meta.title: Vegan Health Dashboard
meta.note: A personal, searchable vegan nutrition hub, Indian foods first. Compiled from this project's Gate-2-approved content: 17 nutrients, 242 foods, 12 health topics, 4 life stages, 14 herbs, 12 myths (1 of 13 drafted candidates still pending its own Gate 2 review and deliberately excluded), and a 46-term glossary. Where to buy and Did you know have no real content yet and are empty by design, not a bug.

sources.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
sources.author: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, Dokras A, Moran LJ, Piltonen TT, Costello MF, Boivin J, Redman LM, Boyle JA, Norman RJ, Mousa A, Joham AE; International PCOS Network
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, pcos-hormonal-health.json Gate 1 pick - THE definitive current international clinical guideline on PCOS. Co-developed across 39 professional/consumer organisations in 71 countries (ASRM, Endocrine Society, ESHRE, ESE, NHMRC-funded), co-published simultaneously in J Clin Endocrinol Metab, Human Reproduction, European Journal of Endocrinology and Fertility and Sterility. GRADE-evidence-graded; the guideline itself states overall PCOS evidence remains 'low to moderate quality.' Key honest caveat used directly in this card: the guideline's own dietary-intervention recommendation (3.3.1) states there is no evidence to support any one diet composition over another for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological PCOS outcomes - so this card does NOT claim a fibre-rich/vegan dietary pattern is guideline-endorsed as superior to other diets, only that healthy lifestyle/dietary intervention generally is recommended for all women with PCOS (3.1.1/3.1.2). The guideline also notes inositol is generally considered secondary to metformin for some outcomes (4.7.2) - used to support this card's instruction not to lead with inositol. PMID 37580314.

sources.title: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome
sources.author: Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine
sources.asOf: 2024 (most recent cited reference; page undated on current fetch)
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, pcos-hormonal-health.json Gate 1 pick - this project's established PCRM tier (Moderate per BRIEF.md rule 1). This is the vegan-specific anchor for the fibre/insulin-resistance mechanism: cites two real low-fat vegan-diet RCTs (Barnard ND et al., Diabetes Care 2006;29(8):1777-1783; Kahleova H et al., JAMA Netw Open 2020;3(11):e2025454) on insulin sensitivity generally (not PCOS-specific trials themselves - PCRM applies the general vegan-diet/insulin-sensitivity finding to PCOS's insulin-resistance mechanism), and a PCOS-specific fibre RCT substudy (Nybacka A, Hellstrom PM, Hirschberg AL, 'Increased fibre and reduced trans fatty acid intake are primary predictors of metabolic improvement in overweight polycystic ovary syndrome,' Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2017;87(6):680-688) finding fibre intake was the strongest predictor of metabolic improvement - none of these three independently read by this project, cited via PCRM's own reference list. Also covers inositol, chromium, omega-3 and soy protein with their own cited trials - inositol and chromium are supplement-tier leads, not given the same confident framing as fibre per the owner's explicit instruction.

sources.title: Impact of dietary fiber on PCOS: a systematic review
sources.author: Swanson CM, Barker Y, Patterson R
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, pcos-hormonal-health.json Gate 1 pick - an independent, open-access, PRISMA-based systematic review (Food, Nutrition and Health, vol 2, article 30, 2025), found separately from PCRM, corroborating fibre's association with improved metabolic/anthropometric PCOS outcomes (reductions in BMI, waist circumference, fasting blood sugar, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR across reviewed studies). Honestly hedged: 'the mechanism between decreased IR by increased fiber intake is not yet apparent,' hormonal (LH/FSH) effects described as 'unclear,' and the review's own conclusion calls for more research - this card must not overstate fibre's PCOS-specific causal mechanism beyond what this review itself claims. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via the publisher's own article page (Springer Nature, matching the cited DOI 10.1007/s44403-025-00043-y exactly), Semantic Scholar, and EBSCOhost.

sources.title: Effectiveness of mineral supplements (magnesium, chromium, zinc, selenium, chromium picolinate) in reducing insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sources.author: Ye J, Cen S, Qi Q, Wang C, Wang J, Wang J, Yaping G, Wang J
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, pcos-hormonal-health.json Gate 1 pick - a genuine meta-analysis (BMC Endocrine Disorders, 2025) of 11 RCTs, 618 women with PCOS, Cochrane RoB2 bias assessment. Found significant reductions in fasting glucose/insulin/HOMA-IR with mineral supplementation (magnesium, chromium, zinc, selenium, chromium picolinate pooled together), mixed lipid effects. Important limitation for this card: the meta-analysis pools MULTIPLE different minerals across the 11 trials together - it cannot isolate a zinc-only or magnesium-only effect size from this abstract, so this card must not attribute the pooled effect size to either nutrient individually. Conclusion is appropriately hedged: 'further large-scale, well-designed trials are needed.' This is supplement-trial evidence, not dietary-food-adequacy evidence like the fibre sources above - framed with that distinction in this card, per the owner's instruction not to lead with supplement claims.

sources.title: Efficacy and safety of Shatavari root extract in women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
sources.author: Mhatre Y, Jadhav P, Malik A, Srivathsan M, Langade D
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, pcos-hormonal-health.json Gate 1 pick - a genuine, independently-readable primary RCT (Frontiers in Endocrinology, PMID 41816216), CTRI-registered (CTRI/2024/10/074660), double-blind, placebo-controlled, 70 participants (66 completed), 12 weeks. No declared conflict of interest. MIXED RESULT, not a clean positive finding - graded Moderate rather than Strong because the primary endpoint missed significance: ovarian volume (the trial's own primary outcome) showed NO significant difference between groups (p=0.254); BMI, hormonal levels and lab parameters also showed no significant difference. Follicular count significantly decreased (p<0.0001) and perceived-stress-scale score significantly improved (p<0.0001) - genuine positive findings, but on secondary outcomes, with the trial's own chosen primary outcome not confirmed. Mild-to-moderate adverse events occurred in 11.4% of the Shatavari group vs 8.5% placebo (stated not intervention-related). This project's first independently-readable shatavari evidence - also relevant to the future herbs section's PCOS link, per the owner's instruction, but not strong enough on its own to support a confident 'shatavari helps PCOS' claim - kept as a candidateAddition with this full nuance, not merged live. RE-VERIFIED DIRECTLY 31 Oct 2026 (Phase 2 Herbs, Shatavari card) against the live Frontiers page, not just re-read from this note - three further things worth recording: (1) the paper is internally inconsistent about which outcome is primary - the Discussion calls ovarian volume the primary endpoint (as used above), but the Abstract and Conclusion instead emphasise follicle count and endometrial thickness, which reads as moving the goalposts toward the outcomes that were significant; (2) endometrial thickness also increased significantly with Shatavari vs placebo (+1.33mm vs +0.20mm, p=0.028) - a finding not previously recorded in this note, included in the herb card neutrally (without assuming it is 'good' or 'bad' in a PCOS context, since the paper itself does not interpret the clinical meaning of this specific change); (3) the dose used was one 300mg capsule/day of root extract standardised to a minimum of 10% total Shatavarins by HPLC - a real standardisation detail worth having for howToUseVegan; and (4) while the paper declares no conflicts of interest, its own acknowledgments state the extract was supplied by Ixoreal BioMed, a detail the conflict-of-interest statement itself does not mention - the same kind of undisclosed-supplier-relationship pattern already flagged for Jamshidi & Cohen's Tulsi review, not a reason to discard the trial but worth knowing.

sources.title: Can the right diet get rid of acne?
sources.author: American Academy of Dermatology
sources.asOf: 2013 (news release date cited in references; page itself undated on current fetch)
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, skin-hair-health.json Gate 1 pick - the official US dermatology professional body's public patient-education page, treated as a Strong/health-body source the same way this project treats other national professional-society pages. Cites multiple real cohort/case-control studies (e.g. Adebamowo et al., J Am Acad Dermatol 2005/2006/2008, each with full citations on the page) directly linking cow's milk - specifically, not dairy broadly - with higher acne rates (e.g. 44% higher odds with 2+ glasses/day of skim milk in one 47,355-woman cohort). The page explicitly states 'No evidence yogurt or cheese can increase acne breakouts' - this is a milk-specific finding, not a blanket dairy one, and the card must not overstate it as the latter. Separately covers a low-glycemic-diet/acne link (not dairy-related, not vegan-specific, not used in this card). Mechanism is stated as unclear/theoretical (hormones in milk causing inflammation) - the page itself is appropriately hedged, not presented as settled causation.

sources.title: The Role of Vitamins and Minerals in Hair Loss: A Review
sources.author: Almohanna HM, Ahmed AA, Tsatalis JP, Tosti A
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, skin-hair-health.json Gate 1 pick - a peer-reviewed review in Dermatology and Therapy (9(1):51-70, 2019), PMID 30547302, PMC6380979. Confirmed exact quote on zinc: 'Alopecia is a well-known sign of established zinc deficiency with hair regrowth occurring with zinc supplementation' (citing Goskowicz & Eichenfield 1993, Alhaj et al. 2007 Skinmed). Used WITH an important nuance also stated in the same source: evidence correlating zinc LEVELS with the more common, non-deficiency forms of hair loss (telogen effluvium, androgenetic/female-pattern alopecia) is inconsistent across studies - so the established link is specifically about avoiding deficiency, not 'more zinc = more hair' for someone already zinc-replete. On biotin, the same review states average dietary biotin intake in Western countries is adequate, biotin deficiency is rare, and 'severe biotin deficiency in healthy individuals eating a normal diet has never been reported' - efficacy of biotin supplementation for hair/skin/nails outside a true deficiency state is not supported by large-scale studies. A companion, more skeptical source (Thompson KG, Kim N, 'Dietary supplements in dermatology: A review of the evidence for zinc, biotin, vitamin D, nicotinamide, and Polypodium,' J Am Acad Dermatol 2021;84(4):1042-1050, PMID 32360756) was also checked and corroborates this caution directly: 'Current evidence is insufficient to recommend the use of biotin or zinc supplements in dermatology' - not added as a separate source id since it adds no new fact beyond reinforcing the same caution, cited here in this note for the record.

sources.title: The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets: A Guide to Health and Nutrition
sources.author: Jacqueline L. Longe (Editor)
sources.note: A real, structured academic reference encyclopedia (Gale is a legitimate reference publisher), not a popular diet book - by far the richest source for vegan/vegetarian content found in this whole project (287 'vegan', 778 'vegetarian' mentions across 1,115 pages). Pre-2015 in places (its soy/phytoestrogen/breast-cancer claim reads as reflecting early-2000s soy scares that more recent research has generally not supported - flagged explicitly in a new myth candidate, drafts/myths/soy-phytoestrogen-breast-cancer.json, rather than treated as settled). Only a fraction of this book was reviewed this pass given its size (1,115 pages) - a future continuation pass on this specific source is likely to surface more, given its density. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: 1st ed., Gale, 2007 (ISBN 1414429916) - confirmed via AbeBooks' listing and Stanford SearchWorks' library catalog record, both matching this project's own 2007 year field exactly.

Cites a real large epidemiological study (Rosell et al., EPIC-Oxford, Int J Obes 2006, 21,966 participants, weight gain across meat-eating/fish-eating/vegetarian/vegan groups) in its bibliography, but the specific in-body claim/context tied to that citation was not located via keyword search - flagged as present but not actioned, since the claim itself wasn't found.

sources.title: Super Charge with Super Foods

Picked hoping for an older-adults Life-stages lead given its 'reverse the aging process' subtitle - its 'aging' content turned out to be cosmetic/wellness-marketing framing (anti-aging skin, etc.), not age-specific nutrient-requirement science. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via Biblio.com and AbeBooks.

sources.title: Food: What the Heck Should I Eat?
sources.author: Mark Hyman, M.D.
sources.note: Promotes a 'Pegan' (Paleo + vegan) philosophy, explicitly skeptical of strict veganism in places while still acknowledging real vegan-diet advantages. Cites several real studies by name (a 2016 BMC Medicine nut-consumption meta-analysis, a 2014 BMJ Open low-fat-vs-high-fat vegan trial) - treated as secondary citations pending direct verification, not independently read. Also contains one clinical-anecdote claim (vegan/vegetarian patients finding type 2 diabetes harder to reverse) that directly conflicts with a Barnard-RCT citation from The Whole Foods Diet - flagged as an unresolved conflict in diabetes.json, not resolved by us.

sources.title: Digestive Health with REAL Food
sources.author: Aglaee Jacob, RD
sources.note: Explicitly anti-vegetarian/anti-soy in tone (a 'six reasons to skip soy' section, 'animal protein is a safer, superior option' framing). One narrow, legitimate point within it - that high-FODMAP legumes can aggravate symptoms for people with IBS/SIBO specifically - is a real clinical caveat for that subset of patients, not a general anti-legume claim; the book's broader 'animal protein is superior' framing is not adopted anywhere in this project. Not used as a source for gut-health.json. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via Amazon, Goodreads, and a publisher promotional listing, all for the same title (registered dietitian, matching this project's note on the book's practical dietetic framing).

sources.title: Genius Foods: Become Smarter, Happier, and More Productive While Protecting Your Brain for Life
sources.author: Max Lugavere
sources.note: A brain-health-focused book, not vegan-specific (acknowledges algal oil as the vegan omega-3 option, otherwise mostly general brain-nutrient science). Cites a real TMAO/gut-microbiome study but the author's own framing of it is nuanced/non-committal on vegan-vs-omnivore implications - treated as interesting background, not a vegan-advocacy source.

sources.title: Eat Right for Your Metabolism: The Individualized Diet Plan to Balance Body Chemistry, Lose Weight, and Prevent Disease
sources.author: Felicia Drury Kliment
sources.note: A 'metabolic typing' pseudo-science book - proposes people have innate 'metabolic types' (including a 'meat eater' type) that determine whether a vegetarian diet can work for them long-term, supported only by anecdotal case histories, not controlled studies. Deliberately reviewed to mine for objections to plant-based eating (Enhancement Backlog item #4), not as a source of facts to use directly - see drafts/myths/metabolic-typing-meat-eater.json, which still needs a Strong source for its rebuttal before publishing. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via Walmart, BooksRun, eBay, and AbeBooks, all matching the ISBN.

sources.title: Foods that Harm and Foods that Heal
sources.author: Editors of Reader's Digest
sources.note: A general A-Z food-health reference with a dedicated, concise, reasonably accurate 'Vegetarian and Vegan' section (protein, calories, B12, D, minerals) and a short 'Vegan Kids' subsection with practical food ideas - a usable, non-hostile general-audience source, though not deeply cited per individual claim. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via Simon & Schuster's own publisher listing, Amazon, and Barnes & Noble - consistent across editions, so applies regardless of which of the two editions (1997/2004) this project cites; year field correctly left "unknown" per the owner's prior instruction, unaffected by this fix.

sources.title: Nutrition for Sport, Exercise and Performance: A Practical Guide for Students, Sports Enthusiasts and Professionals
sources.author: Regina Belski, Adrienne Forsyth, Evangeline Mantzioris (Editors)
sources.note: A sports-nutrition textbook, cites real studies (e.g. Lukaski 2004 on endurance-athlete zinc status, Rodriguez et al. 2009 on magnesium and submaximal exercise). Still teaches the older 'incomplete/limiting plant protein, must combine' framing superseded by the IOM/Mangels position already used elsewhere in this project - its genuine risk-factor content (vegetarian + female + growth + altitude-training iron risk) is used, its outdated protein-combining framing is flagged, not adopted. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via a PINES (Professionals in Nutrition for Exercise and Sports) book review, a WorldCat catalog record, and the publisher's own listing (Allen & Unwin).

sources.title: Eat Right for Your Type (4 Blood Types, 4 Diets)
sources.author: Peter J. D'Adamo
sources.note: The 'Blood Type Diet' - its core premise (ABO blood type should determine diet, including whether a vegetarian/vegan diet suits someone) lacks mainstream scientific support and is graded Limited accordingly. Deliberately reviewed to mine for objections to plant-based eating (Enhancement Backlog item #4), not as a source of facts to use directly - its specific claims (e.g. blood-type-specific B12 absorption or iron needs) are not supported by better-established, blood-type-independent explanations already used elsewhere in this project. Used only to document the objection itself in drafts/myths/blood-type-diet-vegetarian.json, which still needs a Strong source for its rebuttal before publishing.

sources.title: Handbook of Nutrition and Pregnancy - Chapter 15, "Vegetarian Diets in Pregnancy"
sources.author: Ann Reed Mangels (chapter author); Lammi-Keefe CJ, Couch SC, Philipson EH (volume editors)
sources.note: Graded Moderate per BRIEF.md rule 10 (a book chapter, not a government body or systematic review itself), but notably stronger than most other book sources used in this project: the chapter author, Ann Reed Mangels, is the same named author behind the official American Dietetic Association/VNDPG vegetarian-nutrition position papers this project already cites directly (vndpg-protein, pcrm-kids), and the chapter itself carries 89 numbered citations to the primary literature. Part of the Humana Press "Nutrition and Health" series (same series as book-nutrition-guide-for-physicians). Figures are pre-2015 (2008) - check against current RDA/DRI tables before using any specific number as current guidance; this project's NIH/ICMR-NIN sources remain the primary figures, with this chapter used for vegetarian/vegan-specific practical content (food sources, sample menus, practical counselling points) that NIH/ICMR-NIN don't cover.

sources.title: Vitamin D Secrets: How to Know if You Are Deficient in Vitamin D and How to Easily Overcome This
sources.author: Unknown (self-published-style ebook)
sources.note: Graded Limited, not Moderate, despite citing real resources (WebMD, Healthline, MedlinePlus, Cleveland Clinic as end-of-book links, plus a real NHANES 2013-2016 reference) - it contains a confirmed factual error (states D2 is cholecalciferol/animal-derived and D3 is ergocalciferol/plant-derived, the exact reverse of the truth and of this project's own vitamin-d.json), and makes several overstated health claims (vitamin D 'can prevent breast or colon cancer') with no citation, which is well beyond what current evidence supports per BRIEF.md rule 10. Only the UV-exposed-mushroom vitamin D content figure was used from this source; the specific IU number has not been independently verified against USDA FoodData Central or another Strong source - flagged as needing that check before being treated as settled, in vitamin-d.json's own candidate entry.

sources.title: Minerals and Vitamin Supplementation - Practical Guide
sources.author: medicalnotess.com / Instituto Caffeína ("LOVE SUMMARIES")
sources.note: A Brazilian clinical-nutrition practice guide for nutritionists/prescribers, not a government body or peer-reviewed review itself - but each individual claim in it cites a named, checkable primary or secondary source (e.g. Cochrane reviews, the ESPEN micronutrient guideline, IOM Dietary Reference Intakes, named journal articles), so claims from this source should be checked against their own underlying citation before being treated as Strong, per BRIEF.md rule 10. Written for a clinical/prescriber audience, not vegan-specific (only one of its ~20 nutrient sections - vitamin B12 - directly addresses vegetarians/vegans). Tables in the cached text came through a PDF-to-text extraction that sometimes lost which label matched which number (visual table layout, not raw text) - treat exact figures as needing an independent spot-check, not as beyond doubt.

sources.title: Food Science, Health and Nutrition
sources.author: Logan Bowman (editor)
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 - CONFIRMED MISS for this project's purposes. Full keyword search (vegan/vegetarian/plant-based/phytic acid/bioavailability/tofu/legume-protein/iron-absorption) across the whole 253-page text returned only two trivial hits (a bibliography entry mentioning a lactovegetarian-diet study, and a sentence about insect protein vs 'plant-based' sources) and one generic taste-physiology passage about tannins and non-heme iron (already covered elsewhere in this project, no vegan framing). This is a food-science/sensory-science/food-technology textbook, not a diet-pattern reference - essentially no vegan/vegetarian content exists in it. No candidateAdditions drafted from this book.

sources.title: Food as Medicine Everyday: Reclaim Your Health with Whole Foods
sources.author: Julie Briley, ND and Courtney Jackson, ND
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 - genuine hit. Whole-food-as-medicine genre (same genre as The China Study, Eat to Live, The Whole Foods Diet). Written by two naturopathic physicians (Food as Medicine Institute, National College of Natural Medicine); pragmatic/flexible stance (acknowledges dairy can be part of a healthy diet for tolerant people, not anti-vegan). Gave two real, named, checkable primary-study citations used in candidateAdditions: Heaney & Weaver 1990 and Weaver & Plawecki 1994 (calcium bioavailability, calcium.json); Pawlak, Lester & Babatunde 2014 (vegetarian B12-deficiency prevalence review, vitamin-b12.json). Also directly names 'a vegetarian or vegan diet may be nutritionally risky for some' citing Pawlak 2014 - handled even-handedly, not adopted uncritically.

sources.title: Kidney Stone Diet: Eat to Prevent Kidney Stones
sources.author: Kristie Leong, M.D. and Apollo Leong, M.D.
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 (read in full, all 42 pages) - genuine hit, genuinely new topic area (renal/oxalate nutrition). Year corrected from 'unknown' to 2014 (confirmed from the book's own copyright page). Physician-authored, cites named studies/journals throughout (not primary-read by us). Not anti-vegan - explicitly states vegetarian diets are protective against kidney stones (less urinary calcium/acid, more citrate) and recommends tofu, tempeh, quinoa and lentils as alternative protein sources, though its own default calcium-source list leads with dairy. No candidateAdditions drafted into any nutrient/health-topic file (kidney stones/oxalates has no existing module) - full findings in drafts/llamaparse_findings/kidney-stone-diet.md, a findings handoff recommending whether a future Gate 1 decision for a 'Kidney health/Oxalates' topic is worthwhile.

sources.title: The Food Intolerance Bible: A Nutritionist's Plan to Beat Food Cravings, Fatigue, Mood Swings, Bloating, Headaches, IBS and Deal with Food Allergies
sources.author: Antony J. Haynes and Antoinette Savill

sources.title: Eating Well for Optimum Health: The Essential Guide to Food, Diet, and Nutrition
sources.author: Andrew Weil, M.D.
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 - genuine hit. Author and year corrected from 'unknown' (Andrew Weil, M.D.; copyright 2000) - flagged pre-2015 per BRIEF.md rule 5. Moderate, pragmatic stance: has a dedicated 'THE VEGAN DIET' section listing real pros/cons (not anti-vegan, but author's own preference is reducing rather than eliminating animal foods). Gave several real, named, checkable primary-study citations used in candidateAdditions across diabetes.json (Nicholson et al. 1999 RCT), protein.json (explains the historical origin of, and debunks, the 'incomplete protein/must combine' myth - a useful counter-source to three other books in this project still repeating that outdated framing), iron.json (vegetarian iron/cardiovascular-risk reframing), and calcium.json (Zemel 1988 protein/calcium-loss citation).

sources.title: The Nutritionist - Food, Nutrition and Optimal Health
sources.author: Robert Wildman, PhD, RD
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 - genuine hit. Author confirmed (Robert Wildman, PhD, RD). Pre-2015, flagged every fact per BRIEF.md source rule 5. Has a dedicated 'Nutrition Throughout Life' section with pregnancy/infant/older-adult content - the older-adults/ageing portion specifically is a SIXTH confirmed miss for vegan-specific content on this project's standing older-adults Life-stages search (no vegetarian/vegan mention anywhere in that section). Gave candidateAdditions to protein.json (a fourth instance of the protein-combining myth, somewhat softer-worded than the other three) and omega-3.json (a flagged, high-stakes, pre-2015 pregnancy DHA dosing figure - 200 mg/day with an algal-oil vegetarian option - needing independent verification before any use).

sources.title: The Antianxiety Food Solution: How the Foods You Eat Can Help You Calm Your Anxious Mind, Improve Your Mood, and End Cravings
sources.author: Trudy Scott, CN
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026. Author/year corrected from 'unknown' (Trudy Scott, CN; copyright 2011) - flagged pre-2015 per BRIEF.md rule 5. Evidence grade DOWNGRADED from Moderate to Limited on review: this source is explicitly anti-vegetarian/anti-vegan for mental health ('I am no longer a fan of vegetarian and vegan diets, especially for those with mental health issues'), recommends organ meats/bone broth/red meat as primary mood-food interventions (none usable per BRIEF.md's vegan hard rules), and frames its central mechanism via a fringe 'pyroluria' diagnosis not recognised in mainstream clinical nutrition. No candidateAdditions drafted into any nutrient/health-topic file - the one vegan-compatible fact it offered (pumpkin seeds for zinc/iron/omega-3/B-vitamins) duplicates existing zinc.json content. Full findings in drafts/llamaparse_findings/antianxiety-food-solution.md, which also covers this project's new 'opens a frontier not currently a module' instruction - recommending a future Mood/mental-health module be built from different, more vegan-neutral Strong sources than this one.

sources.title: Chinese Nutrition Therapy: Dietetics in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM)
sources.author: Joerg Kastner, MD, LAc
sources.note: Round 6 hand-picked candidate, 22 Oct 2026 - pre-2015, flag every fact for a current recheck. Turned out to be a genuinely massive academic reference (2,362 pages per PyMuPDF extraction, despite a modest 8.4MB file size) - a full sequential read is not feasible in one pass; review approach must be targeted (keyword search + spot-check of matching sections), same precedent as Food Lipids: Chemistry, Nutrition and Biotechnology's earlier partial review. Graded Limited by default since TCM dietetics is a different evidentiary framework from mainstream nutrition science (parallel to this project's 'Ayurveda is not vegetarian' finding) - any claim needs a Strong mainstream source before being treated as more than an illustration, per BRIEF.md source rule 10. Picked partly for myths-deck potential (food-pairing/food-energy claims), not assumed to be a core nutrient source. sources.title: Nutrition and Enhanced Sports Performance: Muscle Building, Endurance, and Strength
sources.author: Debasis Bagchi, Sreejayan Nair, Chandan K. Sen (editors); Chapter 10 'Vegetarian Athletes' by Jing Zhou, Jia Li and Wayne W. Campbell
sources.note: REVIEWED 22 Oct 2026 - the strongest hit of this whole 9-book batch. Pre-2015, every fact flagged for recheck per BRIEF.md rule 5. Picked as a THIRD cross-confirming source for vegetarian/vegan athlete nutrition, alongside the already-approved Nutrition for Sport, Exercise and Performance and Encyclopedia of Diets' own Sports nutrition article (which surfaced creatine/iron/zinc/B12/D/calcium as an athlete risk bundle) - this call paid off: Chapter 10 is a full dedicated 'Vegetarian Athletes' chapter, considerably more rigorously cited than either existing source (a table mapping each at-risk nutrient to named primary studies, real ADA/DC/ACSM position-statement citations). Found a genuinely new risk-nutrient (beta-alanine/carnosine, a second meat-derived performance compound alongside creatine) and a new, specific lead for the standing older-adults Life-stages search (older vegetarian women, protein source, and muscle mass - see drafts/llamaparse_findings/encyclopedia-of-diets-life-stages.md addendum). Gave candidateAdditions to protein.json, iron.json and bones.json.

Full write-up: reference/pcrm/food-and-mood.md.

sources.title: Plant-Based Diets and Mental and Neurocognitive Health Outcomes: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
sources.author: Bizzozero-Peroni B, Díaz-Goñi V, Fernández-Rodríguez R, Martínez-Vizcaíno V, Jiménez-López E, Visier-Alfonso ME, Garrido-Miguel M, Mesas AE
sources.note: A genuine peer-reviewed systematic review with meta-analysis (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA/MOOSE-compliant, 23 studies, 709,703 adults) - graded Strong per BRIEF.md rule 10. NOT on the rule 12 tappable-link allowlist, cite as plain text. Abstract only read (full text paywalled) - effect sizes are from the published abstract, not independently re-derived. Important nuance to always carry forward: the protective associations are specifically for HEALTHY (whole-food) plant-based diets; an unhealthy (refined/processed) plant-based diet pattern was separately associated with INCREASED anxiety and depression in the same abstract. Added 22 Oct 2026 as the Strong backbone for the new Mood/mental-health topic, pairing with pcrm-food-mood for the vegan-specific practical layer. Full write-up: reference/nutrition-reviews/plant-based-diets-mental-neurocognitive-2025.md. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via Europe PMC's structured author/affiliation record matching the cited DOI (10.1093/nutrit/nuaf080) and PMID 40720633 exactly.

Unlike the other two Round 8 fermented-beverage picks, this book cites dozens of named, dated peer-reviewed journal studies throughout (confirmed by a full-text search) - genuinely better-sourced than most of this project's cookbook-format sources, graded Moderate rather than Limited on that basis. However, most of its best-cited content (its immune, antibiotic-recovery and pregnancy/breast-feeding chapters) is specifically about dairy milk kefir or fermented dairy products - excluded from every vegan candidateAddition per BRIEF.md rule 9, since the book gives no equivalent evidence for water kefir, coconut-water kefir, kombucha or other vegan ferments on those specific points. Content actually used is limited to passages the book itself frames generally, naming no specific animal product as the active ingredient (gut-bacteria diversity, fermented beverages' general digestive-secretion mechanism, lactic acid bacteria and immune cytokines, antibiotic-recovery timelines, stress and gut permeability). A strong lead for a possible future liver-health/detoxification topic (kombucha-specific antioxidant studies and beetroot/beet kvass liver studies, all vegan) was found but not actioned, since no such health topic currently exists among this project's topics - flagged for the owner in the findings file. High-stakes pregnancy/breast-feeding content in chapter 4 was reviewed but deliberately not drafted anywhere: its best-cited claims are dairy-kefir-specific (excluded per rule 9) and its general safety caution (hydration, home-brew testing, timing kombucha away from breast-feeding) is sourced only to a commercial ferment company's founder, not a Strong source, so it fails rule 10's bar for pregnancy-adjacent content.

sources.title: Amino acids and immune function
sources.author: Li P, Yin YL, Li D, Kim SW, Wu G
sources.note: 23 Oct 2026, immune-function.json Gate 1 pick - a peer-reviewed narrative review in the British Journal of Nutrition (98(2), 2007), NIH-grant-funded (R21 HD049449/NICHD), PMID 17403271. Abstract confirms: 'A deficiency of dietary protein or amino acids has long been known to impair immune function and increase the susceptibility of animals and humans to infectious disease', and names a role for amino acids in regulating lymphocyte/macrophage activation and 'the production of antibodies, cytokines and other cytotoxic substances.' Used only for the general, mechanistic protein-immune-function link (deficiency impairs function) - NOT used for its specific-amino-acid-supplementation findings (arginine, glutamine, cysteine), which are about therapeutic supplementation in malnourished/diseased populations, not relevant to this project's general healthy-vegan-diet framing, and not independently read beyond the abstract. Described accurately as 'a review', not as a formal systematic review with its own meta-analysis, since the abstract does not describe PRISMA-style systematic methodology.

sources.title: Low Sugar, So Simple: 100 Delicious Low-Sugar, Low-Carb, Gluten-Free Recipes for Eating Clean and Living Healthy
sources.author: Elviira Krebber
sources.note: Round 9 general-picks batch, 23 Oct 2026 (one of 5 'general picks' reviewed for non-recipe content; 284-page PDF, already cached). Year corrected 23 Oct 2026 Gate 2 review: the book's own copyright page explicitly and repeatedly states 2018 ('First Published in 2018 by Fair Winds Press'); the '2017' originally recorded came from a Library of Congress Cataloging-in-Publication pre-publication line, not the book's own stated publish year. A ketogenic/low-carb lifestyle book, explicitly pro-butter, pro-dairy, pro-eggs and pro-grass-fed-meat, and strongly anti-grain and anti-legume (its own text states cereals, grains and legumes should be avoided 'altogether' by anyone with an autoimmune condition, and separately asserts 'saturated fats don't cause heart disease') - not vegan-aligned in its own framing and none of that framing is adopted here. Flagged for the owner as myths-deck-relevant (the anti-whole-grain/anti-legume framing directly conflicts with this project's existing diabetes.json and fibre.json content) - not actioned into a myths file this round, since a different agent is drafting myths cards this round from a different, disjoint set of books. The book's ~100 recipes are not citable per BRIEF.md. Its own References section (not '~26 citations' as an earlier progress note overstated - a direct count found 14 distinct citations) does include a real, checkable cohort study. Two genuinely useful, vegan-compatible, non-recipe nuggets were used from its front-matter chapters (Ch.1-4, roughly the first 85 pages, before the recipes start): (1) that cohort study (Yang Q, Zhang Z, Gregg EW, 'Added Sugar Intake and Cardiovascular Diseases Mortality Among US Adults,' JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014;174(4):516-524), used in heart-and-cholesterol.json, not independently read by us; (2) its description of stevia and erythritol as non-nutritive, vegan-compatible, low-glycemic sweeteners, used in diabetes.json - the book gives no citation at all for this specific glycemic claim (unlike the Yang et al. citation), so graded Limited and flagged pending an independent Strong-source check (e.g. FDA GRAS status or a systematic review) before any firmer use. Monk fruit is named only once, in passing, as a possible alternative to erythritol - the book never describes monk fruit's own properties, so an earlier draft's claim that monk fruit shares those described properties was corrected during Gate 2 review.

sources.title: The Clinical Efficacy and Safety of Tulsi in Humans: A Systematic Review of the Literature
sources.author: Jamshidi N, Cohen MM
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) pilot - Tulsi Gate 1 backbone source, PMC5376420, Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. Owner's own web research flagged this as Strong/Moderate; independently fetched and read in full before use, which surfaced caveats worth recording rather than just transcribing the owner's summary. Real systematic review of 24 human studies (1,111 participants), grouped into metabolic, immunity/infection, and stress/mood/cognition domains - favourable outcomes reported in all three, consistent with the owner's summary. On safety: 15/24 studies reported no adverse events, 8 did not describe any, 1 reported occasional mild nausea - the abstract's 'no significant adverse events' claim is accurate as far as it goes, but the longest trial was only 13 weeks, so this does not rule out longer-term effects. Graded Moderate, not Strong, for reasons the authors themselves state: only a small minority of the 24 studies were high quality (Jadad 4-5), most lacked double-blinding, only 3 had 100+ participants, doses/formulations/cultivars varied widely and were often unspecified, and the authors' own limitations section warns tulsi's effects 'may be overestimated' by the body of evidence - while the abstract's 'effective treatment' framing reads more confidently than the limitations section supports. Also flagged: the review states internally inconsistent study counts in different sections (e.g. 17 vs 15 metabolic studies), and co-author Cohen discloses consulting for Organic India, a tulsi-product company (stated to have had no input into the article) - neither disqualifying, but both worth knowing. Used here for the traditional-use/general-safety framing, not as proof of any specific dose or formulation.

sources.title: Holy Basil (Consumer Version)
sources.author: Merck Manual editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) pilot - Tulsi safety source, independently fetched and verified (not transcribed from the owner's summary alone). Confirms: pregnancy/breastfeeding - 'might not be safe,' animal studies show reduced implantation chance at large doses, human safety 'not known,' advises pregnant/breastfeeding/trying-to-conceive women to avoid; blood sugar - may lower it, 'may lower blood sugar and thus possibly result in hypoglycemia' combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, advises people with type 2 diabetes to avoid and people on glucose-lowering medicines to talk to their doctor first; thyroid - 'might decrease levels of the thyroid hormone thyroxine,' 'could worsen hypothyroidism,' advises people with hypothyroidism to avoid; bleeding/surgery - taking it with clot-slowing medicines (aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin named) could increase bruising/bleeding risk, and could increase bleeding risk during/after surgery. Treated as Article/blog type per this project's existing taxonomy (a clinical-reference website, not one of the 8 named public reference sources or a peer-reviewed study), consistent with how PCRM pages are graded here. The thyroid and diabetes-drug-interaction specifics are sourced to this page only - RxList (below) independently confirms the pregnancy and bleeding/surgery cautions but does not mention thyroid at all and does not name the specific insulin/sulfonylurea interaction, so those two cautions are NOT cross-corroborated across both sources the way the owner's brief assumed - flagged honestly rather than overstating agreement that isn't there.

sources.title: Holy Basil
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) pilot - Tulsi safety source, independently fetched and verified. Confirms: pregnancy/breastfeeding - 'not enough is known,' advises avoiding; blood sugar - early research suggests it 'might decrease blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes' (does not itself name insulin/sulfonylureas or hypoglycemia specifically); bleeding/surgery - rates the interaction with clot-slowing medicines as 'Moderate,' names aspirin, clopidogrel (Plavix) and warfarin (Coumadin), advises stopping holy basil at least 2 weeks before scheduled surgery, but also states there isn't enough information to know if the interaction is a major concern. Does NOT mention thyroid/hypothyroidism anywhere. Treated as Article/blog type per this project's existing taxonomy, same basis as Merck Manual above.

sources.title: Ayurvedic Science of Food and Nutrition
sources.author: Sanjeev Rastogi (editor)
sources.note: Already Gate-1 approved (GATE1_DECISIONS.md, one of the original 42) and reviewed in an earlier round (CHECKPOINT.md, 22 Oct 2026 entry - 'a real academic volume'), but never previously added to sources.json since no card had cited it yet. A real edited academic volume (Springer, ISBN 978-1-4614-9627-4), not a popular diet book. Used here (31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 Herbs pilot) for its Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) passage: describes 'remarkable adaptogenic and anti-stress activities' and immune-system support as traditionally known and confirmed by 'modern research and clinical studies' (not itself naming which studies, so treated as corroborating the traditional-use framing, not as independent clinical evidence beyond Jamshidi & Cohen above). The same passage also describes in-vitro anticancer findings (pancreatic and prostate cancer cell lines) with full citations to primary lab papers - these are cell-line/preclinical findings only, not human trials, and are NOT used as a human health claim in the Tulsi card; mentioned there only as an honestly-labelled preliminary-research aside, per BRIEF.md rule 10. ADDENDUM 31 Oct 2026 (Phase 2, Moringa, 10th herb): also used for Moringa oleifera, listed in this same book's Ayurvedic anti-cancer herbs name-table (Scientific name/Sanskrit-Hindi name/English name columns: 'Moringa oleifera' / 'Shigru' / 'Horseradish tree', in the chapter 'Food-Based Interventions for Cancer Management: An Ayurvedic Perspective') and separately named as an ingredient, 'Shigru (Moringa olifera)', in a classical 'Yavagu for excessive thirst' gruel formulation elsewhere in the book - excessive thirst being a traditional Ayurvedic marker later associated with what is now understood as diabetes (madhumeha/prameha). Both mentions are plain name-table/ingredient-list entries with no elaboration or outcome data given, so this book is used in the Moringa card only to confirm the plant's genuine traditional Ayurvedic naming and its traditional association with excessive-thirst/diabetes-adjacent and cancer-adjacent formulations - never as evidence that moringa treats cancer or diabetes, per BRIEF.md rule 10. ADDENDUM 31 Oct 2026 (Phase 2, Amla, 11th herb): also used for Amla, via its section 8.6.2 'Fruits and Cancer Prevention' (around p.91), which states 'Emblica officinalis Gaertn. or Phyllanthus emblica Linn, commonly known as Indian gooseberry or amla, is arguably the most important medicinal plant in Ayurveda,' describes antineoplastic effects of its phytochemicals (gallic acid, ellagic acid, pyrogallol, corilagin, geraniin and others) as 'experimental studies have shown' (i.e. preclinical findings, cited to a secondary review, not a human trial - not used as a human cancer claim here, per BRIEF.md rule 10), and separately confirms Triphala's genuine classical composition as three fruits combined: Emblica officinalis, Terminalia chebula and Terminalia bellirica. This book does not mention 'Amalaki' by name but does describe the general Ayurvedic Rasayana-therapy concept at length (pp.16-20), independently corroborating the Rasayana framing given in hc-nhpid-amla-monograph. Note for future readers: this same book elsewhere uses the unrelated word 'amla' to mean the 'sour' taste in classical Ayurvedic taste theory (the six rasas) - a different use of the same word, not a second reference to the fruit.

sources.title: Holy Basil (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) pilot - a 5th, independently-found source (not in the owner's original package), added to clear this project's new 5+-source house rule with real added content rather than padding. A major US academic cancer centre's own clinical integrative-medicine database entry, treated the same way this project already treats AAD's patient-education page (aad-diet-acne) - a professional/academic health body, Strong per rule 1, not a commercial site. States human evidence is limited; small studies suggest possible benefit for stress, sleep, anxiety, cognition, and oral/eye health, plus one topical-formulation finding for oral mucositis in cancer patients on chemoradiation - concludes 'further research is needed to substantiate these findings,' consistent with Jamshidi & Cohen's own hedging above. Lists reported side effects (nausea, headache, agitation) not otherwise in this card's other sources. Explicitly warns not to confuse holy basil with culinary basil - a real, documented mix-up (this project's own cached Dictionary of Food Science and Nutrition makes exactly this error, wrongly giving holy basil the botanical name Ocimum basilicum, which is actually sweet/culinary basil - not used anywhere in this card for that reason). Does not itself cover pregnancy, diabetes-drug, bleeding/surgery or thyroid cautions - those remain sourced to Merck Manual/RxList above, not duplicated here.

sources.title: Effects of Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) on Stress and Anxiety: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.author: Vijayakumar V, et al.
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Ashwagandha Gate 1 backbone source, Explore 2024;20(6):103062, PMID 39348746 - a real, peer-reviewed, PubMed-indexed journal article (not a conference abstract), independently verified before use. Systematic review/meta-analysis of 9 RCTs, 558 participants (MEDLINE/EMBASE/PubMed/PsycINFO/Cochrane, Jan 2000-Jan 2022). Found significant reductions versus placebo on the Perceived Stress Scale (MD -4.72), Hamilton Anxiety Scale (MD -2.19) and serum cortisol (MD -2.58); 4 of the 9 trials reported mild-to-moderate adverse events; authors call for more long-term safety data. Graded Moderate, not Strong, for an honest reason found during Gate 1 verification, not stated in this paper itself: a separate 2025 meta-analysis (Albalawi, Nutrition & Health) pooling a different, more recent set of RCTs found the cortisol reduction again but NO significant effect on perceived stress (SMD -0.355, P=0.40) - a genuine disagreement between reviews on the stress outcome specifically, not settled science. This card's whatEvidenceShows reflects that disagreement rather than only the more favourable result. A separate, unreviewed 2025 BJPsych Open item (conference abstract, explicitly marked by its own journal as reviewed by a conference faculty rather than through standard peer review, and stating it 'should not be quoted as peer-reviewed') was found during the same search and deliberately NOT used as a source here for that reason, despite reporting similar favourable numbers.

sources.title: Ashwagandha (Consumer Version)
sources.author: Merck Manual editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Ashwagandha safety source, independently fetched and verified. States it is 'highly unlikely' one compound has the full breadth of purported benefits; standardized-extract studies suggest modest stress/anxiety reduction (possibly via lower cortisol) and small sleep improvements. Side effects: diarrhoea, headache, sedation, nausea; 'liver problems may occur'; may raise testosterone (flagged as a possible negative for prostate cancer). Cautions: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding (talk to a doctor first for breastfeeding specifically), avoid with stomach ulcers or liver disease. Interactions: may lower blood sugar (diabetes-drug caution) and blood pressure (BP-drug caution); may increase immune activity, a caution with immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, mycophenolate, tacrolimus, prednisone/corticosteroids named); may cause drowsiness, a caution with sedatives/CNS depressants (clonazepam, quetiapine, lorazepam named); may raise thyroid hormone levels, a caution for anyone on thyroid medicine (monitor with blood tests). Treated as Article/blog type, same basis as the Tulsi pilot's Merck Manual citation.

sources.title: Ashwagandha
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Ashwagandha safety source, independently fetched and verified; cross-corroborates most of Merck Manual's cautions above (pregnancy 'likely unsafe' with 'some evidence ashwagandha might cause miscarriages', diabetes-drug hypoglycaemia risk, blood-pressure-drug risk, sedative/benzodiazepine interaction, immunosuppressant interaction, thyroid-hormone interaction) and adds two genuinely new cautions not in Merck Manual: avoid with stomach ulcers, and avoid or use with caution in autoimmune diseases (MS, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis) since it may activate the immune system - plus a specific surgery caution (stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery, since it may slow the central nervous system). Rates stress as the only 'Possibly Effective' use (citing a specific standardised extract, KSM-66, 300 mg twice daily for 60 days); everything else (anxiety, diabetes, cholesterol, male infertility, etc.) is rated insufficient evidence. Treated as Article/blog type, same basis as the Tulsi pilot's RxList citation.

sources.title: Ashwagandha (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - the richest single Ashwagandha source found, same treatment as MSKCC's Holy Basil page above (academic cancer-centre clinical database, Government or health body/Strong). Confirms the stress/anxiety/sleep evidence and most cautions already sourced elsewhere, and adds genuinely new, higher-stakes content not found in Merck Manual or RxList: rare but real case reports of liver injury (including acute steatohepatitis, improving after stopping), thyrotoxicosis (resolved after stopping), kidney transplant rejection in one patient, HPA-axis suppression after prolonged use, and a ventricular tachycardia case possibly linked to a herbomineral product containing ashwagandha. Separately reports a heavy-metal contamination case (hemolytic anaemia and abdominal pain from an ashwagandha/mucuna product with high lead levels - a product-quality issue, not a property of the herb itself, used in this card's cautions as a reason to buy from a reputable brand). Also names a hormone-sensitive-prostate-cancer-specific caution (testosterone-raising), used in the card. Separately reports a lab-test-interference note (may cause falsely elevated digoxin immunoassay results) - genuinely new, but NOT used in the card: Gate 2 verdict (31 Oct 2026) was to drop it as too niche/clinical for this friends-facing dashboard. Notably does NOT cover diabetes-drug interactions, blood-pressure effects, or surgery/anaesthesia precautions - those three remain sourced to Merck Manual/RxList, not duplicated here.

sources.title: Neem in Dermatology: Shedding Light on the Traditional Panacea
sources.author: Gopinath H, Karthikeyan K
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Neem Gate 1 backbone source, Indian Journal of Dermatology 2021;66(6):706, PMCID PMC8906293, PMID 35283494 - independently fetched and verified in full, not transcribed from a summary. An Indian-dermatology-specific peer-reviewed review, directly relevant to this project's own audience. Graded Moderate for an honest reason the review itself states: it explicitly distinguishes traditional use, in vitro/animal data and real human data, and for most skin conditions (acne, eczema, psoriasis broadly, scabies, pruritus, dermatophytosis) it finds only traditional use or preclinical data, not clinical trials. Direct quotes: 'Although there is no evidence of efficacy, neem is extensively used for medicinal purposes in India' and 'the scarcity of human trials has obscured its role in modern medicine.' The only real human trials it names are small and dated: a single 50-patient 1994 trial (oral neem plus topical tar/salicylic acid) for psoriasis, a randomised proof-of-principle study for tungiasis, and a 1992 pilot study for scabies - none treated as settled by the review's own authors. On safety: reports real case-series evidence of allergic contact dermatitis to neem oil and lip leukoderma from chewing neem twigs (states 'the exact compounds and the mechanisms of cutaneous adverse effects remain unclear'); explicitly states neem leaf or oil ingestion is contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation and children under 12, and reports child deaths and other toxicity from neem oil ingestion; flags that home-remedy preparations can carry fungal/aflatoxin contamination risk; and notes product variability (active compound concentration varies by plant part, growing conditions, processing - labels often just say 'neem extract' with no standardisation).

sources.title: Neem
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Neem safety source, independently fetched and verified. Rates most purported uses (fever, malaria, worms, diabetes, heart disease, contraception) as insufficient evidence. Short-term use rated 'Possibly Safe' at studied durations (up to 10 weeks by mouth); large-dose or long-term use rated 'Possibly Unsafe' and 'might harm the kidneys and liver.' Children: oral neem seed/oil rated 'Likely Unsafe' - 'serious side effects in infants and small children can happen within hours after taking neem oil' (vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, blood disorders, seizures, coma, brain disorders, death cited among them). Pregnancy: neem oil/bark 'Likely Unsafe' by mouth, can cause miscarriage. Fertility: 'some evidence that neem can harm sperm' - advises avoiding when trying to conceive. Autoimmune disease: may activate the immune system, advises avoidance. Diabetes-drug interaction (Moderate): insulin, glimepiride, glipizide, pioglitazone named. Immunosuppressant interaction (Moderate): cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate, corticosteroids named - organ-transplant patients specifically advised not to use it. Lithium interaction (Moderate, genuinely new vs. this project's Tulsi/Ashwagandha herb cards): may act like a diuretic and reduce lithium clearance, raising lithium levels. Surgery: stop at least 2 weeks before, since it may interfere with blood sugar control. Separately warns against chewing neem twigs as a toothbrush, since they are 'often contaminated with fungi within 2 weeks of harvest.' Its own reference list cites real case reports (ventricular fibrillation/cardiac arrest from neem leaf poisoning, azadirachtin poisoning, Reye-like syndrome from margosa/neem oil poisoning) - not read directly by us, but their existence corroborates the severity of the ingestion-toxicity caution independently confirmed by Gopinath & Karthikeyan and MSKCC below.

sources.title: Neem (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.asOf: current as fetched 31 Oct 2026 (page states last updated 2023-04-11)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Neem safety source, same Government/health body treatment as this project's other MSKCC herb-page citations. States plainly that 'studies on safety and effectiveness are lacking.' Corroborates the ingestion-poisoning caution independently: 'Swallowing neem oil has caused severe poisoning in both children and adults... In most serious cases, seizures associated with coma and even death have occurred' - described as rare, with specific case reports cited (poisoning/neurotoxicity requiring intensive care and ventilation, toxic encephalopathy, toxic optic neuropathy). Adds genuinely new, skin-relevant case reports not found elsewhere: allergic contact dermatitis after topical neem oil use for alopecia (scalp and face), and a case of neem oil triggering drug-aggravated bullous pemphigoid when applied to blisters - directly relevant to this card's primary link (skin-hair-health) as reasons topical use is not risk-free either. Also names one small positive finding not found elsewhere (increased CD4+ cell count and body weight in a small number of HIV-positive volunteers given neem extract) - used here only as an honestly-labelled preliminary finding, not a treatment claim. Does not cover pregnancy, fertility, infant-specific dosing, diabetes-drug interactions or immunosuppressants - those remain sourced to RxList/Gopinath & Karthikeyan, not duplicated here.

sources.title: Asparagus Racemosus (Shatavari)
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Shatavari safety source, independently fetched and verified. Rates most purported uses (pain, anxiety, stomach spasms, uterine bleeding, PMS, upset stomach, ulcers, diarrhoea, bronchitis, diabetes, dementia, alcohol withdrawal, starting breast milk production) as insufficient evidence - states plainly 'there is not enough information available about asparagus racemosus to know how it might work for any medical use.' Safety overall: 'there is not enough information available to know if asparagus racemosus is safe' - genuinely thinner safety data than this project's other three herb cards. Explicitly and directly warns: 'Don't confuse asparagus racemosus with Asparagus officinalis,' the common vegetable - the exact same kind of species mix-up already flagged for Tulsi/culinary basil, and independently confirmed to be a real, live mistake by this project's own cached 150 Healthiest Foods on Earth, which mislabels ordinary vegetable asparagus as 'also known in India by the name Shatavari.' Pregnancy/breastfeeding: 'not enough is known... stay on the safe side and avoid use.' The one rated drug interaction (Moderate) is lithium - may act like a diuretic and reduce lithium clearance, raising lithium levels; a dose adjustment may be needed. Diabetes interest is based on test-tube research only (insulin-secretion stimulation) - no human blood-sugar or diabetes-drug-interaction data given.

sources.title: Plant Profile, Phytochemistry and Pharmacology of Asparagus racemosus (Shatavari): A Review
sources.author: Alok S, Jain SK, Verma A, Kumar M, Mahor A, Sabharwal M
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Shatavari source, independently fetched and read in full before use, Asian Pacific Journal of Tropical Disease 2013;3(3):242-251. Graded Limited, not Moderate, for real quality problems found during Gate 1 verification: internally conflicting traditional-use claims (cites use for 'threatened abortion' alongside a traditional claim the herb is 'absolutely safe for long term use, even during pregnancy and lactation'), a self-contradicting antiulcer section, at least one section that appears to cite the wrong species (A. cochinchinensis) or an unrelated compound, duplicated references, and no stated quality-grading or inclusion criteria for the studies it reviews - this review is cited here only for one specific, identifiable animal-study finding, not treated as a generally reliable synthesis. The review's own honest headline statement: 'no scintific proof justify aborementioned uses of root extract of A. racemosus is available so far' [sic, exact quote including the source's own typos]. The specific finding used in this project: a rat study (methanolic root extract, 100 mg/kg/day for 60 days) found increased fetal resorption, malformations (including limb swelling), intrauterine growth retardation, smaller placentas and litters, lower pup weight/length, and developmental delays - a real, if animal-only, safety signal that directly complicates the traditional 'safe in pregnancy' claim the same review also repeats uncritically. Also reports an acute-toxicity study (a different preparation, Lactare) finding no deaths up to 64 g/kg orally - a different, reassuring data point for ordinary short-term dosing, not for the pregnancy-specific question above. A human galactogogue (breast-milk-boosting) trial cited in the same review found NO increase in prolactin, directly contradicting the traditional use as a lactation aid - also used in this card.

sources.title: Efficacy and Safety of Shatavari Root Extract for the Management of Menopausal Symptoms: A Double-Blind, Multicenter, Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.author: Gudise VS, Dasari MP, Kuricheti SSK
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - a second, more recent real human RCT found during Gate 1 search, independently fetched and read in full. Cureus 2024;16(4):e57879. Graded Limited, not Moderate, for genuine internal quality problems found during verification, not disqualifying but serious enough to flag: the paper's own tables disagree with its own Methods on sample size per arm (35 randomised per arm stated, but result tables variously report 33/35 or N=68), and it directly contradicts itself on adverse-event severity (stating in one place 'all reported adverse events were mild' and elsewhere that 'none of the adverse events were mild'). It declares 'no competing interests exist,' but its own acknowledgments state the product was supplied by the manufacturer (Waleria Healthtech) and a contract research organisation helped prepare the study protocol and documents - an undisclosed-relationship pattern, same issue flagged for Jamshidi & Cohen (Tulsi) and the Mhatre PCOS trial above. 8-week trial, 70 postmenopausal women, primary outcome (Utian Quality of Life score) improved significantly versus placebo - a real positive finding, but in menopausal women specifically, not PCOS, and the authors' own conclusion ('a safe alternative to modern drugs') overstates what a small, short, single-population trial with these internal inconsistencies can support. Used in this card only as context that human RCTs on shatavari exist beyond the PCOS one, not as independent confirmation of any specific claim.

sources.title: Stinging Nettle
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, fifth herb) - Nettle Gate 1 source, independently fetched and verified. Rates osteoarthritis 'Possibly Effective' (leaf preparations, oral or topical, 'might reduce pain') - the only 'Possibly Effective' rating this project has seen across any herb checked so far, the rest being 'Insufficient Evidence.' BPH rated insufficient/contradictory; a saw-palmetto combination appears comparable to finasteride but it's unclear which ingredient helps. Diabetes evidence conflicts across two cited studies (one null, one positive). Anaemia is explicitly in the 'more evidence needed' bucket, not a supported use. Pregnancy rated 'Likely Unsafe' (may stimulate uterine contractions, miscarriage risk); breastfeeding advised against. Interactions (all Moderate): lithium (diuretic-like effect reduces clearance - the same pattern already seen in Ashwagandha, Neem and Shatavari's own cards), diabetes medicines (hypoglycaemia risk), blood pressure medicines (additive lowering), sedatives (additive drowsiness at large amounts), and warfarin (nettle's vitamin K content may reduce warfarin's effectiveness - the same vitamin-K/warfarin mechanism already in this project's own vitamin-k2.json).

sources.title: Nettle (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.asOf: current as fetched 31 Oct 2026 (page states last updated 2021-12-07)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Nettle safety source, same Government/health body treatment as this project's other MSKCC herb-page citations. Independently corroborates RxList's osteoarthritis and BPH findings. Adds real case reports not found elsewhere: gynecomastia in a man and galactorrhea in a woman from nettle tea; urticaria in a breastfed infant after the mother used nettle-boiled water on cracked nipples (a directly breastfeeding-relevant caution); hypoglycaemia in a 78-year-old man on a nettle-containing BPH remedy; allergic rhinitis from nettle pollen exposure. Separately reports severe reactions (urticaria, pain, ICU admission) from an Australian stinging tree - a different genus entirely, not Urtica dioica, flagged here so it is not mistakenly presented as a common-nettle finding. Notes animal/lab-only evidence for CYP450 enzyme inhibition and for kidney-protective effects - human relevance of both 'has yet to be determined.' Does not cover pregnancy (beyond the infant case), lithium or blood-thinner interactions - those remain sourced to RxList, not duplicated here.

sources.title: The Efficacy and Safety of Urtica Dioica in Treating Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.author: Men C, Wang M, Aiyireti M, Cui Y
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Nettle's only systematic-review-level evidence found, for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) specifically, not a condition this project has a dedicated health topic for and not used as a crossCautionLink target for that reason. African Journal of Traditional, Complementary and Alternative Medicines 13(2):143-150. 5 RCTs, 1,128 patients pooled; favourable results for IPSS symptom score, peak urinary flow and prostate volume, with PSA (a safety marker) unaffected. Graded Limited, not Moderate, for an honest reason found during Gate 1 verification: this 2016 review's own abstract reports no adverse-event data and no risk-of-bias or heterogeneity assessment at all, yet still concludes Urtica dioica is 'an effective and safe treatment' - a safety claim its own abstract does not actually support with safety data. A more recent (2025) systematic review by a different, more methodologically rigorous research group (Edzard Ernst's team, a well-known evidence-based-medicine sceptic group) reassessed a larger pool (6 RCTs, 1,210 patients) and reached a more cautious verdict: risk of bias 'mostly unclear or high,' symptom improvement real but small, and certainty of evidence 'very low' for the main symptom score - not included here as a separate formal source since its exact journal citation could not be fully verified, but its more cautious conclusion is reflected in this card's own wording rather than only citing the more confident 2016 review.

sources.title: Psyllium (MedlinePlus Drug Information)
sources.author: NIH National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 6th herb) - Psyllium Gate 1 source, a government body page (NIH/NLM), Strong per rule 1. Practical safety instructions: powder/granules must be mixed in 8oz (240ml) of liquid immediately before use and taken with a further full glass of water, specifically to work properly and to reduce side effects; don't take for more than 1 week without a doctor's input. Names a specific drug-timing interaction: don't take digoxin, aspirin/salicylates or nitrofurantoin within 3 hours of psyllium. Flags diabetes, heart disease, high/low blood pressure, kidney disease, rectal bleeding, intestinal blockage and swallowing difficulty as things to tell a doctor about before use. A genuinely distinctive caution not found elsewhere: avoid inhaling the powder while mixing a dose, since accidental inhalation can itself cause an allergic reaction - relevant for anyone preparing doses for themselves or someone else repeatedly.

sources.title: Psyllium
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Psyllium safety/dosing source, independently fetched. Lists constipation as the main approved use, with IBS and hypercholesterolemia as off-label uses (no evidence given on this particular page for either). Dosing as listed: adults 2.5-7.5g in 8oz water, up to 30g/day in divided doses; children 6-12y 1.25-15g/day; under 6y not established - no paediatric dosing used in this card per BRIEF.md's standing rule against stating children's doses. Contraindications: GI obstruction, faecal impaction, symptoms of appendicitis/acute surgical abdomen, GI ulceration, dysphagia (swallowing difficulty), rectal bleeding - a more specific and more clinical list than the general caution found elsewhere. Notes sugar-free versions contain phenylalanine (relevant for phenylketonuria). States 'not absorbed systemically' so unlikely to pose a breastfeeding risk, though no direct breastfeeding data exists. This specific page states no known severe/serious/moderate drug interactions (only a mild one with sodium picosulfate) - a narrower interaction picture than MedlinePlus's own digoxin/aspirin/nitrofurantoin timing caution above, which is not contradicted so much as simply a different page with different scope; both are kept, not merged into one claim.

sources.title: The Role and Therapeutic Effectiveness of Plantago Ovata Seed Husk (Psyllium Husk) in the Prevention and Non-Pharmacological Treatment of Gastrointestinal Diseases. Part 1: Clinical Use of Psyllium Husk in the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome, Ulcerative Colitis, and Colorectal Cancer
sources.author: Przybyszewska J, Kuzminski A, Przybyszewski M, Poplawski C
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Psyllium's backbone gut-health evidence source, Gastroenterology Review (Przeglad Gastroenterologiczny) 19(2):121-126, independently fetched and verified. For IBS: cites a 275-patient, 12-week trial finding psyllium superior to placebo in months 1-2 but not month 3 (fading effect, stated plainly rather than only citing the early-month result), plus a smaller 80-patient trial with an 82% vs 53% response rate. For ulcerative colitis: cites a 105-patient open-label trial finding psyllium comparably effective to mesalamine for maintaining remission - a real, if limited (single open-label trial), finding. States psyllium does not meaningfully affect vitamin/mineral absorption in small studies checked. Safety: cites a real case of anaphylaxis and occupational asthma linked to psyllium, notes the FDA's purity requirement (at least 95%) for psyllium products, and gives a specific choking-prevention instruction (mix each dose in about 150-200ml liquid, drink a further glass of water, avoid if swallowing is already difficult) - independently corroborating MedlinePlus's own similar instruction. Graded Moderate, not Strong: a narrative review, not itself a systematic review or meta-analysis, and does not discuss its own cited trials' limitations (sample size, blinding) in detail.

sources.title: Herbal Immune Booster-Induced Liver Injury in the COVID-19 Pandemic - A Case Series
sources.author: Nagral A, Adhyaru K, Rudra OS, Gharat A, Bhandare S
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 7th herb, Giloy/Guduchi) - the single most important safety finding across every herb checked in this entire pass, independently fetched and verified in full. Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hepatology 2021;11(6):732-738. A real, peer-reviewed, single-centre case series: 6 patients (4 women, 2 men, median age 55) presented with jaundice and acute hepatitis after self-prescribed Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy) use - median duration 90 days (range ~3 weeks to 7 months), median peak bilirubin 17.5 mg/dL and peak AST 1,350 IU/L (severe hepatitis-range values). 3 patients received steroids (one deteriorated on tapering); 1 patient (Case 4) DIED of hepatorenal syndrome about 120 days after first presentation; the rest recovered, with liver tests taking a median 86.5 days to normalise after stopping the herb. 4 of 6 had underlying silent autoimmune-featured chronic liver disease on biopsy. Authors propose an autoimmune-like hepatitis mechanism, possibly via the herb's own immune-stimulating action. Graded Moderate, not Strong, for the reasons the authors themselves state: small (6 patients), single-centre, observational, RUCAM causality scores only possible-to-probable, and some viral serologies/plant-content analyses not done - but this does not make the finding dismissible; it is a real, independently reviewable, peer-reviewed clinical finding with a death in it, not a secondhand or folklore safety claim.

sources.title: Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy)-Induced Liver Injury During the COVID-19 Pandemic - Multicenter Nationwide Study From India
sources.author: Kulkarni AV, et al. (Liver Research Club India)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - a second, larger, independent Giloy liver-injury finding, Hepatology Communications 2022;6(6):1289-1300, confirming the Nagral et al. case series above is not an isolated single-centre anomaly. A real multicentre retrospective cohort across 13 tertiary-care hospitals in 9 Indian cities (April 2020-July 2021): 49 patients with Giloy-associated liver injury (acute hepatitis, worsening chronic liver disease, or acute liver failure); causality assessed as probable in 67.4% of cases. Graded Moderate, not Strong, for real, substantive critiques this project found during Gate 1 verification and is recording honestly rather than ignoring: published letters noted the study did not report how many total patients were screened to reach these 49 (no denominator given), that the reported median intake (40 mL/day) may be above typically recommended amounts, and - most seriously for causality - raised the possibility that some cases may involve a different, visually similar plant (Tinospora crispa) rather than Tinospora cordifolia itself. India's government AYUSH Ministry has also publicly and repeatedly disputed the Giloy-liver-injury link on these grounds, without itself publishing a counter-study. None of this resolves the underlying safety question either way - two independent, peer-reviewed clinical case series exist, a serious scientific dispute about species identification and dosing also exists, and this card presents both rather than picking a side.

sources.title: Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy): An Insight on the Multifarious Pharmacological Paradigms of a Most Promising Medicinal Ayurvedic Herb
sources.author: Gupta A, Gupta P, Bajpai G
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Giloy's traditional-pharmacology source, Heliyon 10(4):e26125, independently fetched and verified. A narrative review (no systematic search method described) covering antidiabetic, immunomodulatory, hepatoprotective, anti-arthritic, neuroprotective and anticancer claims - almost all supported only by animal/lab studies, with a handful of small human studies for allergic rhinitis, diabetic foot ulcers and one cognition trial. Graded Limited, not Moderate, for two real problems found during Gate 1 verification: its own highlights claim the herb 'could fight against coronavirus disease,' a claim its own body text does not substantiate with any human data: COVID-19 work is described only as 'in the clinical trial stage' with no results given; and - more seriously - this 2024 review, published three years after Nagral et al.'s peer-reviewed liver-injury case series (above), does not mention hepatotoxicity risk anywhere, describing the herb's liver effects only in protective terms. This is a significant omission in an otherwise recent, citable review, and is exactly why this card does not rely on this source alone for safety information.

sources.title: Tinospora Cordifolia
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs) - Giloy/Guduchi safety source. Rates hay fever 'Possibly Effective' (a specific extract, Tinofend, reduced sneezing/nasal itching after ~2 months); all other uses (diabetes, cholesterol, cancer, liver disease, arthritis) rated insufficient evidence, mostly animal/test-tube data: 'there isn't enough information to know the effects... in the human body.' Short-term use 'seems to be safe'; long-term safety (over 8 weeks) not known. Cautions: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding; may lower blood sugar (diabetes-drug interaction, Moderate, insulin/glimepiride/glyburide/pioglitazone named); may activate the immune system (avoid with autoimmune disease; may reduce immunosuppressant effectiveness - azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus, prednisone/corticosteroids named, Moderate); stop 2 weeks before surgery. Notably, this specific page does NOT mention liver toxicity or DILI at all - flagged here explicitly since this project independently found a real, serious, peer-reviewed liver-injury signal (see Nagral/Kulkarni above) that this otherwise-useful safety page simply omits.

sources.title: Bacopa
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 8th herb, Brahmi) - Brahmi/Bacopa Gate 1 safety source, independently fetched and verified (including a direct exact-quote check of its own wording, not just a paraphrase). Rates memory 'Possibly Effective' (specific extracts KeenMind and BacoMind improve some memory measures in healthy older adults; some evidence of memory/hand-eye-coordination benefit in children aged 6-8) and IBS 'Possibly Ineffective' (no better than placebo at preventing symptom return after remission) - most other claimed uses (anxiety, epilepsy, asthma, backache, hoarseness, mental illness, joint pain, sexual problems, fluid retention) rated insufficient evidence. Short-term use (up to 12 weeks) rated possibly safe; common side effects increased bowel movements, stomach cramps, nausea, dry mouth, fatigue. Cautions: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding (safety data lacking); may slow heart rate (caution with existing slow heart rate); may cause intestinal congestion (caution with intestinal blockage); may increase stomach/intestinal secretions (caution with ulcers) and lung secretions (caution with asthma/emphysema); may increase thyroid hormone levels (use cautiously or avoid with thyroid conditions/thyroid medicine, Minor-rated interaction); may increase urinary tract secretions (caution with urinary obstruction). Drug interactions (Moderate): anticholinergic/'drying' drugs such as atropine, scopolamine and some antihistamines/antidepressants (effects of both may be reduced); Alzheimer's acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (effects and side effects may increase); cholinergic drugs such as pilocarpine, donepezil, tacrine (side-effect risk may increase). Dosing as studied: 300 mg brahmi extract/day for 12 weeks for memory.
