Exact quote confirmed directly from the page's own overview: 'Be careful not to confuse brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) with gotu kola and other natural medicines that are also sometimes called brahmi' - the page names gotu kola by its common name only, not by the botanical name Centella asiatica.

sources.title: The Cognitive-Enhancing Effects of Bacopa monnieri: A Systematic Review of Randomized, Controlled Human Clinical Trials
sources.author: Pase MP, Kean J, Sarris J, Neale C, Scholey AB, Stough C
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 8th herb, Brahmi) - Brahmi's backbone cognition evidence source, Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine 2012;18(7):647-652, PMID 22747190. A genuine systematic review (not a narrative review) of randomised, placebo-controlled human trials: 6 trials met inclusion criteria, each run for 12 weeks in adults without dementia or significant cognitive impairment. Found Bacopa improved performance on 9 of 17 tests specifically in the domain of memory free-recall, with little evidence of enhancement in any other cognitive domain tested. The authors describe research on Bacopa's effects as being 'in its infancy' and call for studies at varied dosages and across different standardised extracts - an appropriately cautious conclusion for a review this size. Independently corroborated via a second route: StatPearls' own 2023 Bacopa monnieri chapter (see statpearls-bacopa-monnieri-2023 below) cites this same review and reports the identical finding (memory free-recall improved, other cognitive domains not) and the identical dose range (300-450mg/day extract standardised to 10-20% bacoside glycosides), confirming this summary was not taken from a secondary source alone.

sources.title: Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials on Cognitive Effects of Bacopa monnieri Extract
sources.author: Kongkeaw C, Dilokthornsakul P, Thanarangsarit P, Limpeanchob N, Scholfield CN
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 8th herb, Brahmi) - a second, independent, Strong-tier evidence source for Brahmi's cognitive effects, Journal of Ethnopharmacology 2014;151(1):528-535, PMID 24252493, independently fetched and verified in full (full abstract read directly, not summarised secondhand). A genuine meta-analysis: searched 9 databases/registries to June 2013, included randomised, placebo-controlled trials of chronic (12+ week) dosing of standardised Bacopa extract without co-medication, assessed methodological quality with Cochrane risk-of-bias and Jadad scales. 9 trials met inclusion criteria (518 subjects total, 437 analysed in the pooled result); overall quality judged low risk of bias. Found statistically significant improvement in speed of attention: shortened Trail B test time (-17.9 ms, 95% CI -24.6 to -11.2, p<0.001) and decreased choice reaction time (10.6 ms, 95% CI -12.1 to -9.2, p<0.001). Conclusion: Bacopa 'has the potential to improve cognition, particularly speed of attention,' but only a large head-to-head trial against an existing medication would give definitive efficacy data. Worth noting for this card's own honesty: this finding (speed of attention) is a different cognitive domain from the one the 2012 Pase et al. systematic review above found benefit in (memory free-recall only, 'little evidence of enhancement in any other cognitive domain') - the two Strong-tier reviews here support different, not identical, specific benefits, which this card's whatEvidenceShows states plainly rather than blurring together into one confirmed claim.

sources.title: Bacopa monnieri
sources.author: Walker EA, Pellegrini MV
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 8th herb, Brahmi) - Brahmi's richest single source, found independently (not in the owner's original package) and fetched/read in full. A StatPearls continuing-education chapter, hosted on NCBI Bookshelf (NIH/NLM infrastructure) but authored and peer-reviewed by named physicians (Eric A. Walker, Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center; Mark V. Pellegrini) and published by StatPearls Publishing LLC - a narrative/CME review, not an official NIH/government work product, so graded Moderate and classed as Study or review (consistent with this project's treatment of other narrative reviews), not Government or health body. Both authors declare no relevant financial relationships. Directly and explicitly confirms the Bacopa/gotu-kola name confusion with an exact quote used in this card's traditionalUse section: 'The term Brahmi has been used to describe Bacopa monnieri, Centella asiatica (Gotu kola), or a combination of the 2 botanicals' (citing Shinomol, Muralidhara & Bharath 2011). States main Ayurvedic indications as memory improvement, insomnia, epilepsy and as an anxiolytic ('medhya rasayana'). Cites both Pase et al. 2012 and Kongkeaw et al. 2014 (above) directly and consistently with this project's own independent reads of those two papers. Safety/mechanism detail used in this card: may inhibit acetylcholinesterase (raising acetylcholine), which could counteract anticholinergic drugs and worsen bradycardia, GI obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, asthma/COPD or urogenital obstruction; inhibits human cytochrome P450 enzymes CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2C19, a mechanism for herb-drug interactions with medicines broken down by those enzymes; an animal (mouse) study found Bacopa extract increased thyroxine (T4) levels by about 40%, the basis for its own thyroid caution. One study (28-56 days, 250mg/kg/day) found decreased sperm count, motility and viability in male mice without affecting libido - an animal-only fertility finding, used in this card as an open question, not an established human effect. States 'no human toxicity demonstrated' in a 270-day high-dose rat study, and 'no significant documented adverse drug reactions' in human clinical/biochemical measures as of the chapter's writing - a reassuring data point for short-term use specifically. Also notes the FDA issued a 2019 warning to supplement manufacturers against making unapproved therapeutic claims about Bacopa monnieri products.

sources.title: Bacopa (Consumer Version, Overview of Dietary Supplements)
sources.author: Merck Manual editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 8th herb, Brahmi) - Brahmi's second consumer clinical-reference source, independently fetched and verified, same Article/blog treatment as this project's other Merck Manual citations (Tulsi, Ashwagandha). Also names Bacopa as 'Brahmi, Indian pennywort, water hyssop, and herb of grace' in its own opening description - an independent, third confirmation (alongside RxList and StatPearls) that 'Indian pennywort' genuinely circulates as an alternative name for Bacopa in some consumer sources, even though it is Centella asiatica's own common English name, which somewhat complicates a clean 'the book got it wrong' reading of the cached-book finding above; this card treats the mix-up as real and worth flagging regardless, since multiple serious sources (StatPearls, RxList) still explicitly warn against conflating the two plants. States plainly that 'no beneficial effects have been confirmed in high-quality human studies' - more skeptical phrasing than RxList's 'Possibly Effective' rating for memory, a real difference in tone this card does not paper over. Side effects: upset stomach, nausea, diarrhoea, fatigue, slowed heart rate, slowed intestinal transit, worsened ulcers, increased lung secretions, raised thyroid hormone levels, increased urinary obstruction. States plainly 'use of bacopa is not recommended' because no confirmed benefit outweighs the possible harms, though probably safe for most people short-term - the single most skeptical overall verdict of any source checked for this card, included for balance rather than smoothed over. Pregnancy: avoid. Thyroid disease: avoid. Drug interactions named: thyroid hormone medication (avoid combining), fluoxetine (possible confusion, agitation, blood pressure/temperature changes), Alzheimer's/glaucoma drugs (pilocarpine, donepezil, tacrine), warfarin, glipizide, diltiazem, losartan, and chemotherapy drugs etoposide/vinblastine/vincristine (Bacopa could raise levels of these in the body).

sources.title: Guggul
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - Guggul's primary consumer clinical-reference source, independently fetched and verified. Scientific names given as Commiphora mukul, also Commiphora wightii, Balsamodendrum mukul and Balsamodendrum wightii - confirming the two main botanical names in circulation are a taxonomic synonym, not a different-plant mix-up. Rates acne 'Possibly Effective' ('seems to work about as well as' tetracycline for nodulocystic acne, based on the Thappa & Dogra 1994 trial below), obesity 'Possibly Ineffective'; cholesterol rated insufficient evidence/inconsistent - states 3000-6000mg/day did not lower cholesterol/triglycerides in people eating a Western diet, though it may help on an Indian diet; osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis rated early/insufficient evidence. Side effects: stomach upset, headache, nausea, vomiting, loose stools, diarrhoea, belching, hiccups, more common at higher doses (~6000mg/day); allergic-type rash/itching also reported. Safety: pregnancy 'Likely Unsafe' (may stimulate uterus/menstrual flow); breastfeeding avoid (not enough known); may slow clotting (bleeding disorder caution); may act like oestrogen (avoid with hormone-sensitive cancers, endometriosis, fibroids); thyroid conditions - use only under medical supervision; stop 2 weeks before surgery. Drug interactions: Major - avoid with oestrogens; Moderate - birth control pills, diltiazem, CYP3A4-metabolised drugs (lovastatin, atorvastatin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, fexofenadine, triazolam named), anticoagulants/antiplatelets (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, heparin, NSAIDs named), propranolol, tamoxifen ('Do not take guggul if you are taking tamoxifen'), thyroid hormone medicine.

sources.title: Guggul (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.asOf: current as fetched 31 Oct 2026, page last updated by MSKCC 5 Jan 2022
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - Guggul's richest single source, independently fetched and verified (academic cancer-centre clinical database, same Government or health body/Strong treatment as this project's other MSKCC About Herbs citations). States plainly that studies on whether guggul can lower cholesterol are 'mixed' - mice fed guggul had lower cholesterol but human results conflict, with one study suggesting guggul may actually raise cholesterol; no benefit seen combined with Triphala. For acne, states 'Evidence is lacking to support this claim for guggul alone' - a notably more skeptical position than RxList's 'Possibly Effective' rating on the same underlying trial, used in this card to show the genuine disagreement rather than picking a side. Mechanism (mostly preclinical/animal): guggulsterone affects liver cholesterol biosynthesis in vitro; cholesterol-lowering in mice attributed to FXR inhibition affecting bile acid production; activates oestrogen receptor alpha, pregnane X receptor and progesterone receptor, and may induce CYP3A genes. Warning: 'Do Not Take if' taking CYP3A4 substrate drugs, since guggul may make these less effective. Adverse reactions: headache, mild nausea, belching, hiccups, loose stools, rash. Case reports: contact dermatitis from guggul in slimming/anti-cellulite creams; a 63-year-old woman developed severe hypertransaminasemia (markedly raised liver enzymes) after 6 months on an over-the-counter product combining guggulsterol with red yeast rice, resolving after stopping; a case of liver failure requiring transplant involved a supplement combining usnic acid, green tea and guggul extract, with usnic acid considered the main suspected cause though the other ingredients may have amplified its effect - MSKCC does not attribute this case to guggul alone. Herb-lab interactions listed: reduced serum triglycerides; elevated TSH, T3 and T4 - used in this card's thyroid caution alongside the Krause's animal-study finding.

sources.title: Guggulipid for the Treatment of Hypercholesterolemia: A Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.author: Szapary PO, Wolfe ML, Bloedon LT, Cucchiara AJ, DerMarderosian AH, Cirigliano MD, Rader DJ
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - the key Western-population negative finding for this card, JAMA 2003;290(6):765-772, PMID 12915429, independently fetched and verified directly from PubMed, not taken from a secondary source. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group RCT, March 2000-August 2001, 103 ambulatory, community-dwelling adults with hypercholesterolemia in the Philadelphia, PA area, eating their usual Western diet. Three arms: placebo (n=36), standard-dose guggulipid 1000mg three times daily (n=33), high-dose guggulipid 2000mg three times daily (n=34), extract standardised to 2.5% guggulsterones, 8 weeks. Primary outcome (LDL-C): placebo fell ~5%; standard-dose rose 4% (P=.01 vs placebo); high-dose rose 5% (P=.006 vs placebo) - guggulipid groups ended up roughly 9-10% higher than placebo. No significant change in total cholesterol, HDL-C, triglycerides or VLDL-C in the intention-to-treat analysis. Six guggulipid-treated participants developed a hypersensitivity rash versus none on placebo; otherwise generally well tolerated. Authors' own conclusion, quoted directly: guggulipid 'did not appear to improve' serum cholesterol over the short term in this population and 'might even raise LDL-C.' Partly funded by Sabinsa, a US guggulipid-extract manufacturer, whose officials disputed the completeness of the results - noted here for transparency, not as a reason to discount the trial. Graded Moderate (a single, well-conducted primary RCT) rather than Strong, consistent with this project's treatment of other individual RCTs.

sources.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Ayurvedic Herbal Preparations for Hypercholesterolemia
sources.author: Gyawali A, et al. (Cochrane Complementary Medicine bursary-funded review)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - Guggul's backbone cholesterol-evidence source, Medicina 2021, PMID 34071454, open access PMC8229657, independently fetched and read in full (not just the abstract) directly from PMC. Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs in hypercholesterolemia, 32 studies/1,386 participants total across three herbs meeting inclusion criteria (garlic, guggulu/Commiphora mukul, black cumin), average intervention 12 weeks, inverse-variance method in RevMan 5.3, two independent reviewers for risk of bias. Guggul-specific: 7 RCTs, 8 trial arms, 380 participants. Total cholesterol: mean difference -16.78mg/dL (95% CI -30.96 to -2.61), p=.02. LDL-C: mean difference -18.78mg/dL (95% CI -34.07 to -3.48), p=.02, from 5 studies/266 participants. Triglycerides not significantly changed; HDL rose 2.19mg/dL (95% CI 0.27 to 4.12), p=.03. Minor adverse effects only in most studies (diarrhoea, headache, rash); the Szapary 2003 RCT above is one of the pooled trials and is itself rated low risk of bias across the board. IMPORTANT CAVEATS the review states about itself, used directly in this card to avoid overclaiming: heterogeneity for the 7 guggul studies was I-squared=75%, at the review's own stated threshold for trusting a pooled result; one single older trial (Verma 1988) 'strongly influenced' the pooled effect; most trials were run in Western populations, by the review's own count, apart from two exceptions; guggul preparations varied (crude gum vs extracted guggulipid - extraction not being an Ayurvedic practice); purification status in the Szapary trial was unclear and its author did not respond to the reviewers' queries; random sequence generation/allocation concealment were mostly unclear across the guggul trials, and attrition bias was rated high in about 7 of 10 guggul-related risk-of-bias entries. Despite these caveats, the authors' own conclusion calls guggul 'moderately effective' for total cholesterol, LDL-C and HDL-C and a possible adjunct to cholesterol-lowering treatment - a more confident-sounding verdict than the underlying 75% heterogeneity and single-study-driven result fully supports; this card flags that gap explicitly rather than repeating the headline conclusion uncritically. No conflicts of interest declared.

sources.title: Nodulocystic acne: oral gugulipid versus tetracycline
sources.author: Thappa DM, Dogra J
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - the single primary trial behind this card's acne discussion, Journal of Dermatology 1994;21(10):729-31, PMID 7798429, independently fetched and verified directly from PubMed. Randomised controlled trial, 20 patients with nodulocystic acne, two arms: tetracycline 500mg twice daily, or gugulipid tablets (equivalent to 25mg guggulsterone) twice daily, both for 3 months. Results: inflammatory lesions fell 65.2% with tetracycline and 68% with gugulipid, both arms showing progressive reduction in most patients; difference between arms not statistically significant (P>.05). At 3-month follow-up, 4 patients on tetracycline relapsed versus 2 on gugulipid. Patients with oily faces responded noticeably better to gugulipid, though the abstract does not report a formal statistical subgroup analysis for this. Graded Moderate, not Strong, given the very small sample (20 patients total) and age of the trial - this is the project's single primary-evidence source for acne, not a review, and this card treats the acne use as a genuine open question rather than a confirmed benefit, especially given MSKCC's more skeptical position (see mskcc-guggul above).

sources.title: NTP Technical Report on the Toxicity Studies of a Gum Guggul Extract (Commiphora mukul) Administered by Gavage to Sprague Dawley Rats and B6C3F1/N Mice
sources.author: US National Toxicology Program (NIH/NIEHS)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - a genuine US government toxicology study, NTP Toxicity Report Series No. 99, June 2020, DOI 10.22427/NTP-TOX-99, found and partially read via its own abstract/background page (PMC8039874) and corroborating search results; the full technical report's detailed organ-by-organ pathology tables could not be fully retrieved in this research pass (NCBI Bookshelf blocked automated access with a bot-check during this session) - flagged here honestly as a limitation rather than inferring specific findings not directly confirmed. What is confirmed: a gum guggul extract (GGE) formulation from Commiphora mukul oleoresin was given by oral gavage (chosen to mirror how people take encapsulated supplements) to male and female Sprague Dawley rats and B6C3F1/N mice, in 28-day and 3-month studies; the study was explicitly motivated by guggul's widespread dietary-supplement use alongside 'reported metabolic and hormone-altering effects and limited safety data.' Secondary reporting on the 3-month rat study states there were 'no dose-related microscopic findings' in that study's pathology (Appendix F) - a reassuring animal-only data point, used cautiously in this card as an open question rather than a confirmed human safety finding, since it does not resolve the human case reports of liver enzyme changes reported elsewhere (see mskcc-guggul).

sources.title: The Encyclopedia of Nutrition and Good Health, Second Edition
sources.author: Robert Ronzio, with Kennedy Associates
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - Gate-1-approved reference encyclopedia (Facts On File Library of Health and Living), not previously given a sourceId despite being Gate-1 approved; added here on first genuine use. Its 'guggul (gum guggulu)' entry (around line 32436 of the cached text) describes a yellowish resin from the mukul myrrh (Commiphora mukul) tree, used in India for arthritis, obesity, skin disorders and high cholesterol; states preliminary studies indicate possible benefit for atherosclerosis (lowering triglycerides/LDL/VLDL, raising HDL) and that it is approved for that use in India, but adds plainly that 'because these studies were limited in scope the results are unreliable' - an appropriately hedged statement this card echoes rather than overriding. Also notes other small studies suggesting possible benefit for acne. Safety: available in the US as a dietary supplement with safety/efficacy not tested or proven by any government agency; some studies indicate it can stimulate the thyroid, possibly countering thyroid medications; side effects named include headache, nausea and skin rashes; 'probably unsafe for pregnant women,' with inadequate breastfeeding safety data. Pre-2015 (2003) - flagged per BRIEF.md rule 5 for a current recheck, though its content here is corroborated independently by newer sources (RxList, MSKCC) rather than relied on alone.

sources.title: Yograj Guggulu (ingredient and preparation listing)
sources.author: Planet Ayurveda (commercial Ayurvedic manufacturer/educational library page)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 9th herb, Guggul) - used only for a plain ingredient/preparation fact (not a health claim), independently fetched and verified: full ingredient list for the classical Yograj Guggulu formulation lists 22 herbs/spices at 10g each, purified guggulu (Commiphora mukul) at 270g, and 'Sarpi - ghee - Sufficient Quantity' as a direct ingredient; the dosage section instructs taking the tablets 'along with Honey or butter milk.' Cross-checked against several other independent commercial/clinical ingredient listings for the same classical formulation (via wider search), which consistently also list ghee as part of the recipe - this is a well-documented, standard feature of this classical formulation, not an isolated or unusual claim from one retailer. Graded Limited and typed Article/blog since this is a commercial source used narrowly for an ingredient fact, not for any efficacy or safety claim.

sources.title: Moringa
sources.author: RxList editorial staff
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - Moringa's primary consumer clinical-reference source, independently fetched and verified. This card's main anchor for the leaf-vs-other-parts safety distinction, which is the single most important thing to get right on this card. By-part safety, quoted/paraphrased directly: leaves, fruit and seeds eaten as food are rated 'LIKELY SAFE'; leaf and seed used as medicine short-term are 'POSSIBLY SAFE' (leaf products used safely up to 90 days, seed products up to 3 weeks); root and root extracts are 'POSSIBLY UNSAFE' by mouth, the page stating the root contains spirochin, 'a toxic substance'. Pregnancy: root, bark and flowers are 'POSSIBLY UNSAFE' - traditional use of root and bark aimed to cause miscarriage, and chemicals in these parts may make the uterus contract; information on other parts is insufficient, so the page advises avoiding use generally in pregnancy. Breastfeeding: short-term maternal use 'seems to be safe', but not enough is known about the nursing infant, so the page advises it is 'best to avoid'. Children: leaf 'POSSIBLY SAFE' short-term, used apparently safely up to 2 months. Uses/evidence: no formal effectiveness rating is given for diabetes or cholesterol specifically; the page notes that adding moringa tablets to a sulfonylurea 'does not improve blood sugar control better than taking sulfonylureas alone' (a specific small trial finding). Other uses with early-research descriptions: asthma (3g twice daily for 3 weeks reduced symptom severity in mild-moderate asthma), breast milk production (a review of 5 studies found a moderate increase after one week when started postpartum day 3, benefit of longer use unclear), malnutrition (powder added to food for 2 months improved weight in malnourished children), menopausal symptoms (fresh leaves added to food for 3 months may improve hot flushes and sleep in healthy postmenopausal women). Drug interactions: levothyroxine (thyroid medicine), rated Moderate - moringa may reduce how much levothyroxine the body absorbs, possibly making it less effective; diabetes medicines, rated Moderate - moringa may lower blood sugar, so combining with insulin, glimepiride, glyburide, pioglitazone or rosiglitazone could cause hypoglycaemia, with close monitoring and possible dose changes advised; blood pressure medicines, rated Moderate - may add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect of captopril, enalapril, losartan, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide and similar; CYP3A4-metabolised drugs, rated Moderate - moringa may slow how the liver breaks these down, raising effects/side effects of lovastatin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, fexofenadine, triazolam and similar. The page states there is 'not enough scientific information to determine an appropriate range of doses for moringa' generally.

sources.title: Moringa Oleifera (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Integrative Medicine
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - independently fetched and verified (academic cancer-centre clinical database, same Government or health body/Strong treatment as this project's other MSKCC About Herbs citations). Patient section: leaves, flowers, seeds and roots 'are used in traditional medicine'; moringa is used to treat infections, to treat diabetes and to lower high cholesterol, with other uses 'doctors haven't studied... to see if they work'. Clinician section narrows which parts reach the table versus the clinic: leaves and seed pods are eaten as food, while bark and root are used in folk remedies specifically - an independent corroboration of RxList's leaf/seed-vs-root-and-bark safety split. States human studies are 'quite limited'; small preliminary findings suggest a modest positive effect on lipid profiles, and one leaf-powder study found increased insulin secretion in healthy subjects; reviews call for 'well-designed studies in diabetic or prediabetic patients' - consistent with this card's own conclusion that the clinical evidence is not yet settled. Safety: 'generally safe to eat moringa leaves, seeds, and to drink moringa powder mixed with liquids'; patients are told to talk with their provider before taking supplements, since 'herbal supplements are stronger than the herbs you would use in cooking' and can interact with medications. Preclinical genotoxicity: a mouse model found moringa genotoxic only at 'supra-supplementation levels of 3,000 mg/kg body weight' - a high-dose preclinical finding, not a normal-use safety concern. Drug interactions (clinician section, preclinical/animal data, clinical relevance undetermined for all): chronic co-administration with the diabetes medicine sitagliptin decreased its antihyperglycaemic effect in an animal model; moringa increased rifampin bioavailability and inhibited CYP3A4 in preclinical data. Side effects: patient section states 'side effects have not been reported', but the clinician section separately lists real case reports of Stevens-Johnson syndrome after eating food containing moringa leaves, cutaneous toxicity in a woman who took moringa powder for weight loss, and anaphylaxis with widespread angioedema after eating moringa leaves - rare but genuine documented reactions, used in this card's cautions. Pregnancy/breastfeeding: clinician section states plainly 'pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid the use of moringa' (a more blanket caution than RxList's by-part distinction; this card notes both positions rather than picking one). Root-specific preclinical finding: in an animal model, root extract showed protective effects on the liver and kidney in a dose-dependent manner - preclinical only, not used here to claim a human root benefit, and not treated as contradicting this card's root-safety caution, which rests on different evidence (traditional abortifacient use, spirochin toxicity).

sources.title: Moringa (LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury)
sources.author: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - the genuine new safety finding of this card's research, independently found (not part of the owner's original package) and fetched/verified via search-engine excerpts after the NCBI Bookshelf page itself returned a browser/reCAPTCHA verification screen on direct fetch (NBK605172; a mirrored PubMed/Bookshelf record elsewhere online lists PMID 39047137 against this same Bookshelf ID). LiverTox is a continuously updated NIH database (hosted by NIDDK via NCBI Bookshelf), graded Government or health body/Strong per this project's convention, distinct from a StatPearls CME chapter. Describes a documented case of acute anicteric hepatitis (no jaundice) attributed to a moringa-containing product, hepatocellular injury pattern, R value 5.0 initially; the product also listed vitamin C on its label, with concentrations not given. The person stopped the product, then restarted it, and the case recurred with a higher R value of 10.6 on rechallenge - a dechallenge/rechallenge pattern, one of the stronger forms of evidence for attributing a liver injury to a specific product, though a co-ingredient (vitamin C) cannot be fully excluded since exact composition wasn't given. LiverTox's own likelihood score for moringa is 'D' (a possible but rare cause of clinically apparent liver injury). The entry frames moringa as not approved by the FDA for any medical condition in the United States, and states that before this recently described case, there had been no published reports of clinically apparent liver injury attributed to moringa extracts - i.e. this is treated as a rare, newly emerging signal, not an established risk, similar in spirit to how this project has already treated single case-report liver signals for Guggul.

sources.title: Effects of Moringa oleifera Lam. Supplementation on Cardiometabolic Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials with GRADE Assessment
sources.author: Crisan D, Gavrilas L, Paltinean R, Frumuzachi O, Mocan A, Crisan G
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - this card's backbone source for both the diabetes and cholesterol evidence sections, and the single most rigorous human review found for either question. Nutrients 2025;17(22):3501, doi 10.3390/nu17223501, PMID 41305552, PMCID PMC12655524, PROSPERO-registered (CRD420251025219), independently fetched and read in full (not just the abstract). RCT-only (unlike the weaker Phimarn 2021 review below, which mixed randomised and non-randomised trials): 9 RCTs/12 study arms, 341 participants in intervention groups versus 308 in control groups, across a mixed adult population (prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, HIV-infected adults, overweight adults, people with hyperlipidaemia - not a diabetes-only or cholesterol-only population). Random-effects standardised mean differences (SMD, 95% CI): fasting glucose -0.12 (-0.38 to 0.14), p=.38, I-squared=0%; HbA1c -0.30 (-0.65 to 0.05) from 3 trials, not significant; total cholesterol -0.20 (-0.76 to 0.35), p=.47; LDL-C -0.30 (-1.10 to 0.51), p=.47; HDL-C +0.18 (-0.60 to 0.96), p=.65; triglycerides -0.14 (-0.71 to 0.44), p=.64 - none of these six outcomes reached statistical significance. GRADE certainty was rated very low for every outcome. Authors' own conclusion, quoted directly: 'Current evidence does not support consistent cardiometabolic benefits of moringa supplementation in adults.' Authors' own stated limitations: risk of bias was high or unclear in several trials (poor randomisation reporting, lack of blinding, selective outcome reporting); 'high between-study heterogeneity was observed across several outcomes', especially anthropometric and lipid markers; each outcome was informed by fewer than 10 trials, so publication bias could not be reliably assessed; most studies lacked dietary control or monitoring; a secondary finding (diastolic blood pressure, SMD -0.41) was not robust and lost significance in sensitivity analyses. This is the Strong source this card relies on to avoid overclaiming moringa's diabetes/cholesterol research as more settled than it is.

sources.title: Efficacy and Safety on Moringa oleifera on Blood Glucose and Lipid Profile: A Meta-Analysis
sources.author: Phimarn W, Sungthong B, Wichaiyo K
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - the earlier, less rigorous positive-finding counterpart to the Crisan 2025 review above, used here specifically to show the genuine disagreement in the literature (BRIEF.md rule 6) rather than being hidden. Pharmacognosy Magazine 2021;17(74):373-378. Searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus and the Thai Library Integrated System through December 2019. Pooled 7 studies, 257 participants, 28-90 days' duration - importantly, this pool mixes randomised AND non-randomised trial designs together (unlike the RCT-only Crisan 2025 review), a real methodological weakness distinct from and additional to its heterogeneity problem. Fasting blood sugar: weighted mean difference -14.81 mg/dL (95% CI -27.99 to -1.63), I-squared=97.8% - heterogeneity this extreme means the pooled estimate is unstable and should be read with real caution, a point this card makes explicitly rather than repeating the headline figure uncritically. Postprandial glucose: WMD -64.73 mg/dL (95% CI -102.87 to -26.59), I-squared=93%. No significant change in HbA1c was found. For lipids, the authors' own conclusion states moringa 'improved fasting blood sugar (FBS) levels and lipid profile significantly... whereas some others reported that it has no or negative effects' and separately describes a rise in HDL - but this card could not independently confirm the exact pooled lipid mean differences/confidence intervals, despite repeated attempts, because the original PDF could not be rendered through this project's available fetching tools (a recurring TLS/certificate error on phcog.com), so the lipid figures here rest on the authors' own stated conclusion via the published abstract/search-engine excerpts, not on an independently re-derived number - flagged here as a genuine verification limit, per BRIEF.md rule 7/11, rather than presented as fully independently checked. The authors state no serious adverse effects were reported, but caution in their own words that 'the long-term benefits and safety of the treatment remain to be determined'. This card grades this review Moderate rather than Strong specifically because of the mixed RCT/non-RCT pooling, and treats its confident-sounding headline conclusion as overclaiming relative to the 97.8% heterogeneity in its own primary outcome and relative to the stricter, RCT-only Crisan 2025 review's null finding on the same outcomes.

sources.title: The Impact of Moringa oleifera Supplementation on Anemia and Other Variables during Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: A Narrative Review
sources.author: Rotella R, Soriano JM, Llopis-Gonzalez A, Morales-Suarez-Varela M
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 10th herb, Moringa) - this card's dedicated pregnancy/breastfeeding source for the leaf side of the leaf-vs-root safety distinction, independently fetched and read in full. Nutrients 2023;15(12):2674, doi 10.3390/nu15122674. Despite its title calling it a narrative review, its own Methods describe a systematic PubMed/EMBASE search from 2018-2023, yielding 12 included studies, all conducted in Southeast Asia, using leaf powder, leaf extract, or leaf-flour biscuits/capsules only - no root, root bark or flower studies are included anywhere in this review. States plainly: 'None of the studies analysed reported contraindications' to this leaf-based use during pregnancy and lactation, also citing an earlier review (Stohs and Hartman) that found no adverse effects from oral intake of leaves and leaf extracts at achievable doses. Important scope caveat this card relies on directly: the review does not mention uterine stimulation, abortifacient effects or miscarriage risk anywhere, and its only cited pregnancy-related traditional uses are promoting fetal growth and relieving nausea, vomiting and constipation - its silence on uterotonic effects reflects that its scope never included root, bark or flower studies, so this 'no contraindications' finding is read in this card as applying to leaf-based forms only, not as reassurance extending to other plant parts. Authors' own conclusion: moringa 'appears to be a useful local food to prevent nutritional deficiencies' at this life stage; they call for further research into dose-dependent effects and possible adverse effects, and recommend pregnant/breastfeeding women consult a healthcare provider before taking any supplement or herbal remedy. Graded Moderate: although its search was systematic, the review is self-labelled narrative, pools small heterogeneous trials without a formal GRADE-style quality assessment, and its central finding is an absence-of-reported-harm observation rather than a positive controlled safety outcome.

sources.title: Amla - Phyllanthus emblica (Natural Health Products monograph)
sources.author: Health Canada, Natural and Non-prescription Health Products Directorate (NNHPD)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - a genuine Canadian government regulatory monograph, independently fetched and read in full (PDF text extracted directly, not taken from a secondary source). This card's primary official anchor, filling the role RxList/MSKCC play for other herb cards - see drugs-com-emblica-monograph's note for confirmation that neither RxList nor MSKCC has a dedicated amla page. Proper name Phyllanthus emblica (fruit, dried); common names given include Amalaki, Amla, Emblic, Emblic myrobalan, Indian gooseberry, Myrobalan. Approved use/purpose claims for Canadian product labels: source of antioxidants that help protect cells against free radicals; traditionally used in Ayurveda as Rasayana (rejuvenative tonic); traditionally used in Ayurveda to relieve symptoms of Amlapitta (hyperacidity/dyspepsia); traditionally used in Ayurveda as a digestive tonic (stomachic) to increase appetite and aid digestion; traditionally used in Ayurveda as a mild laxative for occasional constipation (mode of action unclear, effect mild - not a stimulant or bulk-forming laxative); traditionally used in Ayurveda as an eye tonic. Dose: adults 18+, not to exceed 6 g dried fruit/day for the antioxidant claim, 3-6 g/day for the Amlapitta/digestive-tonic/laxative/Rasayana/eye-tonic claims. Direction: take a few hours before or after other medications or health products (a generic separation caution this monograph applies to amla, not a specific documented interaction). Caution: ask a healthcare practitioner before use if breastfeeding (all products); ask a healthcare practitioner before use if pregnant, specifically for products providing more than 3 g amla/day. Contraindication: do not use as a laxative if you have fever or any undiagnosed gastrointestinal trouble. Known adverse reaction: a laxative effect may occur. This is a regulatory labelling guide (what claims and warnings Health Canada will allow on a product label), not a clinical trial review - it is used in this card for its official confirmation of amla's genuine traditional Rasayana/digestive/laxative/eye-tonic uses and for its pregnancy/breastfeeding caution, not as efficacy evidence for any specific cardiometabolic outcome. Its own reference list separately cites a human trial on Chyawanprash and vitamin C's effect on glucose tolerance and lipoprotein profile (Manjunatha et al 2001) - noted here but not relied on directly, since this card could not independently fetch that paper.

sources.title: Emblica (professional natural-product monograph)
sources.author: Drugs.com, natural products database (Wolters Kluwer Health-licensed professional monograph)
sources.asOf: current as fetched 31 Oct 2026, page states 'Last updated on Jun 22, 2026'
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - this card's main consumer/professional clinical-reference anchor, independently fetched and read in full (direct fetch returned HTTP 403, so content was retrieved via an alternate scraping route and read as markdown, not inferred from a snippet). Confirms, by direct check, that neither RxList (rxlist.com/supplements/amla.htm returned HTTP 404) nor MSKCC's About Herbs database (mskcc.org returned HTTP 404 for an amla page) has a dedicated amla page - a genuine gap from the sources this project used for other herb cards, verified directly rather than assumed, the same way this project's Guggul card confirmed StatPearls and Merck Manual had no guggul chapter; a further direct search confirmed neither StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) nor Merck Manual has a dedicated amla/Phyllanthus emblica chapter either. Clinical Overview: 'Data support benefit of emblica supplementation in dyslipidemic patients as well as antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. There is limited robust clinical evidence to support the use of emblica for any other indication.' Dosing: few clinical studies guide dosage; dyslipidemia 250 mg or 500 mg standardised Phyllanthus embilica extract twice daily for up to 12 weeks (citing Khanna 2015, Upadya 2019, Usharani 2019); diabetes/hyperlipidaemia trials used 1-3 g powdered dried fruit/day in water for 21 days, or 300 mg tablets (50% amla extract/50% dextrin) three times daily. Contraindications: 'have not been identified.' Pregnancy/Lactation: 'information regarding safety and efficacy... is lacking.' Interactions: 'None well documented.' Adverse Reactions: 'little or no information'; Toxicology: 'No major toxicities have been reported' - rat toxicity studies found no liver or renal detriment, no chromosomal aberrations, no toxicity or mutagenicity even at the highest doses tested. GENUINE INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY this card flags directly: despite stating 'Interactions: None well documented,' this same monograph's own 'Platelet aggregation' section cites real clinical trial data (Khanna 2015, standardised CAPROS extract 500 mg twice daily, 12 weeks, obese adults) finding ADP- and collagen-induced platelet aggregation significantly reduced versus baseline, with the collagen-induced effect still measurable after a 2-week washout - a plausible antiplatelet/bleeding-relevant mechanism that its own 'Interactions' section does not mention or connect to bleeding-medicine caution. This card treats the bleeding/antiplatelet caution as a genuine open question on this basis, not as a settled interaction. Immune section (used to support this card's honest immune-function gap): only animal data given - Triphala (not amla alone) raised neutrophil function and lowered cortisone release in noise-stressed rats, but a separate aqueous emblica extract had no effect on cold-stress-induced cortisone release in another experiment; no human immune-outcome clinical data is given anywhere on this page. Also separately notes amla fruit is known by the common name 'Chyavanprash' among many others, and cites a hepatoprotective study titled 'Hepatoprotective activity of Emblica officinalis and Chyavanaprash' (Jose & Kuttan 2000) - supporting that Chyawanprash is a recognised, amla-based classical product, cross-referenced against this card's own independently fetched Chyawanprash composition source below rather than relied on alone for ingredients.

sources.title: Clinical effects of Emblica officinalis fruit consumption on cardiovascular disease risk factors: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.author: Brown PDS, Ketter N, Vis-Dunbar M, Sakakibara BM
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - this card's single most rigorous review and backbone cardiometabolic source, independently fetched and read in full. BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies 2023;23:190, DOI 10.1186/s12906-023-03997-8, PMID 37296402, PMCID PMC10251691. Risk of bias assessed with Cochrane RoB 2 (a more rigorous tool than most reviews this project has used for other herbs), PRISMA-reported. 9 RCTs (6 parallel, 3 crossover), 535 participants total (range 12-150 per trial), ages 20-74; populations: healthy adults (3 trials), male smokers, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, essential and uncontrolled hypertension; 7 trials from India, 1 from Japan, 1 from Iran. Intervention: oral capsules, 8 trials aqueous fruit extract and 1 dried fruit powder, 500-1500 mg/day, 14-84 days. Pooled mean differences vs placebo: LDL-C -15.08 mg/dL (95% CI -25.43 to -4.73, I2=77%, p=.004); VLDL-C -5.43 mg/dL (95% CI -8.37 to -2.49 per the Abstract, though the Results section itself gives -2.94 as the upper bound - a small internal discrepancy noted here rather than silently resolved; I2=44%, p=.0003); triglycerides -22.35 mg/dL (95% CI -39.71 to -4.99, I2=62%, p=.01); hsCRP -1.70 mg/L (95% CI -2.06 to -1.33, I2=0% - the single least heterogeneous, most internally consistent finding in the whole review, p<.00001); HDL-C +2.09 mg/dL (95% CI -0.91 to 5.08, I2=86%, p=.17, NOT statistically significant); systolic blood pressure -2.75 mmHg (95% CI -10.41 to 4.90, I2=96%, p=.48, NS); diastolic blood pressure -0.83 mmHg (95% CI -5.87 to 4.21, I2=89%, p=.75, NS). Total cholesterol was deliberately excluded by the authors as an outcome; fasting glucose was never measured or pooled (diabetic status was only an eligibility characteristic, not a tested outcome) - a real gap this card relies on directly when describing how thin the dedicated blood-sugar evidence is. GENUINE OVERCLAIMING FLAG: despite HDL-C not reaching statistical significance (p=.17), the paper's own Discussion and Conclusions sections describe HDL-C improvements as statistically significant alongside the genuinely significant outcomes - this card treats the HDL-C finding as not significant, per the paper's own Results table, rather than repeating its more confident-sounding Discussion wording. Risk of bias: 5 of 6 parallel trials rated 'some concern', 1 (Biswas 2014) rated 'high risk' (randomisation process); all 3 crossover trials rated 'some concern', none assessed carryover effects explicitly. No GRADE or equivalent overall certainty rating was given. Authors' stated limitations, in their own words/paraphrase: considerable clinical and statistical heterogeneity across populations, baseline values, design and duration; possible variation in proprietary extract preparation; one trial used raw fruit rather than extract; possible publication bias from commercial interests; three trials had only 12-13 participants; too few trials for funnel-plot/Egger testing; crossover trials were analysed as parallel trials (a unit-of-analysis error the authors call conservative); non-English articles were excluded; safety was not formally investigated. Verbatim conclusion: 'Emblica officinalis has beneficial effects on LDL-C, VLDL-C, HDL-C, TG, and hsCRP that are statistically significant' but 'these results should be interpreted with caution'; E. officinalis 'may offer an efficacious, affordable, and convenient option' for CVD prevention pending further research.

sources.title: The Efficacy and Safety of Emblica officinalis Aqueous Fruit Extract among Adult Patients with Dyslipidemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.author: Acampado LRT, Chiu HHC, Larrazabal RB Jr, Arcellana AES, Añonuevo-Cruz MCS
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - independently fetched and read in full from the journal's own PDF (not a secondary source). Acta Medica Philippina 2023;57(5):90-96, DOI 10.47895/amp.vi0.5047. Eight-database search (MEDLINE/PubMed, MEDLINE/Ovid, Google Scholar, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov) to 31 Jan 2022, PRISMA flow from 730 records to 4 included RCTs, all conducted in India (2008-2019), 227 participants total, mean ages 35-68, random-effects model, Cochrane RoB 2.0 (one study, Antony 2008, rated high risk for lack of blinding). Dosage form across trials: aqueous fruit extract in 250 or 500 mg capsules, typically twice daily. Pooled effects at 12 weeks vs placebo: total cholesterol -21.23 mg/dL (95% CI -34.22 to -8.25, p=.001, I2=72%); LDL-C -25.12 mg/dL (95% CI -40.24 to -10.00, p=.001, I2=83%); HDL-C +4.74 mg/dL (95% CI 0.40 to 9.07, p=.03, I2=91%); triglycerides -22.28 mg/dL (95% CI -53.33 to 8.76, p=.16, NOT statistically significant, I2=93%). Adverse events, reported in 3 of 4 studies, all mild: dyspepsia (7 events, treatment arm), mild diarrhoea (3), fever (1) and headache (1) (placebo arm). The abstract labels these pooled values 'SMD' (standardised mean difference) but reports them in mg/dL, which is actually consistent with an unstandardised mean difference - likely a labelling error in the paper itself, noted here rather than silently corrected. Authors' own verbatim conclusion: results are 'based on low certainty of evidence,' and 'trials with a larger sample size that directly compare E. officinalis extract to statins, preferably local data, are needed.' This is one of three overlapping amla-and-lipids reviews this card draws on (alongside Brown 2023 and Setayesh 2023) - given how few amla RCTs exist worldwide, these reviews likely draw on substantially the same small pool of underlying trials sliced by different inclusion criteria, so this card treats them as one evidence base presented three ways, not as three independent confirmations, and states this explicitly.

sources.title: The impact of Emblica Officinalis (Amla) on lipid profile, glucose, and C-reactive protein: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sources.author: Setayesh L, Haghighat N, Rasaei N, Rezaei M, Casazza K, Nadery M, Yamrali I, Zamani M, Asbaghi O
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - independently fetched and read directly from PubMed (abstract only; full text not accessible through this project's tools, a genuine verification limit noted honestly). Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Research & Reviews 2023;17(3):102729, PMID 36934568, DOI 10.1016/j.dsx.2023.102729, literature search to December 2022 across ISI Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus and Embase. 5 RCTs pooled; total participant count is not given in the abstract itself; populations generally aged 40-58, mean BMI ~25.5, intervention length 3-12 weeks. This is the only one of the three amla-and-cardiometabolic reviews this card found that assessed fasting blood glucose as an outcome at all - the more rigorous, RoB2-assessed Brown 2023 review above did not test glucose. Reported results (direction and p-value only; the abstract gives no pooled effect size, confidence interval or heterogeneity/I-squared figure for any outcome, a real reporting gap distinguishing this review from the more fully reported Brown and Acampado reviews above): CRP significantly reduced (p=.002); fasting blood glucose significantly reduced (p<.001); LDL cholesterol significantly reduced (p<.001); total cholesterol significantly reduced (p<.001); triglycerides significantly reduced (p<.001); HDL cholesterol significantly increased (p<.001). Verbatim conclusion: 'Amla supplementation shows promise for improving metabolic parameters in adults,' with the authors adding that further investigation is warranted. Graded Moderate and treated cautiously in this card specifically because of this missing effect-size/heterogeneity detail - its blood-glucose finding is the main basis for this card's blood-sugar discussion, but it cannot be checked the way Brown's or Acampado's lipid figures can.

sources.title: A Randomized, Triple-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Add-On Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy of Emblica officinalis in Uncontrolled Hypertension
sources.author: Ghaffari S, Navabzadeh M, Ziaee M, Ghobadi A, Ghods R, Hashem-Dabaghian F
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - independently fetched and read in full. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine 2020;2020:8592869. Triple-blind, placebo-controlled, add-on RCT in Tabriz, Iran: 287 assessed, 92 enrolled, 81 completed 8 weeks (41 Emblica officinalis, 40 placebo), 500 mg capsules three times daily after meals (or matching placebo) added on top of each patient's existing antihypertensive medicine, in adults with uncontrolled hypertension. Results: systolic blood pressure fell 15.6+/-8.23% with EO vs 6.3+/-7.49% with placebo (p<.001; week-8 values 126.7 vs 136.7 mmHg, p=.009); diastolic blood pressure fell 12.3+/-7.87% with EO vs 3.88+/-7.98% with placebo (p<.001; week-8 values 81.2 vs 87.6 mmHg, p<.001). A unit inconsistency in the paper itself is noted here: the abstract reports the changes as percentages while the Results text separately reports them in mmHg - both are given above rather than only the more impressive-sounding figure. Response rates (SBP<140 and/or DBP<90): 82.9% EO vs 62.5% placebo for SBP; 95.1% vs 72.5% for DBP. No confidence intervals were reported. Secondary outcomes - heart rate, fasting blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, ALT, AST, BUN and creatinine - showed no statistically significant between-group differences at baseline or week 8 (specific values not given in the accessible text), supporting this card's safety discussion. Authors reported no side effects and no significant complications. This is a single add-on trial, not a review, and stands in direct contrast with the pooled, null blood-pressure finding in Brown's 2023 systematic review above (brown-amla-cvd-risk-meta-analysis-2023) - this card shows both rather than picking a side, per BRIEF.md rule 6.

sources.title: Clinical evaluation of Emblica Officinalis Gaertn (Amla) in healthy human subjects: Health benefits and safety results from a randomized, double-blind, crossover placebo-controlled study
sources.author: Kapoor MP, Suzuki K, Derek T, Ozeki M, Okubo T
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - this card's main dedicated safety-parameters source, independently fetched and read in full. Contemporary Clinical Trials Communications 2019;17:100499 (collection March 2020), PMID 31890983, PMCID PMC6926135, DOI 10.1016/j.conctc.2019.100499. Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in healthy Japanese adults: 24 screened, 15 randomised (7 male, 8 female), 13 completed (6 male, 7 female, mean age 51.9+/-2.8). Intervention: 500 mg/day standardised amla fruit extract (SunAmla-PD1, 2 capsules after breakfast and dinner) vs dextrin placebo, two 4-week periods separated by a 3-week washout (~18 weeks total). Lipids: HDL rose significantly at 2 weeks (p=.03) and stayed elevated; LDL fell at 2 weeks but not significantly vs placebo (p=.09); triglycerides, total cholesterol and HbA1c showed no significant between-period differences. Oxidative stress/vascular markers: 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) fell significantly vs placebo at 4 weeks (p=.002) and post-intake (p=.003); von Willebrand factor fell significantly during amla intake (p<.05); blood fluidity (the trial's primary endpoint, measured in vitro via microchannels) improved significantly vs placebo at 2 weeks (p=.012), 4 weeks (p=.024) and post-intake (p=.036); blood pressure and pulse were unchanged. SAFETY (used directly in this card's cautions): liver - ALT lower at 2 weeks (p=.02), total bilirubin lower (p=.04), AST unchanged, all liver values stayed within normal range; kidney - no significant change in creatinine or urea nitrogen, urinalysis unchanged; haematology - no significant between-group difference in WBC, RBC, haematocrit or platelet count; prothrombin time (PT) was significantly lower with amla at 4 weeks (p=.01) - a real, if small, clotting-relevant finding this card uses alongside the platelet-aggregation finding in drugs-com-emblica-monograph to support an open-question bleeding/antiplatelet caution; APTT unchanged. Authors state plainly: 'no adverse events, changes [in] safety parameters or tolerance issues were observed after consumption of amla'; minor complaints (diarrhoea, loose stools, constipation, a cold) occurred during the placebo period instead; compliance was 100%. GENUINE OVERCLAIMING FLAG: the paper's own Discussion states amla lowered LDL, triglycerides and total cholesterol, but its own Results section reports no significant change in triglycerides or total cholesterol, and the LDL change was not significant either (p=.09) - this card relies on the Results figures, not the more confident Discussion wording. Limitations acknowledged by the authors: very small sample (13 completers); the blood-fluidity assay is an in-vitro microchannel measure that may not reflect real vascular conditions. Several authors are affiliated with Taiyo Kagaku, the product's manufacturer, though the paper declares no conflicts of interest - noted here for transparency, not to discount the safety data, which is this card's most direct human liver/kidney/haematology evidence for amla.

sources.title: The effect of an oral product containing Amla fruit (Phyllanthus emblica L.) on female androgenetic alopecia: A randomized controlled trial
sources.author: Akhbari M, Firooz A, Rahimi R, Shirzad M, Esmaealzadeh N, Shirbeigi L
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - this card's only dedicated oral-amla-and-hair-loss trial, citation independently confirmed directly on PubMed (title, full author list, journal, volume and PMID all verified there), but the PubMed abstract page itself could not be rendered as readable text through this project's tools (it returned only a cookie-notice placeholder) - a genuine verification limit. Journal of Ethnopharmacology 2024;318(Pt A):116958 (published online 2023), DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2023.116958, PMID 37487962. Per a secondary summary of the trial (naturalhealthresearch.org, cross-checked against the Iranian clinical trial registry record for the same study, IRCT entry for a 60-participant, two-arm, 10cc-three-times-daily, 12-week design, which matches): triple-blind RCT, 60 women with female androgenetic alopecia (FAGA), randomised 30:30 to oral amla syrup or placebo, 10 cc three times daily after meals for 12 weeks; 27 of 30 completed in the amla group, 25 of 30 in placebo. The placebo was a colour- and taste-matched syrup made from honey dissolved in boiled water with rose water added - a detail about the COMPARATOR, not the active amla product, so it does not by itself establish whether the active amla syrup itself contains honey; this card could not independently verify the active product's own ingredient list, so it is not described here as vegan or non-vegan, only as unverified. Reported outcome (figures as given by the secondary summary, not independently re-derived from the primary paper - flagged honestly per BRIEF.md rule 7/11): significant improvement in anagen percentage (F=24.7, p<.001), telogen percentage (F=12.6, p<.001) and anagen:telogen ratio (F=10.4, p<.002) in the amla group vs placebo. Only adverse event: one case of mild constipation. Authors' conclusion (as reported by the secondary summary): amla syrup may help treat androgenic hair loss in women and increase the anagen phase, but further studies are needed before it can be considered an established treatment. Graded Moderate rather than Strong given this is a single trial (not a review) and its detailed statistics are secondhand; this card treats it as a genuine but thin, unreplicated signal for ORAL amla specifically, not as evidence for amla hair OIL - see majeed-amla-hair-serum-trial-2020 below for the distinct, weaker topical evidence picture.

sources.title: Clinical Safety and Efficacy of a Novel Topical Hair Growth Serum Formulation [containing amla (Emblica officinalis) extract]
sources.author: Majeed M, Majeed S, Nagabhushanam K, Mundkur L, Neupane P, Shah K
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - independently fetched and read in full; this card's only located trial testing a TOPICAL product containing amla, used specifically to show how much weaker this evidence is than the oral syrup trial above, and that it cannot show what amla itself contributes. Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology 2020;13:691-700, DOI 10.2147/CCID.S271013. Open-label, single-arm, non-comparative, monocentric study (MS Clinical Research, Bangalore, India; CTRI/2019/08/020742). 46 screened, 42 completed (21 men, 21 women, aged 25-45) with MSCR grade 3-6 hair loss. Intervention: a leave-in hair serum applied nightly for 90 days (2 mL men, 3.5 mL women) whose active ingredients include amla (Emblica officinalis) extract ALONGSIDE freeze-dried coconut water, a selenium-containing peptide (PeptiSeLect), peanut shell extract, sandalwood odorant and tetrahydropiperine - a multi-ingredient product, so no result can be attributed to amla specifically. No placebo or comparator arm. Results (all subjects combined, sexes not reported separately): hair density (TrichoScan) +7.97%; hair growth rate +17.36%; terminal hair density +5.93%, vellus density +13.51%; anagen:telogen ratio showed no significant change; hair comb test showed 57.53% reduction in hair fall with bulb, 81.60% without; hair pull test fell from 2.27 to 1.33 hairs per pull (41.4%); dermatologist-rated hair thinning improved 17.55%; photo-numeric hair-fall scale showed no significant change; self-assessment improved for hair fall, texture, volume and itching. Stated p-values (p<.0001 for density, growth rate and hair-fall measures) come from an open-label, uncontrolled design, so cannot separate a genuine treatment effect from a placebo/regression-to-mean effect. No adverse events reported. Funded by Sami Labs and Sabinsa Corporation, whose affiliated authors hold related patents on the formulation - a direct commercial interest, disclosed in the paper. The paper's own conclusion claims effectiveness in 'more than 98%' of subjects, a figure this card's reading of the Results section could not clearly verify - noted here as a possible overclaim rather than repeated as fact. Graded Limited: no control group, single small open-label sample, multi-ingredient product, manufacturer-funded. This card uses it only to state plainly that no isolated-amla topical hair-oil trial could be found - traditional amla hair-oil use remains a traditional/folk practice in this card's reading of the evidence, not a clinically tested one.

sources.title: Chyawanprash: A Traditional Indian Bioactive Health Supplement
sources.author: Sharma R, Martins N, Kuca K, Chaudhary A, Kabra A, Rao MM, Prajapati PK
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - independently fetched and read (first 100,000 of 167,807 characters; the ingredient/composition and clinical-evidence-summary sections used here appeared well within that range). Biomolecules 2019;9(5):161, DOI 10.3390/biom9050161, PMCID PMC6571565. THE KEY VEGAN-CHECK FINDING THIS CARD RELIES ON: Chyawanprash (an 'Awaleha', herbal jam/electuary) is built on an amla-pulp base combined with roughly 50 herbs and extracts (organised into classical groups: Dashmula/ten roots, Chaturjata/four aromatics, Ashtavarga/eight herbs often substituted today, plus a general class). Ghee AND honey are both confirmed as FORMAL, STANDARD ingredients of the classical preparation method, not merely a traditional way of taking the product (contrast with Triphala below): the standard process fries the amla paste with 500 g each of cow ghee and sesame oil, and 250 g of honey is stirred in after the mixture cools - honey and ghee are also described by the review as a traditional 'anupana' (absorption-aiding transporter) within the recipe itself. This is not vegan as classically made. Clinical evidence summarised by the review is for CHYAWANPRASH AS A WHOLE MULTI-HERB PRODUCT, not for amla alone, so none of it is used in this card as amla-specific evidence (per BRIEF.md rule 9 - a combination product's evidence does not transfer to one ingredient): an RCT in 90 tuberculosis patients found it eased symptoms and improved haemoglobin as an adjunct to antitubercular drugs; an observational study in 99 TB patients reported symptom relief and improved isoniazid/pyrazinamide bioavailability; a 6-month open-label RCT in children aged 5-12 reported improved immunity, energy and quality of life; a placebo-controlled trial of 60 participants reported reduced depression scores; an RCT of 128 college students reported improved alertness/attention/concentration; an RCT of 75 head-and-neck cancer patients reported reduced radiotherapy mucosal reactions; a randomised study of 121 people with type 2 diabetes found NO significant change in HbA1c or blood sugar, which the review's own authors read as a safety reassurance rather than an efficacy finding. The authors' own stated conclusion: mechanistic studies and sufficient clinical data are still lacking, and larger, longer, multicentre RCTs and product standardisation are needed - an appropriately hedged position this card does not override by treating any of the above as settled.

sources.title: Triphala churna/kwatha - composition and traditional anupana (vehicle) practice
sources.author: Cross-checked commercial Triphala product listings (Govinda, Vitacost and others) and the NCBS GRAYU Ayurvedic formulary database (Triphala Kwatha entry)
sources.note: 31 Oct 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 11th herb, Amla) - used only for a plain ingredient/preparation-practice fact (not a health claim), the same way this project's planetayurveda-yograj-guggulu source was used for Guggul. This card's own independently-fetched and read Book source (book-ayurvedic-science-food-nutrition, p.91) already confirms Triphala's actual composition is three fruit powders only - Emblica officinalis (amla), Terminalia chebula (haritaki) and Terminalia bellirica (bibhitaki) - with no ghee, honey or other animal ingredient in the formula itself; several independent commercial Triphala product listings cross-checked via web search consistently confirm the same three-fruit-only composition for plain Triphala churna/capsules, and several independent product pages describe some owners taking the powder mixed with warm water, milk OR honey - describing honey as one optional vehicle for taking the powder, not an ingredient of the product. Separately, the NCBS (National Centre for Biological Sciences) GRAYU classical-formulary database's Triphala Kwatha (decoction, a different preparation from the plain churna/powder) entry could not be directly re-fetched in this session (the live page returned a connection error), so this specific detail is relayed from a search-engine excerpt of that page, not independently re-verified in full text - flagged honestly: it reportedly lists honey as the anupana (accompanying vehicle) for Vata- and Kapha-type conditions and ghee (with buttermilk or, in one listed case, cow's urine) for Pitta-type conditions, for that specific kwatha formulation. Taken together, this card treats a plain Triphala powder or capsule product as vegan by composition, while flagging that classical instructions for HOW to take it (not what is in it) sometimes suggest honey or ghee as the accompanying vehicle - a different, milder kind of vegan check than Chyawanprash's, where ghee and honey are actual formula ingredients (see sharma-chyawanprash-review-2019). Graded Limited/Article or blog given the mix of commercial sources and one unverifiable formulary excerpt.

sources.title: Hibiscus sabdariffa (Flora & Fauna Web)
sources.author: National Parks Board, Singapore
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - species-identity source, independently fetched and verified. Government horticultural database entry (Singapore's National Parks Board) confirming the accepted scientific name Hibiscus sabdariffa L., family Malvaceae, with synonyms Hibiscus gossypiifolius, Abelmoschus cruentus, Hibiscus digitatus, Sabdariffa rubra and Hibiscus sanguineus. Common names given: Roselle, Jamaica Sorrel, Red Sorrel, Sorrel, Indian Sorrel, Asam Susar, plus Chinese names. Confirms this is the same plant that is also called 'sorrel' in parts of the world - used in this card to establish, from a government source, that 'sorrel' is a genuine, recognised common name for Hibiscus sabdariffa itself (not evidence on its own of the separate, unrelated Rumex acetosa plant also called sorrel - see diffordsguide-hibiscus-roselle-names for that specific confusion warning). Describes the plant (woody shrub, 1-2m, red-purple stems, pinkish flowers with red centre, fleshy red calyx), its food uses (young shoots eaten raw/cooked; calyces steeped as a drink, used as food colouring and in jams), and states plainly that 'research supports the traditional use of roselle for ulcers' while animal/human studies reported antioxidant and cholesterol-lowering effects and animal-only studies reported pain-relieving, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic and antimicrobial effects - this card treats the anti-diabetic line as animal-only per the page's own wording, not human evidence. The page explicitly states it is not medical advice and recommends consulting a physician before medicinal use.

sources.title: Hibiscus sabdariffa
sources.author: WebMD editorial staff (ingredient monograph)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - consumer supplement-monograph source, independently fetched and verified. Confirms scientific name Hibiscus sabdariffa (family Malvaceae), common names Roselle/H. sabdariffa/HS, and separately lists 'Jamaica sorrel' and 'red sorrel' as names used for allergy-labelling purposes - independent confirmation that 'sorrel' genuinely attaches to this plant's own name, not just a folk alias. Classified as an over-the-counter dietary supplement the FDA has not reviewed for safety or effectiveness; chemical content (organic acids, anthocyanins, polyphenols, polysaccharides, flavonoids) varies by product and the FDA does not verify label contents. Proposed mechanism: may help blood vessels relax via increased nitric oxide production, linked mainly to polyphenols - a proposed mechanism, not a confirmed human finding. High blood pressure is named as the most common use but the page gives no formal evidence rating and cites a blood-pressure/cardiometabolic meta-analysis without reporting its actual findings - a real information gap this card does not fill in on the page's behalf. Side effects: common/mild (gas, stomach discomfort, constipation); serious - possible liver damage (hepatotoxicity) with risk described as higher with regular high doses or combined with other liver-affecting medicines, and a named symptom list (nausea, abdominal pain, fever, fatigue, itching, poor appetite, pale stools, dark urine, jaundice); serious allergic reaction also named. Pregnancy: human effects unknown, but animal data suggest possible harm including miscarriage - advises telling a provider if pregnant or planning pregnancy. Breastfeeding: unknown whether it passes into breast milk. Advises telling a provider before use if taking acetaminophen, blood-pressure medicines/supplements, or diabetes medicines/supplements, and says interactions are 'not fully understood' with research 'incomplete.' Notably, this particular page does NOT name chloroquine or antimalarial drugs anywhere - a genuine gap in this specific source, which is why this card also checked webmd-hibiscus-uses-risks and showande-hibiscus-cyp450-chloroquine-interaction-review-2013 independently for that specific interaction rather than relying on this page alone.

sources.title: Hibiscus: Uses and Risks
sources.author: WebMD editorial staff
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - second WebMD consumer source, independently fetched and verified, used specifically because it covers ground the ingredient-monograph page (webmd-hibiscus-sabdariffa-monograph) does not. States plainly: 'Hibiscus tea may interfere with some anti-malaria drugs' - a real, independently found confirmation of an antimalarial-drug interaction caution, though this particular page does not name chloroquine specifically (see showande-hibiscus-cyp450-chloroquine-interaction-review-2013 for the chloroquine-specific primary literature). Also separately notes it 'can also interact with drugs for diabetes and high blood pressure.' Describes 'promising research' on blood pressure but says more study is needed - deliberately non-committal wording this card does not upgrade. Side effects named: possible dermatitis, headache, nausea, and ringing in the ears (tinnitus); may also cause blood pressure to drop (relevant to anyone already on blood-pressure medicine or with naturally low blood pressure). Advises against use if pregnant or nursing ('may be unsafe for you and your baby'), and against use if allergic/sensitive to hibiscus or other Malvaceae-family plants. Dosing forms named: tea and supplements/extract capsules; states no optimal dose has been established for any condition and that supplement quality and active-ingredient content vary widely between manufacturers - the same product-variability caution this project has flagged for other herb supplements.

sources.title: Hibiscus Flower (Red) Petals
sources.author: Difford's Guide editorial staff
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - a drinks-reference source (not a health or scientific source, graded Limited accordingly), independently fetched and verified, used only for its specific, quotable naming claim. Lists regional names: bissap (West Africa), karkade (Egypt), flor de Jamaica (Mexico), gudhal (India), gongura (Brazil), and roselle as the general common name. States that in Jamaica and Trinidad hibiscus is 'known as sorrel,' traditionally steeped with herbs and spices into a sweetened Christmas cordial sometimes mixed with rum (an alcoholic serving variant, not evidence either way about the plain plant's vegan status). Crucially, the page explicitly warns: 'This should not be confused with sorrel (Rumex acetosa), a perennial herb' - direct, independently-fetched confirmation that the plain English name 'sorrel,' used for Hibiscus sabdariffa in Caribbean usage, genuinely collides with the unrelated leaf vegetable Rumex acetosa (garden/common sorrel, family Polygonaceae, a wholly different plant family from Hibiscus's own Malvaceae per nparks-hibiscus-sabdariffa above). This card treats the ambiguity as real and worth flagging, the same honest approach this project has already taken for Tulsi, Shatavari and Brahmi naming mix-ups, rather than silently picking one plant.

sources.title: The effectiveness of Hibiscus sabdariffa in the treatment of hypertension: a systematic review
sources.author: Wahabi HA, Alansary LA, Al-Sabban AH, Glasziou P
sources.asOf: published Feb 2010 (Epub 3 Oct 2009); current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - Phytomedicine 2010;17(2):83-6, PMID 19801187, independently fetched and verified (PubMed abstract). Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, the Cochrane Hypertension Group register and Google through January 2009. Found only 4 RCTs, 390 patients total, meeting inclusion criteria for primary hypertension in adults: 2 compared Hibiscus sabdariffa with black tea, 1 with captopril, and 1 with lisinopril - no placebo-controlled trial met inclusion. Finding: hibiscus produced a greater blood-pressure reduction than tea but a smaller one than the two ACE-inhibitor comparators. Quality assessment: apart from one study, trials were short-term and of poor quality (Jadad scores below 3), not meeting international reporting standards. Authors' own conclusion, quoted directly: the four trials 'do not provide reliable evidence to support recommending Hibiscus sabdariffa' for primary hypertension in adults. This is the single most cautious of the blood-pressure reviews this card checked, and is kept alongside the more positive later reviews (hopkins-hibiscus-hypertension-lipids-review-2013, ellis-hibiscus-bp-cardiometabolic-meta-analysis-2022) rather than treated as superseded, since it independently confirms that even the two head-to-head drug-comparison trials did not find hibiscus at least as good as the ACE inhibitor it was tested against.

sources.title: Hibiscus sabdariffa L. in the treatment of hypertension and hyperlipidemia: a comprehensive review of animal and human studies
sources.author: Hopkins AL, Lamm MG, Funk JL, Ritenbaugh C
sources.asOf: published March 2013; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - Fitoterapia 2013;85:84-94, doi:10.1016/j.fitote.2013.01.003, PMID 23333908, independently fetched and verified (full text). Covers 10 RCTs in total (5 on blood pressure, 5 on cholesterol/lipids), roughly 650 participants by this card's own rough tally of the paper's own enrollment tables (the authors give no single combined total). Authors describe many of the included RCTs as 'of low quality,' with inconsistent reporting of the extract used, and note that preparations, doses and plant parts varied so widely across trials that findings were hard to compare - this card treats that heterogeneity warning as a genuine limitation, not resolved by the paper's own 'promising' framing. Calls hibiscus extracts 'promising' for hypertension and hyperlipidaemia while explicitly calling for 'more high quality animal and human studies informed by actual therapeutic practices,' and notes only one placebo-controlled trial (McKay et al.) was rated high quality. Gives a head-to-head drug-comparison table: Herrera-Arellano 2004 (vs captopril) found SBP fell 16.4 mmHg with captopril vs 14.2 mmHg with hibiscus, DBP fell 13.1 vs 11.2 mmHg - differences not significant, i.e. hibiscus performed about as well as captopril in that one trial; Herrera-Arellano 2007 (vs lisinopril, a separate, larger trial) found SBP fell 23.3 mmHg with lisinopril vs only 17.1 mmHg with hibiscus, DBP 15.4 vs 12.0 mmHg - hibiscus was less effective than lisinopril in that trial. The two head-to-head trials therefore point in somewhat different directions depending on which ACE inhibitor hibiscus was tested against - this card shows both rather than picking one. Diuretic effect: states plainly 'there is evidence that HS acts as a diuretic' - a 500 mg/kg/day dose produced diuresis in animal hypertensive models over 3 weeks with mostly unchanged electrolytes, and two human studies reported statistically significant rises in sodium or chloride excretion (natriuretic/chloruretic effect). The authors compare hibiscus's effect profile to potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, and separately warn against combining hibiscus with hydrochlorothiazide on the strength of animal data suggesting a possible interaction - the primary basis for this card's kidney-health crossCautionLink.

sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of Hibiscus sabdariffa on blood pressure and cardiometabolic markers
sources.author: Ellis LR, Zulfiqar S, Holmes M, Marshall L, Dye L, Boesch C
sources.asOf: published 5 May 2022, Nutrition Reviews 80(6):1723-1737; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - the largest and most recent pooled review this card found, independently fetched and verified (full text, two passes covering the whole 125,758-character article). Pooled 17 chronic trials (18 arms; one trial, Izadi et al., excluded from the blood-pressure analysis because its reported BP values looked implausible).
