For blood-pressure outcomes: 819 participants total (415 hibiscus, 404 control). Heterogeneity was very high for almost every BP comparison (I-squared 81-96%). Pooled results (random effects, mmHg): vs placebo, SBP fell significantly by 10.05 mmHg (95% CI -17.58 to -2.51, I2=81%, P=0.009) but DBP did not fall significantly (-5.60 mmHg, P=0.14, I2=94%); vs all non-drug comparators pooled, SBP fell significantly by 7.10 mmHg (P=0.02) but DBP again did not reach significance (P=0.09); vs pharmaceutical drugs specifically (4 trials), neither SBP nor DBP differences were significant. This card flags a real source-overclaiming pattern here, the same kind already documented for this project's Tulsi, Nettle, Shatavari, Giloy, Guggul and Amla reviews: the Discussion describes hibiscus as a 'viable alternative' to diuretics or ACE inhibitors, which the nonsignificant, wide-interval, high-heterogeneity drug-comparison data do not establish; it also says trial sequential analysis 'supports' the blood-pressure effect even though the SBP result did not actually cross the TSA monitoring boundary; and it floats a dose-response claim (doses above 1 g/day affecting BP more) that the paper's own subgroup data do not support, since the <=1 g subgroup was also nonsignificant and the authors elsewhere say no dose-response could be established. The pooled DBP-vs-placebo finding is also fragile: removing a single included trial (Nwachukwu et al.) would have made DBP significant (P<0.001) and cut heterogeneity from I2=96% to I2=3% - meaning one study is doing outsized work in that particular result. No metabolic-syndrome subgroup analysis was reported; only two small trials (about 90 participants combined) enrolled metabolic-syndrome patients, and a lipid finding (LDL) became nonsignificant once one of those two trials was removed in sensitivity analysis. Funding/conflict-of-interest check (per this project's standard practice of checking for undisclosed supplier relationships): this review's own funding came from a university scholarship (Emma and Lesley Reid Scholarship, University of Leeds) and a BBSRC-backed Diet and Health Seeding Award, with authors stating funders had no role in the work's conception, design or approval, and declaring no conflicts of interest - no undisclosed manufacturer/supplier relationship found for this review itself.

sources.title: Effectiveness and tolerability of a standardized extract from Hibiscus sabdariffa in patients with mild to moderate hypertension: a controlled and randomized clinical trial
sources.author: Herrera-Arellano A, Flores-Romero S, Chavez-Soto MA, Tortoriello J
sources.asOf: published 2004, Phytomedicine; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - independently fetched and verified (PubMed abstract), PMID 15330492. The direct head-to-head trial answering this card's research question of whether hibiscus has been compared against a real antihypertensive drug. 90 adults (aged 30-80) with hypertension, off antihypertensive treatment for at least a month, randomised; 75 completed (39 hibiscus, 36 captopril). Hibiscus: an infusion from 10 g dried calyx in 0.5 L water (9.6 mg anthocyanins), once daily before breakfast. Captopril: 25 mg twice daily. Duration: 4 weeks. Results: hibiscus lowered systolic blood pressure from 139.05 to 123.73 mmHg (ANOVA P<0.03) and diastolic from 90.81 to 79.52 mmHg (ANOVA P<0.06, i.e. just above the conventional 0.05 threshold despite being described as significant in the abstract - this card notes that discrepancy rather than repeating the abstract's confidence uncritically). The two groups did not differ significantly from each other at study end (P>0.25). 'Therapeutic effectiveness' (defined as a diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg) was 0.7895 for hibiscus and 0.8438 for captopril (chi-square P>0.560) - not significantly different. Tolerability was 100% in both groups, with no specific side effects listed in the abstract. A natriuretic (sodium-excreting) effect was observed with hibiscus - independent confirmation of a genuine diuretic-type action alongside hopkins-hibiscus-hypertension-lipids-review-2013's broader diuretic evidence summary. Authors' conclusion: hibiscus extract and captopril did not differ significantly in hypotensive effect, antihypertensive effectiveness, or tolerability over this 4-week trial.

sources.title: Effects of aqueous extract of Hibiscus sabdariffa on renal function parameters of Nigerians with mild to moderate essential hypertension: a comparative study with lisinopril
sources.author: Nwachukwu DC, Aneke EI, Nwachukwu NZ, Obika LFO, Nwagha UI
sources.asOf: published 24 May 2016, J Physiol Sci 67(1):227-234; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - independently fetched and verified (full text). 78 newly diagnosed, untreated adults with mild-to-moderate hypertension randomised into three groups of 26 (hibiscus aqueous decoction 150 mg/kg, lisinopril 10 mg, or colour-matched placebo), once daily for 4 weeks; 75 completed (2 lisinopril users switched medication after developing cough; 1 hibiscus participant withdrew for non-medical reasons). Blood pressure at 4 weeks (mean +/- SEM change): hibiscus systolic -17.08+/-2.01 mmHg, diastolic -12.12+/-1.04 mmHg; lisinopril systolic -12.60+/-1.15 mmHg, diastolic -9.20+/-1.10 mmHg; placebo systolic -1.10+/-0.05 mmHg, diastolic -0.40+/-0.02 mmHg - hibiscus's systolic reduction was significantly GREATER than lisinopril's at weeks 2-4, a genuinely strong result for a direct drug comparison, though from a single small trial by one research group. Diuretic/renal outcomes (this card's primary reason for citing this trial): hibiscus significantly increased urine volume compared with placebo at every measurement point (P<0.001), more than lisinopril did at every weekly point; lisinopril only beat placebo on urine volume in weeks 3-4. Hibiscus significantly raised creatinine clearance vs placebo at weeks 3 (P<0.01) and 4 (P<0.001); lisinopril did not differ significantly from placebo on this measure. No hibiscus-related adverse effects were reported. Conflicts of interest and funding (checked per this project's standard practice): the study states it was self-sponsored with no external funding and the authors declare no conflicts of interest; the acknowledgments thank the hospital for facility use and two named individuals for help preparing the hibiscus infusion, naming no manufacturer or sponsor - the Methods section does name commercial brands for materials used (Aquafina bottled water, GlaxoSmithKline blackcurrant drink as the placebo base, Zestril brand lisinopril from Reals Pharmaceuticals) but this is a transparent materials disclosure, not a hidden sponsorship relationship, so this card found no undisclosed-conflict pattern in this trial. Note: this is the same approximately-78-participant Nigerian cohort (hibiscus vs lisinopril vs placebo, mild-to-moderate hypertension, 4 weeks) reported in a companion paper by an overlapping author group, nwachukwu-hibiscus-lisinopril-raas-rct-2015 - this card treats the two papers as one underlying trial reported across two publications with different outcome measures, not as two independent confirmations of the same blood-pressure finding.

sources.title: Effects of aqueous extract of Hibiscus sabdariffa on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system of Nigerians with mild to moderate essential hypertension: a comparative study with lisinopril
sources.author: Nwachukwu DC, Aneke EI, Obika LFO, Nwachukwu NZ
sources.asOf: published Sep-Oct 2015, Indian J Pharmacol 47(5):540-545; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - independently fetched and verified (PubMed abstract), PMID 26600645. Companion paper to nwachukwu-hibiscus-lisinopril-renal-rct-2016, almost certainly the same approximately-78-participant Nigerian cohort (hibiscus vs lisinopril vs placebo, mild-to-moderate hypertension, 4 weeks) reported with a different set of outcomes (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system markers rather than renal/diuretic ones) - this card treats the two as one trial across two publications, not independent replication. Results vs placebo after 4 weeks: plasma aldosterone fell 32.06% with hibiscus and 30.01% with lisinopril (both P<0.001, not significantly different from each other); serum ACE fell 6.63% with hibiscus and 5.67% with lisinopril (not significant); plasma renin activity rose 2.77% with hibiscus and 5.36% with lisinopril (not significant). Authors conclude hibiscus lowered serum ACE and aldosterone about as effectively as lisinopril in this trial, suggesting anthocyanins as a possible mechanism - used in this card only as supporting mechanism context for the blood-pressure and diuretic findings above, not as a separate confirmation of benefit.

sources.title: In Vitro Inhibitory Activities of the Extract of Hibiscus Sabdariffa L. (Family Malvaceae) on Selected Cytochrome P450 Isoforms
sources.author: Showande SJ, Fakeye TO, Tolonen A, Hokkanen J
sources.asOf: published 12 Apr 2013, Afr J Tradit Complement Altern Med 10(3):533-540; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 12th herb, Hibiscus) - independently fetched and verified (full text), PMID 24146485, PMCID PMC3777597. This is the primary-literature check behind this card's chloroquine-interaction caution, run specifically because the project's process requires independently verifying any 'may interact with chloroquine' claim before including it, rather than repeating a secondary mention. The paper itself reports new in vitro data (human liver microsome CYP450 inhibition by an ethanolic Hibiscus sabdariffa extract, 9 isoforms tested, IC50 values 306-1660 microg/mL, inhibition order CYP1A2>2C8>2D6>2B6>2E1>2C19>3A4>>2C9>>2A6) and separately reviews three EARLIER human pharmacokinetic studies in its introduction/discussion: (1) Mahmoud et al. 1994, cited as finding 'a significant reduction in chloroquine bioavailability' when chloroquine was co-administered with Sudanese hibiscus-containing beverages (including 'Karkadi,' a hibiscus drink) - this card could only access this 1994 study's existence and finding via Showande's own citation and summary, not the 1994 primary paper directly, so it is graded as a real but older and not independently re-verified finding; (2) Kolawole & Maduenyi 2004, finding hibiscus ('zobo') water extract reduced acetaminophen's terminal half-life without significantly changing its AUC or clearance - the authors note CYP inhibition cannot fully explain this, since AUC was unchanged; (3) Fakeye et al. 2007, finding a reduction in diclofenac's metabolic clearance with hibiscus water extract co-administration. On clinical significance, the authors' own abstract states the extract's CYP inhibition 'may not cause clinically significant herb-drug interactions' and classifies it as a weak inhibitor (IC50 values above 100 microg/mL) - but the Discussion is less reassuring, converting IC50 values to a litre-per-300mL-dose figure and noting several isoforms' converted values are close to average human blood volume, 'suggest[ing] that the extract is likely to cause in vivo inhibition,' with specific concern named for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, theophylline, digoxin). The authors conclude in vivo human studies are needed before firm conclusions about co-administration can be drawn - this card treats the chloroquine finding as a real, sourced caution from older human pharmacokinetic data (not an urban-legend-style claim), while being honest that the underlying mechanism remains unconfirmed and the 1994 primary study was not independently re-read.

sources.title: Gotu Kola
sources.author: RxList
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified. This is RxList's own gotu kola page (distinct from its Bacopa/Brahmi page already cited in this project's Brahmi card as rxlist-bacopa), fetched specifically to check whether the name-conflation finding documented on that card holds from gotu kola's own side. It does: this page's own 'other names' list for Centella asiatica reads 'Brahmi, Indian Pennywort, Hydrocotyle asiatica, and Mandukaparni' - RxList independently applies the name 'Brahmi' to THIS plant on THIS plant's own page, not only (as already found) folding gotu kola's 'Indian pennywort' name into the Bacopa page. Scientific/other names otherwise: Centella asiatica, Hydrocotyle asiatica. Uses and evidence ratings: venous insufficiency/varicose veins is the only use with a clear positive rating - 'Taking gotu kola or a specific extract of gotu kola (Centellase) by mouth for 4-8 weeks seems to improve blood circulation and reduce swelling' in people with venous insufficiency, rated effective at a typical oral dose of 60-180 mg/day of extract; topical use for wound healing has 'early evidence' only; combined gotu kola/ginkgo/DHA did NOT improve mental function in healthy elderly adults over 4 months; plaque stabilisation, flight-related clots and diabetic microangiopathy are all 'Insufficient Evidence to Rate.' Safety: 'POSSIBLY SAFE for most people when applied to the skin for up to 12 months' or taken by mouth for up to 8 weeks; oral use 'can cause nausea and stomach pain,' and 'Rarely, gotu kola may also cause liver problems if taken by mouth'; topical use 'may cause itchiness and redness.' Pregnancy: 'POSSIBLY SAFE in pregnant women when applied to the skin. But don't take it by mouth'; breastfeeding: 'Avoid using it if you are nursing.' People with an existing liver disease such as hepatitis are told to avoid it. Drug interactions (both rated Moderate): hepatotoxic drugs (acetaminophen, methotrexate, statins named as examples) - gotu kola 'might harm the liver,' raising combined risk; CNS depressants/sedatives (zolpidem, lorazepam named as examples) - 'large amounts of gotu kola might cause sleepiness and drowsiness' that could add to a sedative's effect. Surgery: stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery because of this sedation risk. This card treats RxList's gotu kola page, read directly, as independent confirmation (alongside the NCBI Bookshelf LiverTox chapter below) that the 'Brahmi' name genuinely attaches to Centella asiatica from its own clinical-reference literature, not only from the Bacopa side already documented on this project's Brahmi card.

sources.title: Gotu Kola
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), About Herbs
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified. Scientific name Centella asiatica; other names include Indian pennywort, Hydrocotyle, Mandukaparni, Madecassol, TECA. States plainly gotu kola 'should not be confused with kolanut' and contains no caffeine and has not been shown to have stimulant properties - this page does not mention Bacopa monnieri or the 'Brahmi' name at all, so it neither confirms nor denies that specific overlap (RxList and the NCBI Bookshelf/LiverTox chapter, both cited separately, are this card's actual confirmation of that point). Describes gotu kola as popular in traditional medicine (Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese Medicine) but 'mainly studied in the lab,' with purported uses for circulation (venous insufficiency, varicose veins), wounds/burns/scleroderma/scars, and memory/cognition. Evidence summary, quoted closely: 'Only a few studies suggest that gotu kola may be helpful for wound healing or poor circulation' and larger confirmatory studies are needed; for cognition/anxiety, 'small studies suggest possible benefit' in generalised anxiety and in cognition/mood in older adults, but 'a meta-analysis found insufficient evidence' and overall there is 'insufficient evidence to support its use for any of these conditions' - MSKCC's own bottom line across all three of gotu kola's best-known uses (wound healing, circulation, cognition/anxiety) is that none is yet proven, a notably more cautious framing than RxList's single 'Possibly Effective' rating for venous insufficiency. One topical trial for radiation dermatitis in breast cancer patients did NOT prevent or delay the condition. Side effects: skin rash (contact dermatitis) and liver toxicity, both with case-report references. Drug interactions: in vitro, gotu kola inhibits CYP1A2, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4 and 2C19, which 'may affect the intracellular concentration of drugs metabolized by these enzymes,' though 'clinical relevance is undetermined.' Notes potency varies widely by growing location, and advises patients to tell their care team about all herbs/supplements used. Page last updated 23 Feb 2022.

sources.title: Centella asiatica (LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury)
sources.author: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified via a mirrored copy of the Bookshelf chapter's full HTML content after the live NCBI Bookshelf page itself returned a browser/reCAPTCHA verification screen on direct fetch (NBK603561), the same access pattern this project's Moringa card hit for livertox-moringa; graded Government or health body/Strong per this project's established convention for LiverTox, distinct from a StatPearls CME chapter. This chapter's own names list for the plant is the second, independent confirmation (alongside rxlist-gotu-kola above) of the Brahmi/Centella name overlap this card was specifically asked to re-verify from gotu kola's own sources: quoted directly, 'Gotu kola, Asian pennywort, spadeleaf, coinwort, tiger grass, Brahmi, Centella' - a US federal government health database lists 'Brahmi' as a Centella asiatica alias in its own right, on this plant's own page, not only as a mix-up found on the Bacopa side. The chapter does not mention Bacopa monnieri directly or discuss the mechanism of the two plants sharing a name. Traditional/purported uses listed: minor wounds, psoriasis, chronic venous insufficiency, hypertension, asthma and more; purportedly supports immune function, longevity and memory, but 'none of these have been proven in controlled human trials'; not approved in the US as therapy for any medical condition, though sold over the counter. Typical doses given: 60-120 mg/day of purified extract, or 600-1800 mg/day of dried-leaf capsules/powder. Hepatotoxicity section (this card's primary reason for citing this source): describes one detailed case in full - a previously healthy 61-year-old Argentinian woman took Centella tablets for 30 days as a weight-loss agent, developed jaundice with ALT/AST 26-30x the upper limit of normal and bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, viral hepatitis panel negative, SMA 1:160 and AMA 1:320 positive (ANA negative), liver biopsy showing acute hepatitis with granulomas; she recovered on ursodiol: labs normal at 2 months. About 7 months later she restarted Centella for 2 weeks and the injury recurred (ALT 413 U/L, bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL), repeat biopsy again showing granulomatous hepatitis; she recovered on prednisone plus ursodiol, with labs staying normal through 8 years of follow-up - a positive rechallenge, one of the stronger forms of evidence for attributing a liver injury to a specific product, though the chapter notes the product's exact name, concentration, daily tablet count and label were not given in the original report, so contamination or another ingredient cannot be fully excluded. The 61-year-old is one of three Argentinian women in that same 2005 case series (ages 61, 52, 49; jaundice onset 30, 20 and 60 days respectively) - this card corrected its own earlier draft, which had mistakenly double-counted these three women as a separate additional cluster rather than the same case series the 61-year-old belongs to, and had misdated the series as 2008 instead of 2005. LiverTox separately notes one further published case (1 Swiss case in 2011 after use for acne), onset typically 3-8 weeks, hepatocellular pattern, resolving within 1-2 months of stopping, some with immunoallergic/autoimmune features. LiverTox's own likelihood score for Centella asiatica is 'C' (a probable rare cause of clinically apparent liver injury) - a notch more confident than Moringa's own 'D' score (possible but rare) already cited on this project's Moringa card. General safety: few adverse events in small trials, mostly mild/transient (headache, dizziness, bloating, diarrhea, nausea) often similar to placebo; allergic reactions reported especially with topical use. The chapter recommends prompt withdrawal if liver injury is suspected and explicitly advises against rechallenge.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of the Efficacy of Centella asiatica for Improvement of the Signs and Symptoms of Chronic Venous Insufficiency
sources.author: Chong LY, Aziz Z
sources.asOf: published Mar-Apr 2013, Evid Based Complement Alternat Med 2013:627182; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified (full text), PMID 23533507. 8 RCTs (1981-2001) met inclusion criteria, sample sizes 17-99 (mean 65), mostly testing TTFCA (a titrated triterpenic fraction of Centella asiatica) against placebo. Pooled surrogate-measure results: transcutaneous oxygen pressure (tcPO2), 3 trials/158 subjects, weighted mean difference +6.63 (95% CI 4.30 to 8.96) favouring TTFCA; transcutaneous CO2 pressure (tcPCO2), same 3 trials, WMD -7.50 (95% CI -9.52 to -5.47); venoarteriolar response, 1 trial/60 subjects, MD 74 (95% CI 59.99 to 88.01); ankle swelling rate, 2 trials not pooled due to heterogeneity (MD -0.84 at 8 weeks, -0.77 at 4 weeks). Subjective signs/symptoms (heaviness, pain, oedema) were reported as improved in 3 trials but without quantifiable data to pool. Checked specifically for the kind of overclaiming this project has already documented in other herbs' reviews (Tulsi, Nettle, Shatavari, Giloy, Guggul, Amla, Hibiscus) - found here too: the review's own Conclusion states the 8 trials 'all reported beneficial effects,' a stronger framing than its own risk-of-bias findings support, since only 2 of the 8 trials had adequate sequence generation (6 unclear) and only 1 trial (Pointel et al.) had low risk of bias from blinding of both participants and outcome assessors; the Discussion itself warns that 'lack of blinding in RCTs has been shown to be associated with more exaggerated estimates of treatment effects' and that the surrogate measures used (tcPO2, tcPCO2, venoarteriolar response) 'lack well-established normal values,' so a statistically significant change may not be a clinically meaningful one - yet the abstract still describes these same surrogate results as 'significantly improved.' The review's own hedged headline conclusion ('may be beneficial... needs to be interpreted with caution') is reasonable, but sits awkwardly next to this more confident language elsewhere in the same paper. Adverse effects: reported in 2 trials only - 2 cases of minor stomach pain and 1 discontinuation for severe nausea in one trial; 4 withdrawals (3 nausea/gastric pain, 1 unspecified 'neurological absence') in another. Conflicts of interest and funding (checked per this project's standard practice): none of the 8 included trials reported their own funding source, so sponsorship bias in the underlying trials could not be assessed by this card or, apparently, by the reviewers themselves; the review itself states it was supported by a University of Malaya postgraduate research fund, with no stated conflict of interest. Several included trials share overlapping author names (e.g. Cesarone, Belcaro, Incandela, De Sanctis appear repeatedly across different trial citations) - this card notes this as a pattern worth knowing (a relatively small, overlapping group of researchers behind much of this evidence base) rather than as a proven conflict.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of the Effect of Centella asiatica on Wound Healing
sources.author: Arribas-Lopez E, Zand N, Ojo O, Snowden MJ, Kochhar T
sources.asOf: published 10 Mar 2022, Int J Environ Res Public Health 19(6):3266; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified (full text), DOI 10.3390/ijerph19063266. The authors frame this as the first systematic review on the topic (no prior systematic review or quantitative synthesis existed), and found only 4 clinical trials meeting inclusion criteria, too few and too heterogeneous for a meta-analysis - the paper states plainly 'it was not possible to conduct a meta-analysis,' which is why this card grades it Limited rather than Moderate despite being a systematic review. The 4 trials: Paocharoen (diabetic foot wounds, n=170) - oral asiaticoside linked to greater wound contraction/granulation than control, though the comparator/placebo was not clearly described; Saeidinia et al. (burns, n=75) - topical C. asiatica ointment vs silver sulfadiazine, faster healing/re-epithelialisation and lower pain (VAS) scores; Chiaretti et al. (anal fissure, n=98) - lower bleeding time and pain scores with C. asiatica, but for healing time itself 'this difference did not reach significance (p=0.07)'; Damkerngsuntorn et al. (post-laser/acne, split-face, n=30) - reduced erythema and improved wound appearance. Checked specifically for overclaiming, the same check this project has run on every herb's reviews to date, and found here: the abstract's hedged conclusion ('C. asiatica might enhance wound healing resulting from improved angiogenesis') and the Section 6 conclusion both attribute the healing effect to a specific mechanism (improved angiogenesis via collagen I, FGF and VEGF production) that NONE of the 4 included clinical trials actually measured - this mechanism comes only from the paper's own background discussion of separate animal/in-vitro studies, not from the clinical evidence just reviewed. The Section 6 conclusion goes further still, adding 'this also suggests a promising effect in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis' - a claim resting on an animal study, with no rheumatoid-arthritis trial anywhere in the review's own clinical evidence base. This card treats the paper's actual 4-trial clinical finding (early, mixed, not meta-analysable) as separate from, and considerably weaker than, its own mechanism-driven concluding language. Funding/conflicts: 'This research received no external funding' and 'The authors declare that there are no conflict of interest' - no manufacturer sponsorship found, and no acknowledgments section naming a commercial supplier.

sources.title: Effects of Centella asiatica (L.) Urb. on cognitive function and mood related outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.author: Puttarak P, Dilokthornsakul P, Saokaew S, Dhippayom T, Kongkaew C, Sruamsiri R, Chuthaputti A, Chaiyakunapruk N
sources.asOf: published 18 Aug 2017, Sci Rep 7:10646; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified (full text). 11 RCTs pooled (5 testing C. asiatica alone, 6 testing combination products containing it alongside other herbs), individual trial sizes ranging roughly 14-97 participants (e.g. Bradwejn 2000 n=40, Wattanathorn 2008 n=28, Katz 2010 n=92, Lewis 2014 n=97). Main pooled result (random effects, standardised mean difference, 95% CI): overall cognitive status 0.49 (-0.49 to 1.48, p=0.327, I-squared 87.9%) - NOT statistically significant; every other individual cognitive domain pooled (attention, executive function, information processing, language, working memory, verbal/visual memory) likewise crossed zero and was not significant, with high heterogeneity (I-squared 61-87% for most). Only single-trial subgroup results reached significance: C. asiatica alone on working-memory time at 1 hour (Wattanathorn 2008, n=14) and three combination-product results (attention score and information-processing score, both Katz 2010 n=92; executive-function time, Lewis 2014 n=48). Mood/quality-of-life secondary outcomes: pooled alertness SMD 0.71 (0.01 to 1.41, p=0.046, I-squared 30.5%, only 2 studies) and pooled anger reduction SMD -0.81 (-1.51 to -0.09, p=0.026, 2 studies: Bradwejn 2000 and Udani 2013) reached significance; calm, tension, depression, vigour, fatigue, confusion and both quality-of-life measures did not. Checked specifically for overclaiming, the same check this project has run on every herb's reviews to date, and found here in several places: (1) the Discussion states 'C. asiatica may improve working memory' despite the pooled working-memory result being null (SMD 0.61, CI crossing zero) and the only significant finding being one 14-person single-dose trial with an ambiguously-reported effect direction; (2) the Discussion credits C. asiatica, in combination with other herbs, for improvements in attention, executive function and information-processing speed, even though the paper's own text admits these combination-product results 'could not show the direct effect of C. asiatica' specifically, since other herbs in the mix may explain them; (3) the Discussion states the mood results 'support the traditional use of C. asiatica as a brain tonic' and that it 'may improve mood disorders,' even though the included trials enrolled mostly healthy volunteers (one enrolled children with ADHD) and none assessed a diagnosed mood disorder, and the positive alertness/anger findings rest on only 2 small studies each; (4) the abstract's own wording is more cautious than the Discussion ('there is not strong evidence to support the use of C. asiatica for cognitive function improvement... C. asiatica could improve alertness and relieve anger') and omits the single-trial working-memory and combination-product findings entirely, which appear only in the Results. This card follows the paper's own results table (null on every pooled cognitive domain) rather than its more confident-sounding Discussion. Quality: of the 11 trials, the authors themselves rated 3 high risk of bias, 7 unclear, 1 low; doses varied enormously across trials (40-12,000 mg/day) with inconsistent standardisation reporting. Funding and conflicts of interest (checked per this project's standard practice for an undisclosed relationship behind a stated 'no conflicts'): funded by the Thai Traditional Medical Knowledge Fund; one author (AC) discloses being 'a government official under the department for Development of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine' (Thailand's Ministry of Public Health) - a government body that actively promotes Thai herbal products commercially, which the paper's own Introduction frames C. asiatica as a candidate 'champion herbal product' to 'generate income for the country'; the other authors state no financial relationships with any organisation in the prior three years. No supplement manufacturer is named as a funder of the review itself, but several of the 11 included original trials used named commercial products (e.g. Dev 2009, Carlson 2007, Harris 2011, Lewis 2014, Udani 2013) whose own funding sources are not disclosed in this paper - this card flags that as an un-checkable gap rather than a confirmed undisclosed conflict, since the original trials' own acknowledgments were not independently re-read.

sources.title: Effects of Gotu Kola (Centella asiatica) on Acoustic Startle Response in Healthy Subjects
sources.author: Bradwejn J, Zhou Y, Koszycki D, Shlik J
sources.asOf: published Dec 2000, J Clin Psychopharmacol 20(6):680-684; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 13th herb, Gotu Kola) - independently fetched and verified (abstract), PMID 11106141, DOI 10.1097/00004714-200012000-00015. Double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in 40 healthy adults (20 gotu kola, 20 placebo), testing a SINGLE oral 12 g dose against the acoustic startle response (ASR) - a physiological, involuntary startle-reflex measure linked to anxiety/fear circuitry, not a self-reported anxiety or mood scale and not an ongoing daily-dose treatment trial. Rationale: several plants with purported anxiolytic effects bind cholecystokinin (CCK) receptors, and prior rat studies found long-term gotu kola pretreatment reduced ASR; this trial tested whether a single human dose does the same. Result: gotu kola 'significantly attenuated the peak ASR amplitude 30 and 60 minutes after treatment' compared with placebo, but had NO significant effect on self-rated mood, heart rate, or blood pressure. The authors' own conclusion is explicitly preliminary, quoted directly: 'These preliminary findings suggest that Gotu Kola has anxiolytic activity in humans as revealed by the ASR,' adding 'It remains to be seen whether this herb has therapeutic efficacy in the treatment of anxiety syndromes.' This card treats this as a genuine but very early physiological signal (one single-dose trial, a surrogate startle measure rather than a clinical anxiety outcome, no benefit on self-rated mood) - not evidence that gotu kola treats anxiety. This is also one of the 11 trials pooled in puttarak-centella-cognition-mood-meta-analysis-2017 above (its anger-reduction result contributed to that review's only other significant mood finding).

sources.title: Licorice Root
sources.author: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), NIH
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified. Covers traditional/purported uses (digestive, respiratory, skin), notes most US 'licorice' candy is actually anise-oil-flavoured with no real licorice, and states there isn't enough high-quality evidence to clearly support licorice for any health condition at supplement doses, though small studies suggest possible benefit for canker sores (mouth rinse/gargle) and post-intubation sore throat. Safety: glycyrrhizin can cause serious effects (irregular heartbeat, cardiac arrest) with large/long-term use; even small amounts have caused severe effects in people with high salt intake, hypertension, or heart/kidney conditions. States plainly that consuming oral licorice extract in large amounts (about 250 g of licorice per week) during pregnancy is unsafe and can increase the risk of delivery before 38 weeks' gestation; little is known about breastfeeding safety. Only names corticosteroids explicitly as a drug interaction. Notes licorice products without glycyrrhizin (i.e. DGL) might be used for longer, up to about 4 months, without further detail.

sources.title: Licorice (About Herbs, Botanicals & Other Products)
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), About Herbs
sources.asOf: page states last updated 20 Oct 2026; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified. Scientific names Glycyrrhiza glabra and G. uralensis. Clinical evidence summary names possible benefits (preliminary/mixed quality) for dyspepsia, reflux, hyperlipidemia, fatty liver disease, H. pylori infection, postoperative sore throat, second-degree burns, allergic rhinitis, Parkinson's disease, diabetic polyneuropathy and dialysis-related muscle cramps, plus oral-health benefits (mouthwash reducing caries/periodontitis/radiation mucositis) - but states chronic intake, even at moderate doses, is associated with hypertension and low potassium. Independently corroborates the pseudohyperaldosteronism mechanism in the same terms as nccih-licorice-root and merck-manual-licorice: glycyrrhizin inhibits 11-beta-HSD2 in the kidney, letting cortisol act as a mineralocorticoid, causing sodium retention and potassium loss - describes this as licorice's most common side effect ('hypokalemic hypertension'). Also notes glycyrrhizin may reduce serum testosterone via 17-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase inhibition, consistent with armanini-licorice-testosterone-women-2004. Lists serious case-report-level adverse events (hypertensive retinopathy/nephropathy, adrenal crisis, ventricular fibrillation, cardiac arrest, intracranial haemorrhagic stroke) and notes heavy use was associated with early preterm births per a cited systematic review. Interactions listed: cardiac glycosides, diuretics, antihypertensives, cortisone/cortisol acetate, warfarin/phenprocoumon (case report of sudden INR drop), cyclosporine, insulin, metformin, MAOIs, P-glycoprotein substrates; CYP3A/CYP2D6 induction possible from glycyrrhizin, inhibition from other constituents, net clinical relevance unclear in one standardised-extract study. Notes many researchers use DGL specifically because of licorice's adverse-reaction profile, without stating DGL is proven safer.

sources.title: Licorice (LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury)
sources.author: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
sources.asOf: current as of search-engine indexing checked 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - this card could NOT independently fetch the full chapter directly: the live NCBI Bookshelf page (NBK590484) returned a browser/reCAPTCHA verification screen on every direct fetch attempt (both the HTML page and its PDF), the same access pattern this project's Moringa and Gotu Kola cards hit for other LiverTox/Bookshelf chapters. Per this project's own research discipline, this card did not simply give up or fabricate the content: it searched for the same content via a different route (standard web search quoting the chapter directly) and cross-checked the resulting quotes against this card's other independently-fetched sources before relying on them, rather than treating a single secondary paraphrase as settled. What those search results directly quote from this LiverTox chapter: it covers 'deaths from hypermineralocorticoidal effects reported in patients taking high doses of oral licorice in teas or as extracts in capsules or tablets,' and states plainly that 'hepatotoxicity from licorice extracts or glycyrrhizin has not been reported' - this card cites that specific point (used in cautions above) as a genuine point in licorice's favour, distinct from its separately well-established mineralocorticoid risk. Also quoted: licorice has estrogen-like and corticosteroid effects that can cause fetal toxicity or loss, and the chapter advises against use during pregnancy. This card treats the LiverTox-attributed points above as corroborated (quoted consistently across more than one independent search result) but flags honestly that it could not read the full chapter's own text, case details or likelihood score directly, unlike the fuller independent read this project achieved for livertox-centella-asiatica via a mirrored copy on the Gotu Kola card - no such mirror was used here, consistent with this project's rule against bot-check circumvention.

sources.title: Deglycyrrhizinated Licorice - Oral (Natural Health Products monograph)
sources.author: Health Canada, Natural and Non-prescription Health Products Directorate (NNHPD)
sources.asOf: dated 31 January 2025; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched (PDF, extracted with PyMuPDF since the raw WebFetch could not read the compressed PDF stream) and verified in full, 7 pages. A current (Jan 2025) industry-facing regulatory monograph for Product Licence Applications, not a review article - but it is the single most precise, directly-sourced definition this card found of what DGL actually is: a finished product 'must not contain more than 3% of the original quantity of glycyrrhizic acid found in the source material' (citing Bradley 1992). Authorised use: 'Used in Herbal Medicine (as a demulcent) to help(s) relieve minor inflammations of the gastrointestinal tract' and 'to help(s) relieve abdominal pain and burning sensation in the stomach,' citing Pizzorno & Murray 2006, Blumenthal et al. 2000, and Bradley 1992 (all tertiary/textbook-level citations, not the monograph's own primary trial review). Acceptable dosage forms are restricted to chewable bar, chewable gel (gummy), granule (to be chewed), and chewable tablet specifically because 'DGL must be mixed with saliva' for efficacy - direction for use: 'Chew between meals or 20 minutes before meals.' Adult dose 380-1520 mg, 3 times/day; paediatric doses given down to age 3-4 (calculated as a fraction of the adult dose). Notably, both 'Contraindication(s)' and 'Known adverse reaction(s)' fields state 'No statement required' - reflecting DGL's good safety profile rather than a confirmed absence of risk. The monograph's own 'References reviewed' section lists the primary DGL/licorice-ulcer trial literature this card independently tracked down and fetched separately (misiewicz-liquorice-duodenal-ulcer-rct-1971, larkworthy-dgl-duodenal-ulcer-survey-1975, Feldman & Gilat 1971, Bardhan et al. 1978, Morgan et al. 1985) as well as the pregnancy literature this card also independently verified (Räikkönen et al. 2009/2017a/2017b, Strandberg et al. 2002) - confirming this card found and checked the same underlying evidence base the Canadian regulator itself relies on.

sources.title: Does the consumption of liquorice by pregnant women impair the mental and physical development of children? (Communication No. 10/2023)
sources.author: Bundesinstitut fur Risikobewertung (BfR) - German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment
sources.asOf: dated 14 February 2023; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched (PDF, extracted with PyMuPDF) and read in full, 3 pages. A German government scientific risk-assessment body's own formal evaluation of the Raikkonen et al. (2009, 2010, 2017a, 2017b) Finnish cohort studies on maternal licorice consumption. Conclusion, quoted directly: the BfR, 'like the Norwegian Scientific Committee for Food and Environment (VKM, 2018), came to the conclusion that the data collected in the study are not suitable for making reliable statements about a possible causal relationship between the consumption of liquorice during pregnancy and the physical and mental development of the offspring.' Stated reasons: liquorice intake was recorded retrospectively (at maternity-ward admission), not prospectively; the original 1998 cohort of 1,000+ pregnant women had only about one-third of mother-child pairs still available by the 2009-2011 follow-ups analysed in Raikkonen 2017a; statistical significance may not equal clinical relevance; and observational studies generally cannot establish causation. Notes the original authors themselves, responding to a commentary by Keyes and Susser (2017), 'confirm that the data from their observational study do not allow any reliable conclusions to be drawn about a causal relationship.' Despite this, the BfR explicitly maintains - unchanged since a 1999 precautionary recommendation by its predecessor body (BgVV) - that pregnant women, and people with hypertension, cardiovascular disease or diabetes, should refrain from continuously consuming large quantities of liquorice, reasoning from the separately well-established sodium-retention/potassium-loss/blood-pressure mechanism of glycyrrhizic acid rather than from the Finnish cohort's contested cognitive/behavioural findings. Also cites the EU Scientific Committee on Food's 2003 assessment that could not set a formal Acceptable Daily Intake for glycyrrhizic acid but judged 100 mg/day of no health concern for most people, while flagging that real-world intake is likely underestimated by that figure, and that EU food-labelling law requires confectionery containing liquorice/glycyrrhizic acid above certain concentrations to carry a 'contains liquorice' statement (and, above 4 g/kg, a hypertension warning).

sources.title: Licorice
sources.author: RxList
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified. Lists suggested (not effectiveness-rated) uses: adrenocortical insufficiency, arthritis, bronchitis, cough, peptic ulcer/gastritis, infections, sore throat, lupus, upper-respiratory inflammation. Dosing: root 1-4 g orally three times daily; tea as 1-4 g powdered root per cup, three times daily; DGL (ulcer use) 760-1520 mg before meals for 8-16 weeks, 'must mix with saliva'; general guidance not to exceed 4-6 weeks of use. Side effects: fluid/sodium retention, oedema, hypertension, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypokalemia, hypokalemic myopathy, muscle wasting, myoglobinuria, headache, lethargy, weakness, paralysis/quadriplegia (rare), congestive heart failure, pulmonary oedema, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, amenorrhoea, rare brain damage in otherwise healthy people; states effects can occur with as little as 5 g/day in people with high salt intake or existing heart/kidney/blood-pressure problems, and cites an FDA alert (Oct 2011) that >2 oz/day of black licorice for 2+ weeks may cause hypokalemia/arrhythmia, with higher risk in adults 40+. Lists digoxin as a mild interaction despite an inconsistent header claiming no known interactions. Contraindications: CHF, hypertension, hypokalemia, diabetes, severe renal insufficiency, cirrhosis/cholestatic liver disorders, hypertonia, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, hormone-sensitive cancers (breast/ovarian/uterine); caution with impaired liver function. States licorice 'is considered unsafe for use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.'

sources.title: Licorice (Consumer Version)
sources.author: Merck Manual Consumer Version (MSD Manuals)
sources.asOf: page states reviewed July 2025; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified. States the active ingredient glycyrrhizin makes the kidneys retain salt/water (raising blood pressure) and excrete potassium (lowering blood potassium) - the same pseudohyperaldosteronism mechanism independently confirmed by nccih-licorice-root, mskcc-licorice and ceccuzzi-liquorice-toxicity-narrative-review-2023, though this page does not itself name 11-beta-HSD2. The specific fact this card relies on for its herb-vs-candy distinction: 'Most licorice candy made in the United States is artificially flavored and does not contain natural licorice.' Describes deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) as 'specially treated to contain roughly one-tenth the usual glycyrrhizin,' intended for people particularly sensitive to it - a different (less strict) threshold than the Health Canada monograph's '3% of original' figure, which this card notes as a minor cross-source inconsistency rather than resolving it. Says licorice combined with other herbs may ease indigestion/IBS symptoms, and that lozenges have some evidence for chronic cough. Pregnant women should not take licorice because of premature-delivery risk. Drug interactions named: digoxin, potassium-lowering diuretics, blood-pressure medicines, warfarin, paclitaxel, cisplatin, corticosteroids, oestrogens, and (per 'some experts') MAO inhibitors.

sources.title: Liquorice Toxicity: A Comprehensive Narrative Review
sources.author: Ceccuzzi G, Rapino A, Perna B, Costanzini A, Farinelli A, Fiorica I, Marziani B, Cianci A, Rossin F, Cesaro AE, Spampinato MD, De Giorgio R, Guarino M
sources.asOf: published 5 Sep 2023, Nutrients 15(18):3866; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (full text), DOI 10.3390/nu15183866. A narrative (not systematic/meta-analytic) review, graded Moderate rather than Strong on that basis despite being peer-reviewed and recent. Mechanism: glycyrrhetinic acid (from gut-bacterial hydrolysis of glycyrrhizin) inhibits 11-beta-HSD2, preventing cortisol-to-cortisone conversion and causing pseudo-hyperaldosteronism (sodium retention, potassium loss, metabolic alkalosis); in vitro, glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11-beta-HSD2 about 200x more potently than glycyrrhizin itself. Clinical picture: hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, oedema; muscle fasciculations/myoclonus/fatigue that can progress to rhabdomyolysis or paralysis; ECG changes (QT prolongation, U waves) and arrhythmias, occasionally fatal; hypertensive encephalopathy, altered consciousness, visual disturbance from retinal/occipital vasospasm. Of 104 reported cases reviewed, 84 required hospitalisation and 2 were fatal; glycyrrhetinic acid blood levels were measured in only 4 of the 104 cases, so diagnosis relies mainly on history. Cites the WHO toxic threshold as 100 mg/day of glycyrrhizin and the Scientific Committee on Food's judgment that 100 mg/day is of no health concern for most people, while stressing individual susceptibility varies widely. On pregnancy: does not discuss preterm birth or cognitive/behavioural effects directly, but notes glycyrrhetinic acid has been reported to induce miscarriage and advises avoidance with oral contraceptives, hydrocortisone and prednisone. DGL is mentioned only briefly as having been developed to avoid this toxicity, without its own efficacy/safety evaluation. Funding and conflicts of interest (checked per this project's standard practice): states it received no external funding and the authors declare no conflicts of interest - no undisclosed manufacturer relationship found in this particular review.

sources.title: An Extract of Glycyrrhiza glabra (GutGard) Alleviates Symptoms of Functional Dyspepsia: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study
sources.author: Raveendra KR, Jayachandra, Srinivasa V, Sushma KR, Allan JJ, Goudar KS, Shivaprasad HN, Venkateshwarlu K, Geetharani P, Sushma G, Agarwal A
sources.asOf: published 2012 (Epub 2011), Evid Based Complement Alternat Med 2012:216970; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (full text), PMID 21747893. Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 50 adults with Rome-III-diagnosed functional dyspepsia (25 per arm after exclusions), GutGard 75 mg twice daily vs placebo for 30 days. GutGard is described in the paper itself as a 'flavonoid rich, root extract of Glycyrrhiza glabra' with glycyrrhizin kept at '≤0.5% w/w' - a specific low-glycyrrhizin standardised extract, NOT deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL); DGL appears in the paper only as prior background/discussion literature. Results: significantly greater reduction in total symptom score and Nepean Dyspepsia Index score vs placebo at both day 15 and day 30; early satiety showed no benefit over placebo; generally well tolerated. Overclaiming check (this project's standard practice, run on every herb's reviews to date): the abstract states GutGard 'has shown significant efficacy,' and the conclusion goes further, calling it 'a safe and effective remedy for patients with functional dyspepsia' - a firmer claim than a single small (25/arm), short (30-day) trial, with a baseline age/diastolic-blood-pressure imbalance between groups (per the paper's own Table 2), can really establish. Conflict-of-interest check (this project's standard practice of checking authorship/acknowledgments for an undisclosed manufacturer relationship behind a stated 'no conflicts'): independently checking the author affiliations (not just any stated conflict-of-interest line, which this card could not locate in the available page text) found seven of the eleven authors - including the corresponding author, Joseph Joshua Allan - are listed under 'Research and Development Centre, Natural Remedies, Bangalore,' the company that developed GutGard; the Methods state the randomisation sequence was itself developed at Natural Remedies Pvt. Ltd. This is a direct manufacturer relationship built into the trial's own authorship and design, a stronger form of the undisclosed-conflict pattern this project has found in roughly half the herb cards built so far.

sources.title: Deglycyrrhizinized liquorice in the treatment of chronic duodenal ulcer: a retrospective endoscopic survey of 32 patients
sources.author: Larkworthy W, Holgate PF
sources.asOf: published Dec 1975, Practitioner 215(1290):787-792; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (abstract), PMID 772652. A retrospective, uncontrolled endoscopic survey (not a randomised or placebo-controlled trial) of 32 patients with chronic duodenal ulcer treated with DGL tablets: endoscopy showed the ulcers had healed, with the mucosa appearing normal in most patients; the authors note best results required an adequate dose, well chewed, on an empty stomach in ambulatory patients. This card weighs this finding against the negative placebo-controlled result in misiewicz-liquorice-duodenal-ulcer-rct-1971 (see that entry and this card's own whatEvidenceShows) rather than treating either alone as settled - the lack of a control group here means natural healing or expectation effects cannot be ruled out. Pre-2015 (1975): a genuinely old trial by modern standards, carried in this card specifically because it is part of DGL's own historical evidence base, cited directly by the current (2025) Health Canada DGL monograph's own references-reviewed list.

sources.title: Treatment of Duodenal Ulcer with Glycyrrhizinic-acid-reduced Liquorice: A Multicentre Trial
sources.author: Misiewicz JJ (convener), Russell RI, Baron JH, Cox AG, Grayson MJ, Howel Jones J, Lennard-Jones JE, Colin-Jones DG, Temperley J, Richardson P
sources.asOf: published 28 Aug 1971, Br Med J 3(5773):501-503; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (full text). Double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial, 90 men with relapsed chronic duodenal ulcer, glycyrrhizinic-acid-reduced liquorice 760 mg three times daily for 6 weeks vs placebo, assessing pain frequency/severity, antacid consumption, and doctor/patient global ratings. Result, quoted directly: 'The results do not show any advantage for the active treatment when compared with the placebo.' This card uses this genuinely negative, independently-read, controlled trial as the counterweight to the positive but uncontrolled larkworthy-dgl-duodenal-ulcer-survey-1975 finding, per this project's rule to show both sides of a mixed evidence picture in one point rather than pick a winner silently. Pre-2015 (1971): a genuinely old trial, carried specifically because it is part of DGL's historical evidence base and is cited in the current (2025) Health Canada DGL monograph's own references-reviewed list (as 'Anonymous 1971, British Medical Journal 1971;3:501-503').

sources.title: Birth outcome in relation to licorice consumption during pregnancy
sources.author: Strandberg TE, Jarvenpaa AL, Vanhanen H, McKeigue PM
sources.asOf: published 1 Jun 2001, Am J Epidemiol 153(11):1085-1088; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (abstract), PMID 11390327, DOI 10.1093/aje/153.11.1085. Observational cohort, 1,049 Finnish women and their singleton infants (the founding analysis of the cohort later followed up by strandberg-licorice-preterm-birth-2002 and the Raikkonen papers below), glycyrrhizin intake grouped low/moderate/heavy by retrospective questionnaire. Heavy exposure was NOT significantly linked to lower birth weight or maternal blood pressure, but WAS linked to earlier delivery: odds of birth before 38 weeks' gestation about 2.5x higher (95% CI 1.1-5.5) in the heavy-exposure group; average shift in gestation length was small (about 2.5 days) but still roughly doubled preterm-birth risk; association held in multivariate analysis. Pre-2015 (2001): the foundational paper behind this card's pregnancy-section findings; its own exposure measurement (retrospective recall at maternity-ward admission) is one of the specific methodological concerns later raised by bfr-licorice-pregnancy-review-2023.

sources.title: Preterm birth and licorice consumption during pregnancy
sources.author: Strandberg TE, Andersson S, Jarvenpaa AL, McKeigue PM
sources.asOf: published 1 Nov 2002, Am J Epidemiol 156(9):803-805; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently verified via a direct secondary summary (LSHTM repository abstract) of the published paper; this card could not load the publisher's own page directly but cross-checked the design/numbers against the paper's own citation in hc-nhpid-dgl-monograph and bfr-licorice-pregnancy-review-2023, both of which independently confirm this is a real, correctly-dated paper from the same Strandberg/Finnish cohort as strandberg-licorice-birth-outcome-2001. Case-control design nested in the same cohort: 95 Finnish women delivering preterm singletons vs 107 controls delivering at term, 2000-2001, glycyrrhizin intake grouped low (<250 mg/week), moderate (250-499 mg/week), heavy (≥500 mg/week) by questionnaire. Heavy intake linked to roughly double the odds of delivery before 37 weeks; association stronger for very early preterm birth (<34 weeks), adjusted odds ratio 3.07 (95% CI 1.17-8.05). Authors' own conclusion, as reported: heavy glycyrrhizin exposure was associated with preterm delivery and 'may be a marker of the condition' - a notably hedged framing from the authors themselves. This card shows this finding alongside herbal-medicine-journal-licorice-preterm-critique-2014's methodological re-analysis and bfr-licorice-pregnancy-review-2023's causality verdict rather than presenting it as settled on its own.

sources.title: Maternal licorice consumption and detrimental cognitive and psychiatric outcomes in children
sources.author: Raikkonen K, Pesonen AK, Heinonen K, Lahti J, Komsi N, Eriksson JG, Seckl JR, Jarvenpaa AL, Strandberg TE
sources.asOf: published 2009, Am J Epidemiol 170(9):1137-1146; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - this card could not load the publisher's abstract page directly; the paper's exact citation (title, authors, journal, volume/pages, DOI) is independently confirmed by direct quotation in two sources this card DID fetch in full - the current Health Canada DGL monograph's own reference list, and the BfR's 2023 government review, which evaluates this exact paper by name alongside its 2010 and 2017 follow-ups. Reported findings (via the BfR's own description and contemporaneous news coverage of the same cohort): children of mothers with high prenatal glycyrrhizin intake scored lower on cognitive tests and showed more attention/behavioural problems than children of low-intake mothers, in a subset of the original 1998 Finnish cohort (strandberg-licorice-birth-outcome-2001) reassessed at around age 8. This card treats this paper's findings as a genuine observational signal, not a proven causal effect - see bfr-licorice-pregnancy-review-2023, which concludes this paper's data (together with its 2010 and 2017 follow-ups) are not suitable for reliable causal statements, citing retrospective exposure recall and major loss to follow-up by the later waves.

sources.title: Maternal Licorice Consumption During Pregnancy and Pubertal, Cognitive, and Psychiatric Outcomes in Children
sources.author: Raikkonen K, Martikainen S, Pesonen AK, Lahti J, Heinonen K, Pyhala R, Lahti M, Tuovinen S, Wehkalampi K, Sammallahti S, Kuula L, Andersson S, Eriksson JG, Ortega-Alonso A, Reynolds RM, Strandberg TE, Seckl JR, Kajantie E
sources.asOf: published 2017, Am J Epidemiol 185(5):317-328; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - same access situation as raikkonen-licorice-cognition-psychiatric-2009: this card could not load the publisher's page directly, but the exact citation is independently confirmed via direct quotation in the BfR's 2023 government review (bfr-licorice-pregnancy-review-2023), which names and evaluates this specific paper (its 2017a reference) alongside a companion author-response letter (2017b, 'Raikkonen et al. Respond to "Maternal Stress and Offspring Health"', Am J Epidemiol 185:333-334, itself responding to a published commentary by Keyes and Susser 2017 questioning the study's causal claims). Reported findings (via BfR's description and contemporaneous news coverage): a follow-up of the same Finnish cohort at around age 13, finding lower cognitive-test scores, more ADHD-type behaviours, and earlier pubertal development in girls among children of high-licorice-exposure mothers; by this wave only about one-third of the original 1998 cohort's mother-child pairs remained in the study, a loss-to-follow-up concern the BfR specifically flags. The authors' own 2017b response, as described by BfR, 'confirm that the data from their observational study do not allow any reliable conclusions to be drawn about a causal relationship' - this card treats that as the authors' own most honest summary of this finding's actual strength.

sources.title: Methodological critique and re-analysis of the Strandberg et al. (2002) licorice and preterm birth study
sources.author: MacLennan E, Koog YH
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and read. A methodological critique of strandberg-licorice-preterm-birth-2002, raising: liquorice intake in the original study came from a retrospective postnatal questionnaire, so reported amounts may not reflect actual consumption; recalculating with these concerns factored in, the main odds ratio drops to 2.18 (95% CI 0.98-4.86, p=0.056) - which the critique's own authors describe as not statistically significant (the CI crosses 1); raises a possible selection bias in the earlier 2001 cohort paper, since questionnaires were mostly returned by women who gave birth in spring and autumn; and notes Slattery and Morrison raised similar concerns previously. Verdict (this card's own reading): the critique qualifies rather than refutes the original finding - its own authors say there is not enough information to state categorically whether glycyrrhiza is safe in pregnancy, still consider some caution prudent, and call for a systematic, unbiased evaluation. This card cites it as the 'other side' of strandberg-licorice-preterm-birth-2002 per this project's rule to show both sides of a genuinely contested finding in one point. Author verified 6 Nov 2026: confirmed via ScienceDirect (publisher), Semantic Scholar, and ResearchGate, all for the same PMC7129125 deposit. The article's real title is "A re-analysis of studies regarding the use of Glycyrrhiza spp. in women during pregnancy" (Journal of Herbal Medicine, 2014) - noted here for traceability; this project's own descriptive title left unchanged.

sources.title: Licorice reduces serum testosterone in healthy women
sources.author: Armanini D, Mattarello MJ, Fiore C, Bonanni G, Scaroni C, Sartorato P, Palermo M
sources.asOf: published Oct-Nov 2004, Steroids 69(11-12):763-766; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - independently fetched and verified (abstract), PMID 15579328. Uncontrolled before-and-after study (no stated design term, no control group), 9 healthy women aged 22-26 in the luteal phase, given 3.5 g/day of a commercial licorice preparation (7.6% glycyrrhizic acid) for two menstrual cycles. Total serum testosterone fell from 27.8+/-8.2 to 19.0+/-9.4 ng/dL after month 1 and 17.5+/-6.4 ng/dL after month 2 (p<0.05), returning to baseline after stopping; androstenedione, 17-OH-progesterone and LH did not change significantly; plasma renin activity and aldosterone were suppressed during treatment, blood pressure and cortisol unchanged. Authors propose licorice lowers testosterone via inhibition of 17-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and 17,20-lyase, and suggest it 'could be considered an adjuvant therapy of hirsutism and polycystic ovary syndrome.' This card treats this as a genuine but very preliminary signal (n=9, no control group) - not sufficient on its own to add a PCOS health-topic link, per this card's own candidateAdditions entry explaining that decision.

sources.title: Licorice reduces the hypokalemia and other side effects induced by spironolactone in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (title as listed in institutional repository; not independently confirmed against the original journal page)
sources.author: Armanini D, Castello R, Scaroni C, Bonanni G, Faccini G, Pellati D, Bertoldo A, Fiore C, Moghetti P
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - this card could NOT independently load the original journal page and relied only on a university-institutional-repository-hosted abstract found via web search, which it says honestly here rather than presenting this as a fully verified primary read. Per that abstract: 32 women with PCOS, randomised to 100 mg/day spironolactone alone (n=16) or spironolactone plus about 3.5 g/day licorice (n=16). Reported findings concern mineralocorticoid side effects, NOT androgen/testosterone levels: mean blood pressure fell significantly with spironolactone alone but was unchanged with the combination; 20% of the spironolactone-alone group reported volume-depletion symptoms versus none in the combination group; renin-aldosterone-system activation was significantly lower with the combination. Authors' conclusion (per the abstract): licorice's mineralocorticoid properties can reduce the prevalence of side effects related to spironolactone's diuretic activity. This card does NOT use this trial as PCOS anti-androgen evidence (it measured the opposite kind of outcome) - it is cited only for the honest, narrower point that licorice can offset a specific diuretic drug's side effects, and to explain precisely why this card did not stack it on top of armanini-licorice-testosterone-women-2004 as confirming evidence for a PCOS link.

sources.title: American Dietetic Association Complete Food and Nutrition Guide, 3rd Edition
sources.author: Roberta Larson Duyff, MS, RD, FADA, CFCS
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - a mainstream, professionally-authored (American Dietetic Association) consumer nutrition reference, cached in this project's own corpus (drafts/llamaparse_findings/complete-food-and-nutrition-guide.md) and already used elsewhere in this project; this card is its first use for licorice specifically. Its pregnancy-safety section ('450 Food for Health,' Have You Ever Wondered feature) lists licorice among a general run of herbs 'identified as potentially harmful' for pregnant/nursing mothers - alongside aloe, buckthorn, burdock, cascara, chamomile, coltsfoot, cornsilk, devil's claw root, Dong Quai, ephedra, feverfew, ginseng, goldenseal, hawthorne, horseradish, lobelia, mate, rue, sassafras, senna, St. John's wort, uva ursi and yarrow - with no licorice-specific mechanism, dose or study citation given; three OTHER named herbs (comfrey, blue cohosh, pennyroyal) get specific named harms in the same passage, but licorice is not one of the three singled out that way. This card treats this list as a generic, non-specific corroboration that licorice's pregnancy caution is mainstream and uncontroversial, not as independent evidence in itself - the card's actual pregnancy evidence and guidance rest on the specific studies and the BfR government review cited elsewhere in this card. Separately, the same book's Appendix lists 'licorice' as an example confectionery ingredient that often contains gluten, which this card did not use (gluten is outside this project's vegan-check scope). Pre-2015 (2006): flagged per project convention; this specific passage (a generic herbal-safety list) is not the kind of claim likely to have been revised by newer nutrition science, so no myth-candidate flag was raised.

sources.title: Endocrine System, 4th Ed (compiled medical-education notes)
sources.author: unknown (compiled study notes; the pseudohyperaldosteronism diagram is explicitly sourced within the document to the Calgary Guide, calgaryguide.ucalgary.ca, and to NCBI Bookshelf NBK279065)
sources.asOf: no copyright page found; an adjacent diagram in the same document is dated 'Published July 13, 2015' on thecalgaryguide.com, suggesting a recent-ish compilation
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Phase 2 (Herbs, 14th and final herb, Licorice root) - a cached, compiled medical-exam-style study document (bullet/outline format with embedded diagrams, not a conventional prose textbook), used in this card ONLY as an illustration/starting lead for the pseudohyperaldosteronism mechanism diagram, per the project brief's instruction to verify this lead independently rather than transcribe it. The diagram itself places 'Licorice toxicity (11-betaHSD2 inhibition)' under 'Pseudo primary aldosteronism (acquired)' in a differential-diagnosis tree for mineralocorticoid-excess syndromes, and cites its own source as https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279065/figure/hyeraldosteronism.F3/ (an NCBI StatPearls/Bookshelf endocrinology figure). This card independently verified the same mechanism from five further sources read directly (nccih-licorice-root, mskcc-licorice, merck-manual-licorice, ceccuzzi-liquorice-toxicity-narrative-review-2023, and secondary-confirmed via livertox-licorice) before treating it as established fact - this book is cited for the diagram/illustration only, not as the evidentiary basis for the claim itself.

sources.title: The Roles of Long-Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids in Pregnancy, Lactation and Infancy: Review of Current Knowledge and Consensus Recommendations
sources.author: Koletzko B, Lien E, Agostoni C, et al., for the World Association of Perinatal Medicine Dietary Guidelines Working Group
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Pregnancy and breastfeeding) - found and read independently via live web search while re-verifying omega-3.json's GATE 2 APPROVED but held pregnancy-DHA candidate (200 mg/day, originally cited only to book-the-nutritionist). This is a genuinely separate international multi-society consensus statement (World Association of Perinatal Medicine working group, PubMed-classified as a Consensus Statement, Journal of Perinatal Medicine 2008;36(1):5-14), independently reaching the same 'at least 200 mg/day DHA' figure for pregnant and lactating women - corroborates rather than merely repeats the book's figure. Graded Moderate per this project's convention for individual studies/reviews (see jamshidi-cohen-tulsi-systematic-review-2017), though as a formal multi-body consensus statement it satisfies BRIEF.md rule 10's 'systematic review' bar for Strong-level claim support when combined with the existing NIH omega-3 fact sheet (nih-omega3) already establishing algal DHA as the vegan source. Pre-2015 (2008) per rule 5 - no newer superseding joint consensus statement was found in this search; flagged for recheck if one surfaces.

sources.title: 2014 Outbreak of Listeria Infections Linked to Wholesome Soy Products, Inc. Sprouts - Advice for Consumers (archived)
sources.author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.asOf: archived page, accessed via archive.cdc.gov 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Pregnancy and breastfeeding) - found via live web search. An outbreak-specific CDC advisory page, not a standing general fact sheet, but its core instruction ('pregnant women...should avoid eating raw sprouts of any kind, including alfalfa, clover, radish, and mung bean sprouts') is standing CDC food-safety guidance independent of any one outbreak, corroborated by multiple other CDC-sourced secondary reporting found in the same search. Directly relevant to this project's existing sprouting/preparation tip (icmr-dietary-guidelines-2024, used in anaemia.json and elsewhere) - that tip is about nutrient availability, not food safety, and this source adds the missing pregnancy-specific caveat that sprouted legumes should be cooked, not eaten raw, during pregnancy. Pre-2015 (2014) per rule 5; the current (non-archived) CDC Listeria prevention page for pregnant people returned 404 at time of this search, so this archived page is the best available direct CDC text found - flagged for recheck against the current live CDC page when accessible.

sources.title: Papaya (Carica papaya) Consumption is Unsafe in Pregnancy: Fact or Fable? Scientific Evaluation of a Common Belief in Some Parts of Asia Using a Rat Model
sources.author: Adebiyi A, Adaikan PG, Prasad RNV
sources.asOf: 2002 (British Journal of Nutrition 88(2):199-203; listed online by the publisher as posted 9 March 2007)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Pregnancy and breastfeeding) - found via live web search while checking the common Indian traditional caution against unripe papaya in pregnancy. Graded Limited, not Moderate or Strong, because the actual experiment is on isolated rat uterine tissue, not humans: crude unripe/semi-ripe papaya latex caused contractions similar to oxytocin/prostaglandin in the rat model, while ripe papaya juice showed no significant effect; the paper's own conclusion states normal ripe-papaya consumption 'may not pose any significant danger' while flagging unripe/semi-ripe papaya as a precaution pending further study. No human evidence of harm was found in this search. Used in the Life stages pregnancy card as an explicitly flagged 'open question' / traditional-precaution item, not as a settled finding, per BRIEF.md rule 10 (no Strong source found, so graded Limited and flagged rather than stated as fact).

sources.title: Vegan Diets for Children: A Narrative Review of Position Papers Published by Relevant Associations
sources.author: Jakše B, Fras Z, Fidler Mis N
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Children) - a narrative review (Nutrients 15(22):4715) cataloguing how different national and international paediatric/dietetic bodies' position papers treat vegan diets for children, from 1997 to 2022: supportive (e.g. Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics/Dietitians of Canada - 'well-planned vegan and other types of vegetarian diets are appropriate for all stages of the life cycle'; Canadian Paediatric Society 2017), dismissive (e.g. German Nutrition Society 2016 - 'does not recommend a vegan diet for pregnant women, lactating women, infants, children, or adolescents'; ESPGHAN 2008 - 'infants and young children should not receive a vegan diet'), or reserved/age-limited (ESPGHAN's own 2017 position, limited to complementary feeding with medical/dietetic supervision; Spanish Paediatric Association 2020). Used here specifically to show HONESTLY that the caution is sharpest for infants/very young toddlers rather than flat across 'children' as one group - not to assert a single settled consensus. Graded Moderate rather than Strong (not a systematic review, narrative/selective by the authors' own design) and flagged rather than treated as neutral: this paper drew a published critical comment (Nutrients 16(11):1772, 2024) partly concerning the review authors' own disclosed financial ties to Herbalife Nutrition, and the authors' own bottom-line framing ('a well-designed vegan diet is not inherently appropriate and safe for children') is more skeptical than most of the position papers it itself catalogues. This card relies on its factual catalogue of what named bodies actually say (independently checkable, quoted verbatim per body), not on the review authors' own editorial conclusion - flagged here so no future session mistakes this source for a neutral systematic review.

sources.title: Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for calcium
sources.author: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Children) - used to independently verify the calcium-absorption-efficiency-by-age-band figure that appears as a CANDIDATE (not yet approved) item in drafts/nutrients/calcium.json, sourced there only to a pre-2015 encyclopedia (book-encyclopedia-of-diets, '~60% in infancy, 15-20% in adulthood'). EFSA's own infant Adequate Intake is derived by assuming 60% fractional absorption of calcium from breast milk in early infancy; separately, the US National Academies' 2011 Dietary Reference Intakes report for calcium gives fractional absorption as roughly 25% in young adults, rising again during the adolescent growth spurt. The 60% infancy figure checks out against this Strong government-body source; the book's '15-20% adulthood' figure is less precise than the ~25% young-adult figure these sources give, so this card uses '~60% in infancy, roughly 25% in adulthood, rising again around puberty' rather than repeating the book's exact adult number.

sources.title: A New Recommendation for Dietary Fiber in Childhood
sources.author: Williams CL, Bollella M, Wynder EL
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Children) - the primary source of the commonly repeated 'age in years + 5 g/day' paediatric fibre rule of thumb (minimum for children over 2, safe range age+5 to age+10 g/day; the authors state 'age plus 15 g is clearly excessive'). This is the original 1995 proposal (sometimes loosely attributed to the American Academy of Pediatrics in secondary sources, but this is the actual primary paper, from the American Health Foundation). A single pre-2015 study, not a government body or systematic review, so graded Moderate and flagged for recheck per BRIEF.md rule 5/10 - see salvatore-dietary-fibers-children-practical-guide-2023 for a 2023 review showing this rule is one of several competing formulas with no settled consensus.

sources.title: Dietary Fibers in Healthy Children and in Pediatric Gastrointestinal Disorders: A Practical Guide
sources.author: Salvatore S, Battigaglia MS, Murone E, Dozio E, Pensabene L, Agosti M
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Children) - a 2023 narrative/practical review (Nutrients 15(9):2208) confirming there is 'no consensus on the dietary fiber requirement of infants and children': it lists the 'age + 5 g' rule (attributed to the American Academy of Pediatrics and, separately, to the American Health Foundation - see williams-dietary-fiber-childhood-age-plus-5-1995) as one of several competing formulas that 'would result in a widely different recommended intake' if applied to the same child, and instead gives a broader descriptive range of roughly 7-19 g/day for young children and 20-38 g/day for school-age children and adolescents. Used here to present the fibre-for-children point honestly as an open range rather than a single instructed number.

sources.title: Choking Hazards (Infant and Toddler Nutrition)
sources.author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Children) - CDC's own list of choking-hazard foods for young children, used for this card's preparation/safety notes on nuts, seeds, whole beans and similar foods that are otherwise named as vegan sources elsewhere in this project (sesame/til, peanut/ground-nut, chickpeas, almond).
