The page itself sits within CDC's 0-24-month infant/toddler nutrition section and gives no single numeric age cutoff in the text pulled; this card does not invent one, and notes the caution applies while a child is still learning to chew hard or small foods safely, not as a fixed age rule.

sources.title: Evidence-Based Recommendations for Optimal Dietary Protein Intake in Older People: A Position Paper From the PROT-AGE Study Group
sources.author: Bauer J, Biolo G, Cederholm T, et al., for the PROT-AGE Study Group
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Older adults) - a multi-society geriatric/clinical nutrition expert consensus (confirmed directly via its PubMed abstract, PMID 23867520), treated as a Strong source per BRIEF.md rule 10 (expert consensus position paper, not a single study). States healthy adults over 65 should average at least 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day, rising to 1.2-1.5 g/kg for most older adults with acute or chronic disease and at least 1.2 g/kg for those who are exercising and otherwise active; names an exception for severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR <30, not on dialysis), who may need to limit protein. Cites declining anabolic responses to ingested protein and high splanchnic extraction as mechanisms, and states evidence on protein quality, timing and supplements is 'not yet sufficient to support specific recommendations' - the leucine/plant-protein-source detail used on the Older adults card instead comes from the independently-read Lonnie et al. 2018 review below, not from this paper's own abstract. Funding note carried through transparently: the PROT-AGE group's meeting was funded by a Nestlé Nutrition grant to the European Union Geriatric Medicine Society; authors reported no personal honoraria.

sources.title: Protein for Life: Review of Optimal Protein Intake, Sustainable Dietary Sources and the Effect on Appetite in Ageing Adults
sources.author: Lonnie M, Hooker E, Brunstrom JM, Corfe BM, Green MA, Watson AW, Williams EA, Stevenson EJ, Penson S, Johnstone AM
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Older adults) - independently read in full via its PMC full text (PMC5872778), not just an abstract. A systematic review specifically on protein needs, sustainable/plant sources and appetite in an ageing (40+) population - the direct Strong-source check requested for the leucine/sarcopenia mechanism before use (the held candidate in drafts/nutrients/protein.json citing book-food-what-the-heck-should-i-eat). Confirms PROT-AGE/ESPEN's 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day consensus for healthy over-65s and the anabolic-resistance mechanism; adds the plant-specific nuance that plants generally contain under 8% leucine as a share of total protein versus roughly 8-14% in animal foods (maize an exception at ~12%), cites PROT-AGE's own per-meal anabolic threshold of roughly 2.5-2.8 g leucine (higher than in younger adults), and lists leucine-rich plant foods per 100g including dry-roasted soybeans (3.22 g) and cooked lentils (1.29 g/cup) - these specific per-food figures are the review's own, not independently re-verified against USDA FoodData Central here, so used descriptively rather than as a precise meal-planning target. The review's own conclusion is that whether plant protein alone reliably prevents muscle/strength loss in older adults is still unproven and an open research question ('more studies are needed'), and that soy is the best-studied plant option but 'may not be optimal' for appetite reasons in frail older adults specifically - this card follows the review's own cautious framing rather than overstating either direction.

sources.title: Definition & Facts for Constipation
sources.author: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Life stages Gate 1 (Older adults) - confirmed directly via live fetch. States about 33 of 100 adults aged 60+ have symptoms of constipation, and names older adults, low fibre intake, and certain medicines or supplements among the groups/factors more likely to become constipated (alongside women during/after pregnancy and non-Caucasians, neither used on the Older adults card). Used to support that card's fibre/constipation point; this project's own Gut health card's existing fibre/fluid/activity framing is cross-referenced for general management rather than repeated here.

sources.title: Soy and Cancer Risk: Our Expert's Advice
sources.author: American Cancer Society (ACS) - Dr Marissa Shams-White, Senior Principal Scientist, ACS Population Science department
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (soy/breast cancer card) - confirmed directly via live fetch, the current Strong-source check this card's own status note said was needed before any confident wording could be published. ACS states soy foods are 'healthy and safe' and that 'a large body of evidence supports the safety of soy foods as part of a healthy diet', with human studies finding soy isoflavones either have no effect or may reduce breast cancer risk - especially in Asian populations with lifelong higher soy intake - directly contrasting the earlier rodent studies (which used much higher doses and a different isoflavone metabolism than humans) that originally drove the cancer-risk fear. Important caveat carried through faithfully: for cancer prevention specifically, ACS does NOT recommend soy supplements - it recommends getting nutrients through whole soy foods instead, noting supplements can contain much higher isoflavone amounts than naturally occur in food and that more research on supplements specifically is still needed. This is the single best anchor source for this card: current (2025), directly on-topic, and from a major cancer body rather than a general nutrition reference.

sources.title: Soy and Breast Cancer: Myths and Misconceptions
sources.author: American Institute for Cancer Research (AICR) - Karen Collins, MS, RDN, CDN, FAND, AICR Nutrition Advisor
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (soy/breast cancer card) - confirmed directly via live fetch. A second, independent current health-body source corroborating the ACS reversal above, with more mechanistic and survivor-specific detail. States isoflavones bind oestrogen receptors differently from the body's own oestrogen (a 'lock and key' effect that can act as a tumour suppressor rather than a growth promoter) and that studies show soy protein/isoflavone intake has no effect on breast-cancer-risk markers (hormone levels, breast cell growth, breast density). Specifically addresses breast cancer SURVIVORS: cites the AICR/WCRF Continuous Update Project (CUP) Global systematic-review report rating the evidence as 'limited suggestive' that eating soy is associated with greater survival and decreased recurrence, including in women with ER-positive cancer, at roughly one to two standard servings/day (no added benefit found above that). On the whole-food-vs-supplement question this card needs to address honestly: AICR's own reading is that isolated soy protein/soy protein powder does not contain MORE isoflavones than whole soy (some processing methods strip out 80-90% of isoflavones) and has not been shown to carry excess risk, but it lacks the fibre and full nutrient range of whole soy foods - so AICR's practical advice, like ACS's, is to favour whole soy foods (tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk, soy yogurt, soy nuts) as the primary approach, not because isolated soy is known to be risky, but because whole foods are better-evidenced and more nutritionally complete. Used together with the ACS source, these are not conflicting (both reach the reassuring conclusion and both prefer whole foods), just differently worded - no 'show both sides' conflict-flag needed here.

sources.title: Soy intake and breast cancer risk: a prospective study of 300,000 Chinese women and a dose-response meta-analysis
sources.author: Wei Y, Lv J, Guo Y, Bian Z, Gao M, Du H, Yang L, Chen Y, Zhang X, Wang T, Chen J, Chen Z, Yu C, Huo D, Li L, for the China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB) Collaborative Group
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (soy/breast cancer card) - independently read via PMC full text (PMC7320952, PMID 31754945), not just an abstract. A large prospective cohort (300,852 Chinese women in the main CKB analysis) combined with a dose-response meta-analysis pooling 631,498 women across prospective studies - treated as Strong per BRIEF.md rule 10 (systematic/pooled analysis, not a single study). Found moderate soy intake was NOT associated with increased breast cancer risk among Chinese women, with no meaningful difference between pre- and post-menopausal subgroups; the pooled dose-response meta-analysis found each 10 mg/day increment in soy isoflavone intake was associated with a 3% (95% CI 1-5%) REDUCED risk of breast cancer. This is the direct epidemiological evidence (large population with lifelong higher soy intake) that the ACS and AICR sources above both reference in general terms - read here directly rather than taken on their word.

sources.title: Association between a soy-based infant diet and the onset of puberty: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.author: Oliveira FRK, Silva e Gustavo AF, Goncalves RB, Bolfi F, Mendes AL, Nunes-Nogueira VDS
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (soy/breast cancer card) - independently read via PMC full text (PMC8130953, PMID 34003856), the direct check this project ran specifically for the 'precocious puberty' half of the original uncited claim. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies (598 children on a soy-based diet vs 2957 not) found no statistically significant difference in precocious puberty risk (OR 0.51) or age of menarche (mean difference 0.14 years) between the groups, concluding there is no conclusive evidence that a soy-based diet causes either premature or delayed puberty in girls or boys. Important scope caveat carried through honestly: every included study was about soy-based INFANT FORMULA specifically (not about the diet of a breastfeeding/pregnant vegan mother, which is what the original myth claim actually describes), and the review itself flags a low number of relevant studies and mixed methodologies as limitations - so this is the closest and most directly relevant systematic-review evidence found on the puberty-timing question, and it does not support the original claim, but it answers a narrower question (infant soy formula) than the claim poses (maternal vegan diet).

sources.title: You are what your mother eats: evidence for maternal preconception diet influencing foetal sex in humans
sources.author: Mathews F, Johnson PJ, Neil A
sources.asOf: published 2008-04-22 (Proc Biol Sci 275(1643):1661-1668) - FLAGGED PRE-2015 per BRIEF.md rule 5
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (soy/breast cancer card) - independently read via PMC full text (PMC2602810, PMID 18430648), added specifically to trace what real research (if any) underlies the card's 'vegan mothers have a disproportionate number of female babies' claim, per this task's instructions to check that claim directly rather than just dropping it. This is the only remotely-related real study found, and it does NOT support the myth claim: it studied total maternal preconception ENERGY (calorie) intake in 740 UK women (via the Trivers-Willard resource-allocation hypothesis), not veganism, soy, or phytoestrogens specifically, and found the OPPOSITE direction to the myth - HIGHER energy intake was associated with more SONS (56% boys in the highest-energy-intake group vs 45% in the lowest), not more daughters. Graded Limited (rather than Strong) despite being a peer-reviewed study: it is a single study on a contested, hard-to-replicate topic (facultative human sex-ratio adjustment), it is pre-2015, and most importantly it is being cited here only to show what the actual literature says on a loosely related question, not as support for the claim in the card, which this project found no genuine scientific backing for at all under any search term tried (vegan diet, soy, phytoestrogens, or sex ratio together).

sources.title: The Alkaline Diet: Does It Work?
sources.author: Cleveland Clinic (quoting Anthony DiMarino, RD)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (acid-alkaline-diet-theory candidate) - read directly in full via live fetch. A hospital patient-education page (Cleveland Clinic - a qualifying Strong source type per this project's brief, in the same tier as Mayo/MSKCC patient-education pages). States plainly that diet does not change blood pH: dietitian Anthony DiMarino is quoted, 'Your body is a smart machine. It regulates pH very well on its own,' and 'Our lungs and kidneys work to remove metabolic waste and keep our body pH where it needs to be,' and the page states directly that 'nothing you eat will change your blood pH.' Separately states urine pH 'doesn't signify anything about the quality of your diet' - directly addressing the litmus-paper urine self-testing method named in the mined naturopathy book. Calls the alkaline diet's core premise 'unproven' and says it 'doesn't stand up to scientific rigor,' while noting any real benefit from the diet (e.g. weight loss, fewer chronic-disease risk factors) likely comes from its emphasis on whole foods, not from any actual pH change. Does not address cancer, bone or the other specific conditions named in the mined book's claim list - see the companion Fenton & Huang 2016 systematic review (below) for the cancer-specific evidence gap. Used for this card's core 'why diet can't change body pH' mechanism point.

sources.title: Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer
sources.author: Fenton TR, Huang T
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (acid-alkaline-diet-theory candidate) - read directly via its PubMed abstract page (PMID 27297008; BMJ Open 6(6):e010438). A genuine systematic review (published and grey literature searched separately) of randomised and observational studies testing dietary acid/alkaline load or alkaline water against any cancer outcome or cancer-treatment outcome. Screened 8,278 citations, reviewed 252 abstracts in full, and found only 1 study meeting inclusion criteria (a low-risk-of-bias cohort study on bladder cancer, finding no association: OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.86-1.55, p=0.36). No randomised trials were found at all, and no studies addressed cancer treatment. Authors' own conclusion, quoted directly: 'there is almost no actual research to either support or disprove these ideas,' and 'Promotion of alkaline diet and alkaline water to the public for cancer prevention or treatment is not justified.' Used for this card's point that even the most specific, testable version of the alkaline-diet health claim (cancer) has essentially no evidence base either way - not disproven by trials so much as never properly tested, which is a more honest framing than a flat 'false.' Satisfies BRIEF.md rule 10's systematic-review bar; post-2015 per rule 5.

sources.title: Gout Symptoms, Causes, & Risk Factors
sources.author: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), NIH
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (acid-crystals-apple-cider-vinegar candidate) - confirmed directly via live fetch. Used to independently verify the gout/crystal-arthropathy contrast already drafted as this card's third explanation bullet, which had previously been the project's own unsourced observation (sourceIds: []). NIAMS confirms gout is a real, specific, named condition: 'Gout happens when urate, a substance in your body, builds up and forms needle-shaped crystals in your joints,' described as 'a type of inflammatory arthritis' with a characteristic pattern (flares 'often begin in your big toe or a lower limb'), not a universal explanation for ordinary joint stiffness, arthritis in general, or ageing. The page gives no support for a general 'acid crystal' mechanism outside gout, and does not mention apple cider vinegar or any dietary crystal-dissolving agent. Used to turn the card's previously unsourced gout contrast into a properly cited point.

sources.title: Apple Cider Vinegar
sources.author: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), Integrative Medicine service
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (acid-crystals-apple-cider-vinegar candidate) - read directly in full via live fetch. A hospital patient-education page (a qualifying Strong source type per this project's brief). Its clinical summary lists arthritis only among claims people make for ACV ('dyslipidemia, arthritis, and skin conditions such as acne, eczema and dandruff'), with no supporting evidence discussed for any of them - the page records that the claim exists, it does not confirm a benefit. States overall that 'available evidence to support ACV use is not conclusive due to heterogeneity between studies' and that 'larger, methodologically-robust trials are needed to generate more definitive data.' Separately states there is 'no scientific evidence that ACV can prevent or cure skin or any other type of cancer' - not directly relevant to this card's arthritis/crystal claim, but confirms the source's general evidence standard. Does not mention 'acid crystals' or any crystal-dissolving mechanism at all. Used for this card's overall 'inconclusive, not supported' evidence verdict on ACV generally.

sources.title: 10 Arthritis Food Myths
sources.author: Arthritis Foundation
sources.asOf: unknown (no date shown on page; accessed 2 Nov 2026)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (acid-crystals-apple-cider-vinegar candidate) - read directly in full via live fetch. Graded Moderate, not Strong: a patient-advocacy non-profit's own myths page, undated, with no named author and no cited studies, rather than a government body, a hospital clinical page, or a systematic review. Lists cider vinegar as myth #7 and states plainly: '[Its] anti-inflammatory benefits aren't backed by science,' while noting it is separately being studied for weight loss and blood-sugar effects. Does NOT mention 'acid crystals,' gout, or any crystal-dissolving claim on this live page - an earlier web search surfaced secondary (CNN-sourced, not independently confirmed) reports that the Foundation elsewhere states gout is the only form of arthritis genuinely involving acid crystals and that vinegar cannot dissolve them, but that specific wording was not found on this directly-read page and is NOT relied on in this card; only the directly-read 'not backed by science' line above is used. Used as Moderate corroboration alongside the Strong MSKCC and NIAMS sources, not as this card's primary evidence.

sources.title: Do Brassica Vegetables Affect Thyroid Function? A Comprehensive Systematic Review
sources.author: Galanty A, Grudzinska M, Pazdziora W, Sluzaly P, Pasko P
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (cruciferous-vegetables-thyroid candidate) - read directly in full via its PMC full text (PMC11012840), not just an abstract. A PRISMA-guided systematic review (Medline, Scopus and Google Scholar searched through January 2024; 273 articles screened, 123 included) of human, animal and in vitro evidence on brassica/cruciferous vegetables and thyroid function - more specific and more recent than this card's existing sourceId (book-end-of-heart-disease), and satisfies BRIEF.md rule 10's systematic-review bar directly. Overall conclusion, quoted: including brassicas in the daily diet 'particularly when accompanied by adequate iodine intake, poses no adverse effects on thyroid function' - the negative effect seen in some older/animal studies 'was most pronounced in the regions with concurrent iodine deficiency,' and iodine supplementation reversed goitrogenic effects in several livestock studies. On cooking: cooking inactivates the myrosinase enzyme that produces the active goitrogenic breakdown products; in a human radioiodine-uptake study, raw rutabaga inhibited uptake but cooked rutabaga had no effect, and boiled/steamed Brussels sprouts (150 g/day for 4 weeks) caused no change in thyroid hormones or TSH in healthy adults. On large/raw amounts: uptake inhibition was only seen with unusually large or concentrated amounts - e.g. a purified extract equivalent to 2,617 g of raw rutabaga in one subject, and a case report of hypothyroidism in a woman eating up to 1.5 kg/day of raw Chinese cabbage - not normal dietary portions. On existing thyroid conditions: the review found the common advice for hypothyroid patients to avoid brassicas 'often rely on outdated animal studies' using seed forms humans rarely eat, and found no clean human trial isolating brassica intake from levothyroxine use or iodine status in this group; it does not conclude normal amounts are proven safe for people on thyroid medication, only that the evidence commonly cited against them is weak. Review's own limitations: human data are limited and many included studies are small, old, or use animal models or concentrated extracts rather than food-form intakes; some survey studies are confounded by iodine intake, salt type and medication use and lack control groups. Used for this card's precise, non-oversimplified rewrite: normal cooked amounts are not a practical concern given adequate iodine, raw/very large/juiced/concentrated amounts are the real area of caution, and advice for people with existing thyroid conditions should still go through a clinician, since the evidence specific to that group is thin rather than reassuring either way.

sources.title: Dietary fiber
sources.author: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sources.asOf: 2025 (citing the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans; page updated periodically, exact last-review date not shown on page)
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (high-fiber-diet-harm candidate) - read directly via live fetch. States the current adult/adolescent target as 21-38 g/day (citing the Dietary Guidelines for Americans), well above typical US intake of about 16 g/day. Lists established benefits: bulk/fullness supporting weight control, aiding both constipation and diarrhoea, helping lower cholesterol, and supporting glycaemic control for people with diabetes. Advises increasing fibre gradually (gas, bloating, cramps if too fast) and notes a balanced diet usually makes a fibre supplement unnecessary. Used as this card's general Strong source for what current mainstream guidance on fibre actually says - it contains no warning resembling the myth's claims, and no mention of fibre causing mineral-absorption harm, osteoporosis, Alzheimer's or rickets at these recommended intakes.

sources.title: Ask the Experts: Can certain fibers bind essential minerals and lessen their bioavailability?
sources.author: Robert M. Russell, MD (emeritus professor, Tufts Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy), for Tufts Health & Nutrition Letter
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (high-fiber-diet-harm candidate) - read directly via live fetch. A named, credentialled expert's answer in a university nutrition-newsletter Q&A, not a government body or systematic review, so graded Moderate per BRIEF.md's PCRM-style convention for expert-authored but non-governmental sources. Directly addresses the fibre-vs-phytate distinction this card turns on: 'many foods that are high in fibre (particularly cereals) can inhibit the absorption of iron and zinc,' but these same foods also contain phytate, which 'also has an inhibitory effect on these minerals['] absorption,' so 'it is hard to pick apart how much of the inhibition... is due to phytate alone' versus fibre itself. States that 'most of the inhibition for calcium and magnesium absorption is thought to be due to phytate rather than fibre' (with a separate, smaller effect of cellulose reported for calcium). Also states that at typical/ordinary fibre intake levels, no chronic adverse effects from mineral malabsorption have been seen. Used as this card's clearest single source on the fibre-vs-phytate mechanism distinction, corroborating this project's own nih-zinc/icmr-dietary-guidelines-2024-sourced phytate content already in zinc.json and calcium.json.

sources.title: Alzheimer's & Memory Loss Myths
sources.author: Alzheimer's Association
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (high-fiber-diet-harm candidate) - read directly via live fetch. Graded Strong on the same basis as this project's existing vndpg-protein entry: a major medical/scientific nonprofit with its own Medical and Scientific Advisory Council, not a government agency but a recognised health body, distinct from PCRM's advocacy-grade Moderate rating. The current (2026) version of this page no longer carries a dedicated aluminium myth (an older, now-retired version did - archived copies state plainly that 'studies have failed to confirm any role for aluminum in causing Alzheimer's'); the current page's closest standing item, Myth 8, states that 'no single food, ingredient or supplement has been shown to prevent, treat or cure Alzheimer's.' Used for the general organisational position that mainstream Alzheimer's science does not treat any specific dietary factor as an established cause. This project could not find any current or historical source, mainstream or otherwise, connecting fibre-driven aluminium absorption specifically to Alzheimer's risk - the aluminium-Alzheimer's hypothesis itself remains a contested, unproven minority position in the wider scientific literature even on its own terms (e.g. Tomljenovic 2011, J Alzheimers Dis, arguing a case for it; mainstream bodies such as this one and the UK's Alzheimer's Society conclude no causal role has been confirmed), which is itself a weaker and quite separate claim from the fibre-specific mechanism this myth card addresses - a claim not found stated anywhere outside the one 1997 book.

sources.title: A Brief History of Nutritional Rickets
sources.author: Wheeler BJ, Snoddy AME, Munns C, Simm P, Siafarikas A, Jefferies C
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths deck Gate 1 research (high-fiber-diet-harm candidate) - read directly via live fetch (Frontiers in Endocrinology, open access). States plainly that vitamin D deficiency, 'usually in concert with dietary calcium deficiency, is the leading cause' of nutritional rickets, historically linked to overcrowding, indoor living, poor air quality and reduced calcium intake from a greater dietary reliance on bread, and in its modern 'third wave' to reduced UVB/sun exposure. Does not mention dietary fibre or bran anywhere as a cause, and does not discuss phytate or plant-based/vegetarian diets as a contributing factor. Used as this card's direct rebuttal source for the myth's rickets claim: the current, mainstream peer-reviewed account of what causes rickets has no place for fibre or bran, and centres on vitamin D and calcium intake plus sun exposure instead.

sources.title: ABO Genotype, 'Blood-Type' Diet and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors
sources.author: Wang J, Garcia-Bailo B, Nielsen DE, El-Sohemy A
sources.asOf: published 2014-01-15, PLoS ONE 9(1):e84749; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (blood-type-diet-vegetarian card) - independently fetched and read full text, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0084749, PMID 24454746. The first study to directly test the 'Blood-Type' diet theory: 1,455 healthy young Toronto adults were genotyped for ABO blood group and scored for adherence to each of D'Adamo's four Blood-Type diets (A, B, AB, O), then cardiometabolic risk markers (fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, lipids) were compared. Key, precise finding (quoted from the paper's own Discussion, this project's exact nuance requirement): adherence to the Type-A, Type-AB and Type-O diets WAS associated with more favourable levels of several cardiometabolic risk factors, but 'these associations were not related to an individual's ABO blood group' - when the authors directly tested whether people with the MATCHING blood group benefited more than people with a mismatched blood group following the same diet, no significant interaction was found for most outcomes. The authors attribute the Type-A diet's benefit to its general healthy-diet pattern (high fruit/vegetable, low meat) rather than to ABO matching. Also notes a related claim check: existing lectin-agglutination studies found no ABO-specific agglutination, undermining the diet's own stated mechanism. This is the precise 'diets may have individual merit, but not because they match your blood type' finding this card needed, read directly rather than assumed.

sources.title: Blood type diets lack supporting evidence: a systematic review
sources.author: Cusack L, De Buck E, Compernolle V, Vandekerckhove P
sources.asOf: published 2013-07 (Epub 2013-05-22), Am J Clin Nutr 98(1):99-104; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (blood-type-diet-vegetarian card) - independently read via PubMed abstract and corroborating secondary summaries (ScienceDirect, NCBI Bookshelf), DOI 10.3945/ajcn.113.058693, PMID 23697707. A genuine systematic review (GRADE methodology) asking directly: 'In humans grouped according to blood type, does adherence to a specific diet improve health and/or decrease risk of disease compared with nonadherence to the diet?' Result: the search found only one study even tangentially related (MNS blood-type variation in LDL response to a low-fat diet, a different blood-group system to ABO) and 'no studies that showed the health effects of ABO blood type diets were identified.' Conclusion, quoted directly: 'No evidence currently exists to validate the purported health benefits of blood type diets.' Used alongside wang-abo-blood-type-diet-plos-2014 (which positively tested and found an ABO-independent diet-quality effect) and barnard-blood-type-cardiometabolic-jand-2021 below - together the three give a consistent, precise picture: no blood-type-specific effect exists, though the underlying diets themselves may still have ordinary nutritional merit.

sources.title: Blood Type Is Not Associated with Changes in Cardiometabolic Outcomes in Response to a Plant-Based Dietary Intervention
sources.author: Barnard ND, Rembert E, Freeman A, Bradshaw M, Holubkov R, Kahleova H
sources.asOf: published 2021-06 (Epub 2020-12-04), J Acad Nutr Diet 121(6):1080-1086; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (blood-type-diet-vegetarian card) - independently fetched and read full abstract/metadata, DOI 10.1016/j.jand.2020.08.079, PMID 33288495. A secondary analysis of a 16-week randomised clinical trial (the Kahleova et al. JAMA Network Open low-fat vegan diet trial): 68 intervention-group participants were ABO-genotyped and outcomes (body weight, fat mass, visceral fat, blood lipids, fasting glucose, HbA1c) compared between blood type A vs all others, and type O vs all others. Result: no significant difference in ANY outcome by blood type (e.g. mean weight change -5.7 kg for type A vs -7.0 kg for others, P=0.09; -7.1 kg for type O vs -6.2 kg for others, P=0.33). Conclusion, quoted directly: 'Blood type was not associated with the effects of a plant-based diet on body weight, body fat, plasma lipid concentrations, or glycemic control.' Directly on point for this card: type O is the type the Blood-Type diet claims most needs meat, and here type O did at least as well as everyone else on a vegan diet. CONFLICT-OF-INTEREST NOTE (this project's standard practice): the corresponding author (Neal Barnard) and 4 of 6 co-authors are affiliated with the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, a vegan-advocacy nonprofit that also runs this project's own cited pcrm.org source - a real affiliation to disclose, though the actual trial design (randomised, with a no-change control group, pre-registered outcome measures) and the small-but-genuine sample (n=68) make this a legitimate RCT-derived finding, not an opinion piece; it corroborates rather than stands alone against the independently-run Toronto cohort (wang-abo-blood-type-diet-plos-2014) and the Belgian Red Cross systematic review (cusack-blood-type-diets-systematic-review-2013).

sources.title: Mammalian intestinal allometry, phylogeny, trophic level and climate
sources.author: Duque-Correa MJ, Codron D, Meloro C, McGrosky A, Schiffmann C, Edwards MS, Clauss M
sources.asOf: published 2021-02-10, Proc Biol Sci 288(1944):20202888; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (human-anatomy-proves-herbivore-diet card) - independently fetched and read full text (PMC7893215, PMID 33563126), DOI 10.1098/rspb.2020.2888, Proceedings of the Royal Society B (peer-reviewed). Tests the 'textbook knowledge' assumption (the same assumption behind this card's claim) that herbivores reliably have longer intestinal tracts than carnivores, across a large comparative mammal dataset. Finding: the paper 'corroborates intuitive expectations that diet has a main effect' on large-intestine measures in the expected direction (longer in herbivores on average), BUT the significance of these relationships depends heavily on large sample sizes and which taxonomic groups are included, so the relationship 'cannot be considered a fixed biological law' - i.e. gut-length-vs-diet is a loose statistical tendency across mammals generally, not a clean two-category rule that can be read off any one species (including humans) with confidence. Does not discuss humans specifically or give the 12x/3x body-length figures the draft card repeats; used here as the general methodological corrective to the oversimplified 'gut length proves diet type' reasoning pattern itself, with clemente-suarez-human-digestive-physiology-evolutionary-diet-2025 below supplying the human-specific numbers.

sources.title: Human Digestive Physiology and Evolutionary Diet: A Metabolomic Perspective on Carnivorous and Scavenger Adaptations
sources.author: Clemente-Suarez VJ, Redondo-Florez L, Beltran-Velasco AI, Yanez-Sepulveda R, Rubio-Zarapuz A, Martin-Rodriguez A, Navarro-Jimenez E, Tornero-Aguilera JF
sources.asOf: published 2025-07-04, Metabolites 15(7):453; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (human-anatomy-proves-herbivore-diet card) - independently fetched and read via targeted full-text extraction (PMC12297991, PMID 40710552), DOI 10.3390/metabo15070453, a peer-reviewed review in Metabolites (MDPI). Directly addresses this card's central question and gives the numeric comparisons needed to check the draft's specific claim. Conclusion: humans are classified as omnivores showing 'omnivorous flexibility and partial carnivorous specialization', not strict herbivores. Key numbers, which CORRECT the draft card's '12x body length for humans vs 3x for carnivores' claim rather than confirming it: human small-intestine-to-body-length ratio is approximately 5:1 (adult small intestine roughly 5 metres long) - closer to carnivores/dogs (approx. 6:1) than to ruminant herbivores (approx. 12:1, the figure vegetarian-advocacy sources like this card's source books misattribute to humans). Stomach pH: carnivores approx. 1-2, herbivores approx. 4-7, HUMANS approx. 1.5 - i.e. humans' gastric acidity is carnivore-like, not herbivore-like, the opposite of what the draft card's 'alkaline saliva/acid-stomach' framing implies. Salivary amylase: humans have high salivary amylase activity (2-15 copies of the AMY1 gene) where obligate carnivores like cats have minimal/no salivary amylase - this point does cut toward starch-adapted omnivory, so the overall picture is genuinely mixed rather than one-sided, consistent with 'omnivore' being the accurate classification rather than either 'herbivore' or 'carnivore'. Used together with duque-correa-mammalian-intestinal-allometry-2021 above.

sources.title: Metabotyping and its role in nutrition research
sources.author: Hillesheim E, Brennan L
sources.asOf: published online 2019-08-22, print Nutrition Research Reviews 33(1):33-42, June 2020; current as fetched 2 Nov 2026
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (metabolic-typing-meat-eater card) - independently fetched and read abstract/metadata, DOI 10.1017/S0954422419000179, peer-reviewed review in Nutrition Research Reviews (Cambridge). IMPORTANT DISTINCTION this card relies on: 'metabotyping' as defined and reviewed in this real, legitimate scientific field is the DATA-DRIVEN clustering of individuals into subgroups by MEASURED metabolic biomarkers (blood/urine metabolite profiles from clinical testing), used in personalised-nutrition research to find who responds differently to a given diet intervention - a genuinely active, peer-reviewed research area with real evidence behind it (per this review: 'strong evidence that metabolic phenotyping is a promising strategy'). This is NOT the same concept as the commercial 'metabolic typing diet' this card is actually about (Kelley/Wolcott's self-assessed 'meat eater' type, determined by simple symptom checklists or reactions to niacin/vitamin C, not laboratory metabolite measurement). This source is cited here specifically to draw that distinction clearly and avoid the error (found during this research) of citing legitimate metabotyping science as if it validated or tested the commercial diet book's claim, which it does not address at all.

sources.title: Metabolic diet: Fact vs. fiction
sources.author: Maeve Ginsberg (writer); medically reviewed by Gia Eapen, MD; contributions by Daniel Chavez, RD
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (metabolic-typing-meat-eater card) - independently fetched and read in full. A dietitian-contributed, MD-medically-reviewed consumer health article (Fay Nutrition, a telehealth dietitian service), graded Moderate rather than Strong per BRIEF.md rule 10 (not a government body or systematic review). Directly addresses 'the myth of metabolic typing': states plainly that 'the concept of metabolic typing has been around for decades, but it remains largely unsupported by rigorous scientific research' and 'there is little evidence to support the idea that metabolic typing leads to better weight loss or health outcomes.' NOTE on this source's own citation error, caught and NOT repeated by this project: the article cites hillesheim-brennan-metabotyping-nutrition-research-2020 (above) as its evidence for 'little evidence', but that paper is actually about a different, legitimate research concept (measured-biomarker metabotyping), not the commercial metabolic-typing diet - so this article's own debunking conclusion is used here as a dietitian's informed opinion, not as if its cited reference were itself a direct test of the diet claim. No formal systematic review or RCT testing the specific 'meat eater metabolic type' claim was found anywhere in this research pass - this remains the best available source, which is why this card stays graded Limited overall rather than being promoted to Gate 2.

sources.title: Metabolic typing (Wikipedia article)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors, citing Stephen Barrett MD / Quackwatch and Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center
sources.note: 2 Nov 2026, Myths Gate 1 (metabolic-typing-meat-eater card) - independently fetched and read in full. Tertiary source, graded Limited accordingly (BRIEF.md rule 10 requires a government/health body or systematic review for Strong; this is neither). Background/history only: documents that 'metabolic typing' was introduced by William Donald Kelley, a dentist (not a physician or nutrition scientist), convicted in 1970 of practising medicine without a licence; states 'the validity and effectiveness of metabolic typing have yet to be established,' citing a Quackwatch (Stephen Barrett, MD) investigation in which a single person's two separate blood/urine samples, sent to the same metabolic-typing testing firm, produced two drastically different 'metabolic type' results and diet plans - a direct test-retest reliability problem with the diagnostic method itself, independent of whether the underlying theory has merit. Used here only for this historical/practitioner-credibility context, not as the card's scientific rebuttal.

nutrients.name: Calcium

whatItDoes.text: Builds and maintains bones and teeth, and is needed for muscles to move, nerves to signal, and hormones to be released. Vitamin D helps the body absorb it.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 1,000 mg/day (does not increase over the non-pregnant adult amount, per PCRM)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: NIH names vegans directly: people who do not eat dairy must find other calcium sources, such as kale, broccoli, Chinese cabbage, calcium-fortified plant milks (soy, almond) and juices, tofu, and fortified cereals.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: On a plant-based diet, good sources include tofu, dark leafy greens, beans, figs, sunflower seeds, tahini, almond butter and fortified soy milk, cereals or juice.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: A well-known study (the Harvard Nurses' Health Study) found women who ate a serving of lettuce or another leafy green vegetable daily had half the hip-fracture risk of women eating a serving only about once a week - an association from an observational study, not proof the greens alone caused the lower risk, but a specific, checkable finding worth having on file for a vegan reader asking about bone health without dairy.
veganContext.label: open question

absorptionTips.text: Calcium absorbs best in single doses of 500 mg or less - split a larger daily target across two or more meals or snacks rather than one go.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Only around 30% of the calcium in dairy is absorbed by the body, compared with roughly 40-64% of the calcium in broccoli, Brussels sprouts, mustard greens, turnip greens and kale - dairy's own phosphorus content is part of the reason its calcium absorbs less efficiently.
absorptionTips.label: open question

absorptionTips.text: Diets high in protein - particularly dense animal protein - are linked to increased calcium loss in urine. Wheat bran, raw spinach, fructose (as in sugary soft drinks), salt, caffeine, alcohol and tobacco are also everyday factors that can interfere with calcium absorption, alongside the phytic/oxalic-acid effect already noted above.
absorptionTips.label: open question

cautions.text: Calcium supplements can reduce absorption of levothyroxine (a thyroid medicine) - take them about 4 hours apart. Long-term lithium use together with calcium supplements can raise blood calcium too high. Talk to your doctor if you take either.
cautions.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Have a calcium-fortified plant milk or juice, tofu set with calcium, or a katori of cooked greens most days, split across meals.
gaps: No source found for calcium needs specific to older vegan adults (71y+) broken down separately from the general IOM/NIH figure already listed.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Fills the currently-empty whenToTest field. Note: this clinical reference book's tables are extracted from a visually-formatted PDF and some surrounding labels came through jumbled - the two figures below were cross-checked against their own in-book citation (Goldstein 1990, a standard clinical-chemistry reference) and look internally consistent, but worth a quick independent check before treating as final.
candidateAdditions.text: A blood test for calcium status usually reports total serum calcium (normal range about 8.5-10.5 mg/dL) and sometimes ionized serum calcium (about 4.7-5.2 mg/dL) separately - a doctor interprets these alongside vitamin D and parathyroid hormone levels.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Calcium article in The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets (2008) - flagged pre-2015, recheck current absorption-science consensus before use. Adds a nuance to the existing single absorptionTips entry (500mg split-dose tip) rather than duplicating it: this is about which specific foods' own calcium is affected, not about supplement dosing.
candidateAdditions.text: The phytic acid naturally found in beans and the oxalic acid naturally found in spinach and other leafy greens reduce how much calcium the body absorbs from THOSE particular foods specifically - but the book states this does not reduce absorption of calcium from other foods eaten at the same meal. Fibre such as wheat bran also somewhat reduces calcium absorption. This is a reason to get calcium from a variety of plant sources rather than relying on spinach or beans alone, not a reason to avoid either food.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Calcium article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Partially speaks to this card's existing 'gaps' note about no older-adult-specific calcium source, but only partially - it explains WHY absorption efficiency drops with age, it does not supply a separate 71y+ RDA breakdown, so the gap itself should stay open.
candidateAdditions.text: How efficiently the body absorbs dietary calcium changes a lot with age: infants absorb as much as 60% of the calcium they eat, this falls to roughly 15-20% in adulthood, and falls further still in old age. Pregnancy increases absorption efficiency to help meet the growing baby's needs.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Calcium article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015 - medicine interactions can change, so this should be rechecked against a current source before publishing). Expands the existing cautions entry, which currently only names levothyroxine and lithium - no dosing given, framed as 'talk to your doctor' per BRIEF.md Safety rule 3.
candidateAdditions.text: Beyond levothyroxine, calcium absorption can also interact with several other prescription medicines, including fluoroquinolone and tetracycline antibiotics, digoxin, anticonvulsants, thiazide-type diuretics, corticosteroids, mineral oil and stimulant laxatives, and antacids. Anyone taking these should check with their doctor or pharmacist about timing calcium intake or supplements around their medication.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Calcium article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015, recheck exact mg figures against USDA FoodData Central before use). Only vegan-compatible foods pulled from this source's food-content table (dairy, cheese, sardines and salmon figures from the same table were excluded per BRIEF.md's strictly-vegan rules) - adds specific numbers the existing veganContext entries do not currently give.
candidateAdditions.text: Approximate calcium content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: calcium-set firm tofu, half cup, about 204 mg; fortified orange juice, 6 oz, about 200-260 mg; fortified breakfast cereal, 1 cup, about 100-1,000 mg (varies widely by brand - always check the label); cooked spinach, half cup, about 120 mg; cooked white beans, half cup, about 113 mg; cooked bok choy, half cup, about 61 mg; cooked pinto or red beans, half cup, about 43 mg; whole wheat bread, 1 slice, about 20 mg.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From book-pharmacology-toxicology-4th-ed (Round 7b targeted drug-nutrient-interaction search). A MORE COMPLETE/specific version of the generic 'antacids' entry already listed among the medicines in this card's existing expanded cautions candidateAddition - names the actual recognised clinical syndrome rather than just the drug category. Not a new drug class.
candidateAdditions.text: Taking large amounts of a calcium-containing antacid (calcium carbonate) over time can cause a specific recognised condition called milk-alkali syndrome - high blood calcium and metabolic alkalosis that, if it continues, can affect the kidneys. This is about large or frequent antacid doses specifically, not calcium from food. Anyone using a calcium-based antacid regularly, especially alongside a calcium or vitamin D supplement, should check with their doctor rather than self-dosing indefinitely.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

nutrients.name: Choline

whatItDoes.text: Supports brain and nervous system function (memory, mood, muscle control) and helps build cell membranes. The body makes a small amount itself, but most comes from food.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Plant sources include potatoes, cruciferous vegetables (brussels sprouts, broccoli, cauliflower), beans, nuts, seeds and whole grains. PCRM highlights soybeans as a particularly good plant source.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Most people in general - vegan or not - get less choline than recommended from diet and supplements combined, so this is a general population shortfall, not only a vegan one; plant sources are more limited than the richest animal ones, though, so it is worth a vegan's attention.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate choline content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: toasted wheat germ, 1 cup, about 172 mg; cooked Brussels sprouts, 2 cups, about 63 mg; cooked broccoli, 1 cup, about 62 mg; peanut butter, 2 tbsp, about 20 mg. Soybeans and peanuts are also named as choline-rich plant sources. Lecithin supplements (a choline source) are commonly soy-derived and so can be a vegan-friendly option, but lecithin supplements carry a smaller and more variable amount of choline than choline-chloride or choline-bitartrate supplement forms - worth checking the label either way.
veganContext.label: established fact

cautions.text: Pregnant women are a group NIH flags as being at higher risk of not getting enough choline. Very high intakes from supplements can cause a fishy body odour, low blood pressure or liver problems.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: The official upper limit for choline is 3,500 mg/day for adults (men and women) - well above the recommended daily amount, giving a wide safety margin before the high-dose side effects above would be expected.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Low choline intake in pregnancy is linked (in one source) to effects on the developing fetal brain, and may contribute to learning, memory and attention difficulties in the child later in life. This adds the 'why it matters' behind the existing caution that NIH flags pregnant women as a higher-risk group for low choline above - it is not a reason to worry, but a reason to make sure choline-rich plant foods are a regular part of a vegan pregnancy diet alongside other known pregnancy nutrients.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Methotrexate (a medicine used for certain cancers, psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis) has been linked to choline deficiency in animal studies. Anyone taking methotrexate should discuss this with their doctor.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A theory exists that gut bacteria metabolise choline (from any dietary source) into a compound called trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), which some researchers have linked to atherosclerosis. This association has not been proven and the theory has real gaps, including that TMAO's role seems to depend heavily on each person's specific gut-bacteria mix rather than choline intake alone - worth knowing as reassurance that an ordinary vegan diet's plant choline sources are not something to worry about on this basis.
cautions.label: open question

whenToTest.text: There is no routine blood test for choline status in general clinical practice; a research-only fasting plasma free-choline range of roughly 7-9.3 micromol/L has been reported, but this is not something a person would typically have tested.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Include soy foods, beans, nuts, seeds and cruciferous vegetables like broccoli regularly for choline.
gaps: No Indian RDA figure for choline found in the ICMR-NIN 2020 brief note's summary tables - only NIH figures shown here.
No source found quantifying exactly how much lower typical vegan choline intake runs compared with the recommended amount - flagged rather than estimated.

The 750 mg/day pregnancy-choline figure (Derbyshire & Obeid 2020) remains HELD (not used anywhere in this card) pending a direct read of that systematic review - see candidateAdditions, and also flagged for the Life stages module.

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): higher priority than most holds despite having the best citation of this book's findings - a stronger source doesn't buy down the risk of a dosing figure well above NIH's RDA and closing in on the UL, especially since it will eventually feed the Life stages pregnancy section. Needs Derbyshire & Obeid 2020 read directly before this figure goes anywhere near Life stages content. Also flagged in CHECKPOINT.md's Life stages section so it isn't lost before that module starts.
candidateAdditions.text: One cited trial found that choline supplementation of 750 mg/day during pregnancy was linked to babies performing better on child development tests at 6 months of age (cited to Derbyshire E, Obeid R, 'Choline, Neurological Development and Brain Function: A Systematic Review Focusing on the First 1000 Days,' Nutrients, 2020) - this is a systematic review in a real peer-reviewed journal, a stronger citation chain than most book-sourced findings reviewed in this project so far, though still worth a direct read before treating the specific 750 mg figure as settled guidance.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Fibre

whatItDoes.text: Delays and slows digestion of carbohydrates and fats, increases fullness, and adds bulk to stools, which supports regular bowel movements.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: Diets rich in fibre can help reduce blood glucose and blood fats (lipids).
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: Dietary fibre includes several distinct types grouped by function rather than just 'soluble/insoluble' - cellulose, hemicellulose, polyfructoses (inulin/oligofructans, in onions, garlic, artichokes, soybean), gums, mucilages, pectins, lignin, and resistant starches (in legumes, potatoes, bananas and plantains). Fermentable fibres are broken down by gut bacteria into short-chain fatty acids (such as butyric acid) that fuel and support the health of the colon's lining.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: A high-fibre diet is believed to play a role in preventing or treating breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, colon cancer, diabetes, gallstones, high cholesterol, irritable bowel syndrome, obesity and metabolic syndrome - but this broader list is given without a specific study citation in the source reviewed, so it should be treated as an open, broad claim rather than a settled one, pending a check against a current systematic review.
whatItDoes.label: open question

whatItDoes.text: Studies on whether a high-fibre diet protects against colon cancer specifically are inconclusive - some supporting studies suggest fibre may reduce exposure to carcinogens in waste by speeding food through the bowel, but the evidence is not settled. Separately, a low-fat, high-fibre diet combined with daily exercise is associated with reduced breast cancer risk in this source, but no specific study citation is given for this, so it is graded Limited rather than stated as settled.
whatItDoes.label: open question

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 30-38 g/day (also expressed as the Dietary Reference Intake of 14 g of fibre per 1,000 kcal eaten)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 21-25 g/day (same 14 g/1,000 kcal basis, at typical female calorie intakes)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: around 25 g of fibre per 1,000 kcal eaten
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.group: IOM 2001 age/sex bands (second citation, corroborating the ranges above)
dailyRangeByGroup.amount: children 1-3y about 19 g/day, 4-8y about 25 g/day; boys 9-13y about 31 g/day, girls 9-13y about 26 g/day; boys 14-18y about 38 g/day, girls 14-18y about 26 g/day; men 19-50y about 38 g/day, women 19-50y about 25 g/day; men over 50y about 30 g/day, women over 50y about 21 g/day; pregnancy about 28 g/day; breastfeeding about 29 g/day
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Fibre comes only from plant foods, so a varied whole-food vegan diet (whole grains, pulses, vegetables, fruit) naturally runs higher in fibre than a diet that includes animal foods - this is one of the nutrients that tends to look after itself on a vegan diet.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: At least half a katori of beans daily is a simple, practical way to add fibre.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Approximate fibre content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: cooked lima beans, half cup, about 6.6 g; canned baked beans, half cup, about 6.3 g; cooked black beans, half cup, about 6.1 g; cooked kidney beans, half cup, about 5.7 g; cooked winter squash, 1 cup, about 5.7 g; cooked whole wheat spaghetti, 1 cup, about 5.6 g; bran flake cereal, 3/4 cup, about 5.3 g; shredded wheat cereal, 1 cup, about 5.2 g; a medium pear, about 5.1 g; cooked turnips, half cup, about 4.8 g; cooked brown rice, 1 cup, about 3.5 g; an apple with skin, about 3.3 g; cooked oatmeal, 3/4 cup, about 3.0 g; cooked broccoli, half cup, about 2.6 g; cooked spinach, half cup, about 2.2 g; whole wheat bread, 1 slice, about 1.9 g.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Further approximate fibre values from the same source, for foods not already listed above: raw pear, about 5.1g; raw pineapple, about 1.9g; raw tangerine, about 1.9g; blueberries, about 4.0g; cranberries, about 4.0g; raspberries, about 8.3g; cooked asparagus (4 spears), about 1.2g; cooked Brussels sprouts, about 4.0g; cooked cabbage, about 3.0g; cooked carrot, about 4.6g; cooked cauliflower, about 3.4g; raw celery, about 2.1g; romaine lettuce, about 1.2g; raw tomato, about 1.0g; cooked white rice, about 0.6g (included for contrast with brown rice). All figures are per medium fruit or 1 cup of vegetable/grain, per the source.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A further, larger fibre-food table from the same source (herbs and spices given per 2 tsp unless noted; vegetables, fruit, legumes and grains per 1 cup unless noted): cinnamon 2.5g, basil 1.2g, coriander seeds 1.4g, oregano 1.3g, thyme 1.1g, rosemary 0.9g, cloves 1.5g, dried chili pepper 2.6g, black pepper 1.1g, cayenne pepper 1.0g, mustard seeds 1.1g, turmeric powder 1.0g; turnip greens (cooked) 5.0g, mustard greens (boiled) 2.8g, collard greens (boiled) 5.3g, swiss chard (boiled) 3.7g, celery (raw) 2.0g, fennel (raw) 2.7g, bell peppers (raw) 1.8g, tomato (raw) 2.0g, onions (raw) 2.9g, beetroot (boiled) 3.4g, corn (cooked) 4.6g; raspberries 8.3g, romaine lettuce (2 cups) 1.9g, cranberries (1/2 cup) 2.0g, strawberries 3.3g, kiwifruit (1 each) 2.6g, orange (1 each) 3.1g, apricot (1 each) 0.8g, blueberries 3.9g, papaya (1 each) 5.5g, apple (1 each) 3.7g, grapefruit (1/2) 1.7g, pear (1 each) 4.0g, plum (1 each) 1.0g, banana (1 each) 2.8g, pineapple 1.9g, cantaloupe 1.3g; split peas (cooked) 16.3g, lentils (cooked) 15.6g, black beans (cooked) 15.0g, pinto beans (cooked) 14.7g, lima beans (cooked) 13.2g, barley (cooked) 13.6g, navy beans (cooked) 11.7g, kidney beans (cooked) 11.3g, chickpeas 12.5g, soybeans (cooked) 10.3g, green peas (boiled) 8.8g; bulgur wheat (cooked) 8.2g, rye (whole grain, 1/3 cup) 8.2g, buckwheat (cooked) 4.5g, oats (whole grain, cooked) 4.0g; flaxseeds (2 tbsp) 5.4g, avocado (sliced) 7.3g, olives 4.3g, miso (1 oz) 1.9g, yam (cubed, cooked) 5.3g, sweet potato (1, baked with skin) 3.1g, potato (baked with skin) 2.9g.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Fibre reduces how much cholesterol the gut reabsorbs and increases how much leaves the body, which is one reason higher-fibre, plant-based diets are linked with better cholesterol levels.
absorptionTips.label: official recommendation

absorptionTips.text: Increase fibre gradually and drink enough water alongside it, to avoid bloating or discomfort as the gut adjusts.
absorptionTips.label: illustration

absorptionTips.text: When increasing fibre intake, also increase fluid intake up to about 2 litres (8 cups) a day - a specific water-intake figure alongside the general gradual-increase advice already in this card.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: A sudden large jump in fibre (for example from very low intake to a lot of beans and whole grains at once) can cause temporary bloating or loose stools - increase gradually instead.
cautions.label: illustration

cautions.text: Fibre supplements such as psyllium can reduce how well the body absorbs certain medications if taken at the same time. As a general rule, medications should be taken at least one hour before or two hours after a fibre supplement - check with a doctor or pharmacist about any specific medicine.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Total daily fibre intake above about 50g may raise the risk of intestinal blockage, and excessive fibre intake has been linked to reduced absorption of vitamins, minerals, protein and calories generally - though this is unlikely to be a problem for healthy people eating fibre within the usual recommended ranges above. Most of this effect is thought to come from phytate (a separate compound that travels alongside fibre in whole grains, legumes and seeds) rather than fibre itself, and no chronic harm has been seen at typical intakes - see this project's own myths deck entry on this topic for the fuller picture. Parents should also be careful about adding a lot of extra fibre to a child's diet, since it can fill a child up and reduce appetite for other needed nutrients.
cautions.label: open question

nutrients.oneLineAction: Build meals around whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit rather than refined/processed versions, and increase fibre gradually with plenty of water.
gaps: No dedicated NIH ODS consumer fact sheet exists for fibre (confirmed during Step 4 caching) and no ICMR-NIN RDA/EAR figure for fibre was found in the brief-note summary tables used for this batch - the general adult target above comes from Nutrition Guide for Physicians (2010), a pre-2015 core-reference book, so it is flagged for recheck against a current Strong source if one becomes available.

No separate Indian adult fibre target (outside the pregnancy-specific 25 g/1,000 kcal figure) was found in the ICMR Dietary Guidelines for Indians - flagged rather than assumed to equal the pregnancy figure.

The food-content gram figures sourced from book-encyclopedia-of-diets (a pre-2015 reference encyclopedia, author unstated) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

The GI-specific paediatric 'age in years plus 5 g/day' fibre rule remains pending (not used anywhere in this card) - see candidateAdditions; it needs a direct check of the primary source (Williams et al.) before use, especially since it is high-stakes children's content.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the primary source (Williams et al.) before use - not promoted this round despite being otherwise well-documented, because the card's own author-attribution correction (owner's call, 22 Oct 2026) still leaves the exact citation, year and clinical age-range/context independently unverified, and this is high-stakes children's content (rule 9). From the dedicated Irritable bowel syndrome diet AND Diverticular disease diet articles (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - gut-health continuation pass. ATTRIBUTION CORRECTED (owner's call, 22 Oct 2026): this book attributes the 'age in years plus 5 g/day' formula to the IOM/National Academy of Sciences, but the owner identifies this as a mis-attribution by the book - it is actually a separately-published, GI-specific paediatric fibre guideline in its own right, commonly known in the literature as the 'age+5' rule (Williams et al.), which is exactly why it turns up in these two GI-specific articles rather than in the book's own general Fiber article. NOT a conflict with this file's IOM 2001 age-band table - the two measure different things for different purposes (a general-population adequate-intake standard vs a GI-specific paediatric target) and can both be kept, clearly scoped.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states (twice, in two different articles, both mis-attributing it to the IOM) that children older than 2 should get dietary fibre equal to or greater than their age in years plus 5 grams per day (e.g. about 10g/day at age 5) - in gastroenterology/paediatric literature this is known separately as the 'age+5' rule (Williams et al.), a GI-specific target, not the general-population IOM figure above. The source separately notes there are no published studies establishing an optimal fibre intake for infants and children under 2 - for them, it suggests simply introducing a variety of fruit, vegetables and easily-digested cereals after weaning, without a specific target.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Folate

whatItDoes.text: Needed to make DNA and other genetic material, and for cells to divide.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 400 mcg DFE/day (NIH); 300 mcg DFE/day men, 220 mcg DFE/day women RDA 2020 (ICMR-NIN)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: NIH's adult figure (400 mcg DFE) is notably higher than ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian adults (300 mcg men / 220 mcg women). Both shown rather than merged into one number - worth asking the owner which to lead with.

dailyRangeByGroup.group: Women/teen girls who could become pregnant
dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 400 mcg/day folic acid specifically, from supplements or fortified food, in addition to dietary folate
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Folate's natural food sources are mostly plant foods already: vegetables such as asparagus, brussels sprouts and dark leafy greens (spinach, mustard greens), fruits such as oranges and orange juice, nuts, beans and peas. This is one of the nutrients an ordinary varied vegan diet covers well.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Folic acid (the synthetic form) is also added to enriched bread, flour, pasta, rice and fortified cereals in many countries.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: The American Cancer Society states: 'Folate deficiency may increase the risk of cancers of the colorectal and breast, especially in people who consume alcoholic beverages. Current evidence suggests that to reduce cancer risk, folate is best obtained through consumption of vegetables, fruits, and enriched grain products.' The ACS does not endorse taking megadoses of folic acid to prevent cancer - this supports this card's existing food-first framing. Separately, the American Heart Association's 2006 Diet and Lifestyle Recommendations stated that 'available evidence is inadequate to recommend folic acid and other B vitamin supplements as a means to reduce CVD risk' - an honest open question, not a settled benefit, kept here as a caution against over-claiming what folate supplements can do for heart health.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Approximate folate content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: fortified breakfast cereal (100% fortified), 3/4 cup, about 400 mcg; cooked pinto beans, half cup, about 147 mcg; cooked turnip greens, half cup, about 135 mcg; cooked asparagus, half cup, about 132 mcg; cooked spinach, half cup, about 131 mcg; cooked navy beans, half cup, about 127 mcg; cooked great northern beans, half cup, about 90 mcg; steamed broccoli, half cup, about 85 mcg; boiled beets, half cup, about 68 mcg; enriched white rice, cooked, half cup, about 65 mcg.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: The elderly are named as the largest group at risk of folate deficiency overall (ahead of pregnant women), with low intake also commonly reported in teenage girls in some countries - a general-population risk pattern, not a vegan-specific one. Causes of deficiency beyond low intake include poor absorption (coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, certain medicines), increased needs (pregnancy, cancer) and increased loss (kidney dialysis, heavy alcohol use).
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Cooking vegetables can reduce their folate content by up to 40%, depending on the vegetable and cooking method - gentler cooking (such as light steaming rather than prolonged boiling) keeps more folate intact. This matters because leafy greens and other vegetables are a main vegan folate source.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Large folate or folic acid supplement doses can mask a vitamin B12 deficiency on a blood test, without stopping the nerve damage B12 deficiency can also cause. This matters for vegans, who are already the main group at risk of low B12 - do not treat a high folate intake as a reason to skip a reliable B12 source.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: The official upper limit for folic acid (the supplement/fortification form, not food folate, which has no set upper limit) is 1,000 mcg/day for adults.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Besides masking B12 deficiency, several medicines can interfere with the body's ability to absorb or use folate: seizure medications (such as phenytoin/dilantin and primidone), metformin (used for type 2 diabetes), sulfasalazine (used for Crohn's disease and inflammatory bowel disease), triamterene (a diuretic), barbiturate sedatives, methotrexate (used for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis), and some GERD medicines (such as omeprazole, lansoprazole, cimetidine, famotidine, nizatidine or ranitidine). Anyone taking these should check with their doctor about their folate levels.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Methotrexate works partly by blocking dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme the body needs to activate folate for building DNA - this is the actual mechanism behind methotrexate's already-noted effect on folate status above. Doctors prescribing methotrexate for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis manage this as part of the treatment itself; it is not something to address with an ordinary folate supplement on one's own.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Sulfasalazine (already noted above as a folate-interfering medicine) and the antibiotic trimethoprim both work partly by blocking enzymes the body needs to use folate (dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase) - broadly the same mechanism family as methotrexate, though these two are chosen because bacteria rely on that pathway far more than human cells do. Trimethoprim specifically carries a higher risk of birth defects and is generally avoided in pregnancy for this reason. Anyone taking trimethoprim who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy should raise this with their doctor.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Anti-epileptic (anticonvulsant) medicines taken during pregnancy carry a raised risk of certain birth defects, including spina bifida (a neural tube defect) - this risk varies by specific drug, with valproate and phenytoin named as carrying some of the higher risk among anticonvulsants. Folate supplementation is specifically noted as something that can further reduce the added risk of spinal cord defects in this situation. Anyone on anticonvulsant medication who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy should discuss their specific medicine and any extra folate need directly with their doctor, rather than self-dosing.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Cholestyramine and colestipol (bile acid-binding resins, used to lower cholesterol) can interfere with absorption of folate, alongside the fat-soluble vitamins A, D and K. Anyone taking one of these medicines long-term should ask their doctor or pharmacist whether their folate intake needs attention.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for folate status usually reports serum folate (deficiency indicated below roughly 10 nmol/L) or the more stable red-blood-cell folate (deficiency indicated below roughly 340 nmol/L).
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat leafy greens, citrus fruit, beans and nuts regularly - and still keep a separate, reliable B12 source alongside them.
gaps: A real randomized controlled trial (folic acid plus zinc supplementation in men undergoing infertility treatment) found no meaningful effect on semen quality or live birth rate, cited to Schisterman EF, et al., JAMA, 2020 - worth keeping in mind if a claim about folic acid and male fertility ever needs checking, though this single trial does not settle the question on its own.

The food-content gram/mcg figures sourced from book-encyclopedia-of-diets (a pre-2015 reference encyclopedia, author unstated) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

The 4 mg/day higher-dose folic acid figure for women with a previous neural-tube-defect-affected pregnancy remains HELD (not used anywhere in this card) pending a primary clinical-guideline source (NICE, ACOG or ICMR-NIN directly) - see candidateAdditions.

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): no primary citation was actually attached to this specific line in the source, which is disqualifying on its own for a pregnancy dose. Needs a primary clinical-guideline source (NICE, ACOG, or ICMR-NIN directly) before use.
candidateAdditions.text: For women with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, the usual recommended dose is higher than the standard preconception amount - 4 mg/day, starting one month before conception and continuing for the first three months of the next pregnancy. This is a specific higher-risk-group figure, separate from the standard 400 mcg/day preconception amount already in this card, and should only be followed under a doctor's guidance.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

nutrients.name: Iodine

whatItDoes.text: Needed to make thyroid hormones, which control metabolism. Especially important for bone and brain development in pregnancy and infancy.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

veganContext.text: NIH states plainly that people on a vegan diet, or who eat little or no dairy, seafood or eggs, might not get enough iodine.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Vegan-friendly sources: iodised salt and sea vegetables (seaweed). Processed foods rarely use iodised salt, and speciality salts (sea salt, kosher, Himalayan) usually are not iodised, so check the label.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A simple everyday way to work seaweed in: a small daily pinch of kelp added to a salad.
veganContext.label: illustration

veganContext.text: Iodised salt gives roughly 77 mcg of iodine per gram, or about 400 mcg per teaspoon. Kelp is highly variable but one source gives roughly 415 mcg per quarter cup (wet weight), and dried seaweed can carry up to 18,000 mcg per ounce - a huge range that shows why 'a bit of seaweed' is a poor way to judge iodine intake compared with iodised salt or a labelled supplement.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Soy foods and cruciferous vegetables (like cabbage and cauliflower) contain compounds that can mildly reduce iodine uptake if someone's iodine intake is already only just enough - this is a reason to make sure a reliable iodine source (iodised salt or seaweed) is part of the regular diet, not a reason to avoid these foods.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Beyond soy and cruciferous vegetables, flaxseed, millet, sorghum, cassava and lima beans also interact with iodine/thyroid metabolism. As with soy and cruciferous vegetables, the practical takeaway is the same: this is a reason to make sure a reliable iodine source is part of the regular diet, not a reason to avoid these foods (several of which, like flaxseed, this project separately recommends for other nutrients).
absorptionTips.label: open question

absorptionTips.text: Canola oil, turnips and peanuts also contain goitrogens, substances that can interfere with the body's ability to absorb or use iodine, alongside broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts already noted above - these foods should not cause iodine deficiency unless they become the mainstay of a very limited diet.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Selenium deficiency makes the effects of iodine deficiency worse, and vitamin A deficiency may also worsen iodine deficiency. This is a reason iodine should not be thought of in isolation - a varied vegan diet that also covers selenium (nuts and seeds) and vitamin A (leafy greens and orange vegetables) supports healthy thyroid function overall, not iodine intake alone.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Too much iodine (from supplements or concentrated seaweed) can itself cause goitre or thyroid problems. See a doctor before taking an iodine or kelp supplement, especially with thyroid disease or antithyroid medicine.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Iodine and iodine-containing supplements (like kelp) can interact with several medicines - including amiodarone, lithium, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics and antithyroid drugs. Anyone taking these should check with their doctor before adding an iodine or seaweed supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Long-standing, more severe iodine deficiency can cause a goitre (a visible swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck) alongside memory and language changes; in children, IQ can be affected, and some effects can be reversed in children (not adults) once iodine intake improves. One extra nuance worth knowing: in an adult who already has a goitre, suddenly increasing iodine intake can occasionally push the thyroid to overdrive (hyperthyroidism) instead of helping - so anyone who already has a goitre or known thyroid condition should talk to their doctor before significantly changing iodine intake, rather than assuming 'more is always better.'
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: Thyroid function is usually checked with a TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) blood test; this reflects thyroid status rather than iodine intake directly.
whenToTest.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: Besides the TSH blood test, a 24-hour urinary iodine test is the WHO-standardised way to check iodine intake adequacy specifically (as opposed to thyroid function itself) - this is a research/clinical tool more than a routine test an individual would ask for, but worth knowing it exists.
whenToTest.label: open question
