candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): hold until someone reads the actual papers directly, not just Fuhrman's citation of them; then they can likely sit as a second citation next to NIH.
candidateAdditions.text: Two studies on iodine status specifically in vegetarians/vegans are cited for this topic in one of our cached books (not independently read by us - this is a secondary citation, flagged per BRIEF.md rule 10 rather than graded Strong on that basis alone): Krajcovicova-Kudlackova M, Buckova K, Klimes I, et al. 'Iodine deficiency in vegetarians and vegans.' Ann Nutr Metab. 2003;47:183-85; and Leung AM, Lamar A, He X, et al. 'Iodine status and thyroid function of Boston-area vegetarians and vegans.' J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2011;96:E1303-7. Worth a direct primary-source check before use as a citation beyond the existing NIH ODS statement.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying source before use (secondary citation, not independently verified) - not promoted this round for that reason. A new caution not yet in the cautions field above.
candidateAdditions.text: Beyond the risk of too much iodine itself, regularly eating sea vegetables also raises a separate question of heavy-metal contamination, since seaweed can absorb heavy metals from seawater. A reliable iodine supplement sidesteps both the overconsumption risk and this contamination question at once.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.oneLineAction: Use iodised salt and include a vegan iodine source like seaweed regularly, since few other plant foods carry reliable iodine.
gaps: No source found for a specific coverage of iodine content in common Indian sea vegetables (e.g. kelp bought locally) - flagged for the Foods module rather than invented here.

nutrients.name: Iron

whatItDoes.text: Makes haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells, and myoglobin, which supplies oxygen to muscles.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.note: Owner's decision, 21 Oct 2026: use ICMR-NIN's figure as-is, not NIH's general-population 8 mg/day doubled again for vegetarians - ICMR-NIN's RDA is already derived from a largely plant-based Indian diet, so re-doubling it would likely overstate the target.

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.note: Same owner's decision as for men: ICMR-NIN's Indian-diet-adjusted figure used as-is.

veganContext.text: NIH states explicitly that vegetarians who eat no meat, poultry or seafood need almost twice the standard iron amount, because the body absorbs nonheme (plant) iron less well than heme (animal) iron.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Good plant iron sources: iron-fortified cereals and breads, white beans, lentils, spinach, kidney beans, peas, nuts and dried fruit such as raisins.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Pair iron-rich plant foods with a vitamin C food in the same meal - citrus fruits, strawberries, peppers, tomatoes or broccoli - to boost how much nonheme iron the body absorbs. See this project's own vitamin C nutrient card for vitamin C's daily target and food sources in full - this is the main cross-reference that card exists for.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Tannins in tea reduce nonheme iron absorption; having tea between meals rather than with them helps iron-rich meals absorb better.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Fermenting or sprouting grains and legumes can improve how available their iron is.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Reversing iron-deficiency anaemia, once it has developed, is a slow process - typically three to six months - a useful timeframe for a worried reader wondering why their levels haven't improved immediately after changing diet or starting a supplement.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Iron supplements can cause stomach upset or constipation at normal doses, and are dangerous in overdose, especially for young children - keep them well out of reach. People with hereditary haemochromatosis should avoid extra iron and vitamin C supplements. Calcium can interfere with iron absorption if taken at the same time.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: Iron status is usually checked with a full blood count and ferritin (the body's iron-storage protein) level.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Pair lentils, beans or fortified cereal with a vitamin C food at the same meal, and keep tea away from mealtimes.
gaps: NIH's separate general-population figures (8 mg/day men, 18 mg/day women) are not shown above, since the owner decided (21 Oct 2026) to use ICMR-NIN's Indian-diet-adjusted RDA as-is rather than re-apply NIH's vegetarian doubling on top of it.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. An upgrade to the existing whenToTest entry, with specific normal ranges and how they shift across the three stages of iron depletion.
candidateAdditions.text: A fuller iron panel (beyond the full blood count and ferritin level already noted) can include transferrin, transferrin saturation and total iron-binding capacity. As iron reserves run low, the first change is a drop in ferritin alone (normal roughly 12-35 ng/mL) with everything else still normal; next, transferrin and iron-binding capacity rise while serum iron and transferrin saturation fall (still no anaemia yet); only once this progresses further does haemoglobin itself drop (normal roughly 12-15.5 g/dL for women, 13.5-17.5 g/dL for men) to confirm iron-deficiency anaemia. This staged picture can help explain why a normal haemoglobin result does not always rule out low iron reserves.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Adds specific risk-factor nuance relevant to active/athletic vegan readers, not yet in this card.
candidateAdditions.text: Athletes and active people face several compounding iron-deficiency risk factors that can stack with being vegetarian/vegan: being female (iron lost through menstruation), being on an energy-restricted diet, being an adolescent (rapid growth increases iron needs), and altitude training (increases red blood cell production). A vegetarian or vegan athlete who is also female, growing, or dieting for weight may be at meaningfully higher combined risk than the general vegan-diet caution alone suggests - worth a doctor's attention rather than assuming diet alone explains any fatigue.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article in The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets (2008) - flagged pre-2015, recheck against current absorption-science consensus before use. Quantifies why nonheme (plant) iron needs are higher, which backs up the existing NIH-sourced veganContext line about vegetarians needing almost double the iron.
candidateAdditions.text: Of the iron in food generally, only about 10-20% is absorbed. Heme (animal) iron absorbs at roughly 20-25%; nonheme (plant) iron absorbs at only roughly 2-10%, and its absorption is much more affected by what else is eaten at the same meal. This is the underlying reason vegetarians and vegans are advised to pay closer attention to pairing iron-rich plant foods with absorption-boosting foods.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Expands the existing absorptionTips, which currently only names tea tannins - adds dairy, eggs, soy protein and chocolate as other absorption inhibitors, and organic acids (beyond vitamin C) as enhancers. The soy-protein point is worth a vegan reader knowing, since tofu/soy milk are common vegan staples - framed as a reason to still include a vitamin C food at the same meal, not a reason to avoid soy.
candidateAdditions.text: Besides tea, coffee, dairy products, eggs, soy protein and some chocolate can also reduce how much nonheme iron the body absorbs from a meal when eaten at the same time. Vitamin C and other organic acids (such as those in citrus, tomatoes and other acidic fruits) increase nonheme iron absorption. This is a reason to pair iron-rich plant foods with a vitamin C food at the meal where iron matters most, rather than worrying about any single food in isolation.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A caution not yet in this card - relevant to the Life stages module's older-adults section too (cross-referenced in the Life stages findings handoff file), and reinforces this card's existing 51y+ lower RDA by explaining why. No dosing given; framed as 'talk to your doctor' per BRIEF.md Safety rule 3.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that men and women over about 55 are generally not at risk of iron deficiency, and advises they should only take an iron-containing multivitamin on their doctor's instruction, not by default - because excess iron carries its own risks. Pregnant women are advised to discuss any iron supplement with their healthcare provider rather than starting one on their own.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015, medicine interactions can change so recheck before publishing). Expands the existing cautions entry (which already names calcium) with further interactions - no dosing given, framed as 'talk to your doctor'.
candidateAdditions.text: Besides calcium, iron absorption can also be affected by antacids and acid-reducing medicines (such as cimetidine or ranitidine), pancreatic enzyme supplements, and copper. Iron supplements can also change how well some other prescription medicines work. Anyone starting an iron supplement should review their other medicines with a doctor or pharmacist.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015, recheck exact mg figures against USDA FoodData Central before use). Only vegan-compatible foods pulled from this source's nonheme-iron table - its separate heme-iron table (chicken liver, beef, turkey, oysters, shrimp, tuna, halibut, crab, pork loin) was excluded entirely per BRIEF.md's strictly-vegan rules. Adds specific numbers this card's existing veganContext entries (food names only, no amounts) do not currently have.
candidateAdditions.text: Approximate iron content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: iron-fortified cereal, 1 cup, about 18 mg; boiled soybeans, 1 cup, about 8.8 mg; firm tofu, half cup, about 6.2 mg; cooked kidney beans, 1 cup, about 5.2 mg; cooked lima beans, 1 cup, about 4.5 mg; cooked pinto beans, 1 cup, about 3.6 mg; blackstrap molasses, 1 tbsp, about 3.5 mg; a medium potato with skin, about 2.75 mg; cashew nuts, 1 oz, about 1.7 mg; whole wheat bread, 1 slice, about 0.9 mg; raisins, a small 1.5oz box, about 0.9 mg.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Iron article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A calm, non-alarming symptom list for the 'quietly worried' reader - written as information, not a diagnostic checklist, with a clear doctor line kept.
candidateAdditions.text: Possible signs of iron-deficiency anaemia include ongoing tiredness, feeling weak, feeling cold often, getting more infections than usual, irritability, lower performance at work or school, and a sore, swollen tongue. An unusual craving to eat non-food items like dirt or clay (called pica) is a less common but specific sign. These symptoms have many possible causes - see a doctor for a blood test rather than assuming iron is the cause.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified accurate by independent review against book-eating-well-for-optimum-health p.141 (exact match). KEPT HELD, not merged into any live field - no specific citation was given for this exact claim in the source text, so per BRIEF.md rule 10 it stays an open question on file rather than a reader-facing line, even though it's an interesting reframing worth knowing about for the long-time-vegan reader (Vegan Reader Walkthrough persona 2).
candidateAdditions.text: This source notes that vegetarians tend to have slightly lower iron and haemoglobin levels than meat eaters, but observes that some experts think this difference may actually correlate with a LOWER risk of cardiovascular disease, reasoning that it reduces exposure to iron's own pro-oxidant (cell-damaging) effects in the body. This reframes the usual 'vegetarians need more iron' caution as not purely a downside - though it should not be read as a reason to ignore iron status, since iron-deficiency anaemia itself is still a real risk this card already covers.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified accurate by independent review against book-nutrition-enhanced-sports-performance p.107 (exact match, including the anaemia-recovery timeframe, which has been separately merged into absorptionTips above). KEPT HELD, not merged into dailyRangeByGroup: this source's doubled figures (14 mg/day men, 32 mg/day premenopausal women) differ from both NIH's general-population figures and the ICMR-NIN RDA this card already uses as-is per the owner's 21 Oct 2026 decision - shown here as a documented conflict/alternative figure per BRIEF.md rule 6, not adopted in place of the existing dailyRangeByGroup values. Full citation [20] still not independently read - flagged pre-2015 (2013) per rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that nonathletic vegetarians are advised to take in roughly double the standard iron amount - approximately 14 mg/day for adult men and 32 mg/day for premenopausal women - and suggests vegetarian athletes, who lose more iron through training, may benefit from even more than this.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Magnesium

whatItDoes.text: Important for many processes in the body, including regulating muscle and nerve function, blood sugar levels and blood pressure, and making protein, bone and DNA.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian men (440 mg/day) is somewhat higher than NIH's US figure (400-420 mg/day). Both shown rather than merged into one number.

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian women (370 mg/day) is notably higher than NIH's US figure (310-320 mg/day).

veganContext.text: Magnesium's main food sources are already vegan staples: legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains, and green leafy vegetables (such as spinach), plus fortified breakfast cereals and other fortified foods. NIH does not name vegans or vegetarians as a specific at-risk group - the groups it names (men over 70, teenage girls and boys generally, people with GI diseases, type 2 diabetes, or long-term alcoholism) are general-population risk groups, not vegan-specific ones.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A separate general food-health reference independently gives a closely matching adult RDA by age band (400 mg for men 19-30y, 420 mg for men 31+; 310 mg for women 19-30y, 320 mg for women 31+) and names a similar vegan-compatible food list - leafy green vegetables, legumes, whole grain cereals and breads, and nuts (its meat/poultry/fish/egg entries from the same table are excluded here per this project's strictly-vegan rules).
veganContext.label: established fact

cautions.text: Magnesium naturally present in food and beverages is not harmful and does not need to be limited - in healthy people, the kidneys clear any excess in urine. Magnesium from dietary supplements and medications should not exceed the upper limit unless a health care provider recommends it, because the limit only covers supplement/medication magnesium, not food: 350 mg/day for adults and children 9-18y, 110 mg/day for children 4-8y, 65 mg/day for children 1-3y (not established for infants under 1).
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: High intakes of magnesium from dietary supplements and medications can cause diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal cramping. Extremely high intakes can lead to irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Magnesium supplements can interact with several medicines: bisphosphonates (used for osteoporosis) and antibiotics are not well absorbed if taken too soon before or after a high-magnesium supplement; diuretics can either increase or decrease magnesium loss through urine depending on type; long-term use of prescription acid-reflux or peptic-ulcer drugs can cause low blood magnesium; and very high-dose zinc supplements can interfere with the body's ability to absorb and regulate magnesium. Anyone taking these should mention their magnesium intake to their doctor or pharmacist.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: The elderly are named as most at risk of low magnesium levels, since magnesium absorption decreases and excretion increases with age. As of the source's own 2007 review, no studies recommended magnesium supplementation specifically for preventing or treating osteoporosis, despite magnesium's general role in bone health - worth knowing so this card does not overstate what a magnesium supplement can do for bone health specifically.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Abnormally high blood magnesium (hypermagnesemia) is rare and mainly occurs with severe (end-stage) kidney failure or overdose of magnesium-containing intravenous fluids - symptoms include exhaustion, low blood pressure, a depressed heart and breathing rate, and slow reflexes. Abnormally low blood magnesium (hypomagnesemia) is most common among people with alcoholism, severe malnutrition, or digestive disorders that interfere with magnesium absorption - symptoms include vomiting, weight loss, leg cramps, muscle spasms, seizures and irregular heartbeat. These are general clinical causes, not specific to diet or to vegans.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: For people who form calcium-oxalate kidney stones specifically: magnesium forms a soluble complex with oxalate and may help reduce oxalate absorption, giving it a possible protective role - this mechanism is corroborated by two independent sources. A specific supplement dose (magnesium oxide, 400 mg/day) has been suggested for this purpose in one source, but that figure is not independently verified and is deliberately not repeated here - see the Kidney health topic's own candidateAdditions, where it remains held pending a direct check against NIH or another Strong source. Anyone considering a magnesium supplement for kidney stone prevention should do so under a doctor's guidance, not by self-dosing from this mechanism alone.
cautions.label: illustration

whenToTest.text: A blood test for magnesium status usually reports serum magnesium; normal levels are approximately 1.7 to 2.5 mEq/L, though only around 70% of serum magnesium is free/active, the rest bound to protein and inactive. There is no standard screening recommendation for healthy people without symptoms or a risk factor noted above.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Include legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains and leafy greens regularly - an ordinary varied vegan diet usually covers magnesium well.
gaps: NIH does not name vegetarians or vegans as a magnesium risk group anywhere in its consumer fact sheet - this card exists because magnesium is a genuinely common general-population shortfall and a real cross-reference for kidney-stone content, not because vegans specifically fall short.
The magnesium-oxide 400 mg/day kidney-stone dose remains unverified and intentionally not used in this card - see the Kidney health topic's candidateAdditions for its Gate 2 status.

nutrients.name: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)

whatItDoes.text: Builds healthy cell membranes, especially in the retina, brain and sperm cells. ALA is an essential fat the body cannot make itself.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

veganContext.text: ALA comes from plant foods (flaxseed, chia, walnuts, soybean and canola oils). EPA and DHA mainly come from fish, but the body converts only a small amount of ALA into EPA/DHA, so ALA alone may not match what a fish-eater gets.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Algal oil, made directly from algae, is explicitly named by NIH as the vegetarian/vegan source of ready-made EPA and DHA - the same compounds fish get from eating algae.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: An algae-based DHA/EPA supplement is a reasonable option in pregnancy; discuss it with a doctor.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Approximate ALA amounts per everyday portion, cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central's SR Legacy dataset: flaxseed (1 tbsp, ~10.3 g) gives roughly 1.7-2.3 g ALA; flax oil (1 tsp, ~4.5 g) gives roughly 2.2-2.4 g; walnuts (12 halves, ~24 g) give roughly 2-2.2 g - all a reasonably close match between the two sources. (Green soybeans and tofu figures from the same original table diverged substantially from USDA's own data - roughly 4-5x higher than USDA's figure for the same portions - and are held back from this card rather than used, since USDA SR Legacy does not separately break out ALA for those two foods, only a combined fatty-acid total used as an imperfect stand-in for the comparison.)
veganContext.label: illustration

veganContext.text: Diets have shifted from roughly an even (1:1) balance of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids to around 10:1 in a typical modern diet, according to research cited in one source - omega-3 fats are anti-inflammatory while excess omega-6 tends to promote inflammation, so an over-supply of omega-6 can blunt some of omega-3's benefit. Some experts suggest a ratio of one to four times more omega-6 than omega-3 is more reasonable. Vegan omega-6-rich foods (sunflower seeds and oil, corn oil, soybean oil, sesame oil, pecans, pine nuts, wheat germ oil) are healthy in moderation, but worth balancing with regular omega-3 sources (flaxseed, chia, walnuts) rather than relying heavily on omega-6-rich oils alone.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Ground flaxseed and chia give ALA more reliably than whole seeds, which can pass through the gut undigested.
absorptionTips.label: illustration

cautions.text: The American Heart Association does not recommend omega-3 supplements for people without high cardiovascular risk; for people with heart disease, guidance is around 1 g/day EPA+DHA under medical advice. High doses may increase bleeding risk with blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin. Talk to your doctor before starting a high-dose supplement.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Anyone planning to take more than 3 grams/day of omega-3 fatty acids in supplement form (such as a vegan algal-oil supplement) should get their doctor's approval first, for the same bleeding-risk reason already noted in this card's caution about blood-thinning medicines.
cautions.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Have ground flaxseed, chia or walnuts most days for ALA, and consider a vegan algal-oil supplement for a direct EPA/DHA source.
gaps: No official RDA exists for EPA/DHA specifically (only ALA has a set daily range) - NIH is explicit about this, so no EPA/DHA gram target is stated here rather than estimated.
No source found for an older-adult-specific ALA daily range beyond the general adult figure.

Green soybean and tofu ALA figures from book-eat-to-live diverged substantially (roughly 4-5x) from USDA FoodData Central's own data and are deliberately not used anywhere in this card - see candidateAdditions history for the comparison.

candidateAdditions.status: MERGED/ACTIONED (2 Nov 2026) - Life stages Gate 1 draft for pregnancy-breastfeeding now underway. Independently re-verified: found a genuinely separate international multi-society consensus statement (Koletzko et al. 2008, World Association of Perinatal Medicine working group, Journal of Perinatal Medicine - new source koletzko-dha-pregnancy-lactation-consensus-2008) reaching the same 'at least 200 mg/day DHA' figure for pregnant and lactating women, independent of this book. Used in drafts/life_stages/pregnancy-breastfeeding.json's whatToFocusOn field, cited to both book-the-nutritionist and the new Koletzko consensus source together with nih-omega3 for the algal-DHA vegan-source point. Originally GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) via independent review against book-the-nutritionist p.325 (exact match), sanity-checked as a clinically plausible dose, not a unit-slip (unlike this project's earlier 45mg/day K2 and '5mg/day' B12 extraction errors). Pre-2015 (2009) per rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: This source recommends pregnant and lactating women get at least 200 mg/day of DHA, linking adequate DHA intake in pregnancy/lactation to a healthier pregnancy length and, in one citation it references without giving the study details in the text captured, better cognitive development assessed at age 4. It explicitly names an algal-oil DHA supplement with a vegetarian pill coating as the option for vegetarian women who do not want a fish-oil source - consistent with, and specific enough to extend, this card's existing general 'algae-based DHA/EPA supplement is a reasonable option in pregnancy' line.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Potassium

whatItDoes.text: Needed for almost everything the body does, including proper kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve transmission.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Potassium's main food sources overlap heavily with everyday vegan staples: fruits (dried apricots, prunes, raisins, orange juice, bananas), vegetables (acorn squash, potatoes, spinach, tomatoes, broccoli), and lentils, kidney beans, soybeans and nuts. This is not a nutrient vegans are specifically short on - NIH names most people in general (diet-pattern-wide, not vegan-specific) as falling below the recommended amount, mainly because of low fruit and vegetable intake overall.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A separate general food-health reference independently gives a very similar adult target (4,700 mg/day, not split by sex) and names a closely matching vegan-compatible food list - avocados, bananas, citrus and dried fruits, legumes, many vegetables, and whole grain products (its dairy-product entry from the same table is excluded here per this project's strictly-vegan rules). It also independently confirms that no upper limit is established for potassium, matching this card's existing NIH-sourced point.
veganContext.label: established fact

cautions.text: ACE inhibitors (e.g. benazepril/Lotensin) and ARBs (e.g. losartan/Cozaar), and potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. amiloride/Midamor, spironolactone/Aldactone), all reduce how much potassium is lost in urine and can push blood potassium too high (hyperkalemia) - especially with existing kidney problems. This can happen even at an ordinary dietary potassium intake, not just from supplements. Anyone on these medicines should ask their doctor before increasing potassium intake or using a potassium-based salt substitute.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide/Lasix, bumetanide/Bumex) and thiazide diuretics (e.g. chlorothiazide/Diuril, metolazone/Zaroxolyn) increase potassium lost in urine and can cause abnormally low blood potassium (hypokalemia) instead. Talk to a doctor about monitoring if taking these.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: People with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are a specific exception to potassium's general food-tier/green status: a damaged kidney struggles to clear potassium, so CKD management often means limiting high-potassium plant foods rather than favouring them. This is a condition-specific caution, not a general vegan one - see the Kidney health topic for detail.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Hypokalemia (low blood potassium) caused by loop or thiazide diuretics can increase the risk of digoxin toxicity in people also taking digoxin (a heart medicine). Anyone on both a diuretic and digoxin should have their potassium levels monitored by their doctor, not managed by diet changes alone.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: For CKD specifically, dried beans and peas, nuts, and several whole grains (amaranth, brown rice, millet, oats, quinoa, spelt) are 'double trouble' foods - high in both potassium and phosphorus, which a damaged kidney struggles to clear. Suggested swaps for someone managing CKD: green beans or wax beans instead of dried beans or peas, and lower-potassium/phosphorus whole grains such as barley, buckwheat, bulgur, popcorn or wild rice.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Potassium is an ingredient in many salt substitutes used to replace table salt. People with kidney disease, or who take the medicines named above, should talk to their health care provider before using them, since these products could push potassium levels too high.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Beyond medicines and CKD, hyperkalemia (too much blood potassium) can also result from severe burns or injury (potassium released from injured cells), inadequate adrenal hormones (Addison's disease), and excessive use of potassium supplements - symptoms include nausea, diarrhoea, weakness, muscle pain and irregular heartbeat, and severe cases can be life-threatening. Hypokalemia (too little) can also result from excess adrenal hormones (Cushing's disease), long-term diuretic use, laxative abuse or bulimia - symptoms include increased urine production, muscle pain, paralysis and irregular heartbeat. These are general clinical causes, not specific to diet or to vegans, but useful context for why a doctor manages potassium imbalance rather than diet alone.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: For CKD patients who want to eat certain high-potassium vegetables anyway, one specific preparation method ('leaching') can remove some of the potassium: repeatedly rinsing and boiling the vegetable in a large amount of water (the exact method varies by vegetable). This is a CKD-specific technique, not a general vegan cooking tip, and does not replace a renal dietician's guidance.
cautions.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat fruit, vegetables, beans and lentils regularly - an ordinary varied vegan diet usually covers potassium well, unless a doctor has said otherwise because of kidney disease or a medicine you take.
gaps: ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA brief note (the project's primary Indian reference) has no potassium value at all - checked directly against both the male and female nutrient tables, confirmed absent (it covers calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc, iodine, B-vitamins, vitamin A/C/D, nothing else). NIH's AI figures above are currently the only daily-target source on file for this card.

No tolerable upper limit (UL) is set for potassium by NIH - excess is eliminated in urine in people with normal kidney function, so this card has no UL field content, unlike most other nutrient cards. A second, independent source (book-foods-that-harm-and-heal) confirms this 'not established' status.

nutrients.name: Protein

whatItDoes.text: Protein is made of amino acids, the building blocks for muscles, bones and skin. Nine amino acids are 'essential' - the body cannot make them, so they must come from food.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 0.8 g/kg body weight/day (about 0.36 g per pound)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 54.0 g/day (RDA), 42.9 g/day (EAR), for a 65 kg reference body weight
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 45.7 g/day (RDA), 36.3 g/day (EAR), for a 55 kg reference body weight
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: about 70 g/day total (around 0.5 g/lb body weight) by PCRM's figure; +17.6 to +22.0 g/day on top of the adult EAR/RDA by ICMR-NIN's 2020 figure
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: PCRM's absolute target (~70 g/day) and ICMR-NIN's add-on figure land in a broadly similar range once added to the Indian adult RDA, but the two sources frame it differently (a US total vs an Indian EAR/RDA addition) - shown separately rather than merged into one number.

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: protein needs similar to later pregnancy, per PCRM; ICMR-NIN 2020 adds +13.6 to +16.9 g/day (0-6 months) and +10.6 to +13.2 g/day (6-12 months) to the adult EAR/RDA
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: approx. 1.3-1.8 g/kg/day - about 10% more than the equivalent omnivore-athlete target, to offset the somewhat lower digestibility of some plant protein sources
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Plant foods provide all nine essential amino acids, in varying amounts. Vegetarians and vegans meet or exceed their protein needs at every life stage on a well-planned diet.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Beans and rice do not need to be eaten at the exact same meal - a varied mix of plant foods across the day covers essential amino acid needs.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: The 'incomplete protein, must combine plant proteins' idea traces largely to a popular 1970s book, Frances Moore Lappe's Diet for a Small Planet, which described animal protein as 'complete' and plant protein as 'incomplete', suggesting conscious same-meal 'protein combining'. Research has since discredited the idea that plant protein is incomplete or less valuable - the body can draw on amino acids from the digestive tract's own bacteria and shed cells over the course of a day, so meals do not need to be consciously combined.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Legumes (beans, lentils, dried peas, soy) are the richest plant protein group; whole grains, seeds, nuts and some vegetables also contribute. For example, half a katori (about 1/2 cup) of cooked lentils or beans gives roughly 7-9 g protein, and the same amount of firm tofu gives roughly 15-23 g.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Clinical trials matching protein intake and training found plant protein (soy-matched) builds muscle as well as animal or whey protein.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Include a protein source at each meal and most snacks, and eat a variety across the day - beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, nut or seed butter.
absorptionTips.label: official recommendation

absorptionTips.text: The traditional Indian dal with rice or roti combination is a practical way to combine a legume with a grain across a meal.
absorptionTips.label: illustration

cautions.text: A diet based mainly on low-quality cereal protein (rather than a mix including pulses) needs a higher total protein intake to meet needs - ICMR-NIN's own guidance recommends a cereal:legume:milk-equivalent ratio of about 3:1:2.5 for good protein quality; for vegans, replace the milk-equivalent share with soy or other pulses and fortified foods.
cautions.label: official recommendation

nutrients.oneLineAction: Include a katori of beans, lentils, tofu or tempeh at most meals, alongside grains, rather than relying on one single food for protein.
gaps: No source found for a protein figure specific to older vegan adults beyond the general adult RDA.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Not a new fact - a documented conflict worth knowing about, to understand why some other sources (including some readers' doctors or trainers) may still repeat the older 'must combine' framing.
candidateAdditions.text: Two older academic textbooks reviewed in this project (Nutrition and Diet Therapy, 2010, and Nutrition for Sport, Exercise and Performance) still teach the pre-2000s 'incomplete/limiting plant protein, must combine complementary proteins' framing that the IOM and this project's lead pregnancy-nutrition source (the Handbook of Nutrition and Pregnancy chapter, citing the IOM directly) have since superseded - the IOM's own conclusion is that vegetarian protein requirements eating a variety of plant proteins are not different from non-vegetarians, and conscious same-meal combining is not necessary. This project's existing content already reflects the newer, IOM-backed position; this entry is flagged mainly so the conflict with older sources is documented, not silently papered over.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a Strong-source check on the leucine/sarcopenia mechanism before use. Relevant to the not-yet-started Life stages module's older-adults section too.
candidateAdditions.text: As people age, the body becomes less efficient at using dietary protein to maintain muscle (a change sometimes called 'anabolic resistance'), and older adults need somewhat more total protein than they did when younger. One source raises a specific concern for older vegans: beans are relatively low in leucine, an amino acid particularly important for triggering muscle protein synthesis, compared to animal protein or certain plant sources. This is presented in the source as a reason older vegans may struggle to maintain muscle on a bean-heavy diet - but the same source doesn't address that soy, lentils and quinoa are comparatively higher-leucine plant options, so this reads as a solvable nuance (vary plant protein sources, not a reason to add animal protein) rather than a vegan-specific dead end. Held as an open question pending that mechanism being checked against a Strong source.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Protein article in The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets (2008) - flagged pre-2015. This is a THIRD book in this project repeating the same outdated 'must combine' framing already documented in this card's first candidateAdditions entry above (Nutrition and Diet Therapy, 2010, and Nutrition for Sport, Exercise and Performance) - added here rather than merged into that entry so each source is traceable, but it is the same conflict, not a new one. This source is even more specific/dated than the other two: it names a precise four-hour combining window.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that animal proteins (meat, poultry, fish, milk, egg, cheese) are 'complete' because they supply all essential amino acids, while plant proteins are 'incomplete', and that combining incomplete plant proteins to get all essential amino acids 'must be consumed at the same time, or within a short period of time (within four hours)' to get the full nutritive value. This directly conflicts with this project's existing, newer IOM-backed position already reflected elsewhere in this card (conscious same-meal combining is not necessary) - flagged per BRIEF.md rule 6 as a conflict to be aware of, not acted on, since the newer position is already the one this project follows.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Protein article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015, recheck exact gram figures against USDA FoodData Central before use). Only vegan-compatible foods pulled from this source's protein-content table - hamburger, pork chop, beef, chicken, fish, tuna, oysters, yogurt, milk and cheese figures from the same table were excluded per BRIEF.md's strictly-vegan rules. FLAGGING A REAL CONFLICT per BRIEF.md rule 6: this source's tofu figure (10.1 g per half cup) is notably lower than this card's existing vndpg-protein-sourced figure (roughly 15-23 g per half cup) - plausibly reflecting a softer/less-dense tofu type here versus firm tofu in the existing figure, but not confirmed; shown as a range note rather than silently picking one number.
candidateAdditions.text: Approximate protein content of some vegan foods, per typical serving, from this source: tofu, half cup, about 10.1 g (note: this project's existing tofu figure elsewhere is 15-23 g per half cup for firm tofu specifically - the gap is likely a tofu-firmness difference, not confirmed); cooked lentils, half cup, about 9.0 g; cooked kidney beans, 1 cup, about 7.6 g; soy milk, 1 cup, about 6.7 g; peanut butter, 1 tbsp, about 4.6 g; a medium baked potato, about 3.0 g; whole wheat bread, 1 slice, about 2.7 g; pecans, 1 oz, about 2.2 g.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified accurate by independent review against book-the-nutritionist pp.147-150. KEPT HELD, not merged into any reader-facing field: a FOURTH book in this project repeating some version of the protein-combining framing (after Nutrition and Diet Therapy 2010, Nutrition for Sport/Exercise/Performance, and Encyclopedia of Diets 2008), same documented-conflict pattern as the existing entries above, not a new conflict - kept here as a traceable record, consistent with how the Encyclopedia of Diets entry was also kept separate rather than merged. Notably softer than the Encyclopedia of Diets version (no four-hour window; same-day combining is called 'fine' for less restrictive vegetarians, with same/adjacent-meal combining called merely 'best', not required, even for strict vegans with lower protein intake) - flagged pre-2015 (2009) per BRIEF.md rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: This source frames plant proteins as 'incomplete' (one or more limiting amino acids) and recommends combining complementary plant foods - legumes with grains (rice and beans, hummus, peanut butter on whole-grain bread), or legumes with nuts/seeds - calling this 'best' done within the same or adjacent meals for strict vegetarians/vegans with lower overall protein intake, but saying same-day combining is fine for less restrictive vegetarians. Soy is noted as already a complete protein but still sometimes used in combining schemes since it is relatively low in lysine.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

nutrients.name: Selenium

whatItDoes.text: Needed for thyroid hormone production, reproduction, DNA building, and protecting cells against damage.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Breads, cereals, grains, beans, lentils and nuts all carry selenium - Brazil nuts are especially high, at roughly 68-91 mcg per nut.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: NIH flags that people eating mostly plant foods grown in low-selenium soil may be at risk, since a plant's selenium content depends on the soil it grew in - relevant for any strict plant-based diet depending on region.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate selenium content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: Brazil nuts, 1 oz, about 544 mcg (matches this card's existing 1-2-nuts-a-day guidance); enriched noodles, macaroni or white rice, 1 cup, about 10 mcg; brown rice, 1 cup, about 7 mcg; walnuts, 1 oz, about 5 mcg; oatmeal or bran, 1 cup, about 3-4 mcg; garlic, 1 oz, about 0.25 mcg. On absorption: one study cited in this source found the body absorbs only around 50% of selenium from yeast, compared with a much higher rate from fish - relevant because 'high-selenium yeast' (selenomethionine) is a common vegan-friendly supplement form, so it is worth knowing its absorption is not as efficient as the figure on the label alone might suggest.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Wheat germ, whole-wheat bread, bran, oats, turnips, brown rice and orange juice are separately named as everyday selenium food sources - a plain, vegan-compatible list that corroborates the Brazil-nut-and-grains picture already in this card.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Mushrooms are a notably selenium-dense vegan food: one source reports that a 5-ounce serving (dry weight before cooking) of cremini (white button) mushrooms gives more than 50% of the Daily Value for selenium, alongside other minerals - worth naming alongside Brazil nuts as a non-nut vegan selenium source.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A separate general food-reference table lists Brazil nuts and other nuts, whole grain products, onions, garlic, mushrooms and brown rice as selenium sources (its fish, seafood and organ-meat entries from the same table are excluded here per this project's strictly-vegan rules) - broadly consistent with, and a further independent confirmation of, the vegan selenium food sources already named in this card.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Selenium works alongside vitamin E as part of the body's antioxidant defences, and animal studies suggest selenium can offset some of the damage from vitamin E shortfall. A selenium-dependent enzyme (thioredoxin reductase) also helps maintain vitamin C's antioxidant action. Separately, selenium deficiency may worsen the effects of iodine deficiency on the thyroid - another reason a varied vegan diet covering several nutrients at once, not any single one, supports healthy thyroid and antioxidant function.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Selenium is separately confirmed as an antioxidant mineral that assists vitamin E's own antioxidant action in cell membranes and body fluids - the same pairing already noted above, corroborated independently by a second source.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: It is easy to get too much selenium from just a few Brazil nuts or a supplement. Excess causes garlic-smelling breath, metallic taste, hair loss and brittle nails; severe excess can affect organs. One to two Brazil nuts a day is usually plenty - avoid a handful daily plus a supplement at the same time.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A separate general food-reference table gives a tolerable upper intake level of about 400 mcg/day for selenium (adults), alongside an RDA of 55 mcg/day that matches NIH's own figure above - a useful specific ceiling to have alongside the qualitative excess-symptom caution already in this card.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Selenium has an unusually narrow safe range between too little and too much. Supplementing when selenium status is already adequate is specifically discouraged in clinical guidance, not just a matter of avoiding obvious excess symptoms - a blood test, not guesswork, is the way to know whether a supplement is actually needed.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: The anticonvulsant medicine valproic acid has been found to lower blood selenium levels. Anyone taking it should discuss their selenium status with their doctor.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for selenium status usually reports plasma selenium (roughly 60-120 mcg/L is considered an adequate range) or erythrocyte selenium (roughly 90-190 mcg/L).
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Have a Brazil nut or two most days, or a handful of mixed nuts and seeds, rather than relying on a supplement as well.
gaps: No Indian RDA figure for selenium found in the ICMR-NIN 2020 brief note (it was not included in the summary tables extracted) - only the NIH figures are shown here.
No source found confirming typical selenium levels in Indian soil/produce specifically - flagged rather than guessed.

nutrients.name: Vitamin A

whatItDoes.text: Supports vision, the immune system, reproduction, growth and the function of the heart, lungs and other organs.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: ICMR-NIN's figure is somewhat higher than NIH's; both shown rather than merged.

veganContext.text: Preformed vitamin A comes only from animal foods. The vegan-relevant pathway is provitamin A carotenoids (such as beta-carotene) from plant foods, which the body converts into vitamin A.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Rich plant sources: green leafy vegetables, carrots, sweet potatoes, broccoli, winter squash, cantaloupe, mango and apricot, plus fortified breakfast cereals.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: ICMR recommends everyone eat at least 300 g of vegetables a day (50 g green leafy, 200 g other vegetables, 50 g roots and tubers) plus 100 g of fresh fruit, which supplies much of this carotenoid intake in an Indian diet.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Strict vegans - especially vegan children - are named as one of the groups with a somewhat greater likelihood of vitamin A shortfall in industrialised countries, alongside people with certain gut conditions (Crohn's, coeliac disease), pancreas disorders, anorexia or alcoholism. This is specifically about people who do not regularly eat carotenoid-rich vegetables and fruits (not an inevitable risk of veganism itself) - a well-planned vegan diet with regular dark leafy greens and orange/yellow vegetables, as this card already recommends, covers vitamin A needs well.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate vitamin A (as provitamin A carotenoids) in some vegan foods, per typical serving: cooked spinach, half cup, about 11,460 IU; cooked kale, half cup, about 9,560 IU; one whole raw unpeeled carrot, about 8,670 IU; cantaloupe, 1 cup, about 5,410 IU; raw spinach, 1 cup, about 2,800 IU; papaya, 1 cup, about 1,530 IU; mango, 1 cup, about 1,260 IU; tomato juice, 6 oz, about 820 IU; vitamin-A-fortified breakfast cereal, 1 serving, about 500-770 IU. For reference, the conversion is 1 Retinol Activity Equivalent (RAE) = 12 mcg beta-carotene = 24 mcg of other provitamin A carotenoids = about 3 IU - useful context for why plant sources need a much larger gram amount than an animal-sourced retinol equivalent would.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Carotenoids absorb better from cooked or lightly oiled vegetables than raw, since they are fat-soluble - a little oil or ghee-alternative with a vegetable dish helps.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Beta-carotene from food or ordinary amounts is not dangerous in excess - at most it can turn skin yellow-orange, which is harmless and reversible. The one exception: in smokers, ex-smokers or people exposed to asbestos, high-dose beta-carotene supplements raise lung cancer risk. Preformed vitamin A supplements in pregnancy at high doses can cause birth defects - pregnant women should avoid high-dose preformed vitamin A supplements and check with a doctor before any vitamin A supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Vitamin A can interact with several medicines: it may enhance the blood-thinning effect of warfarin with long-term use (a bleeding-risk interaction worth flagging to a doctor); birth control pills raise blood vitamin A levels; cholesterol-lowering drugs and the weight-loss drug orlistat can reduce how much vitamin A the body absorbs; and regular alcohol use raises the risk of vitamin A excess by affecting the liver, where vitamin A is stored. Separately, because vitamin A excess can worsen bone loss, some researchers have linked high blood retinol levels to increased hip fracture risk in people over 50, and have questioned whether a standard multivitamin (often containing 5,000 IU, a dose based on an old 1968 RDA, well above today's RDA) is a good idea for people over 55 specifically because of this. This is about supplement/multivitamin use, not food - the vegan food sources already in this card's veganContext are not implicated.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Cholestyramine and colestipol (bile acid-binding resins, a specific type of cholesterol-lowering medicine) are named specifically as reducing absorption of vitamin A, alongside vitamin D, vitamin K and folate. Anyone on these particular medicines long-term should ask their doctor about their vitamin A status, rather than assuming all cholesterol-lowering drugs behave the same way.
cautions.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat a katori of dark leafy greens or orange/yellow vegetables most days, lightly cooked with a little oil.
gaps: The food-value IU figures sourced from book-encyclopedia-of-diets (a pre-2015 reference encyclopedia, author unstated) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

nutrients.name: Vitamin B12

whatItDoes.text: Keeps blood and nerve cells healthy and helps the body make DNA.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 2.4 mcg/day (NIH); 2.2 mcg/day (ICMR-NIN, same for men and women)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: NIH and ICMR-NIN figures are close but not identical (2.4 vs 2.2 mcg/day). Both shown; ask the owner which to lead with on the card.

veganContext.text: Vitamin B12 is made only by bacteria. It naturally occurs only in animal foods, so a vegan diet has no reliable natural source and needs a fortified food or supplement.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Good vegan sources: B12-fortified breakfast cereals, fortified plant milks, fortified nutritional yeast, or a B12 supplement.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: A literature review found B12 deficiency is common among vegetarians who do not have a reliable B12 source - consistent with, not a change to, this card's existing message that a vegan diet needs a planned fortified food or supplement.
veganContext.label: open question

absorptionTips.text: Older adults absorb B12 from food less well because of reduced stomach acid, so a supplement or fortified food is a more reliable route at any age on a vegan diet.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: The body stores years' worth of B12, so a shortfall can take a long time to show - this is a reason to start a reliable source early, not a reason to skip one.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Acid-reducing medicines (such as omeprazole or ranitidine) and the diabetes medicine metformin can lower B12 absorption or blood levels. Talk to your doctor if you take these long-term.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Large folate intakes can mask a B12 deficiency on some blood tests, without stopping the nerve damage it can still cause - another reason not to rely on diet alone for B12. See a doctor if you have persistent tiredness, tingling hands/feet, or memory problems.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: Serum B12 alone can miss some deficiencies; doctors sometimes also check methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, which are more sensitive to a true B12 shortfall.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Take a vitamin B12 supplement or have a reliable fortified food daily - this is the one nutrient every vegan needs a planned source for.
gaps: No source found for a specific older-adult (over 65) daily range beyond the general adult figure - NIH groups older adults with other adults at risk, but does not give a separate older-adult mcg/day target.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A real journal citation, but explicitly flagged by the source itself as insufficient evidence - worth having on file precisely so this project's own 'no reliable plant source' line doesn't get contradicted by a reader who's seen this claim elsewhere, without addressing it directly.
candidateAdditions.text: Nori (a sea vegetable) and shiitake mushrooms have sometimes been proposed as plant B12 sources, citing a real study: Watanabe F, Yabuta Y, Bito T, Teng F, 'Vitamin B12-Containing Plant Food Sources for Vegetarians,' Nutrients, 2014;6(5):1861-73. However, the source reviewing this (itself, not independently verified by us) concludes 'the available studies and literature are not sufficient to support this claim, so supplementation is strongly recommended' - i.e. even the source citing the study doesn't treat nori/shiitake as a reliable B12 source. This project's existing 'no reliable natural vegan source' line is NOT contradicted by this - if anything, it's reinforced by a source that could have claimed otherwise but didn't.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct check against the ADA's own published position paper before use - this is a secondary quotation of the ADA, not independently verified. If confirmed, this fills the exact gap already named in this card's own gaps field (no older-adult-specific B12 guidance found) - and is a universal recommendation (applies to everyone over 50, not just vegans), which may be worth a line of its own regardless of diet type.
candidateAdditions.text: A secondary source quotes the American Dietetic Association directly: 'The Institute of Medicine has recommended that all people over the age of 50, regardless of type of diet, take vitamin B12 in the form found in supplements and fortified foods for optimal absorption' - because absorption of the natural food-bound form of B12 declines with age (reduced stomach acid), regardless of whether someone eats animal products. The same quote gives a dosing figure, but the number came through the source's own text in a form that reads as a likely transcription error ('at least 5 mg' daily, alongside 'a weekly supplement of 2,000' with no unit given) - the figures don't make clinical sense as written (5 mg/day would be 5,000 mcg, an unusually large daily B12 dose) and are held back rather than repeated as stated, pending a direct check of the real ADA figure.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. INCIDENTAL FINDING: encountered while reading this book's dedicated Soy article in full (per this task's Priority 3 instructions) - the Spirulina entry begins on the very next page, and this specific point was too directly relevant to this card's safety message to leave uncaptured, even though reading the Spirulina article itself was not part of this task's assigned scope (noted transparently here so it isn't mistaken for a full Spirulina-article read). Parallels the existing nori/shiitake candidate above - another commonly-recommended 'vegan B12 source' that this source says does not actually work, worth having on file for the same reason.
candidateAdditions.text: Spirulina (blue-green algae, sold as a nutritional supplement) is often recommended as a vegan B12 source because it tests as high in B12 - but this source states that much of that B12 is in an analogue form the body cannot use, and that these unusable analogues may even block the active B12 the body gets from other, reliable sources. This directly reinforces this card's 'no reliable natural vegan source' line and 'take a planned B12 supplement or fortified food' action - spirulina should not be treated as a substitute for either.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From Krause's Food & Nutrition Therapy (2008), Chapter 10 'Nutrition in Aging' - read as part of the search for an older-adults Life-stages lead (see drafts/llamaparse_findings/krauses-nutrition-in-aging.md for the full chapter writeup; this was a fifth miss on vegan-specific content, but this one point independently backs an existing held candidate above). A cleaner citation chain (DGA 2005, via a credentialed clinical textbook) than the existing held Encyclopedia of Diets candidate above, though it gives no numeric dose either - useful to cross-reference both when resolving this card's gap, not to treat as a replacement.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that older adults are at risk of B12 deficiency both from low dietary intake and from declining stomach acid (which is needed to release B12 from food protein), and separately reports that the Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2005 recommend that everyone over age 50 eat B12 in its crystalline (fortified food or supplement) form rather than relying on food-bound B12 - a second, independent, universal (not vegan-specific) confirmation of the same 'over 50, use a supplement/fortified source regardless of diet' point already flagged above via a different, less cleanly-cited source.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

nutrients.name: Vitamin C

whatItDoes.text: A water-soluble antioxidant that helps protect cells from free-radical damage. Needed to make collagen, a protein required for wound healing. Improves absorption of iron from plant-based foods, and helps the immune system work properly.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: Vitamin C and the common cold: a Cochrane systematic review (Hemila & Chalker, 2013) found regular vitamin C supplementation did not reduce the risk of catching a cold in the general population, but did modestly shorten how long a cold lasted (about 8% shorter in adults, 18% shorter in children) once someone was already sick. Separately, people under heavy physical stress (elite athletes, soldiers training in Arctic conditions) who took vitamin C supplements had around 50% fewer colds than those who did not - a specific finding for people under extreme physical stress, not a general population effect. This is a modest, honest picture - vitamin C is not a reliable way to avoid catching a cold for most people.
whatItDoes.label: open question

whatItDoes.text: Vitamin C and cataracts: a 7-year follow-up study found vitamin C supplements gave no benefit in preventing cataracts, despite earlier hopes based on its antioxidant properties. Worth knowing so this card does not overstate what vitamin C can do for eye health.
whatItDoes.label: open question

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: NIH's US adult-male figure (90 mg/day) is notably higher than ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian men (80 mg/day). Both shown rather than merged into one number.

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: Same pattern as for men - NIH's figure is notably higher than ICMR-NIN's 2020 RDA for Indian women.

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: add 35 mg/day to the figure for their age/group above
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Vitamin C is not a nutrient vegans are specifically short on - unlike most of this project's other nutrient cards, this one exists for its cross-reference value (it meaningfully boosts iron absorption and supports immune function - see this project's iron and immune-function cards) rather than because vegans are at particular risk of falling short on it. NIH's own food-source list is almost entirely fruits and vegetables (citrus fruits and juices, red and green pepper, kiwifruit, broccoli, strawberries, cantaloupe, baked potatoes, tomatoes) - foods that feature heavily in an ordinary varied vegan diet, likely more so than in a typical diet with less fruit and vegetable intake. This card should not read as 'another nutrient vegans need to watch' - it isn't one.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate vitamin C content of some everyday foods: orange, 1 medium, about 70 mg; orange juice, 3/4 cup, about 75 mg; grapefruit, half, about 44 mg; grapefruit juice, 3/4 cup, about 60 mg; strawberries, 1 cup, about 82 mg; papaya, 1, about 94 mg; tomato, 1 medium, about 23 mg; red bell pepper, half cup raw, about 141 mg; broccoli, steamed, half cup, about 62 mg; cauliflower, boiled, half cup, about 27 mg; potato, 1 medium baked, about 26 mg.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: The American Cancer Society recommends meeting vitamin C needs by increasing healthy foods in the diet rather than relying on a dietary supplement - studies on vitamin C supplements and cancer risk specifically have given mixed results. Separately, the American Heart Association recommends increasing vitamin C (and other vitamins and minerals) through more fresh vegetables rather than through supplementation for cardiovascular health, and notes vitamin C does not reduce blood cholesterol levels. Both reinforce this card's existing food-first framing.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Vitamin C is considered safe for women to take during pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and passes into breast milk.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: A separate general food-health reference independently gives the same RDA figures already in this card (90 mg men, 75 mg women) and names a similar vegan-compatible food list (citrus fruits and juices, melons, berries, peppers, broccoli, potatoes and many other fruits and vegetables) - a second, independent confirmation of this card's existing figures and food sources.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: This is this card's main practical job: vitamin C meaningfully improves how much nonheme (plant) iron the body absorbs when eaten in the same meal - NIH states this directly as one of vitamin C's functions. This is the anchor source for this project's existing iron-card advice to pair iron-rich plant foods (lentils, beans, spinach) with a vitamin C food (citrus, peppers, tomatoes, broccoli) at the same meal - see the iron nutrient card for the food-pairing detail itself, not repeated here.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Vitamin C content is reduced by prolonged storage and by cooking - steaming or microwaving loses less than boiling. Many of the best vitamin C sources (fruit, salad vegetables) are usually eaten raw anyway, which avoids the issue.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Ordinary high intake (well above the official upper limit of 2,000 mg/day for adults, usually from supplements rather than food) can cause diarrhoea, nausea and stomach cramps.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: People with haemochromatosis (a condition that causes the body to store too much iron) are a specific exception to vitamin C's general food-tier/green status: because vitamin C increases iron absorption, high-dose vitamin C could worsen their existing iron overload and damage body tissues. This is a real, named caution for that specific condition, not a general population risk - NIH separately notes that in healthy people, vitamin C's iron-absorption-boosting effect is only a theoretical concern, not an actual one. Vitamin C supplementation is also specifically flagged as something to avoid in a few other blood disorders - thalassemia, G6PD deficiency and sickle cell disease - because of similar iron-handling or oxidative-stress concerns; anyone with one of these conditions should check with their doctor before taking a vitamin C supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: High vitamin C intake can raise urinary oxalate and uric acid, which could contribute to kidney stone formation, especially in people with an existing kidney/renal disorder - NIH's own health-professional guidance is careful here: studies on this have had conflicting results, it is not generally considered a risk in healthy people, and the best evidence for an actual contribution is specifically in people who already have hyperoxaluria (an existing high-oxalate condition). Worth knowing rather than worth fearing for most readers - see this project's kidney-health card for oxalate detail generally.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Large daily doses of vitamin C may interfere with the body's absorption of vitamin B12 - worth knowing for vegans specifically, since a reliable B12 source (supplement or fortified food) is already essential on a vegan diet; taking a large vitamin C dose at the same time as a B12 source is not an ideal pairing.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Generally, parents should have few concerns about children getting too much or too little vitamin C from food. Children under age one should not be given a vitamin C dietary supplement specifically - their needs should be met through the foods they eat.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for vitamin C status usually reports plasma ascorbic acid; a level below roughly 23 micromol/L (0.4 mg/dL) indicates hypovitaminosis C. This is mainly a research/clinical tool - true clinically visible vitamin C deficiency is rarely seen outside hospital patients with high inflammation or oxidative stress (such as major surgery, burns or sepsis), not something a person would typically have tested as part of routine care.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat citrus fruit, peppers, tomatoes or other vitamin-C-rich produce alongside your iron-rich meals (dal, beans, spinach) - that pairing is this nutrient's single most useful everyday job for a vegan diet.
gaps: No source found for a vitamin-C-specific blood test reference range tied to a specific symptom threshold beyond the general hypovitaminosis cutoff above - vitamin C status is not typically checked with a routine standalone blood test the way iron or B12 are.

The food-content figures sourced from book-encyclopedia-of-diets (a pre-2015 reference encyclopedia, author unstated) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

nutrients.name: Vitamin D

whatItDoes.text: Helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones, and supports muscle, nerve and immune function.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: The American Cancer Society's 2006 guidelines stated: 'There is a growing body of evidence from population studies (not yet tested in clinical trials) that vitamin D may have helpful effects on some types of cancer, including cancers of the colon, prostate, and breast.' The ACS made no recommendation on the amount of vitamin D needed for any such effect - this is an open research question, not a reason to take extra vitamin D beyond the amounts already in this card's dailyRangeByGroup.
whatItDoes.label: open question

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 15 mcg/day (600 IU) - NIH; 15 mcg/day (600 IU) RDA 2020 - ICMR-NIN
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Very few foods naturally contain vitamin D. Most dietary vitamin D comes from fortified foods: many fortified plant milks (soy, almond, oat) carry it, as do some fortified cereals.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Most D3 supplements are made from a traditional animal-derived source and are not vegan - check the label. D3 made from lichen is now available as a vegan option, alongside plant/fungal-derived D2.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Raw white mushrooms that have been deliberately exposed to UV light (sold specifically as 'UV-treated' or 'vitamin D mushrooms' in some markets) carry meaningfully more vitamin D than ordinary mushrooms - NIH's own fact sheet confirms this qualitatively ('mushrooms exposed to UV light provide some'). One source gives a rough illustrative figure of about 366 IU per half cup for UV-exposed mushrooms versus only about 4 IU per half cup for ordinary portabella mushrooms with no UV treatment, but this specific source has a confirmed factual error elsewhere (it swaps D2 and D3), so its exact numbers are not treated as settled and need an independent cross-check against USDA FoodData Central before being stated as precise. This is still worth knowing as one of the few naturally-occurring (not fortified) vegan vitamin D sources, distinct from fortified plant milks/cereals already in this card.
veganContext.label: illustration

veganContext.text: Exclusively breastfed infants are named as a recognised vitamin D risk group, since breast milk alone provides only a small amount of vitamin D - the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends talking to a paediatrician about a vitamin D supplement starting in early infancy for babies who are only breastfed, rather than waiting for a sign of deficiency. No specific dose is stated here, consistent with this project's rule against stating dosing for children.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

absorptionTips.text: Skin makes vitamin D from direct sunlight on bare skin. Clouds, smog, older age, darker skin, sunscreen and glass windows all reduce this, so sunlight alone is not a guaranteed source.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: D3 may raise and hold blood levels higher than D2, so check which form a fortified food or supplement uses.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Darker skin needs roughly three times as long in the sun as fair skin to make the same amount of vitamin D, because melanin slows vitamin D production - directly relevant for many Indian readers. Sunscreen with SPF 8 or higher also meaningfully slows skin vitamin D production. On the plus side, people living north of about 40 degrees latitude (roughly the Philadelphia-to-San Francisco line) may not get enough winter sun for vitamin D - Bengaluru, at about 13 degrees north, does not have this particular problem, so year-round sun availability is one advantage for readers based there, even though darker skin still needs more time in it.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Taking high-dose vitamin D for a long time without medical guidance can raise blood calcium too high, causing nausea, vomiting or kidney problems. See a doctor before taking a high-dose supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Thiazide diuretics combined with vitamin D and calcium supplements can push blood calcium too high; steroids can lower vitamin D levels. Talk to your doctor if you take these.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Some medicines may raise the amount of active vitamin D in the body (birth control pills, hormone replacement therapy, the tuberculosis medicine isoniazid, and thiazide diuretics) while others may lower it (long-term daily antacids, calcium-channel blockers, certain cholesterol-lowering medicines that block fat absorption, some anticonvulsants, daily mineral oil, and the weight-loss drug orlistat). Anyone taking these should check with their doctor before starting a vitamin D supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Cholestyramine and colestipol (bile acid-binding resins, a specific type of cholesterol-lowering medicine) are named specifically as reducing absorption of vitamin D, alongside vitamin A, vitamin K and folate. Anyone on these particular medicines long-term should ask their doctor about their vitamin D status.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Thiazide diuretics reduce how much calcium the body loses in urine - sometimes even considered mildly helpful for bone health in older adults on its own. This is the actual mechanism behind this card's existing caution: less calcium leaving in urine, combined with vitamin D boosting how much calcium is absorbed from food or supplements, can push blood calcium higher than expected when the two are combined. This explains the existing caution more fully; it does not change the advice already given.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: Blood level check uses 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OH-D): roughly 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) or above is adequate for most people; below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) is too low.
whenToTest.label: official recommendation

nutrients.oneLineAction: Get some regular skin-safe sunlight, choose fortified plant milks and cereals, and take a vegan D2 or lichen-D3 supplement if your levels are low.

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): hold until the unit is resolved; even once resolved, label as this one author's personal target, not an official recommendation (keep NIH's ~20 ng/mL as the 'adequate' line).
candidateAdditions.text: One of our cached books gives an 'optimal' 25-hydroxy vitamin D blood-test target of 30-50 - written in the source as 'mg/dl', which does not match the standard clinical unit for this test (ng/mL or nmol/L, as used in the existing NIH-sourced whenToTest entry above). This is almost certainly a units typo in the source for 30-50 ng/mL, but we have not confirmed that correction independently, so the figure is held here rather than merged. Note this target is also notably higher than NIH's own 'adequate' threshold (around 20 ng/mL) - it reads as this single author's personal optimal-health target, not an official recommendation, and should be labelled as such if ever used.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Vitamin K2

whatItDoes.text: Needed for blood clotting and for healthy bones.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

dailyRangeByGroup.amount: 120 mcg/day (total vitamin K - NIH does not separate a K2-only target)
dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone), the main form in most diets, is plentiful in green leafy vegetables, broccoli, lettuce and vegetable oils, so this part is easy on a vegan diet.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Fermented soy foods, especially natto, are the richest vegan source of K2 (menaquinone). Gut bacteria also make some vitamin K the body can use.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Supplement forms of K2 (menaquinone-4 and menaquinone-7) are available and are not automatically animal-derived - check the label for a vegan-suitable source.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Approximate vitamin K1 content of some vegan foods, per typical serving: cooked kale, half cup, about 530 mcg; cooked spinach, half cup, about 445 mcg; cooked Swiss chard, half cup, about 285 mcg; cooked turnip greens, half cup, about 265 mcg; fresh parsley, 2 tbsp, about 120 mcg; cooked Brussels sprouts, half cup, about 110 mcg; cooked broccoli, half cup, about 77 mcg; cooked asparagus, half cup, about 46 mcg; miso (a fermented soy food), 1 oz, about 4 mcg. Little vitamin K is lost during normal cooking, but more is lost when leafy greens are frozen - a reason to favour fresh or lightly cooked greens over frozen ones if vitamin K intake is a concern.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Natto (soybeans fermented with Bacillus subtilis, this card's own richest vegan K2 source) is also high in vitamins B2 and E and the antioxidant selenium, and contains an enzyme called nattokinase, produced during fermentation.
veganContext.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Vitamin K is fat-soluble, so having leafy greens or fermented soy foods with a little oil or other fat helps absorption.
