absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Anyone on the blood thinner warfarin needs a steady, consistent vitamin K intake day to day - a sudden big increase or decrease (for example suddenly eating a lot more or less leafy greens) changes clotting risk. Talk to your doctor before changing your diet if you take warfarin.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: There is no established upper limit for vitamin K, and no reports of toxicity from vitamin K itself in either animal or human studies - the main safety concern is the warfarin interaction above, not a direct overdose risk.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Beyond warfarin, several other things can interact with vitamin K: some broad-spectrum antibiotics can reduce how much vitamin K2 gut bacteria produce; high-dose aspirin taken over a long time, and quinine, may increase the body's need for vitamin K; cholestyramine, mineral oil, orlistat and olestra can all reduce how well vitamin K is absorbed; and vitamin K may reduce the effectiveness of blood-thinning herbs such as American ginseng, alfalfa and angelica. Separately, pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid vitamin K supplements specifically (as opposed to dietary vitamin K from food, which is not a concern) - worth checking with a doctor rather than self-supplementing in pregnancy.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Nattokinase, the enzyme natto produces during fermentation, has its own reported anti-inflammatory and anti-clotting (fibrin-breaking) action, separate from vitamin K2's own clotting role. Anyone on warfarin or another blood-thinning medicine should be aware that regularly eating natto could affect clotting through this separate mechanism too, not just through its vitamin K content, and should mention their natto intake to their doctor along with any dietary changes.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for vitamin K status usually reports serum or plasma phylloquinone (vitamin K1); a level below roughly 0.15 mg/L suggests depletion. This mainly reflects vitamin K1 intake over the past 24 hours rather than longer-term status, and there is no routine blood test specifically for K2.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Eat leafy greens most days for K1, and try a fermented soy food like natto or tempeh sometimes for vegan K2.
gaps: No separate Indian RDA figure for vitamin K found in the ICMR-NIN 2020 brief note's summary tables - only the NIH general figures are shown here.
No source found quantifying how much K2 specifically (versus total vitamin K) a vegan diet typically provides - flagged rather than estimated.

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): hold until the actual RCT review is read directly. Large claim, correctly not trusted on a secondhand citation alone.
candidateAdditions.text: One of our cached books cites a review of randomized controlled trials finding that vitamin K2 supplementation reduced vertebral fracture risk by about 60%, hip fracture risk by about 77%, and other non-vertebral fracture risk by about 81% in people with low bone density. This is a secondhand citation of a study we have not independently read, and the figures are large enough to need their own primary-source check before any use - not confirmed against a Strong source (government body or systematic review read directly) at this time.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): this is the most important hold of the three Gate 2 holds from this book, for a different reason than an evidence-grading question - it's a possible data-integrity error from table extraction. The source lists 4 indications (hypoprothrombinemia, excessive warfarin anticoagulation, osteoporosis, warfarin patients with unstable clotting) against 4 dose lines, and the PDF-to-text extraction may have shuffled which dose maps to which indication. Do not treat this as 'wait for a better source' - treat it as 'don't trust this number is attached to the right thing at all' until someone opens the actual source PDF page and confirms the table layout directly.
candidateAdditions.text: A source cites a K2 (menaquinone) dose of 45 mg/day used in some osteoporosis treatment protocols - a figure many hundreds of times larger than the RDA (120 mcg/day). Not used in the dailyRangeByGroup/cautions fields above pending that check.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

nutrients.name: Zinc

whatItDoes.text: Supports the immune system, wound healing, taste, and growth and development in pregnancy, infancy and childhood.
whatItDoes.label: established fact

whatItDoes.text: A Cochrane meta-analysis (cited but not independently read by us - a secondhand citation, flagged per BRIEF.md rule 10) found that zinc taken within 24 hours of cold symptoms starting roughly halved the chance of still having symptoms at the 7-day mark, and that regular zinc use over several months reduced the risk of catching a cold at all. This is about zinc and common colds generally, not a vegan-specific point, but worth knowing as a reason some readers may already be taking zinc supplements separately from any vegan-diet consideration.
whatItDoes.label: open question

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: ICMR-NIN's Indian RDA (17 mg/day) is notably higher than NIH's US figure (11 mg/day), likely reflecting the lower zinc absorption from a cereal/pulse-heavy Indian diet rich in phytates. Both shown; not resolved to a single number here.

dailyRangeByGroup.label: official recommendation
dailyRangeByGroup.conflict: Same pattern as for men - ICMR-NIN's figure is notably higher than NIH's.

veganContext.text: NIH states that people on vegetarian or vegan diets may not get enough zinc, both because meat (a good zinc source) is absent and because beans and grains contain phytates that reduce how much zinc the body absorbs. NIH notes vegetarians and vegans might benefit from a zinc supplement.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: Plant zinc sources: chickpeas, beans, lentils, peanuts, tofu, tempeh, soy milk, edamame, chia, hemp and pumpkin seeds, nuts, oats, quinoa, brown rice, broccoli, and fortified cereal.
veganContext.label: official recommendation

veganContext.text: Approximate zinc amounts per serving for common vegan foods: raw sesame seeds (2 oz) about 4.4 mg; raw or roasted pumpkin seeds (2 oz) about 4.2 mg; cooked adzuki beans (1 cup) about 4.1 mg; raw pine nuts (2 oz) about 3.6 mg; raw cashews (2 oz) about 3.2 mg; raw sunflower seeds (2 oz) about 2.8 mg; cooked wild rice (1 cup) about 2.2 mg; cooked edamame (1 cup) about 2.1 mg; cooked black or kidney beans (1 cup) about 1.9 mg; cooked shiitake mushrooms (1 cup) about 1.9 mg; cooked fava beans (1 cup) about 1.7 mg; cooked broccoli (2 cups) about 1.6 mg; raw tahini (2 tbsp) about 1.4 mg; cooked kale (2 cups) about 1.2 mg. These figures are illustrative, from a single-author book rather than a nutrient database, and have not been cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central.
veganContext.label: illustration

veganContext.text: 'Strict vegetarians whose major food staples are grains and legumes' are separately named as a group at risk of zinc deficiency because phytic acid in these foods lowers zinc absorption - the same point this card makes via NIH above, now with a second, independent confirmation. Additional vegan food values, per typical serving: canned chickpeas, 1 cup, about 2.6 mg; frozen green peas, 1 cup, about 1.6 mg; cashews, 1 oz, about 1.6 mg; pecans, 1 oz, about 1.4 mg; mixed nuts, 1 oz, about 1.1 mg; almonds or black walnuts, 1 oz, about 1.0 mg each; instant oatmeal, 1 packet, about 0.8 mg.
veganContext.label: established fact

veganContext.text: An estimate cited in one source suggests around 82% of pregnant women worldwide may have inadequate zinc intake (a general population statistic, not specific to vegan diets), and associates low zinc intake in pregnancy with low birth weight and other delivery complications. This is a reason zinc is worth including as a normal part of antenatal nutrition conversations for any pregnant woman, vegan or not, rather than a specific vegan pregnancy risk.
veganContext.label: open question

absorptionTips.text: Soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains before cooking lowers their phytate content and can improve zinc absorption.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

absorptionTips.text: Besides phytates, a few other nutrients affect zinc absorption: calcium may lower zinc absorption in postmenopausal women specifically; iron (for example from a supplement) may reduce absorption of both iron and zinc when taken together; and phosphate salts can also lower zinc absorption. On the helpful side, the amino acids L-cysteine and L-histidine (found in protein-rich foods) may enhance zinc absorption. This is consistent with this card's existing advice to include a protein source alongside zinc-rich foods.
absorptionTips.label: established fact

cautions.text: Too much zinc (from supplements) can cause nausea and, over time, can lower immunity and cause a copper shortage. Zinc supplements should be spaced a few hours apart from quinolone or tetracycline antibiotics.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Zinc supplements can reduce the absorption of tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics if taken together - a 2-hour gap between the two is recommended. Separately, the anticonvulsant sodium valproate, long-term diuretic use, and the metal-chelating medicines penicillamine and DTPA (used for copper or iron overload) have all been linked to zinc deficiency - anyone taking these should mention it to their doctor. On excess: very high intakes (around 150-450 mg/day of supplemental zinc, well above the RDA) have been linked to copper deficiency, impaired iron function, lower immune function and lower 'good' (HDL) cholesterol, and single very large doses (225-450 mg) can cause vomiting - context for why this card already advises against combining a daily supplement with a zinc-rich diet.
cautions.label: established fact

whenToTest.text: A blood test for zinc status usually reports plasma zinc (normal range roughly 75-110 mcg/dL); erythrocyte zinc and 24-hour urinary zinc are sometimes used too, but are less commonly ordered in routine practice.
whenToTest.label: established fact

nutrients.oneLineAction: Include beans, nuts, seeds or tofu daily, and soak or sprout dried beans and grains where you can to help the zinc in them absorb better.
gaps: No source found for an older-adult-specific zinc daily range beyond the general adult figure.

No Strong source found confirming exactly how much a routine zinc supplement helps a typical vegan diet already containing legumes and nuts - NIH's 'might benefit' wording is cautious, so this card does not state a firm supplement recommendation, only NIH's own caveated note.

The food-value figures sourced from book-super-immunity and book-encyclopedia-of-diets (single-author/pre-2015 sources) have not been independently cross-checked against USDA FoodData Central - flagged for a recheck before being treated as precise rather than approximate.

foods.name: Agar (agar-agar)
foods.notes: Basic entry. Figures are real USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy) values for raw agar (fdc_id 169280, per 100 g), not estimated. Agar-agar is used in India mainly as a vegan gelatin substitute for desserts (China grass), bought dried in small amounts rather than eaten as a vegetable; included here for food-group completeness per BRIEF.md's Completeness rules, not as a nutrient-dense staple - a typical serving used in cooking is a small fraction of 100 g. Vitamin A and vitamin K are present in USDA's record but deliberately left off: the vitamin K value is phylloquinone (vitamin K1), not the vitamin K2 (menaquinone) this project tracks separately, and vitamin A, RAE is 0 for this food. USDA's record carries a tiny EPA value (0.008 g) but no ALA (the plant omega-3 this project tracks) and no iodine value (checked directly - both fields are empty for ALA/iodine), so omega-3 and iodine are left off rather than estimated.
foods.localNameStatus: No local name proposed yet - though sold in India as 'China grass', that is a product/brand-style name, not a vernacular translation, so no candidate is proposed here without the owner's confirmation.

foods.name: Almond milk (fortified, unsweetened)
foods.everydayPortion: 1 cup (about 240 ml) is typical, but check your own carton's stated serving size - it varies slightly by brand

pairingTips.text: Among plant milks, soy milk is the most protein-rich choice; almond milk (like oat, rice and coconut milk) is generally much lower in protein, so if protein matters to you, compare brands or choose soy milk instead.
pairingTips.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Not every almond milk brand adds both vitamin B12 and vitamin D - check the ingredients and nutrition panel for each separately, since a milk can be fortified with one and not the other.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Check for added calcium too. Unfortified nut milks are naturally low in calcium, so a plant milk only reaches a useful calcium level if calcium (such as calcium carbonate) has actually been added.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Brand-specific protein, calcium and vitamin figures are not given here because fortification and recipe vary a great deal between almond milk brands - read your own carton's Nutrition Information panel rather than relying on a single generic figure.
preparationNotes.label: open question

foods.oneLineAction: Choose an almond milk fortified with both calcium and vitamin B12, and check the label each time you switch brands, since fortification varies.

foods.name: Burmese tofu (Tohu / Shan tofu / chickpea tofu)
foods.keyNutrientsStatus: NOT BUILT - no gram-level nutrient source found anywhere for this specific prepared food. Checked: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy and Foundation Foods - only soy-based tofu entries exist, nothing chickpea- or split-pea-flour-based), IFCT 2017's own composition table (no tofu entry of any kind), and this project's own Anuvaad INDB composite-dish extraction (no match). This is a regional homemade preparation with no composite-dish nutrient entry on file anywhere checked - do not invent a figure. If a gram-level source becomes available later, this table can be built then.
foods.notes: Gate 1 search found no formal nutrition source for this dish (see keyNutrientsStatus), so this entry is qualitative-only, graded Limited (general knowledge about a named traditional dish, cross-checked across several independent public descriptions - Wikipedia's 'Burmese tofu' article and a dedicated vegan recipe explainer - for consistency, not drawn from this project's Gate 1 document pool or any of its approved reference bodies). No formal sourceIds are attached to any individual claim below because none of them come from an approved source - flagged here plainly rather than citing an unapproved source type (Wikipedia/recipe blogs) as though it had been Gate-1-cleared. What it is: a soy-free, naturally vegan 'tofu' made by cooking legume flour with water (and usually a little salt and turmeric for colour) into a thick, glossy paste that sets like a firm custard once poured into a tray and cooled - no soy, no coagulant (like the calcium sulfate or nigari used for soy tofu) and no pressing needed. There are two related but distinct versions, often both loosely called 'Burmese tofu': the Shan-State original (won ta hpo), made from yellow split-pea flour, and the chickpea-flour version (to hpu, besan-based) that is now the common version across mainland Myanmar and the one most vegan recipe sites outside Myanmar actually mean by 'Burmese tofu' or 'Shan tofu' - whether chickpea tofu itself originated in Shan State or in southern China (it closely resembles a Yunnanese chickpea-flour dish) is openly unresolved, not something to state as settled. Texture is softer, creamier and less firm than soy tofu - more like a cross between custard and silken tofu - but it still holds together well enough to be sliced and pan-fried or deep-fried into firmer pieces, grated into a warm salad (tohu thoke), or simmered into a curry where it softens further and thickens the sauce. Why it is a useful entry for this project: it is a real, naturally-vegan, genuinely soy-free source of plant protein from a pulse (chickpea or split-pea) flour base, worth naming specifically for any reader who avoids soy (allergy, sensitivity, or simply wanting variety) but still wants a tofu-like ingredient - a gap regular soy tofu and tempeh cards don't cover. One serving caution worth naming plainly: some traditional Burmese preparations of the curry version are made with fish sauce - this card does not describe or recommend that preparation; stick to a vegan curry, dip or dressing (soy sauce, rice vinegar, chilli, garlic, peanuts, coriander, as used in the classic salad version) when making this at home.

foods.name: Flaxseed (linseed)
foods.everydayPortion: 1 tablespoon, ground (about 10 g)

pairingTips.text: Flaxseed is one of the richest plant sources of ALA, the essential omega-3 fat; the body converts only a small part of ALA into the longer-chain omega-3s (EPA and DHA) that oily fish provide, so flaxseed is a useful but different kind of omega-3 source.
pairingTips.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Grinding flaxseed just before eating (rather than leaving it whole) makes its fat and fibre more available; whole flaxseed largely passes through undigested.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

foods.oneLineAction: Stir a tablespoon of freshly ground flaxseed into porridge, a smoothie or dal for extra omega-3 and fibre.

foods.name: Fortified breakfast cereal
foods.everydayPortion: a standard bowl (about 30-40 g dry cereal), or the pack's own stated serving size - cereal serving sizes vary enough between brands that the pack's own label is the more reliable guide

preparationNotes.text: FSSAI's food fortification rules set standards for which nutrients (such as iron, folic acid, vitamin B12 and vitamin D) may be added to foods including breakfast cereals in India, but which nutrients are actually added, and at what level, still varies by product - check the Nutrition Information panel for which vitamins and minerals are listed.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: A cereal being fortified does not by itself make it a balanced choice - prefer whole, minimally processed foods as the base of a meal generally, and treat a fortified cereal as one useful source among several rather than a stand-alone solution.
preparationNotes.label: official recommendation

preparationNotes.text: Brand-specific per-100 g fortification figures are not given here because the vitamins and minerals added, and the amounts, vary a great deal between cereal products - read your own pack's label rather than relying on a single generic figure.
preparationNotes.label: open question

foods.oneLineAction: Pick a breakfast cereal fortified with vitamin B12 and iron where possible, and check the Nutrition Information panel each time, since fortification varies by brand and product.

foods.name: Nori (seaweed)
foods.notes: Basic entry. Figures are real USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy) values, per 100 g (fdc_id 168458). USDA's dataset has no entry named 'nori' specifically - the closest real match is 'Seaweed, laver, raw', laver being the type of red seaweed that dried nori sheets are made from. These figures are for the raw, undried seaweed, not the dried, pressed sheets sold as nori, which are far more concentrated per 100 g because almost all the water is removed; we did not scale or estimate a dried-sheet figure, since USDA has no dried-nori row to check that scaling against, and BRIEF.md rule 11 says never fill a gap from memory. Nori is uncommon and mostly imported in Indian kitchens; it is included here for food-group completeness per BRIEF.md's Completeness rules, not as a staple recommendation. Iodine is often cited as high in nori, but USDA's record here carries no iodine value at all (checked directly - the field is empty), so iodine is deliberately left off rather than estimated. Omega-3 (ALA) also has no value in this record, so it is left out for the same reason.

foods.name: Plant-based ice cream
foods.everydayPortion: a small scoop (roughly 60-100 g), or the pack's own stated serving size

preparationNotes.text: Plant-based ice creams are usually made from coconut, soy, oat or cashew bases. Coconut (and coconut oil) is unusually high in saturated fat among plant foods - about 82 g saturated fat per 100 g fat in coconut oil - so a coconut-based ice cream is likely to carry more saturated fat than a soy- or oat-based one; check the label rather than assuming all plant-based ice creams are alike.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Plant-based ice cream is a treat food like any frozen dessert - it does not need to be a regular source of calcium or B12, even where a product carries a vegan logo.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Check the label for a vegan logo or explicit 'vegan' labelling before assuming a frozen dessert is dairy-free - some frozen desserts combine a dairy-free element with a dairy one (for example, a sorbet swirled with dairy ice cream) and should not be assumed vegan without checking.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

foods.oneLineAction: Enjoy plant-based ice cream as an occasional treat, and check the label for a vegan logo and the saturated fat line, since the recipe varies a lot between coconut, soy, oat and cashew bases.

foods.name: Seitan (wheat meat)
foods.everydayPortion: about 100 g (3.5 oz), cooked

pairingTips.text: Seitan's chewy, meat-like texture comes from its gluten structure, and it takes up marinades, soy sauce and spices well.
pairingTips.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: Seitan is made by kneading and rinsing a wheat flour dough until mostly gluten remains, then simmering or steaming it, often in a seasoned broth. This is different from 'vital wheat gluten', the dry gluten powder USDA FoodData Central lists (about 75 g protein per 100 g dry powder) - cooked seitan absorbs much of the broth it is cooked in, so the dry powder's figure cannot be used directly for a cooked portion.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

preparationNotes.text: We could not find a USDA FoodData Central or ICMR-NIN entry for cooked, ready-to-eat seitan itself, so no per-100 g or per-portion nutrient figure is given here for this food; a 100 g cooked serving is understood to carry a large amount of complete protein, per the cited book, but we have not been able to confirm an exact figure from an independent dataset.
preparationNotes.label: open question

preparationNotes.text: Seitan is pure wheat gluten, so it is not suitable for anyone with coeliac disease or a wheat or gluten intolerance.
preparationNotes.label: established fact

foods.oneLineAction: Use seitan as a protein-dense, meat-like ingredient in stir-fries or stews, but skip it if you avoid gluten.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Iron-deficiency anaemia is one of the most common nutrition problems worldwide, and plant (non-haem) iron is absorbed less easily than the iron in meat and fish, so a vegan diet needs a little more planning around iron.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Anaemia can also come from low vitamin B12 or folate, both of which affect how red blood cells are made, separately from iron.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A sensibly planned vegetarian or vegan diet is not linked with more iron-deficiency anaemia than a diet that includes meat - the real risk comes from an unplanned diet, not from being vegan itself.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Iron (for haemoglobin) and vitamin B12 and folate (for making red blood cells) are the key nutrients; a reliable vegan B12 source matters most, since B12 has almost no reliable plant source.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Iron and folate in one everyday katori; pair with a vitamin C side.
One of the richest iron sources among the leafy greens tracked here.
Good iron and very high folate per portion.
A quick-cooking dal with solid iron per katori.
A millet with meaningfully more iron than refined wheat or rice.
Good iron and folate, but its iron is non-haem and partly oxalate-bound - pair with vitamin C.
A useful everyday iron source, though some of it is phytate-bound - fermenting the batter (as in dosa) helps.
A good iron source, classic in idli-dosa batter and in dal.
Another millet with a useful iron contribution to the day's meals.
Only brands fortified with vitamin B12 help here - check the label; plain nutritional yeast has no reliable B12.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tea and coffee contain tannins that reduce how much non-haem iron the body absorbs from a meal; having them between meals rather than with food helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Taking a calcium supplement at the same time as an iron-rich meal can reduce iron absorption; space them apart if taking both.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Relying only on oxalate-rich greens like spinach for iron, without a vitamin C food alongside, gets less benefit than pairing them.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Eating a vitamin C food in the same meal - lemon, tomato, amla, guava or capsicum - meaningfully improves non-haem iron absorption from dal, millets or greens.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti (rajma-chawal, dal-roti) is a classic Indian combination that also happens to carry the dal's iron and folate alongside everyday protein.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking and sprouting dals and legumes reduces phytates that otherwise bind iron, making more of it available.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Fermenting batter, as in idli or dosa, can improve mineral availability compared with the same grains and dals unfermented.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Blanching spinach and similar greens briefly, and discarding the water, cuts some of their oxalate content, which otherwise binds iron.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Wheat-based iron-fortified foods are not suitable for anyone with coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity; millets like ragi, bajra and jowar are naturally gluten-free iron sources.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Heavy menstrual periods and intense endurance exercise both increase the body's iron needs, which food choices alone may not always cover.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A full blood count and a ferritin test (the body's iron-storage level) are the usual first checks for anaemia.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: If iron levels are normal but anaemia persists, a doctor may also check vitamin B12 and folate.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Rajma-chawal with a side of tomato-onion salad and a lemon wedge: the dal's iron and folate, rice for everyday protein pairing, and vitamin C from the tomato and lemon to help absorb the iron.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual tiredness, breathlessness on mild exertion, a rapid heartbeat, dizziness or very pale skin and nails - these need a blood test, not self-treatment with supplements.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Do not start iron supplements on your own without a blood test first; iron overdose is dangerous, and some people have a condition (haemochromatosis) where extra iron is harmful.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can supply the iron, B12 and folate an everyday diet needs, but it cannot diagnose or treat anaemia caused by internal bleeding, heavy periods or an absorption problem - those need a doctor.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Calcium and vitamin D build and maintain bone density; vegans get no calcium from dairy, so they need calcium-rich plant foods and, for vitamin D, mainly sunlight or a supplement.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Calcium (for bone mineral), vitamin D (so the body can use that calcium) and enough protein matter most; vitamin K supports how calcium is laid down in bone.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: 16.6% of adult calcium RDA per tablespoon - one of the strongest everyday plant sources tracked.
314 mg calcium per portion alongside iron and folate.
A everyday millet calcium source; ragi mudde or roti a few times a week adds up.
274 mg calcium per 100 g, a common Indian leafy green.
281 mg calcium per 100 g, plus folate and fibre.
269 mg calcium per 100 g alongside protein and iron.
Calcium-set tofu is also a calcium source - check the label, as not every brand is calcium-set.
A fortified, unsweetened soy milk can add calcium and B12 - check the label each time you switch brands.
171.5 mg calcium per 100 g as a grain alternative to rice.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A large cohort study (EPIC-Oxford) found a 30% higher fracture risk among vegans compared with lacto-ovo-vegetarians or omnivores. The same study points to low calcium and vitamin D intake - common when dairy is dropped without a planned replacement - as the likely driver, not veganism itself: this is a reason to make sure you have a planned calcium and vitamin D source, not a reason to worry if you already do.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Very high salt intake increases how much calcium the body loses in urine over time; keeping salt moderate protects calcium stores.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Relying on raw oxalate-rich greens alone for calcium gets less of it absorbed than from low-oxalate sources like sesame, ragi or fortified plant milk; blanching helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Vitamin D (mainly from sunlight) helps the body absorb and use calcium; spreading calcium intake across the day, rather than one large dose, also helps.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti supplies the everyday protein that bone tissue also needs, alongside a calcium-rich side like til chutney.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Blanching or lightly cooking oxalate-rich leafy greens before eating reduces the oxalates that otherwise bind some of their calcium.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Dry-roasting sesame seeds or grinding them into a chutney powder (til chutney) is a common, everyday way to include them.
preparation.label: illustration

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Sesame and soy (tofu, soy milk) are recognised allergens; check for a suitable fortified alternative plant milk if either is a problem for you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular sunlight on skin is the main way the body makes vitamin D; weight-bearing activity (walking, climbing stairs) also supports bone density.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

testsWorthConsidering.text: A DEXA bone density scan is the standard test for osteoporosis, usually considered for women from their mid-60s or earlier if risk factors are present; a blood test for vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D) is also common.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Ragi mudde or ragi roti with a spoon of sesame (til) chutney powder and a katori of tofu or soy-based curry - a calcium-forward everyday combination.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you break a bone from a minor fall or bump, have ongoing unexplained bone or back pain, or notice a loss of height over time.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can support bone health day to day, but it cannot replace a bone density scan, or the calcium, vitamin D and medication a doctor may prescribe for diagnosed osteoporosis.

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A whole-food vegan diet is naturally higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat than one built around refined grains and animal foods, and fibre-rich meals raise blood sugar more slowly.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre and whole grains over refined ones matter most, since they slow how fast carbohydrate turns into blood sugar; regular meal timing and portion size matter alongside food choice.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Stevia (leaf extract) and erythritol (a sugar alcohol) are vegan-compatible, non-nutritive sweeteners that one source describes as not raising blood glucose, unlike table sugar - a practical everyday option for sweetening food or drink without the blood-sugar rise. The same source notes erythritol can have a mild laxative effect for some people at higher amounts, the same caution that applies to other sugar alcohols, and names monk fruit only once in passing as a possible alternative if erythritol doesn't suit someone - without describing monk fruit's own properties, so it isn't included in the claim above.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: 20.4 g fibre per 100 g, among the highest tracked here.
16 g fibre per 100 g, a seasonal Karnataka favourite.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g; a good whole-grain swap for part of the rice portion.
12.6 g fibre per portion alongside protein.
11.6 g fibre per 100 g.
8.3 g fibre per portion alongside protein and iron.
8.2 g fibre per portion alongside iron and calcium.
6.9 g fibre per portion, a whole-grain millet alternative to refined wheat or white rice.
Fibre and omega-3 together; stirring a spoon into a meal can help it feel more filling.
Whole fruit's fibre slows sugar absorption; several studies cited by PCRM link fruit intake with better blood sugar control in people with diabetes - the fruit itself is not something to avoid.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Refined grains (maida, white bread, polished white rice in large portions), sugary drinks and deep-fried snacks are low in fibre and raise blood sugar faster than whole grains and legumes.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Fruit juice removes the fibre that whole fruit has, so it raises blood sugar faster than eating the fruit itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Powdered fenugreek (methi) seeds are sometimes suggested as a home remedy for blood sugar, but the dose needed from food alone is too large to be practically effective - worth knowing before relying on it rather than diet and medical care.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Tulsi (holy basil), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea or supplement, may lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea medicine specifically, this could cause hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar). Anyone with diabetes considering tulsi should talk to their doctor first, and watch for hypoglycaemia symptoms (shakiness, sweating, confusion) if they do - see this project's own Tulsi herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Ashwagandha, another traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin, a sulfonylurea or metformin specifically, this could cause hypoglycaemia. Anyone with diabetes considering ashwagandha should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Ashwagandha herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Neem, a third traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea specifically, this could cause dangerously low blood sugar. Anyone with diabetes considering neem should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Neem herb card for full detail, including its more serious unrelated cautions (never give neem oil or seed to a child, by mouth).
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Nettle, a fourth traditional herb some readers may take separately, has conflicting evidence on blood sugar (one trial found no effect, another found a benefit in people already on diabetes medication) - but a real case report describes hypoglycaemia in an older adult taking a nettle-containing remedy alongside diabetes treatment. Anyone with diabetes considering nettle should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Nettle herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Giloy (Guduchi), a fifth traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or other diabetes medicines this could cause hypoglycaemia. This herb also has a separate, more serious documented liver-injury risk unrelated to diabetes - see this project's own Giloy (Guduchi) herb card for full detail before considering it for any reason.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Moringa, a sixth traditional herb some readers may take as a leaf-powder or capsule supplement (separate from eating moringa leaves or pods as an everyday vegetable, which this project's Foods entries already cover), may also lower blood sugar - combined with insulin or diabetes medicines such as glimepiride, glyburide, pioglitazone or rosiglitazone this could cause hypoglycaemia. Worth knowing alongside this: the best current human evidence for moringa actually helping blood sugar is unsettled rather than confirmed, so this caution is about a genuine medicine-interaction risk, not about giving up a proven benefit - see this project's own Moringa herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Amla (Indian gooseberry), a seventh traditional herb some readers may take as a concentrated extract or capsule (separate from eating fresh amla as an everyday fruit, which this project's Foods entries already cover), has thin and only partly checkable evidence for lowering blood sugar - the single most rigorous cardiometabolic review located for amla did not even test blood glucose as an outcome, and the one review that did gives no effect size to check its finding against. Even so, combined with insulin or another diabetes medicine, any blood-sugar-lowering effect amla does have could add up to hypoglycaemia. Anyone with diabetes considering an amla supplement should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely if they do - see this project's own Amla herb card for full detail, including its bleeding-risk and blood-pressure-medicine cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

absorption.text: Eating vegetables and dal alongside rice or roti, rather than a large portion of grain on its own, tends to moderate the overall blood sugar rise from the meal - an idea discussed in one of our cached sources, not independently confirmed here by a government or review source.
absorption.label: illustration

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti is a useful everyday combination: the dal's fibre and protein slow the meal's overall effect on blood sugar compared with grain alone.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Choosing whole grains with the bran intact (whole wheat, millets, brown rice) over refined, polished versions keeps more of the fibre that slows sugar release.
preparation.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Soaking and sprouting legumes before cooking is a normal home step that also reduces phytates, without removing their fibre.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi are naturally gluten-free whole-grain options for anyone managing diabetes alongside coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular physical activity improves how well the body responds to insulin, alongside food choices.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Poor sleep is linked with harder-to-control blood sugar in general nutrition guidance, though this is a broader observation rather than one specific to vegans.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c (average blood sugar over about three months) are the usual tests a doctor uses to check and monitor diabetes.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with a modest portion of rice or roti, a generous katori of mixed-dal, a large helping of non-starchy vegetable sabzi, and a side salad - balancing the grain portion against fibre-rich dal and vegetables.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice unusual thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, or numbness or tingling in the feet.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never change or stop a diabetes medicine dose based on diet alone - doing so risks a hypoglycaemic (low blood sugar) episode; any change needs your doctor.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support better blood sugar day to day, but they cannot replace blood glucose monitoring or a doctor's prescribed diabetes medicine.

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): hold, secondary review article not a primary source.
candidateAdditions.text: A few grams of cinnamon, taken either in cooking or as a supplement, is described as having demonstrated benefits for lowering blood glucose and improving lipid levels without apparent side effects - cited via a secondary review article (Nahas R, Moher M, 'Complementary and alternative medicine for the treatment of type 2 diabetes,' Can Fam Physician, 2009), not independently read by us.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (22 Oct 2026): worth prioritising a closer look given karela's everyday relevance here - one primary trial against metformin is a decent lead, not yet a citation-grade fact.
candidateAdditions.text: Bitter melon (karela) is discussed as a mild blood-sugar-lowering food, with one specific primary study cited: Fuangchan A, Sonthisombat P, Seubnukarn T, et al., 'Hypoglycemic effect of bitter melon compared with metformin in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients,' J Ethnopharmacol, 2011;134(2):422-8 - a single study comparing bitter melon with the diabetes medicine metformin, not a systematic review, so graded Limited per BRIEF.md rule 10 pending a Strong-source check. Karela is a common Indian vegetable, so this is worth a closer look for this topic.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying Barnard trial before use - this project has only a secondary citation of it (via The Whole Foods Diet), not the primary paper.
candidateAdditions.text: A randomized controlled trial by Dr. Neal Barnard (cited, not independently read by us) compared a low-fat vegan diet against standard American Diabetes Association dietary guidelines for blood sugar control. The ADA-guideline group reduced HbA1c by 0.4 points on average; the vegan-diet group reduced it by 1.2 points - described as three times more effective, and a bigger reduction than typical oral diabetes medicines achieve. If confirmed directly, this would be a strong, specific, citable effect-size figure for this topic's whyItMattersForVegans section.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CONFLICT FLAGGED, not resolved - 22 Oct 2026. This directly contradicts the Barnard-RCT candidate immediately above (same topic, opposite claim, both secondary citations from different popular-health books). Per BRIEF.md rule 6, shown here rather than silently resolved - the owner should decide which (if either) governs once both underlying sources are read directly.
candidateAdditions.text: A different physician-author (Dr. Mark Hyman) states in his own clinical experience that it is 'very hard' for his vegan/vegetarian patients (including many vegan/vegetarian Indian patients) to reverse type 2 diabetes, compared to his omnivore patients, for whom it is 'fairly simple' - though he notes some vegan patients succeed with a vegan ketogenic approach specifically. This is anecdotal clinical-practice experience, not a cited trial (unlike the Barnard RCT candidate above), so it carries less evidentiary weight on its own - but the direct contradiction on the same question is worth having on record rather than only keeping the candidate that supports the project's existing framing.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified accurate by independent review against book-eating-well-for-optimum-health p.237 (exact match, including the source's own title-vs-body-text inconsistency: the study's title says 'Vegetarian', the book's body text says 'vegan' - faithfully carried through, not introduced here). KEPT HELD, not merged into whyItMattersForVegans: a separate, independent small pilot RCT alongside the existing Barnard-RCT candidate above (different author, different trial, same direction of finding) - kept as its own entry rather than merged with Barnard's, since the two are independent supporting citations, not duplicates, but both stay held pending a direct read of their primary papers, for consistency with how this card has already treated similar-strength single-trial citations. Pre-2015 (1999) per BRIEF.md rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: A cited randomized controlled pilot trial (Nicholson AS, Sklar M, Barnard ND, et al., 'Toward Improved Management of NIDDM: A Randomized Controlled, Pilot Intervention Using a Low-Fat Vegetarian Diet,' Preventive Medicine, 1999;29(2):87-91) found greater weight loss and better blood sugar control in adult-onset (type 2) diabetes patients following a low-fat vegan diet for twelve weeks than in those on a conventional low-fat diet.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying study before use - secondary citation only (via 500 High-Fiber Recipes). Round 7 trade-in. The NEJM 2000 study named here is the same one offered to heart-and-cholesterol.json from this author's companion book this round - cross-reference, not a duplicate claim, since the effect described there is on cholesterol-related outcomes and here specifically on glucose.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that a high-fibre meal can reduce blood sugar levels by as much as 28% (no study named for this specific figure) by slowing the absorption of sugar into the bloodstream, and separately cites a study in the May 11, 2000 issue of The New England Journal of Medicine finding that diabetic patients on a very high-fibre diet lowered their glucose levels by 10%. It also states fibre has been shown to improve insulin sensitivity. This lines up with, and could strengthen with specific figures, this card's existing general fibre/blood-sugar framing.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the same source. The children's 'age in years + 5 grams' rule has now appeared across several of this project's reviewed books (see this project's own notes on this recurring book-wide pattern, and the owner's 22 Oct 2026 correction elsewhere that the rule traces to Williams et al., not the IOM) - flagged again here as a recurring figure, still not independently re-verified against that primary source. The adult IOM figures broken out by age and sex are more specific than this card's current general fibre framing and could usefully sharpen whatToFocusOn if verified.
candidateAdditions.text: This source gives the American Dietetic Association's general adult fibre target as 20-35 g/day (noting average actual US intake is only 12-15 g/day), and separately cites the US National Academy of Sciences' Institute of Medicine for age/sex-specific adult daily targets: men 50 and younger 38 g, men 51 and older 30 g, women 50 and younger 25 g, women 51 and older 21 g. For children under 18, it gives the same 'age in years plus 5 grams' rule seen elsewhere in this project's reviewed books, without a clear citation of its own for that specific children's rule.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A whole-food vegan diet tends to be higher in dietary fibre, which feeds the gut's beneficial bacteria; traditional Indian fermented foods like idli and dosa batter add live cultures on top of that.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Healthy gut bacteria are also linked to gut immune function, not just digestion: one source cites a 2004 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition stating that the gut's main antibody (secretory immunoglobulin A, or IgA, which helps protect the gut lining from harmful bacteria) depends on healthy gut bacteria for its production, and a 2003 study in the American Journal of Nutrition stating that without enough beneficial bacteria, certain gut immune cells work less effectively. Separately, it cites a 2008 study in the Journal of Immunology reporting that lactic acid bacteria from fermented foods and drinks generally (not any one specific food) can increase production of anti-inflammatory signalling molecules (cytokines).
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, standardised extract or DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) supplement, has a long traditional reputation for heartburn, indigestion and peptic ulcers. The actual trial evidence is real but mixed: a 2011 randomised placebo-controlled trial of a specific low-glycyrrhizin extract (GutGard, not plain licorice) found significant symptom improvement in functional dyspepsia over 30 days, though most of its authors worked for the extract's own manufacturer. For deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) specifically in peptic ulcer, one older uncontrolled survey found healing on endoscopy, while a larger older placebo-controlled trial found no advantage over placebo at all - a genuinely mixed, dated evidence picture, not a settled benefit. This card does not treat licorice as a reliably proven digestive remedy, only as a traditional use with some real but limited supporting trial evidence. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate and much better-established blood-pressure/potassium caution.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre (which feeds gut bacteria) and naturally fermented foods (which add live cultures, called probiotics) matter most; variety in plant foods feeds a wider range of gut bacteria.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Onion, garlic and similar vegetables carry a specific fermentable fibre (a prebiotic) that feeds gut bacteria directly, alongside fibre generally.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Research cited in one source (Nature, 2012) found that people living in rural West Africa had a more diverse gut bacteria population, including more fibre-loving bacteria, than people in more industrialised areas, whose gut bacteria were dominated instead by strains linked to a diet heavier in meat and carbohydrate. The source reports that Stanford University researchers have proposed regularly eating fermented foods and drinks as one way to help rebuild a more diverse gut bacteria population - a specific, named-study basis for this card's general fibre/fermented-food framing.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsToFavour.note: A source of prebiotic fibre that feeds gut bacteria directly, on top of general fibre.
Another everyday prebiotic-fibre source, usually used in small amounts across many meals.
Naturally fermented rice and urad dal batter; fermentation adds live cultures and improves some B-vitamin availability.
Fermented cabbage and salt - always vegan as traditionally made; check the label on shop-bought jars.
A fermented vegetable dish made entirely from plant ingredients - check the label, as some non-vegan versions use a non-plant seasoning.
20.4 g fibre per 100 g, feeding gut bacteria.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g, including fibre types that ferment well in the gut.
12.6 g fibre per portion.
8.2 g fibre per portion alongside iron and calcium.
Fibre alongside omega-3; best ground rather than left whole.
6.9 g fibre per portion as a whole-grain staple.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A sudden, large increase in fibre or fermented foods can cause temporary bloating or gas; building up gradually and drinking enough water helps.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Many ultra-processed vegan snacks are low in fibre despite being plant-based; whole foods generally do more for gut health than processed substitutes.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Onion and garlic are praised above as useful everyday prebiotic-fibre foods for gut bacteria generally - but for some people they are also a personal trigger for heartburn/acid reflux (GERD) specifically. Both can be true at once: a food can be good for the gut microbiome in general and still be worth moderating personally if you notice it triggers reflux symptoms for you.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Fermentation itself is a kind of preparation step that improves some B-vitamin availability and reduces antinutrients, rather than a meal-pairing in the usual sense.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Idli or dosa (fermented rice and urad dal) with sambar is a classic combination that already pairs a grain and a dal for everyday protein.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Natural fermentation (idli-dosa batter, sauerkraut, kimchi, dhokla, kanji) grows live bacterial cultures; refrigerating after fermentation slows them down without killing them.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking and sprouting legumes and grains before cooking reduces some of the compounds that can make them harder to digest.
preparation.label: established fact

preparation.text: The sour taste of fermented foods and drinks is reported to stimulate bitter taste receptors, which in turn trigger digestive secretions - one source cites a 1997 study in the journal Gut showing fermented beverages increase gastric acid output and the release of gastrin (a hormone involved in gastric acid and some pancreatic enzyme production), and a 1999 study in the Journal of Clinical Investigation attributing this specifically to the maleic and succinic acid found in fermented foods and drinks. A specific, named-study mechanism for why a fermented food or drink alongside a meal is traditionally felt to aid digestion.
preparation.label: illustration

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Some people with irritable bowel symptoms find certain high-fibre or fermentable foods (like certain beans) harder to tolerate in large amounts; this varies a lot person to person and is worth discussing with a doctor or dietitian rather than guessing.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: open question

allergensAndSensitivities.text: A small study found that food-elimination testing can meaningfully help people with IBS: of 21 patients following a strict elimination diet, symptoms disappeared for 14; when foods were reintroduced one at a time, the most common triggers found were wheat, dairy products, coffee, tea and citrus fruits. This supports a food-diary/elimination approach to finding personal triggers, consistent with this card's existing advice.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: open question

lifestyleLinks.text: Drinking enough water supports regular digestion, especially alongside a higher-fibre diet.
lifestyleLinks.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: Regular physical activity and adequate sleep are both generally linked with healthier digestion, though neither is specific to a vegan diet.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

lifestyleLinks.text: Gut bacteria can take months to recover after a course of antibiotics - one source cites a 2007 article in the International Society for Microbial Ecology journal stating some strains take up to two years to recover, and a 2011 Nature article suggesting some strains may never fully recover. Separately, it cites a 2012 study in the journal Gut reporting that antibiotic treatment can let iron-loving bacteria overgrow in the gut, reducing how much iron the body takes up - meaning an iron supplement taken at that time may partly end up feeding the overgrown bacteria rather than correcting the underlying shortfall. Worth a doctor's input on timing around a course of antibiotics, rather than self-managing.
lifestyleLinks.label: open question

lifestyleLinks.text: Stress is itself a gut-health factor, not just an activity/sleep one: one source cites a 2006 study in the American Journal of Psychology finding that stress can make the gut wall more permeable, raising the likelihood of developing food allergies, and a 2002 article in the journal Gastroenterology reporting that chronic psychological stress is linked to intestinal inflammation.
lifestyleLinks.label: illustration

testsWorthConsidering.text: There is no routine blood test for general gut health; persistent digestive symptoms are usually assessed by a doctor through history, examination and, if needed, targeted tests.
testsWorthConsidering.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: Idli or dosa with sambar (a mixed-dal and vegetable curry) and a small bowl of coconut-curd-style plant yoghurt - fermented grain, fibre-rich dal and vegetables together.

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you have ongoing abdominal pain, blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, or diarrhoea or constipation that lasts more than a couple of weeks.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Fermented and fibre-rich foods can support everyday digestion, but they cannot diagnose or treat a digestive disorder - persistent symptoms need a doctor's assessment.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Constipation article in The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets (2008) - flagged pre-2015, recheck against a current source before use. The population comparison (Asian vs Western diet) is a demographic/epidemiological observation in the source, not a controlled study, so graded as an illustration rather than an established fact.
candidateAdditions.text: This source names a diet high in meat, dairy and refined sugar and low in fibre as the most common cause of constipation in the United States, and notes that people eating a traditional Asian diet report constipation far less often than those who adopt a Western diet, suggesting diet plays a bigger role than race or genetics (it also notes Black and White Americans differ in constipation rates in the US, but that pattern reverses in Africa). This lines up with and adds specific epidemiological colour to this card's existing fibre/whole-food framing.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Constipation article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Adds a specific clinical definition and complication not yet in this card's redFlags.
candidateAdditions.text: A doctor's clinical definition of chronic constipation requires symptoms present for at least 12 weeks out of the past 12 months (the weeks don't need to be consecutive). The most serious complication is an impaction - a hard blockage of stool that usually needs a doctor's help to clear.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Gastroesophageal reflux disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). RESOLVED (owner's call, 22 Oct 2026): the onion/garlic-as-GERD-trigger point is not actually in conflict with this card's prebiotic praise of the same foods - both can be true at once, scoped to different contexts - so that specific point has been merged into foodsOrHabitsToWatch above, scoped explicitly as a GERD-specific caution. The rest of this trigger-food list (below) remains an unmerged candidate. No food in this list is non-vegan, so there is no blocklist concern.
candidateAdditions.text: This source lists common individual triggers for heartburn/GERD symptoms: greasy or fried foods, citrus fruit or juice, caffeinated drinks, tomato-based foods, chocolate, mint-flavoured foods, spicy foods, and alcohol (garlic and onion, also named here, have been merged separately - see foodsOrHabitsToWatch). It stresses triggers vary a lot from person to person, and recommends avoiding personal trigger foods rather than any fixed list.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated GERD article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). General lifestyle advice, not vegan-specific, but a reasonable lifestyleLinks-style addition; pregnancy is named as a GERD risk group here - flagged per BRIEF.md rule 9 as high-stakes-adjacent (pregnancy), not to be used in any pregnancy-specific content without independent, current verification.
candidateAdditions.text: Alongside diet, this source lists smoking, alcohol, being overweight, pregnancy, poor posture, and eating a large meal shortly before bed as things that raise the likelihood of GERD symptoms. It also suggests not eating for at least 3 hours before bed and raising the head of the bed by about 10-15cm (using blocks or a wedge) as simple, low-cost steps that help some people.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Gallstones article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A genuine, if modest, vegan-relevant hit from this article - directly supports a whole-food vegan pattern as protective. No specific study citation given in the text for this prevention line, so graded established fact cautiously rather than treated as a Strong-sourced guideline; worth a current cross-check (e.g. NIH ODS or a systematic review) before firmer wording.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly, and eating a diet high in whole grains and fresh fruit and vegetables and low in fat and cholesterol lowers the chance of developing gallstones. Since fat and cholesterol in the diet come only from food choices, not inherently from being vegan or not, a whole-food vegan diet naturally tends to be lower in saturated fat and has no dietary cholesterol at all.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Gallstones article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Relevant caution for anyone (vegan or not) attempting fast weight loss; not specific to veganism, but worth keeping here as a general watch-item since this card doesn't currently mention gallstones at all.
candidateAdditions.text: Losing weight very quickly (3 or more pounds/about 1.4kg a week) or following a very-low-calorie diet raises the risk of developing gallstones - about a quarter of people on medically supervised very-low-calorie diets (around 800 kcal/day) for several months develop gallstones, and about a third of those need gallbladder surgery. Gradual, steady weight loss is safer for the gallbladder than rapid crash dieting.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Irritable bowel syndrome and Irritable bowel syndrome diet articles (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Fills this card's existing open-question note on IBS/fermentable-food tolerance with specifics. Dairy is named as a common trigger food here in an explanatory, not recommending, context - no blocklist concern.
candidateAdditions.text: Common individual IBS trigger foods named in this source: dairy products, the sweeteners sorbitol and mannitol, caffeine, chocolate, and alcohol - though triggers vary a lot person to person and a food diary is the recommended way to find personal triggers. Separately, the source notes doctors often test for lactose intolerance and coeliac disease when diagnosing IBS, since both can cause very similar symptoms - so someone whose symptoms turn out to be lactose intolerance specifically may find a vegan (dairy-free) diet incidentally helpful, though that is a different condition from IBS itself.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Irritable bowel syndrome diet article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A genuinely useful, specific addition - gives two concrete starting patterns rather than this card's current single open-question line on tolerance varying person to person. All foods named are vegan or vegan-compatible (avocado, peanut butter, tapioca, cream of rice, etc.) - no blocklist concern. The 'limit dairy products' line is explanatory general advice, not a vegan-specific recommendation.
candidateAdditions.text: This source describes two different starting patterns for an IBS diet, since IBS affects people differently: (1) A high-fibre, low-fat pattern - most helpful for constipation-predominant IBS - built around whole grains, bran cereal, brown rice, carrots, cucumbers, oats, dried beans and peas, lentils, apples, pears and citrus fruit. (2) A low-residue, low-fat pattern - for people whose diarrhoea gets worse on high fibre - built around cooked rather than raw fruit and vegetables, with less whole grain; example foods given are applesauce, peeled grated apple, mashed potato, avocado, cream of rice, smooth peanut butter and tapioca. Other diarrhoea-easing tips given: eat and drink at room temperature rather than hot, drink liquids between meals rather than with them, and rest briefly after meals. The source stresses these are starting points to personalise by trial and error, not fixed rules, and that a doctor can advise if fibre supplements are needed.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Irritable bowel syndrome article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A specific, useful addition to this card's existing general redFlags line - distinguishes ordinary IBS from signs that need prompt medical attention.
candidateAdditions.text: This source notes that blood in the stool, vomiting, fever, and diarrhoea that wakes a person up at night are NOT typical symptoms of IBS - anyone with these should see a doctor promptly rather than assume it is ordinary IBS.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Diverticular disease diet article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Strengthens, rather than conflicts with, this card's existing onion/garlic prebiotic-fibre entries by giving the specific fibre-type name and mechanism; also supports the whyItMattersForVegans framing on fibre feeding gut bacteria.
candidateAdditions.text: This source names a specific class of fermentable fibre, polyfructoses (inulin and oligofructans), found in onions, garlic, artichokes and soybean, and explains that gut bacteria ferment this and other fermentable fibre into a short-chain fatty acid called butyric acid, which fuels and supports the health of the cells lining the large intestine. It also notes Asia and Africa, where people eat high-fibre, vegetable-based diets, have much lower rates of diverticular disease than industrialised countries.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Diverticular disease diet article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Useful myth-style reassurance, directly sourced to the book's own words, not this project's own claim - good candidate to also consider for a future Myths deck entry once that module exists.
candidateAdditions.text: Older medical advice sometimes told people with diverticular disease to avoid nuts, popcorn, and small seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, caraway, sesame), worried that bits of these foods might get stuck in the diverticula. This source states plainly that no scientific evidence supports that advice, and that seeds in tomatoes, zucchini, cucumbers, strawberries, raspberries and poppy seeds are generally considered harmless.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Diverticular disease diet article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). A specific, disease-named addition to this card's existing general redFlags line.
candidateAdditions.text: See a doctor promptly for abdominal pain on the left side of the lower abdomen together with fever, nausea, vomiting or chills - this pattern can mean infected diverticula (diverticulitis), which can become a serious infection if left untreated.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Diverticular disease diet article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015). Practical, Indian-relevant tip (millet porridge) - all vegan, no blocklist concern.
candidateAdditions.text: Simple ways this source suggests to raise everyday fibre: a bowl of porridge made with millet, oats or brown rice for breakfast, whole-grain bread instead of white, whole fruit instead of fruit juice, brown rice instead of white rice, and extra vegetables added to pasta dishes.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Digestive diseases overview article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. A genuine, source-given vegan swap (not invented by this project) found while cross-reading lactose intolerance content - satisfies BRIEF.md rule 9's requirement that a swap carry its own evidence.
candidateAdditions.text: For lactose intolerance specifically (relevant since some people whose symptoms were assumed to be IBS turn out to have this instead - see this card's existing IBS/lactose candidate), this source lists non-dairy, calcium-rich foods: kale, collard greens, broccoli and oranges, plus foods fortified with calcium such as soy milk, juices, cereals and pasta.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: HOLD - Gate 2 verdict (owner, 22 Oct 2026): this is a genuine open question in IBS nutrition (depends on fibre type and IBS subtype), not something this one 2008 popular encyclopedia can resolve on its own - needs a dedicated IBS-specific guideline source (e.g. NICE, the British Dietetic Association, or a current systematic review) before anything is drafted from either side. Keep held, not merged, until that source is found.
candidateAdditions.text: The general Digestive diseases article in this source states that people with IBS are 'usually asked to avoid food that is high in fat, insoluble fiber, caffeine, coffee, carbonated sodas, and alcohol' - but the dedicated Irritable bowel syndrome diet article in the very same book recommends a high-fibre diet including plenty of insoluble fibre (whole grains, bran, brown rice, carrots) as its main approach, reserving a separate low-fibre (low-residue) pattern only for people whose diarrhoea gets worse on high fibre. Shown side by side rather than resolved - the general article appears to oversimplify a point its own dedicated article treats with more nuance.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Inflammatory bowel disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. All foods listed are vegan. The source explicitly frames this list for when IBD is 'under control' (remission), not for an active flare - see the separate flare-up candidate below for the different, lower-fibre pattern used then.
candidateAdditions.text: For inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) in remission, this source lists high-fibre foods that can help: whole grain breads/buns/bagels/muffins, bran cereals, oat bran, whole-wheat pasta, barley, popcorn, corn and brown rice; dried fruit (apricots, dates, prunes, raisins), berries, oranges, apple with skin, avocado, kiwi, mango and pear; broccoli, spinach, green peas and other dark leafy greens, and dried peas/beans (kidney beans, lima beans, black-eyed beans, chickpeas, lentils); and almonds, whole flaxseed and soy nuts.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Inflammatory bowel disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. IMPORTANT VEGAN-RULE NOTE (BRIEF.md rules 4 and 9): for the protein/high-protein part of its flare-up advice, this source recommends well-cooked meat, fresh fish and eggs, and yoghurt - these are deliberately NOT carried over or swapped here, because rule 9 says a vegan swap needs its own evidence, and this source gives none for a vegan high-protein option during an active flare. This is an honest GAP to flag to the owner: this card currently has nothing specific to say about protein during an active IBD flare for a vegan reader, and this source doesn't fill that gap either - worth a dedicated look at vegan IBD/flare nutrition guidance from a current clinical source.
candidateAdditions.text: During an active IBD flare-up, this source recommends a gentler, lower-fibre (low-residue) pattern instead of the high-fibre remission pattern above: refined grains (white bread, cornflakes, white rice, refined pasta) rather than whole grains; peeled or cooked fruit (apple sauce, canned fruit, melon, grapes, peaches) rather than raw, dried fruit or berries; and well-cooked vegetables without skin (potato, carrot, celery, cucumber, courgette, mushroom, peppers, lettuce, beetroot, alfalfa sprouts), while avoiding cabbage-family vegetables, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds during this period. Small, frequent meals are suggested during flares.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Inflammatory bowel disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. All foods named are vegan; this is a caution about moderating certain vegan foods during a flare, not a vegan-rule issue.
candidateAdditions.text: During an IBD flare, this source suggests limiting gas-producing foods - cabbage-family vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts), dried peas and lentils, onions and chives, hot/chilli peppers, and carbonated drinks - plus caffeine, alcohol and the sweetener sorbitol, which can worsen symptoms for some people.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Inflammatory bowel disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. The source names fish oil alongside flaxseed oil as possibly helpful; only the vegan option is carried over here per rule 9 (fish oil's evidence is not transferred to any vegan equivalent, and this source says nothing about algal omega-3). Graded open question since the source gives no specific study citation.
candidateAdditions.text: This source notes that some studies suggest flaxseed oil may help manage IBD (alongside, separately, fish oil - not vegan, not carried over here), and that more recent studies suggest a possible role for prebiotics and probiotics, including psyllium (a soluble, plant-derived fibre from the plant Plantago afra), in supporting intestinal healing.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Crohn's disease article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015, a separate standalone article from the Inflammatory bowel disease article above) - Priority 2 continuation. High-stakes content per BRIEF.md rule 9 (children's growth/nutrition) - flagged for independent verification, no dosing given or implied here.
candidateAdditions.text: This source notes Crohn's disease can cause vitamin and mineral deficiencies because the damaged gut lining absorbs nutrients poorly and chronic diarrhoea speeds nutrient loss - it specifically links this to anaemia (iron), bone-thinning/osteoporosis (calcium and vitamin D), and poor blood clotting (vitamin K), and notes children with Crohn's may need special high-calorie, high-nutrient liquid supplements to maintain normal growth, decided with a doctor or dietitian. It also repeats that many people with Crohn's become lactose intolerant and need to limit or avoid dairy, and that alcohol, high-fibre foods such as popcorn, and spicy foods can worsen diarrhoea and cramping for some people.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Dyspepsia article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. Included for balance and honesty, not cherry-picked: this is a case where the source finds NO evidence that a vegetarian diet helps a digestive condition, which is worth reporting as plainly as the positive findings elsewhere in this file.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states there is no good evidence that a strictly vegetarian diet helps functional dyspepsia (a common, usually non-serious form of persistent indigestion), and cites a population-based study that found no real difference in suspected trigger-food intake between people with dyspepsia and people without it. Separately, it lists garlic (along with gingko, saw palmetto, feverfew, chaste tree berry and willow bark) among herbal remedies that can themselves cause or worsen dyspepsia symptoms in some people - another garlic-related caution alongside the GERD one already flagged in this file. It also names peppermint, turmeric and aloe vera (taken by mouth) as complementary approaches being studied, with research still preliminary, and specifically flags aloe vera taken by mouth as not recommended, since it has a laxative effect and can lower absorption of prescription medicines.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Dyspepsia article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. A specific, age-linked red flag not yet covered in this card's redFlags.
