candidateAdditions.text: See a doctor promptly for indigestion that starts suddenly after age 45, or any indigestion with black tarry stools, loss of appetite, painful swallowing, bloody vomit or unexplained weight loss. Indigestion-like discomfort together with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the neck, jaw or arm needs emergency care, since it can be a sign of a heart attack rather than a digestive problem.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Heartburn article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation, largely overlapping the GERD article already drawn on above but with some extra home-remedy detail. All plant-based, no blocklist issue. The source itself shows disagreement on ginger, a good example of BRIEF.md rule 6's 'show both sides' within a single remedy. UPDATE (2 Nov 2026, Phase 2, 14th/final herb): the licorice-root-specific point in this entry's text (licorice as a traditional heartburn/stomach-acid remedy) has now been independently verified and built out in full in the licorice-root herb card's whatEvidenceShows section and in this file's own new whyItMattersForVegans entry above, including real but mixed trial evidence (GutGard RCT, older DGL ulcer trials) and the separate, well-established blood-pressure/potassium caution. The other remedies named in this same entry (banana, aloe vera, chamomile, ginger, citrus, baking soda) remain pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review and were not touched by this update.
candidateAdditions.text: This source lists plant-based home/herbal remedies people traditionally try for heartburn, with mixed evidence: banana, aloe vera gel (taken by mouth - see this file's separate Dyspepsia candidate, which flags aloe vera by mouth as not recommended for a different digestive condition, for the same reason), chamomile, ginger and citrus juice. It specifically flags disagreement on ginger - some people find it helps, while other practitioners say it can relax the muscle that normally keeps stomach acid down, and so may cause heartburn instead. It also mentions licorice root as a traditional remedy claimed to help rebalance stomach acid output, and plain sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) in water as a cheap, fast-acting antacid - not suitable for anyone on a sodium-restricted diet, and not meant as a long-term fix. None of these carry the kind of Strong evidence this project requires for a firm recommendation - shown here as what people traditionally try, not as advice.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Ulcers article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - Priority 2 continuation. Good myth-debunking value, consistent with this project's calm, non-alarming tone. 'Meat extracts' appears only as an explanatory item in the source's own list of things that can worsen symptoms once an ulcer is present (not a recommendation to eat it) - kept as-is since dropping it would misrepresent the source's own list, and BRIEF.md's vegan rules allow factual, non-recommending mentions of a non-vegan item.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states plainly that spicy food does not cause ulcers - the main cause is a bacterial infection (Helicobacter pylori), with frequent use of NSAID painkillers (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen) a distant second cause; stress and diet were the old, now-disproven explanation. That said, some foods can still worsen symptoms once an ulcer is present, though this varies person to person: coffee (caffeinated or decaf), tea, chocolate, chili powder, mustard seed, black pepper, nutmeg, and meat extracts are named as common triggers. Alcohol should be avoided, and small, frequent meals rather than large ones can ease bloating and discomfort. With proper medical treatment, the source says dietary restriction usually isn't needed beyond easing symptoms.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From The Low-FODMAP Diet Cookbook (Sue Shepherd, PhD; recipes copyright 2013/2014, Workman/The Experiment - Shepherd developed the low-FODMAP diet in 1999 and co-authored The Complete Low-FODMAP Diet; the diet's food-FODMAP classifications are credited in this book to Monash University's Department of Gastroenterology). Round 7 trade-in picked specifically for this card's existing HELD 'IBS and insoluble fibre' open question (see below) - that held entry says a dedicated IBS/FODMAP-specific source is needed, and this is one, but it does NOT resolve the held question directly: FODMAP content (a function of carbohydrate fermentability) and fibre solubility (soluble vs insoluble) are two different frameworks answering different questions, not the same axis restated. Flagging this as a new, complementary lead for the owner to weigh when next revisiting the held entry, not a resolution of it. The book's own '75 percent' figure has no inline citation, though the author is the diet's original developer - worth an independent check against a current Monash University, NICE or British Dietetic Association source before treating as Strong.
candidateAdditions.text: This source explains the low-FODMAP diet's mechanism: FODMAPs (Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, And Polyols - specifically fructans, galacto-oligosaccharides/GOS, lactose, excess fructose, and sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and mannitol) are poorly absorbed in the small intestine, travel to the large intestine, and are fermented there by gut bacteria, producing gas that can trigger IBS symptoms (bloating, pain, altered bowel habits). The diet's developer states that clinical studies indicate over 75% of people with IBS find relief by reducing FODMAP intake, and that it also shows promise for persistent symptoms in coeliac disease, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. This reframes IBS food triggers around a food's FODMAP content, not simply its fibre amount or solubility.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the same source. FLAGS A CONFLICT, not resolved, per BRIEF.md rule 6: this card already (a) praises onion and garlic as prebiotic fibre sources generally while separately flagging them as a personal GERD trigger (see foodsOrHabitsToWatch, a live field above), and (b) has an unmerged candidate above (from The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets) recommending dried beans/peas/lentils/chickpeas as the main approach for constipation-predominant IBS. This FODMAP source adds a third angle: onion, garlic and most legumes (beans, chickpeas, lentils) are themselves classified as HIGH-FODMAP foods the diet asks IBS sufferers to restrict, at least during its initial elimination phase, because of their fructan/GOS content - the opposite framing from 'add more fibre/legumes for IBS.' All three points can be true at once without contradicting the science: these foods are good for the general population's gut bacteria, but can still be a personal IBS trigger, and that trigger is FODMAP content specifically, not insoluble fibre as such. Shown here for the owner to weigh when eventually resolving the held entry; no side picked here.
candidateAdditions.text: This source's high-FODMAP food list (credited to Monash University's Department of Gastroenterology) includes, among vegan-relevant foods: legumes (beans of all kinds including some soy forms, chickpeas, lentils), wheat/rye/barley-based breads and cereals, and onions, garlic, leeks and shallots (a fructan source). The diet asks people with IBS to restrict these, at least in an initial multi-week elimination phase, then reintroduce most of them afterwards in tolerated amounts - it is explicitly individualised, not a permanent avoid-list.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the same source's dedicated vegetarian/vegan substitutions section. A genuine, specific, source-given practical point for vegan readers who may also need a low-FODMAP diet for IBS - not previously covered in this card.
candidateAdditions.text: This source flags that vegans and vegetarians following a low-FODMAP diet risk not meeting daily protein needs, since several everyday plant proteins (whole wheat, barley, legumes, some nuts and soy foods) are themselves high-FODMAP. It suggests leaning on nuts and seeds, suitable low-FODMAP grains and cereals, protein-enriched plant milks, and suitable soy products - firm or extra-firm tofu (pressed first) and tempeh (steamed first) are named as generally suitable in these forms. It also names seitan (vital wheat gluten) as a pure-protein, FODMAP-free vegan meat substitute for anyone who does not also need to be gluten-free (seitan is not suitable for coeliac disease, since it is almost entirely gluten).
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the same source. A specific addition to this card's existing testsWorthConsidering line, which currently only says there is no routine blood test for general gut health.
candidateAdditions.text: For suspected fructose, lactose or sorbitol malabsorption specifically (as opposed to general gut health), a doctor can arrange a breath hydrogen/methane test: a baseline breath sample is taken, a specific sugar solution is drunk, and breath samples are taken again over about three hours to measure the gas gut bacteria produce fermenting that sugar. This is optional, not a prerequisite for trying a low-FODMAP diet, but can help plan one.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying studies before use - this project has only a secondary citation (via 500 High-Fiber Recipes, which names the journal but not authors/year for either Lancet study). Round 7 trade-in; cross-relevant to heart-and-cholesterol.json and diabetes.json, which also drew fibre candidates from this same author's two companion books this round.
candidateAdditions.text: Two studies published in The Lancet (named only by journal in this source, no authors or year given) found that people eating high-fibre diets had fewer colon polyps and less colon cancer; this source puts the effect at roughly a 40% lower colon cancer risk for people on a high-fibre diet. A whole-food vegan diet is naturally higher in fibre, so this supports, without being vegan-specific on its own, this card's existing fibre-focused framing.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the same source's fibre-sources chapter. No citation given for the digestion claim; a small, practical, vegan-compatible tip not currently in this card.
candidateAdditions.text: Alongside their flavour, a few everyday spices - fennel, cayenne, cumin and turmeric - are named by this source as traditionally thought to improve digestion and reduce gas and bloating, alongside the general advice already in this card to increase fibre gradually and drink more water.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Round 8 gut-health trade-in from Probiotic Drinks: 75 Recipes for Kombucha, Kefir, Ginger Beer, and Other Naturally Fermented Drinks (Julia Mueller, 2014, flagged pre-2015). No citation is given anywhere in this book for this claim (confirmed by a full-text search - see sources.json's note on this book) - included only as a general, long-held fermentation principle already consistent with this card's live preparation note on fermentation improving nutrient availability, in the same cautious spirit as this card's existing uncited '500 High Fiber Recipes' spice-digestion entry. Flagged as needing independent verification before any firmer wording.
candidateAdditions.text: This source describes fermented foods and drinks as 'predigested', in the sense that the sugars in them have already been broken down by the fermentation process, which it suggests makes them easier to digest and creates less work for the pancreas. No study or source is cited for this specific framing.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: The body makes all the cholesterol it needs by itself; dietary cholesterol comes only from animal products, so a whole-food vegan diet starts with none of it and is naturally lower in saturated fat.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Low-fat, whole-food plant-based diets have reduced LDL ("bad") cholesterol by about 15-30% across reviewed studies.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Guggul, a traditional Ayurvedic gum-resin herb some readers may take separately as a supplement rather than eat as food, is best known for a researched (though genuinely unsettled) cholesterol-lowering use. A 2021 systematic review pooling 7 trials found an average fall in LDL cholesterol, but a rigorous 2003 US trial in people eating a Western diet found the opposite - no benefit, and a possible small LDL rise, plus a skin-rash side effect in some participants. This card does not treat guggul as a reliable way to lower cholesterol. See this project's own Guggul herb card for full detail, including its thyroid-hormone and bleeding-risk cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Amla (Indian gooseberry), a traditional Ayurvedic fruit some readers may take separately as a concentrated extract or capsule rather than eat as food, has a more consistently positive - though still small and short-term - research base for cholesterol than guggul's. The most rigorous review found (using a stricter risk-of-bias tool, 9 trials, 535 people) found significant falls in LDL cholesterol, VLDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and the single most consistent finding of any amla outcome tested was a fall in hs-CRP (an inflammation marker), with the pooled trials agreeing almost perfectly with each other on that one. HDL ('good') cholesterol and blood pressure did not change significantly in that same review, despite the review's own discussion describing HDL as a significant improvement - an overclaim this project does not repeat. No trial has compared amla directly against a statin. See this project's own Amla herb card for full detail, including its bleeding-risk and blood-pressure-medicine cautions.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa, also called roselle, or sorrel in the Caribbean), usually taken separately as a tea, extract or capsule rather than eaten as food, is best known for a researched - though genuinely mixed - blood-pressure-lowering effect. The largest recent pooled review (17 trials in total across all outcomes, with roughly 11-12 of those - 819 participants - pooled for blood pressure specifically) found a significant fall in systolic blood pressure versus placebo, but no significant fall in diastolic blood pressure, and no significant difference from real blood-pressure drugs in the trials that made that comparison directly; an earlier, more cautious review of just 4 trials concluded the evidence did not support recommending hibiscus for hypertension at all. Hibiscus has actually been tested head-to-head against real ACE-inhibitor drugs (captopril, lisinopril) in at least three trials, with results pointing in different directions across them - roughly equal in one trial, worse than the drug in another, better than the drug in a third. This card does not treat hibiscus as a reliable substitute for prescribed blood-pressure medicine. See this project's own Hibiscus herb card for full detail, including its genuine diuretic effect and its chloroquine-interaction caution.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Fibre (lowers cholesterol absorption), plant protein in place of animal protein, and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, flaxseed) in place of saturated tropical fats matter most.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: A strong plant source of omega-3 ALA, plus fibre.
8.7 g omega-3 per 100 g, one of the richest plant sources tracked.
Soy protein has shown LDL-lowering effects in randomised trials cited by PCRM.
A fortified soy milk brings soy protein into an everyday drink.
20.4 g fibre per 100 g, supporting cholesterol excretion.
8.3 g fibre per portion alongside plant protein.
12.6 g fibre per portion.
15.6 g fibre per 100 g, including soluble fibre.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Coconut and palm oil are plant-based but high in saturated fat; the WHO recommends keeping saturated fat under 10% of daily calories.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Trans fats, from hydrogenated or partially hydrogenated oils and some fried or ultra-processed snacks, raise LDL cholesterol and are best avoided.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A large US cohort study (Yang Q, Zhang Z, Gregg EW, 'Added Sugar Intake and Cardiovascular Diseases Mortality Among US Adults,' JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014;174(4):516-524), reported here via a secondary source, found that adults getting 17-21% of daily calories from added sugar had a 38% higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than those getting about 8%; above 21% of calories from added sugar, the risk was about twice as high. Not diet-type-specific - about added sugar generally, not tied to vegan vs non-vegan eating, and distinct from sugar naturally occurring in whole fruit or vegetables.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or DGL supplement, has a real, well-established mechanism for raising blood pressure: its compound glycyrrhizin blocks an enzyme (11-beta-HSD2) that normally breaks cortisol down in the kidney, letting cortisol act like a sodium- and water-retaining hormone. A 2023 peer-reviewed narrative review found 84 of 104 reported toxicity cases required hospitalisation, with hypertension a leading feature; a US consumer clinical-reference source notes effects can occur with as little as 5 g/day of licorice root in people with existing heart or blood-pressure problems or a high-salt diet, and cites an FDA alert that more than 2 ounces/day of black licorice candy for 2+ weeks may cause dangerous heart-rhythm changes, especially in adults over 40. Anyone with hypertension, heart disease, or taking a blood-pressure medicine, digoxin or a diuretic should talk to a doctor before using licorice root in any form, including DGL. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate pregnancy and kidney/potassium cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: Fibre and plant protein together - for example, a bean-rich meal - lower cholesterol more than relying on just one of the two.
absorption.label: established fact

protein.text: Tofu or tempeh with rice or roti gives a soy-based protein pairing, alongside a fibre-rich bean or vegetable side.
protein.label: established fact

preparation.text: Steaming, baking or pressure-cooking instead of deep-frying keeps added saturated and trans fat down.
preparation.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Aiming for at least half a cup of cooked beans a day is a simple, practical fibre target.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk, edamame) and tree nuts (walnuts) are recognised allergens; those avoiding them can lean more on fibre-rich beans and flaxseed instead.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: About 150 minutes of exercise a week is linked with higher HDL ("good") cholesterol, alongside food choices.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

testsWorthConsidering.text: A lipid profile blood test (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides) is the usual check; general targets cited are total cholesterol under 150 mg/dL and LDL at or below 100 mg/dL, with a stricter 70 mg/dL sometimes used for those already at high risk.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Tofu or tempeh bhurji with a jowar or barley roti and a lobia (cowpea) salad with lemon - plant protein, fibre and minimal added oil in one plate.

redFlags.text: Chest pain or pressure, breathlessness, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or a sudden irregular heartbeat need emergency care, not diet changes.
redFlags.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never stop or reduce a prescribed statin or blood pressure medicine because your diet has improved - talk to your doctor first.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food can meaningfully lower LDL cholesterol for many people, but it cannot replace emergency care for a suspected heart attack, or medicine already prescribed for existing heart disease.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying meta-analysis before use - this project has only a secondary citation of it.
candidateAdditions.text: A 2016 meta-analysis in the journal BMC Medicine, combining 29 of the most rigorous studies on nut consumption (cited via a secondary source, not independently read by us), found that eating a handful of nuts daily was associated with roughly 30% lower coronary heart disease risk, 15% lower cancer risk, and 40% lower diabetes risk. A separate, smaller trial (PREDIMED sub-analysis) found nut-eaters lost more belly fat and had greater reductions in blood pressure, LDL cholesterol and inflammation than a low-fat-diet comparison group. If confirmed directly, these are strong, specific, citable figures for why nuts matter in this topic - walnuts are already in this card's foodsToFavour, but not with this strength of evidence attached yet.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified accurate by independent review against book-complete-home-guide-herbs-natural-healing (exact match). KEPT HELD, not merged into any live field - this general-audience herbs/natural-healing book gives no citation at all for the specific numbers, and this project has no evidence-graded source for this exact claim yet, so per BRIEF.md rule 10 it stays an illustration on file rather than reader-facing content. Worth keeping in mind for the busy-sceptic persona (a relative or friend might raise this exact comparison) once a Strong source is found.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states that vegans and vegetarians naturally have lower blood pressure than meat and dairy eaters, giving example average figures of 110/70 for vegetarians versus 120/80 for meat eaters. No study is cited for these specific numbers. The broader association between plant-based diets and lower blood pressure is plausible and consistent with general nutrition science, but this specific numeric comparison needs a Strong source (e.g. a systematic review or government body) before being treated as more than an illustration.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the underlying studies before use - secondary citations only (via 1,001 Heart Healthy Recipes and its companion book 500 High-Fiber Recipes, both by the same author, Dick Logue; neither book gives full author/year detail for all three studies named). Round 7 trade-in (both books picked as cookbook trade-ins directly relevant to this card). Cross-relevant to diabetes.json and gut-health.json, which also drew fibre candidates from these same two books this round - kept here since this book's primary target per this round's instructions is heart-and-cholesterol.json.
candidateAdditions.text: This source cites three studies on fibre and heart-related health: a study in the May 11, 2000 issue of The New England Journal of Medicine found diabetic patients on a very high-fibre diet lowered their glucose levels by 10%; a 1976 Veterans Administration Medical Center (Lexington, Kentucky) study found fibre useful for diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity and lowering cholesterol; and two studies in The Lancet linked high-fibre diets to fewer colon polyps and less colon cancer. Separately, the source states high-fibre diets have reduced LDL ('bad') cholesterol by 10-15% (via two mechanisms it names: fibre encourages gut bacteria to produce propionic acid, which inhibits the body's own cholesterol production, and fibre removes bile acids from the gut, prompting the liver to draw more cholesterol from the blood to make new ones), and have reduced blood pressure by 3 to 7 points, enough to lower heart disease risk by up to 9%. None of this is vegan-specific on its own, but a whole-food vegan diet is naturally higher in fibre, so it supports this card's existing fibre-focused framing with more specific effect sizes than currently sourced here.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Food-composition data (not a clinical claim), from the companion book 500 High-Fiber Recipes (AccuChef/USDA-based figures per its own introduction, not independently re-verified against USDA FoodData Central here). All items vegan. Supports this card's existing legume entries in foodsToFavour with more specific per-serving figures.
candidateAdditions.text: Approximate fibre per standard serving for common legumes, per this source: navy beans 19 g, split peas 16 g, lentils 16 g, black beans 15 g, lima beans 13 g, kidney beans 11 g, black-eyed peas 9 g. The source separately notes a single legume serving provides 15 g or more of fibre on average, and that legumes have been linked to feeling fuller for longer and to reduced risk of heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A varied, whole-food vegan diet that covers zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein well supports the immune system doing its normal job. The CDC states plainly that vitamin D 'helps the immune system resist bacteria and viruses' and that zinc plays 'an important role in... keeping the immune system strong'. Separately, a deficiency of dietary protein or amino acids has long been known to impair immune function and raise susceptibility to infectious disease, and NIH names 'reduced infection resistance' as a symptom of iron-deficiency anaemia. These four nutrients are exactly the ones a vegan diet needs more planning around (see this project's own zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein cards) - so getting them right is also, specifically, an immune-function point, not just a general nutrition one.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: This is about supporting normal immune function through nutrient adequacy, not about 'boosting' immunity beyond normal. None of the sources behind this card describe a food, nutrient or supplement raising immune function above a normal, well-nourished baseline - they describe what happens when a nutrient is short, and what getting enough of it restores. A reader should come away thinking 'make sure I'm not falling short on these,' not 'eating more of this will supercharge my immune system.'
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Covering zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein well is the main lever here - see this project's own nutrient cards for daily targets, vegan food sources and absorption tips for each. This card does not repeat those targets; it exists to connect them to the immune-function reason they matter.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: Vitamin C also matters here - NIH names it directly as helping the immune system work properly - but a vegan diet is not at particular risk of falling short on it (see this project's own vitamin C nutrient card, added specifically to cover this and the iron-absorption link below). It is included in this card's cross-references for completeness, not as a fifth nutrient to worry about alongside zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

foodsToFavour.note: Covers zinc, iron and protein together in one everyday food - already in this project's zinc, iron and protein cards.
A zinc and protein source; calcium-set tofu also covers calcium, useful alongside vitamin D for bone/immune-adjacent nutrition.
Fermented soy - zinc and protein together, already named in this project's zinc card.
High in both iron and zinc per 100 g, among the highest tracked in this project.
A quick-cooking dal with solid iron and protein per katori.
A named zinc source in this project's zinc card.
A named zinc source in this project's zinc card.
An everyday protein source; check the label for vitamin D fortification, since this is one of the main vegan vitamin D routes this project's own vitamin D card names.
A complete-protein whole grain that also contributes zinc.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Phytates in beans and grains reduce how much zinc the body absorbs from them - this project's zinc card already covers this and the soaking/sprouting/fermenting tip that helps. A vegan diet built mostly around unsoaked, unsprouted dried legumes and whole grains, with little variety, is the realistic risk here - not veganism itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: More is not better: this project's zinc card already notes that too much zinc from supplements can, over time, lower immunity rather than help it, alongside causing nausea and a copper shortage. A zinc-rich varied diet does not need a separate supplement on top by default.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: A restrictive or poorly planned vegan diet - low in variety, low in overall calories, or skipping food groups - is the real driver of falling short on zinc, vitamin D, iron or protein, not a well-planned vegan diet as such. This mirrors the same honesty pattern this project uses elsewhere: the risk comes from how a vegan diet is built, not from being vegan.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Giloy (Guduchi), a traditional herb some readers may consider for 'immune support' specifically, carries a real, published liver-injury risk with ordinary weeks-to-months self-prescribed use, including documented cases requiring hospital treatment and one death - this is this project's single most serious herb-safety finding. See this project's own Giloy (Guduchi) herb card for the full detail before considering it.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

preparation.text: Soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains before cooking lowers their phytate content and can improve zinc absorption - the same tip this project's zinc card already gives.
preparation.label: established fact

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) and sesame, both named above, are recognised allergens; chickpeas, lentils, sunflower seeds or quinoa are reasonable substitutes for zinc/iron/protein if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with masoor dal or chana curry, a side of calcium-set tofu or tempeh, rice or roti, and a fortified soy milk alongside - covering zinc, iron and protein together, with fortified soy milk as one route to vitamin D if the label confirms it.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet supporting normal immune function through nutrient adequacy - it is not a substitute for vaccination, and it cannot treat an active infection. See a doctor for a suspected infection, a fever that doesn't settle, or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor if you notice you are getting infections unusually often, infections that take unusually long to clear, or other signs that something beyond ordinary diet and lifestyle may be affecting your immune system - this needs a clinical assessment, not a diet change on its own.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices can support the immune system doing its normal job by covering nutrients like zinc, vitamin D, iron and protein - but no food, diet or supplement 'boosts' immunity beyond that normal baseline, treats an active infection, or substitutes for vaccination or a doctor's care.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND independent reading of the primary Cochrane review before use. Cross-referenced from this project's own zinc.json, where it already sits as an unverified candidate (sourced to book-super-immunity, a popular book, not independently read). Duplicated here deliberately since this is also exactly the right card for it, same pattern as other cross-referenced candidates in this project (e.g. the kidney-health/potassium 'double trouble' entry). Not vegan-specific.
candidateAdditions.text: A Cochrane meta-analysis (cited but not independently read by this project) reportedly found that zinc taken within 24 hours of cold symptoms starting roughly halved the chance of still having symptoms at the 7-day mark, and that regular zinc use over several months reduced the risk of catching a cold at all.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

whyItMattersForVegans.text: For the most common kinds of kidney stones, limiting animal protein (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) and swapping in plant proteins is linked to lower stone risk - a direction a government health body backs directly, not just a vegan-specific claim.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: One source suggests a specific reason why: vegetarian and vegan eating patterns tend to produce lower urinary calcium and acid, and higher citrate (citrate helps stop stones forming), than diets heavy in animal protein, which push the opposite way. The government source above backs the general advice to limit animal protein, but does not itself spell out this exact urinary-chemistry explanation - so treat the mechanism, specifically, as a single source's illustration rather than an independently confirmed official line.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: If you've ever had, or have a family history of, a calcium-oxalate stone (the most common type), a clinician can set a personal oxalate target for you rather than you following a generic list - most people don't need to cut oxalate-rich plant foods out altogether.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Eat a calcium-rich food at the same meal as an oxalate-rich one, rather than avoiding either. This is the single most specific, actionable tip here - see Preparation below.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

whatToFocusOn.text: Drink enough fluid through the day, and keep sodium moderate - both matter alongside food choice.
whatToFocusOn.label: official recommendation

foodsToFavour.note: Named separately by both sources here as comparatively lower in oxalate than most other legumes - a good everyday plant-protein swap for animal protein if you're watching stone risk.

Calcium-set tofu is a plant calcium source named in our kidney-stone book source as a food to pair with an oxalate-rich vegetable at the same meal - the pairing idea itself is government-backed (see Preparation); tofu is one example of a calcium food to use for it.
A fortified, unsweetened soy milk is another everyday calcium source to pair with an oxalate-rich food at the same meal - check the label, as fortification varies by brand.

Named in our kidney-stone book source as a complete, low-glycaemic plant protein that also contains phytic acid, which may help offset oxalate's effect - an interesting single-source lead, not confirmed independently here.

Our kidney-stone book source names fermented soy (tempeh) as lower in oxalate than plain tofu, thanks to fermentation - a specific claim from one source only, worth knowing but not yet independently confirmed.

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: If you're prone to calcium-oxalate stones, a government health body names nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran as foods to limit or avoid, and suggests asking a clinician about other high-oxalate foods for your own personal target.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: official recommendation

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Our kidney-stone book source additionally names beet greens, strawberries and chocolate as oxalate-rich foods worth moderating. Its own list of foods is longer than the government source's - treat these extra items as a single source's lower-confidence addition, not an official recommendation.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: The two sources here don't fully agree on dried beans: the government source names beans, dried peas and lentils generally as lower-oxalate plant-protein options, while the book source separately lists most dried beans (apart from green beans and lima beans) as oxalate-rich foods to moderate. Shown here rather than resolved, since the sources point different ways on this specific point - lentils are the one food both agree is comparatively lower-oxalate.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: open question

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Cooking only reduces the oxalate in a food modestly - our book source puts it at around 15% - so moderating how much and how often you eat an oxalate-rich food matters more than how you cook it.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: This applies to chronic kidney disease (CKD) specifically, not the kidney-stone/oxalate focus of the rest of this card: dried beans and peas, nuts, and several whole grains (amaranth, brown rice, millet, oats, quinoa, spelt) are 'double trouble' foods for CKD - high in both potassium and phosphorus, which a damaged kidney struggles to clear. For someone managing CKD, this source suggests swapping towards green beans or wax beans instead of dried beans or peas, and lower-potassium/phosphorus whole grains such as barley, buckwheat, bulgur, popcorn or wild rice. This is a narrow, CKD-specific caution, not a general vegan one - legumes and whole grains are rightly praised as core vegan protein and fibre staples elsewhere in this project, and that general praise still stands for people without CKD.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Neem, a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, capsule or leaf powder, is rated 'Possibly Unsafe' and might harm the kidneys specifically at large doses or with long-term oral use - a broader caution than, and separate from, the acute poisoning risk in children covered on this project's own Neem herb card. Anyone with existing kidney disease should be especially cautious about taking neem by mouth, and talk to their doctor first.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa, also called roselle, or sorrel in the Caribbean), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or capsule for blood pressure, has a genuine, reasonably well-evidenced diuretic effect - a dedicated review states plainly 'there is evidence that HS acts as a diuretic,' and separate human trials have found it significantly increases urine volume and raises a kidney-filtration marker (creatinine clearance) compared with placebo. The same review specifically warns against combining hibiscus with the diuretic medicine hydrochlorothiazide, based on animal data suggesting a possible interaction. Anyone taking a diuretic medicine, or with existing kidney disease, should talk to a doctor before combining hibiscus with it, and watch for signs of dehydration or excessive fluid loss if they do. See this project's own Hibiscus herb card for full detail, including its blood-pressure evidence and chloroquine-interaction caution.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra), a traditional herb some readers may take separately as a tea, extract or DGL supplement, causes a well-documented kidney-level mechanism called pseudohyperaldosteronism: glycyrrhizin blocks the kidney enzyme 11-beta-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol there, so cortisol instead acts on the same receptor aldosterone uses - causing the kidneys to retain sodium and lose potassium, which can lead to hypokalemia, swelling and high blood pressure. A US consumer clinical-reference source lists severe renal insufficiency as a contraindication for licorice, and a German government risk-assessment review notes that because product labels do not state glycyrrhizin content, people with existing kidney disease cannot easily judge their own risk from a given product. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is specifically made to reduce this risk (required to contain no more than 3% of the original glycyrrhizic acid per a Health Canada monograph), but this card's own research found no dedicated kidney-safety data for DGL itself. Anyone with kidney disease should talk to a doctor before using licorice root in any form. See this project's own Licorice Root herb card for full detail, including its separate blood-pressure and pregnancy cautions.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

protein.text: Dal with rice or roti stays a useful everyday combination here too: it supplies plant protein instead of animal protein, which is the main swap this topic's own advice points towards.
protein.label: official recommendation

preparation.text: Eat a calcium-rich food in the same meal as an oxalate-rich one, rather than taking a calcium supplement separately and expecting the same effect. Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut before it can reach the kidneys - this is why a government health body says not to cut calcium even while watching oxalate, and recommends getting it from low-oxalate plant foods.
preparation.label: official recommendation

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) is a recognised allergen among the plant protein swaps named above; a lower-oxalate legume like lentils, or a fortified alternative plant milk, is a reasonable substitute if soy doesn't suit you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

lifestyleLinks.text: A government health body suggests roughly six to eight 8-ounce glasses of fluid a day as a general figure, but says to ask a clinician for the amount that's right for you personally, especially if you've had a particular stone type before.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

lifestyleLinks.text: Keep sodium under about 2,300 mg a day (roughly one teaspoon of table salt) - this applies even if you're already taking a stone-prevention medicine.
lifestyleLinks.label: official recommendation

testsWorthConsidering.text: If you've had a kidney stone before, a clinician can identify which type it was - calcium oxalate is the most common - since this decides which of the points above matter most for you, rather than following a generic list.
testsWorthConsidering.label: official recommendation

samplePlate.text: Masoor dal with rice or roti, a side of calcium-set tofu or a glass of fortified plant milk, and a cooked (not raw) vegetable sabzi - pairing a calcium source with the rest of the meal, the way the dietary-calcium advice above suggests.

redFlags.text: Sudden severe pain, especially with fever or blood in the urine, or being unable to pass urine, needs urgent medical attention - don't try to manage these with diet alone.
redFlags.label: established fact

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Diet can lower the chance of forming a new stone, but it cannot dissolve a stone that's already there, relieve a sudden attack, or replace a doctor's diagnosis and treatment.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. High-stakes dosing figure per BRIEF.md rule 9: a specific supplement amount, not independently verified by the government source here (NIDDK's own diet page does not mention magnesium at all). Must stay out of any live field until independently checked, ideally against NIH ODS.
candidateAdditions.text: Our kidney-stone book source cites magnesium oxide, 400 mg/day, as possibly reducing stone risk by blocking calcium-oxalate binding.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. No numeric dose given, but flagged as a lead needing its own nutrient card: this project currently has no dedicated vitamin-B6 nutrient card to attach this claim to, and the claim is not independently confirmed by the government source here.
candidateAdditions.text: Our kidney-stone book source notes that vegetarians 'may have low levels of vitamin B6' and could benefit from supplementation, without giving a specific dose.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A genuinely unresolved question per the source's own wording, not something to state as settled either way.
candidateAdditions.text: Soy foods (tofu, tempeh, soy milk) are themselves moderately high in oxalate but also contain phytic acid, which may help offset stone formation. Our kidney-stone book source says plainly that 'no one knows' whether the phytic acid actually offsets the oxalate, while noting that high-soy-consuming cultures don't show increased stone rates.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From Renal Diet Cookbook (Susan Zogheib, MHS, RD, LDN; Rockridge Press, 2015). Round 7 trade-in. SCOPE NOTE: this source covers a different kidney condition from the rest of this card - chronic kidney disease (CKD) and dialysis - not kidney stones/oxalates. It doesn't contradict anything already here; it's a separate condition with mostly separate dietary advice, added as a new sub-area for this topic rather than folded into the existing stone-focused fields.
candidateAdditions.text: In CKD, the kidneys progressively lose the ability to clear potassium, phosphorus, sodium and protein-breakdown waste from the blood. A CKD diet typically limits all four, with the exact limits depending on CKD stage (there are five, from near-normal kidney function to kidney failure/dialysis) and blood test results - this source stresses that the right limits should be set with a doctor or renal dietitian, not read off a generic list, since needs can differ a lot between someone in early-stage CKD and someone on dialysis.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A genuine vegan-specific hit from this source's own dedicated 'No Meat? No Problem' section on adapting a CKD diet for vegetarians and vegans.
candidateAdditions.text: This source names plant protein sources it considers suitable for a CKD-friendly diet: lentils, grains, seitan, tofu, tempeh, unsalted natto (fermented soybeans), and soy-based low-sodium meat substitutes (soy burgers, soy-based deli slices and hot dogs). It recommends choosing three or more different plant-protein sources a day and including at least one soy item daily, while cautioning that several of these (legumes, whole grains, nuts, soy) also carry potassium and phosphorus that need individual monitoring - see the next candidate below.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the primary paper before use. A real, specific, checkable citation found in this source's own Appendix A reference list (not a secondhand citation via another popular book).
candidateAdditions.text: This source cites: Krishnamurthy VM, Wei G, Baird BC, et al., 'High Dietary Fiber Intake Is Associated with Decreased Inflammation and All-Cause Mortality in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease,' Kidney International, 2012;81(3):300-6 - finding that higher dietary fibre intake was associated with lower inflammation and lower all-cause mortality in CKD patients. A real, specific, vegan-relevant citation supporting a high-fibre whole-food pattern as beneficial in CKD specifically, though it should be read directly before being treated as Strong evidence here.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. General CKD safety caution, not vegan-specific, but worth noting since this project recommends vegan supplements (D3, K2, algal omega-3, B12) elsewhere - CKD can change what's safe to take.
candidateAdditions.text: This source cautions that people with CKD, especially those on dialysis, should not take an ordinary over-the-counter multivitamin without medical advice: vitamins A, E and K can build up to harmful levels as kidney function falls, while water-soluble vitamins (B-complex, folic acid) are often lost and may need daily replacing. It recommends asking a doctor about a renal-specific multivitamin instead, rather than a standard one.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From Kidney Cooking, 3rd ed. (Georgia Council on Renal Nutrition, National Kidney Foundation - Georgia Division, 2013). Round 7 trade-in, picked specifically to cross-check this card's existing NIDDK-vs-book dried-beans oxalate conflict (above). OWNER'S SPECIFIC QUESTION, ANSWERED: this book does NOT mention oxalate anywhere in its 144 pages - it is a CKD/dialysis potassium-phosphorus-sodium recipe book (like book-renal-diet-cookbook above), not a kidney-stone book, so it is silent on, not a third data point for, the existing NIDDK-vs-Kidney-Stone-Diet dried-beans conflict. It does list black-eyed peas and lima beans among 'foods to omit' for its dialysis-patient readers, but that is for their potassium content, not oxalate - a different reason, so it does not count as an independent vote either way on the oxalate question.
candidateAdditions.text: This source gives a specific 'double-cooking' method to reduce potassium in tuberous root vegetables (white potatoes, sweet potatoes, yams) for CKD/dialysis patients: peel and thinly slice the vegetable, soak in room-temperature water (twice the volume of the vegetable), bring to a boil, drain, then repeat with fresh water and cook until tender. It states this does not make the vegetable a low-potassium food, only reduces its potassium by a meaningful amount, citing: Burrowes JD, Ramer NJ, 'Changes in potassium content of different varieties after cooking,' Journal of Renal Nutrition, 2008;18:530-4 (page range as given in this source; volume issue number not specified in the text captured).
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From Krause's Food & the Nutrition Care Process (2012), Chapter 36, 'Medical Nutrition Therapy for Renal Disorders' - the targeted renal-chapter read approved for this round (owner's explicit scope: kidney/renal and mood/mental-health chapters only, not the rest of this 1,187-page book). This is a far more clinically authoritative renal source than book-renal-diet-cookbook, but like that source it is NOT vegan-specific anywhere in this chapter - a deliberate check across the full 32-page chapter (pages 799-832) for vegetarian/vegan/plant-based/soy mentions found zero hits. Added here because it gives the actual numeric clinical targets that the existing book-renal-diet-cookbook candidate above only described in general terms ('limits differ by stage, set with a doctor'). Pre-2015 (2012); flag for a recheck against current KDOQI/NIDDKD guidance before any use, per BRIEF.md rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: This source gives specific National Kidney Foundation (KDOQI) and NIDDKD protein targets by CKD severity, each with roughly half to 60% from 'high biologic value' (HBV) protein: about 0.8 g/kg/day for an eGFR above 55 mL/min, 0.6 g/kg/day for an eGFR of 25-55 mL/min, and 0.6 g/kg/day (rising to 0.75 g/kg/day if calorie intake can't otherwise be kept up) alongside 35 kcal/kg/day for an eGFR below 25 before dialysis starts. On dialysis itself, protein needs rise sharply (around 1.2 g/kg/day for haemodialysis, 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day for peritoneal dialysis). It also gives a general phosphorus target of roughly 1,000-1,200 mg/day for earlier-stage CKD, tightening further once on dialysis. None of this is vegan-specific: the source doesn't say whether, or how, a vegan diet can meet the 'HBV protein' share at these lower total-protein levels - a real gap, not an assumption to fill in without its own evidence.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Corroborates, from a second and more clinically authoritative source, the 'double trouble' caution already held above from book-renal-diet-cookbook - not a new unresolved claim, a second vote for the same one. Still CKD-specific, not a general vegan caution (see that existing candidate's own note).
candidateAdditions.text: This source separately confirms that, alongside meat, high-protein plant foods - dried beans, nuts, and legumes generally - are also significant dietary phosphorus sources that a CKD-specific low-phosphorus diet needs to account for, alongside dairy. It notes that eliminating high-phosphorus foods without also restricting protein overall isn't realistically possible, which is part of why CKD phosphorus and protein targets are managed together rather than separately.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A genuinely new vegan-relevant angle, not found in this card's other CKD sources - but held as an open question, not a swap recommendation: the source names 'increased reliance on animal-based proteins' as one of several contributors to a lipid problem in end-stage renal disease, without citing a specific study for that one factor and without ever suggesting a plant-protein alternative or giving one any evidence of its own (BRIEF.md rule 9 - a swap needs its own evidence, which isn't offered here).
candidateAdditions.text: People with end-stage renal disease (on dialysis) commonly develop raised triglycerides and cholesterol. This source lists a few likely contributors, one of which is increased reliance on animal-based proteins (alongside increased fat synthesis and reduced clearance) - named as a factor, not elaborated on with its own citation or a suggested plant-based alternative.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND independent verification before any use. High-stakes dosing per BRIEF.md rule 9, and the source itself is internally inconsistent: its own running text says 2-10 mg/day of vitamin B6 may reduce urinary oxalate in some calcium-oxalate stone formers, while its own Table 36-4 separately states '40 mg or more per day reduces risk. No recommendation made.' Those two figures don't agree, so neither should be treated as a settled number. Cross-reference: a related, dose-free candidate ('vegetarians may have low levels of vitamin B6') already sits above from book-kidney-stone-diet - this is a different claim (B6's specific role in lowering urinary oxalate for stone formers, not vegetarians' general B6 status) and should not be merged with it.
candidateAdditions.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a required cofactor in how the body processes oxalate, and low B6 status should be avoided by anyone managing oxalate-related stone risk. This source's own running text suggests 2 to 10 mg/day of B6 may reduce urinary oxalate in some calcium-oxalate stone formers, but a table in the same chapter separately gives 40 mg/day or more, and adds 'no recommendation made' - an unresolved internal inconsistency, not a number to use.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Corroborates, from an independent source, the mechanism (not the dose) of the magnesium candidate already held above from book-kidney-stone-diet. This source gives no dose at all, so it doesn't resolve that candidate's missing-dose problem - it only strengthens the general mechanism.
candidateAdditions.text: Magnesium forms a soluble complex with oxalate and may help prevent oxalate absorption, giving it a possible role for people who form calcium-oxalate stones repeatedly - consistent with, though not adding a dose to, the magnesium candidate already noted above.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Two genuinely new oxalate-rich items not yet anywhere in this card, from this source's own box of foods to avoid on a low-oxalate diet - worth flagging prominently since turmeric is a staple Indian spice with approved local names elsewhere in this project. Caveats: the box cites a single reference (Siener et al., 2006, on cereals and cereal products specifically) for the whole list, which doesn't obviously cover turmeric or tea - so treat the citation as weaker for these two items than for the cereal-related ones on the same list. The turmeric entry is also qualified as 'high doses' with no definition of what counts as high in ordinary cooking use, which this project would need to interpret with real care before saying anything to a reader.
candidateAdditions.text: This source's low-oxalate-diet food list separately names tea (green, black, iced or instant) and high doses of turmeric as oxalate sources to moderate, alongside the already-covered rhubarb, spinach, strawberries, chocolate, wheat bran, nuts and beets. It separately notes that black and green tea's own oxalate content is reduced by taking it with milk, since the calcium binds oxalate in the gut - the source doesn't say whether a fortified plant milk would do the same, though the stated mechanism (calcium binding) would suggest it reasonably could; that's our own inference, not something this source states, so it needs its own confirmation before being presented as a tip.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From a single named-author Clinical Insight sidebar within the chapter (Sheila Dean, DSc, RD), not the chapter's own main authors - citing Remer & Manz's real, checkable Potential Renal Acid Load (PRAL) methodology (Remer, 1995, cited directly in this chapter's own reference list). Flagged because it complicates a simple 'plant food = kidney-friendly' assumption for readers managing kidney stones specifically - it is NOT a reason to discourage nuts, seeds or whole grains generally, which this project rightly praises elsewhere for unrelated reasons.
candidateAdditions.text: In the Potential Renal Acid Load (PRAL) model this source cites, several everyday vegan foods are classed as acid-forming in the same way meat, fish and cheese are - walnuts, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, sunflower seeds, peanuts and peanut butter, and wheat-based breads and bran. Vegetables (including lentils) and fruit are classed as alkaline regardless of this. For someone specifically managing kidney stones via urinary pH, this means 'plant-based' alone doesn't guarantee a lower acid load - the type of plant food matters.
candidateAdditions.label: illustration

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND a direct read of the primary paper before use. A real, specific, checkable citation (Nouvenne A, et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2009;91:365) supporting the animal-protein-limitation point already live in whyItMattersForVegans above (currently sourced only to niddk-kidney-stones, which doesn't itself name this exact trial).
candidateAdditions.text: A randomised controlled trial cited in this source found that a diet combining adequate calcium, low animal protein, and low salt (under 4 g/day) reduced oxalate excretion more than a traditional low-oxalate diet alone, in people with idiopathic hypercalciuria.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A general clinical caution, not vegan-specific - but potentially relevant to cross-reference with vitamin-d.json's own cautions field in a future pass (NOT edited here, per this round's explicit scope limit to kidney-health.json and mood-mental-health.json only, and per the separate instruction not to touch any nutrient card's cautions field this round). The source doesn't distinguish by vitamin D form (D2/D3/lichen-D3) - it's a blanket caution for anyone who forms calcium-oxalate stones.
candidateAdditions.text: This source's own table of diet and monitoring advice for kidney stone disease lists vitamin D and cod liver oil supplements as 'not recommended' for people managing calcium-oxalate stone risk, without giving a reason in the text captured here beyond the general concern about excess vitamin D raising urinary calcium.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

whyItMattersForVegans.text: A 2025 systematic review pooling 23 studies and over 700,000 adults found that people eating a healthy, whole-food plant-based diet had lower odds of anxiety, depression and psychological distress than people eating the least plant-based diet, and a lower long-term risk of depression, cognitive decline and dementia. These are associations from observational studies, not proof that the diet caused the lower risk, and they are not a substitute for treatment - but it is a reassuring, well-sized body of evidence for a whole-food vegan diet's role in long-term mental wellbeing.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: The same review found the opposite pattern for an unhealthy plant-based diet - one that cuts out animal foods but relies heavily on refined grains, added sugar and heavily processed plant foods - which was linked to a HIGHER likelihood of anxiety and depression. In short: going vegan on its own is not what the evidence supports for mood; eating mostly whole plant foods is the part that matters.
whyItMattersForVegans.label: established fact

whyItMattersForVegans.text: Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri), a traditional Ayurvedic herb some readers may take separately rather than eat as food, is best known for memory rather than mood specifically. Two independent systematic reviews/meta-analyses of human trials found real benefits - one for memory free-recall, a later one for speed of attention - though the two reviews point to slightly different specific benefits rather than confirming one single, settled effect. See this project's own Brahmi herb card for full detail, including an important naming caution (it is easily confused with a different plant, gotu kola, also sometimes called 'Brahmi').
whyItMattersForVegans.label: open question

whatToFocusOn.text: Building meals around whole, minimally processed plant foods - vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds - rather than relying on refined or heavily processed vegan products, since this whole-food pattern is the one the research above actually supports.
whatToFocusOn.label: established fact

whatToFocusOn.text: PCRM's Food and Mood guidance highlights three food threads worth including regularly: plant sources of tryptophan (an amino acid the body uses to make serotonin) - PCRM also names watercress, broccoli and pumpkin seeds alongside the foods listed below; ALA omega-3s such as ground flaxseed, chia seeds and walnuts (see our omega-3 nutrient card for how the body converts ALA into EPA/DHA); and antioxidant-rich fruit and vegetables, especially ones containing the plant compound quercetin, which PCRM also names in kale and green tea. Watercress, broccoli, pumpkin seeds, chia seeds, kale and green tea don't yet have their own food cards in this project, so they're mentioned here rather than linked. None of these three threads are proven treatments on their own - each rests on PCRM's own smaller citations, which this project grades cautiously - but they fit naturally into the whole-food pattern above.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

whatToFocusOn.text: Many of the tryptophan-rich seeds, legumes and leafy greens named below also appear in this project's zinc, iron and folate nutrient cards - a varied vegan diet that already covers those nutrients well tends to naturally include many of the same foods useful here.
whatToFocusOn.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: The 2025 review's protective finding was specifically for a whole-food plant-based pattern. A diet that is vegan but built on refined grains, added sugar, white bread, fried snacks and other heavily processed vegan products was linked to a HIGHER chance of anxiety and depression in the same research. Being vegan is not, by itself, the protective part - what you build your vegan diet from is.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: PCRM's own mechanisms (tryptophan, quercetin, omega-3) rest on smaller, single studies - useful context, not proof on their own. Treat them as encouraging background for choosing whole plant foods, not as a diet that will fix low mood by itself.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: illustration

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Shatavari, a traditional Ayurvedic herb some readers may take separately, may reduce how well the body clears lithium - a medicine used for some mood disorders (such as bipolar disorder). This could raise lithium to harmful levels, and a dose adjustment may be needed. Anyone taking lithium should talk to their doctor before trying shatavari - see this project's own Shatavari herb card for full detail, including its own separate, more serious pregnancy-related caution.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

foodsOrHabitsToWatch.text: Nettle, another traditional herb some readers may take separately, may also reduce how well the body clears lithium, for the same reason as shatavari - a dose adjustment may be needed for anyone taking lithium. See this project's own Nettle herb card for full detail.
foodsOrHabitsToWatch.label: established fact

absorption.text: PCRM's handout cites research suggesting a meal higher in complex carbohydrates (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes) relative to protein makes it easier for tryptophan to reach the brain and support serotonin production, compared with a very high-protein meal. This is a proposed mechanism from a single cited study, not an established population finding like the review above.
absorption.label: open question

allergensAndSensitivities.text: Soy (soybeans) and tree nuts (walnuts), both named above, are recognised allergens; choose another tryptophan or ALA source from this list if either affects you.
allergensAndSensitivities.label: established fact

samplePlate.text: A thali with a spinach or other leafy-green sabzi, a soybean or mixed-dal curry, rice or roti, and a small side of walnuts or sunflower seeds - a tryptophan-rich, whole-food plate built from PCRM's named foods.

redFlags.text: This card is about diet and general wellbeing - it is not a substitute for professional mental health care. If you are having thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call or text the Tele-MANAS national helpline (14416, free, 24x7, in about 20 languages) or seek emergency care immediately. If you notice a sudden, significant change in mood or your ability to function day to day, see a doctor or mental health professional promptly.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If low mood or anxiety is persistent and affecting your daily life - work, relationships, sleep or appetite - see a doctor or mental health professional rather than relying on diet alone. Diet can be a support alongside therapy, medication if prescribed, and a professional diagnosis, never a replacement for them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

whatFoodCannotDo.text: Food choices may support mood as part of a broader approach to wellbeing, but they cannot diagnose, treat or replace professional care for depression, anxiety or any other mental health condition.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Single workplace RCT cited within pcrm-food-mood (Agarwal, Mishra, Xu, Levin, Gonzales, Barnard, Am J Health Promot 2015 - the same Barnard-affiliated 'GEICO Study' pattern already used in this project's diabetes.json candidateAdditions), not independently read by us. Graded Limited per BRIEF.md rule 10 even though it points the same direction as the Strong systematic review - a single trial, held as an open question pending a direct read of the primary paper.
candidateAdditions.text: An 18-week workplace trial at 10 corporate sites found that employees following a low-fat vegan nutrition programme reported significantly less anxiety, depression and fatigue, and better emotional wellbeing and daily functioning, than a comparison group who did not follow the programme.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Two single studies by the same author, both cited within pcrm-food-mood, not independently read by us - a small 2-week RCT (Beezhold et al., presented at APHA 2009) and a cross-sectional study of Seventh-day Adventists (Beezhold, Johnston & Daigle, Nutr J 2010;9:26). Graded Limited per BRIEF.md rule 10; kept here as open questions, not merged, pending direct reads of both primary papers.
candidateAdditions.text: A small 2-week trial found a vegetarian-diet group reported better mood than a fish-eating or general omnivore group, even though the fish group had raised its intake of fish-sourced omega-3. A separate, larger cross-sectional study of Seventh-day Adventists found vegetarian Adventists reported better mood than omnivorous Adventists, despite lower blood levels of EPA/DHA. Both are read by PCRM as suggesting that avoiding animal-food compounds linked to inflammation may matter more for mood than the specific source of omega-3 - an interesting lead, not yet a settled finding.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - unverified lead, pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND independent reading of the primary paper. Not sourced from pcrm-food-mood or the 2025 systematic review - surfaced in this project's earlier findings handoff on an explicitly anti-vegan book (book-antianxiety-food-solution), which cited it only in passing (to support a generic iron-deficiency point) and did not read it directly. Flagged there as a possible future lead for a vegetarian-specific mood/wellbeing source, not yet verified by this project.
candidateAdditions.text: Baines S, Powers J, Brown WJ, 'How does the health and well-being of young Australian vegetarian and semi-vegetarian women compare with non-vegetarians?', Public Health Nutrition, 2007;10(5):436-442 - a study specifically about vegetarian women's health and wellbeing. Not independently read; kept here as an unverified lead for a possible future addition to this card, not as a citable fact.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND independent reading of the primary paper. From Krause's Food & the Nutrition Care Process (2012), Chapter 42, 'Medical Nutrition Therapy for Psychiatric Conditions' - the targeted mood/mental-health chapter read approved for this round (owner's explicit scope: kidney/renal and mood/mental-health chapters only, not the rest of this 1,187-page book). The source states this in passing, without naming a direction (better or worse) or a number, and points to Davis & Kris-Etherton 2003 as the underlying reference, which should be read directly before this is used for anything beyond 'worth checking'. Pre-2015 (2012); flag for recheck per BRIEF.md rule 5.
candidateAdditions.text: Beyond the already-known low overall conversion rate of ALA to EPA/DHA in humans (roughly 5-10% to EPA, under 3% to DHA), this source notes that recent research had suggested a possible difference in that conversion rate specifically between vegetarians and non-vegetarians - without saying which group converts more efficiently. The same source separately states that most nutrition and mental-health experts do not recommend relying on ALA alone (flax, chia, walnut) as a source of EPA/DHA - a caution that sharpens, rather than contradicts, this card's existing walnut/flaxseed entries, which already point to the omega-3 nutrient card for the same conversion issue.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A genuinely new, specific gap worth flagging, not a recommendation: this source states that, across many of the psychiatric conditions it covers, EPA (more than DHA) appears to matter most for a clinical mood benefit, and separately confirms an algal (vegetarian) DHA source exists - but it never states whether algal-source supplements can supply enough EPA specifically to match the EPA-weighted targets it gives elsewhere in the chapter. This project's own omega-3 nutrient card (not edited in this round, per this round's scope limit) would be the right place to address this gap if it recommends algal omega-3 for mood specifically.
candidateAdditions.text: This source repeatedly notes that EPA, more than DHA, appears necessary for a clinical mood benefit in several of the conditions it covers (e.g. depression, anxiety), and gives official (fish-oil-framed) dosing figures of around 1 g/day combined EPA+DHA for people with mood, impulse-control or psychotic disorders, rising to 1-9 g/day under medical supervision for some mood disorders. It separately confirms an algal (vegetarian) source of DHA is commercially available, but does not say whether algal-source products can supply enough EPA specifically to meet the EPA-weighted targets it describes - a real, unaddressed gap for a vegan reader relying on algal omega-3 for mood, not something to assume either way.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review AND independent verification. High-stakes dosing per BRIEF.md rule 9. The American Psychiatric Association's own figures here are framed entirely around fish and fish oil, with no vegan swap offered or evidenced by this source - held here as a reference figure only, not something to present to a reader without its own vegan-appropriate evidence (e.g., whether an algal supplement at this dose is equivalent - see the EPA-weighting gap candidate above).
candidateAdditions.text: The American Psychiatric Association is cited as recommending that people with mood, impulse-control or psychotic disorders consume about 1 g/day of combined EPA and DHA, and that people with mood disorders specifically may use a supplement providing 1-9 g/day of combined EPA and DHA, with more than 3 g/day monitored by a physician.
candidateAdditions.label: official recommendation

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Brief corroboration only, from a mental-health-specific angle (B12's role in neurotransmitter-related homocysteine handling) - not new information relative to vitamin-b12.json, included here because it's this chapter's own direct statement.
candidateAdditions.text: This source states plainly, in a section on B-complex vitamins and brain health, that vitamin B12 is found in animal sources only and that vegans must choose foods and supplements wisely - consistent with, and said independently of, this project's existing vitamin B12 guidance.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. A vegan-compatible food list (the source's own non-vegan item, liver, excluded here per BRIEF.md's strictly-vegan rules), named specifically in the context of brain/neurotransmitter health rather than general nutrition - several items are new to this card's own foodsToFavour list (broccoli, brussels sprouts, asparagus, kale, brewer's yeast, orange juice, legumes generally), one already appears (spinach).
candidateAdditions.text: This source names brewer's yeast, mushrooms, spinach, broccoli, brussels sprouts, asparagus, kale and other leafy greens, legumes, and orange juice as good folate sources, in a section specifically about folate's role in neurotransmitter (serotonin, dopamine) production relevant to mental health.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact

candidateAdditions.text: This source names oatmeal, bananas, potatoes, avocado, sunflower seeds, brewer's yeast, and brown rice among vitamin B6 sources, in the context of B6's role in neurotransmitter production relevant to mental health.
candidateAdditions.label: established fact
