myths.claim: Over time, the body's tissues and joints accumulate hard 'acid crystals' - a waste product the book attributes mainly to protein metabolism and ageing - and this buildup is presented as the specific, identifiable cause of arthritis, joint stiffness, muscle cramps and premature ageing. Apple cider vinegar (ACV), the book claims, dissolves these crystals back into solution so the kidneys can flush them out, thereby relieving or reversing these conditions - typically taken as an ACV-and-honey drink three times daily.
myths.verdict: Not supported as a general mechanism for arthritis, joint stiffness, cramps or ageing. 'Acid crystals' depositing throughout the body as a cause of ordinary joint problems is not a recognised mechanism in mainstream medicine. The one genuine crystal-deposition joint disease mainstream medicine does recognise - gout, caused by urate crystals - is a specific, diagnosed condition with its own distinct pattern and cause (the body producing too much urate or clearing too little), not a universal explanation for stiff or ageing joints in general, and nothing in mainstream sources suggests apple cider vinegar dissolves urate or any other joint crystal. Separately, the broader evidence for apple cider vinegar's claimed health benefits (including the anti-inflammatory effect this claim relies on) is judged inconclusive, not proven, by the hospital source reviewed here.

explanation.text: The book states this mechanism repeatedly and names it directly: a section titled 'What Becomes of the Acid Crystals Precipitated in the Body That Age Us?' states 'the answer to premature ageing is unhealthy living and potassium deficiency' and that stiff joints and tough flesh result from these crystals; another section, 'All Through Life You Fight Acid Crystals,' states that 'when body tissues hold all the precipitated acid crystals they can, the crystals then appear in the bursae and the joints of the body, resulting in bursitis and arthritis'; a third, 'Toxic Acid Arthritic Crystals Make Joints Grind,' attributes the grinding sound of a rolled neck directly to crystals deposited on the spine. The book's recommended fix in each case is the same ACV (traditionally with raw honey) cocktail, taken three times daily, which it says allows the crystals to 'enter into a solution and pass out of the body.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The same mechanism is extended to muscle cramps ('when precipitated acid crystals get into the circulation of the legs and other parts of the body, they can cause severe cramps') and to general premature ageing and stiffness - treating a single, named, mechanical substance ('acid crystals') as the explanation for several distinct, otherwise-unrelated complaints (arthritis, bursitis, cramps, age-related stiffness), the same oversimplified single-cause pattern as this project's other myth candidates (TCM's 'too yin' vegetable food, the blood-type diet's ABO-linked meat need).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Mainstream medicine does recognise a real, narrow case of a crystal-deposition joint disease - gout, caused by uric acid crystals, and a small number of other crystal arthropathies (e.g. calcium pyrophosphate deposition) - but these are specific, diagnosed conditions with known mechanisms and treatments, not a universal explanation for ordinary joint stiffness, arthritis in general, muscle cramps or ageing itself. NIH's own patient page on gout confirms this directly: 'Gout happens when urate, a substance in your body, builds up and forms needle-shaped crystals in your joints,' described as 'a type of inflammatory arthritis' with its own distinctive pattern (flares 'often begin in your big toe or a lower limb') and its own distinct cause (the body making too much urate or clearing too little) - not a generic 'acid crystal' process affecting ageing joints everywhere in the body. The book does not distinguish gout from its general 'acid crystal' claim or cite any diagnostic criteria; the claim as written is presented as applying to anyone with stiff or ageing joints, which is a materially broader and vaguer claim than the real, narrow phenomenon it resembles.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: A hospital integrative-medicine review of apple cider vinegar's evidence base lists arthritis only among the claims people make for it, with no supporting evidence discussed, and concludes more broadly that 'available evidence to support ACV use is not conclusive due to heterogeneity between studies' and that 'larger, methodologically-robust trials are needed to generate more definitive data.' The page does not mention 'acid crystals' or any crystal-dissolving mechanism at all.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: A patient-advocacy arthritis charity's own food-myths page lists cider vinegar as a myth, stating plainly that its 'anti-inflammatory benefits aren't backed by science' - corroborating, from a second and differently-typed source, that the broader anti-inflammatory claim this remedy leans on is unsupported, separately from the specific 'dissolving acid crystals' mechanism addressed above.
explanation.label: established fact

gaps: The three new sources above establish that (a) gout is the one real, narrow crystal-deposition joint disease and is not evidence for a general 'acid crystal' mechanism, and (b) the broader evidence for ACV's claimed effects (including anti-inflammatory benefit) is inconclusive-to-unsupported. None of the three sources discuss muscle cramps or premature ageing specifically in relation to 'acid crystals' or ACV; this card's verdict addresses the shared underlying mechanism claim (acid-crystal buildup, dissolved by ACV) rather than asserting each named symptom has itself been individually tested.

The book's companion claim that potassium deficiency is itself a root cause of a long list of unrelated diseases (arthritis, kidney stones, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, hypothyroidism, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, lupus, diabetes, stroke and more - attributed in the book to a named source, Linda Page N.D.) was considered as an alternative or additional myths-deck candidate for this same book. It was not drafted as a separate card to avoid duplicating this one (potassium deficiency and 'acid crystals' are presented in the book as the same underlying mechanism - crystal buildup is explained by/linked to potassium deficiency throughout), but is recorded here in case the owner wants it drafted as its own, more sweeping card instead of or alongside this one. That companion claim has NOT been separately Strong-sourced by this research pass.
myths.calmLanguageNote: Needs its own calm-tone pass before publication - written here mainly to record the claim and its rebuttal accurately, not as finished reader-facing text. The book's own recommended remedy traditionally pairs ACV with raw honey; per BRIEF.md's vegan hard rules, a published version of this card may name honey only within the claim being debunked (as done here), and must never present the ACV-and-honey drink as something to try. For the eventual reader-facing card, keep the gout contrast gentle and reassuring rather than clinical - the point for an anxious reader is simply that ordinary joint stiffness is not a toxin buildup needing a vinegar flush, not that they should worry about gout.

myths.claim: A bodybuilding nutrition book states, as a general rule for anyone trying to build muscle, that protein needs are 'best met by animal sources' because animal-based proteins (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) contain 'high but balanced amounts of essential amino acids', treating only two named plant proteins (rice and pea protein) as exceptions that are 'high quality as well' - framing animal protein as the superior default for muscle-building rather than treating a well-planned plant-protein diet as equivalent by default.
myths.verdict: Not supported as a general rule by mainstream sports-nutrition evidence - flagged here as a claim to address, but this project has not yet located a Strong source to cite for the rebuttal (see gap below, though a promising existing lead is noted).

explanation.text: The book states directly: 'Animal-based proteins like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy are particularly popular among athletes because they contain high but balanced amounts of essential amino acids, but certain plant-based proteins like rice and pea protein are high quality as well. Generally speaking, your protein needs are going to be best met by animal sources, but with a bit of creative meal planning, vegetarians and vegans can get enough amino-acid-rich protein to build plenty of muscle and strength.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: No citation, study or named source is attached to the specific 'best met by animal sources' sentence itself. The book is otherwise reasonably well-referenced elsewhere (its surrounding paragraphs on calorie-restriction research and on high-protein diets and kidney/osteoporosis/cancer risk each carry their own numbered endnote), which makes the absence of any citation for this particular comparative claim about protein quality notable rather than simply an oversight of an unreferenced book.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Usefully, the book's own very next sentence already softens the claim for an anxious reader: vegetarians and vegans 'can get enough amino-acid-rich protein to build plenty of muscle and strength' with 'a bit of creative meal planning' - the same internal-inconsistency pattern already seen in this project's other myth candidates, where the source's own text concedes the plant-based path works even while framing animal protein as the default-best option.
explanation.label: illustration

myths.claim: Ayurvedic 'food combining' rules hold that certain food pairings are inherently 'incompatible' in the gut - most famously fruit eaten together with other foods (especially milk, as in a banana-and-milk smoothie) - and that eating these combinations causes fermentation, gas, bloating, and the buildup of a sticky, toxic by-product called ama, which traditional Ayurveda names as the root cause of disease in the body, regardless of the combination's actual nutrient content or how well any individual digests it in practice.
myths.verdict: Not supported by mainstream nutrition science as stated - flagged here as a claim to address, but this project has not yet located a Strong source that directly tests or rejects Ayurvedic food-combining theory as such (see gap below). General advice to keep meals simple is not itself harmful, but the specific mechanism claimed (ama) and the specific forbidden pairings (e.g. fruit eaten with milk) go beyond what mainstream digestive physiology describes.

explanation.text: The book states this directly: 'Certain combinations of foods are incompatible, meaning they are likely to ferment in the gut, resulting in gas and bloating, or be too heavy to digest fully, resulting in the creation of ama, the thick, sticky by-product of incomplete digestion. It is considered the substance that begins to cause disease.' It singles out raw fruit eaten with other foods ('the stomach will hold the fruit even after it is digested, while it's still breaking down all of the other food... this fermentation will give a sour quality... to the meal') and names the banana-and-milk smoothie specifically as 'the king of incompatible meals,' with the stated reason that 'both are mucus forming, and together they create too much mucus for the stomach to burn through.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: This food-combining claim sits inside the same broader Ayurvedic 'dosha' and food-energetics framework as the existing TCM yin/yang myth candidate already on file: foods and bodily states are classified by qualities (hot/cold, heavy/light, dry/moist) that are treated as causing specific symptoms - for example, the book states 'too many vata qualities might cause' gas, constipation, cold hands and feet, and anxiety, and 'too many pitta qualities might cause' acid indigestion/reflux, dysmenorrhea, and acne/rosacea - independent of a food's measurable nutrient content. As with the TCM claim, this is a traditional explanatory system rather than one built on the mainstream physiology this project otherwise requires for a health claim (BRIEF.md rule 10).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Unlike the previously-reviewed TCM source, which explicitly concedes in its own preface that 'current Western scientific methods are not yet able to offer plausible explanations' for its energetics framework, this book makes no such concession anywhere found in a full read - it presents the ama/food-combining mechanism as settled fact throughout, with no clinical citation, study reference or acknowledgement of an evidentiary gap. A targeted search of the full cached text for research-type language ('study', 'clinical', 'research shows', 'published', 'journal', 'evidence suggests') found no hits anywhere in the book that constitute an actual citation to a clinical study - the only non-author-bio-page hits are a passing mention of 'culinary research' behind the recipes, a section heading introducing anecdotal client vignettes ('Three Case Studies in Internal Climate'), and a resources/further-reading section naming Ayurveda study organisations, none of which cite or reference a clinical study supporting the ama/food-combining mechanism - confirming this is a purely traditional-knowledge text with no scientific framework offered for any of its health claims, food-combining included.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Notably, the book's own text already softens the claim considerably, in a way worth keeping prominent for an anxious reader: 'remember that an overzealous approach can create stress. One is likely to eat incompatible combinations sometimes, and unless you notice they make you feel bad or you have chronic digestive disorders, relax.' This is the same internal-inconsistency pattern already noted in the TCM myth candidate (its own 'For vegetarians' clinical note) - even within the book's own framing, occasional 'incompatible' combinations are described as harmless for most people, not as an urgent health risk.
explanation.label: illustration

myths.claim: Your blood type determines whether a vegetarian or vegan diet is right for you - some blood types (the claim goes) are 'natural' meat-eaters and do poorly without it, while others thrive on plant foods.
myths.verdict: Not supported - three independent Strong sources (a 1,455-person cohort study, a systematic review, and a randomised-trial secondary analysis) all directly tested this specific theory and found no effect of ABO blood type on how well a person does on a given diet. One of the three (Wang et al. 2014) did find that some 'Blood-Type' diets were associated with healthier biomarkers in everyone who followed them - but explicitly NOT because of blood-type matching; the benefit tracked the diet's own general quality (more fruit/vegetables, less meat), not the dieter's blood type. The precise, honest finding is: these diets may have real merit for anyone, but not for the reason the theory claims.

explanation.text: This claim comes from the 'Blood Type Diet' (Eat Right for Your Type, D'Adamo), which assigns each ABO blood type a 'natural' ancestral diet - Type O is framed as needing meat and doing poorly on vegetarian diets, while Type A is framed as 'the first vegetarian' and thriving on plant foods.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book supports this with individual patient anecdotes (a person feeling worse on a vegetarian diet, recovering after adding meat; a vegetarian with digestive problems improving on a high-protein animal-food diet) rather than controlled studies - anecdote is a weak form of evidence per BRIEF.md rule 10, and a single person's experience on a diet change does not establish a blood-type-specific cause.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book also attributes specific nutrient issues to blood type that have better-established, blood-type-independent explanations - for example, claiming Type As have unusual difficulty absorbing B12 (B12 absorption problems are actually caused by low stomach acid, intrinsic-factor issues, or diet composition, not blood type) and that iron is 'seriously lacking in the Type A vegetarian diet' (true that plant-only diets need attention to iron, but this is a feature of the diet's composition, not a Type-A-specific biological difference).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: A 2013 systematic review (Cusack et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) searched specifically for studies testing whether matching diet to ABO blood type improves health or reduces disease risk. It found only one tangentially related study (on a different blood-group system entirely) and concluded plainly: 'No evidence currently exists to validate the purported health benefits of blood type diets.'
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: A 2014 study (Wang et al., PLoS ONE) went further and directly tested the theory in 1,455 genotyped adults: it did find that people who more closely followed the Type-A, Type-AB or Type-O 'Blood-Type' diets had somewhat better cardiometabolic markers (blood sugar, insulin, cholesterol) - but when the researchers checked whether this benefit was bigger for people whose actual blood type matched the diet they were following, it was not. Quoted directly from the study: these associations 'were not related to an individual's ABO blood group.' The researchers attribute the Type-A diet's benefit to its general healthy pattern (high fruit and vegetables, low meat) - the same kind of diet already recommended by mainstream health bodies for everyone, regardless of blood type.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: A 2021 analysis (Barnard et al., Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics) of a 16-week randomised vegan-diet trial specifically checked whether blood type A or O people did any differently on the plant-based diet than everyone else. There was no significant difference on any measure (weight, body fat, cholesterol, blood sugar) - type O, the type this claim says needs meat most, did at least as well on the vegan diet as everyone else. Four of the six authors are affiliated with a vegan-advocacy organisation (Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine), a real affiliation worth noting, though the trial itself was a proper randomised design with a no-change control group.
explanation.label: established fact

gaps: This card's Strong-source gap is now closed with three independently-read sources. Remaining for a human reviewer before final publication: a calm-tone, reader-facing rewrite (see calmLanguageNote) and confirmation that the 'diets may still have ordinary merit, just not because of blood type' nuance survives simplification for a phone-first card without becoming a backhanded endorsement of the Blood-Type diet book itself.
myths.calmLanguageNote: Needs its own calm-tone pass for the final reader-facing card, written here mainly to record the evidence accurately. Keep the nuance prominent for the busy-sceptic and long-time-vegan readers: this isn't a flat 'the book is nonsense' takedown - it's 'the diets themselves may be fine, because they're just generally healthy diets, but your blood type has nothing to do with it.' That nuance is more credible and less preachy than an absolute dismissal, and it quietly reassures a Type-O reader who may have been told a vegan diet 'isn't for their type.'

myths.claim: Eating cabbage, kale, broccoli or other cruciferous vegetables regularly hurts your thyroid, especially if you already have a thyroid problem.
myths.verdict: Not supported for normal cooked amounts, with adequate iodine intake - a 2024 systematic review of 123 studies found including cruciferous vegetables in the daily diet 'poses no adverse effects on thyroid function' when iodine intake is adequate. The real areas of caution are narrower than the claim suggests: large amounts of raw or juiced cruciferous vegetables (far beyond a normal portion), and iodine intake that is already too low - not an everyday cooked serving. For people who already have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medication, the review found that common advice to avoid these vegetables often rests on outdated animal research rather than solid human evidence either way - so this remains an open question for that group specifically, worth raising with a doctor rather than treating as settled in either direction.

explanation.text: Cruciferous vegetables contain compounds (glucosinolates) that break down into substances (including thiocyanate and, in a few specific vegetables, goitrin) that can compete with iodine for uptake by the thyroid or interfere with thyroid hormone production. This is a real biochemical mechanism, which is why the worry exists, and it is confirmed by a 2024 systematic review of 123 studies on the subject.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: In practice, that same 2024 systematic review concludes that including cruciferous vegetables in the daily diet, 'particularly when accompanied by adequate iodine intake, poses no adverse effects on thyroid function' - the negative effects seen in older or animal studies were strongest in regions with iodine-deficient soil and water, and iodine supplementation reversed the effect in several livestock studies. Adequate iodine, not avoiding this vegetable family, is the safeguard that actually matters.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: Cooking matters, and in the direction most readers would hope: cooking inactivates the plant enzyme (myrosinase) that produces the active goitrogenic compounds. In a human radioiodine-uptake study, raw rutabaga reduced iodine uptake but cooked rutabaga had no effect; in another trial, boiled or steamed Brussels sprouts eaten daily for four weeks caused no change in thyroid hormone or TSH levels in healthy adults. The clearest caution the evidence supports is around raw, juiced or very large amounts specifically, not ordinary cooked servings - uptake was only meaningfully blocked in cases involving concentrated extracts or unusually large raw amounts (for example, a case report of hypothyroidism in a woman eating up to 1.5 kg a day of raw Chinese cabbage), far beyond a normal portion.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: For people who already have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medication, this is honestly an open question rather than a settled reassurance: the 2024 review found that the common advice to limit cruciferous vegetables in this group often relies on outdated animal studies using seed forms rarely eaten by humans, and it found no clean human trial separating cruciferous vegetable intake from medication use or iodine status in people with existing thyroid disease. This means the usual warning is on weak evidence, but it does not mean normal amounts are proven safe for this group either - so this project flags it as a genuine open question, best discussed with a doctor, rather than stating either 'avoid them' or 'they're completely fine' with confidence.
explanation.label: open question

explanation.text: A frequently-cited scary case (acute myxedema coma after eating raw bok choy) involved an unusually large amount of raw bok choy, not a normal portion - Chu M, Seltzer TF, 'Myxedema coma induced by ingestion of raw bok choy,' N Engl J Med, 1986 (cited secondhand via our cached book, not independently read).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: An animal study on dietary brussels sprouts and thyroid function is also cited (McMillan M, Spinks EA, Fenwick GR, Hum Toxicol, 1986) as part of why the theoretical concern exists - again a secondhand citation, not independently read.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The practical takeaway: eat ordinary cooked cruciferous vegetables freely as part of a varied diet, and separately make sure iodine intake is adequate (iodised salt or a vegan iodine source) - adequate iodine is the actual safeguard, not avoiding this vegetable family. The genuine areas of caution are narrower and more specific than 'cruciferous vegetables are risky': very large or raw/juiced amounts (well beyond a normal portion) rather than an everyday cooked serving, and - as an open question, not a settled answer - anyone with a diagnosed thyroid condition or on thyroid medication is better off raising diet questions with their own doctor rather than relying on this card either way.
explanation.label: official recommendation

gaps: This card's new Strong source (Galanty et al. 2024) is a systematic review of the existing literature, not new primary research - its own stated limitation is that human data are limited, many included studies are small, old, or use animal models or concentrated extracts rather than normal food-form intakes, and some survey studies are confounded by iodine intake, salt type and medication use with no control group. The review does not, and this card does not, claim normal cooked cruciferous vegetable intake is proven safe for people with existing thyroid disease or on thyroid medication - only that the evidence commonly used to warn them away is itself weak. That group should still raise the question with their own doctor.

This card has not independently re-read the two older secondhand citations carried over from the original book (Chu & Seltzer 1986 on the bok choy case, and McMillan et al. 1986 on the Brussels sprouts animal study) - they remain secondhand illustrations, flagged pre-2015 per BRIEF.md rule 5, and are not relied on for the card's verdict, which rests on the independently-read 2024 systematic review instead.
myths.calmLanguageNote: Written to reassure, not alarm - no 'you are at risk' framing, per BRIEF.md's calm-language rule. The one open-question point (existing thyroid conditions/medication) should still be phrased calmly in the eventual reader-facing card: frame it as 'worth a quick chat with your doctor' rather than a warning, per rule 15's render convention of gathering open-question points into their own section rather than scattering alarm through the card. Keep this tone if this becomes a published myth card.

myths.claim: A popular low-carb/ketogenic-diet book argues that the conventional low-fat, high-carbohydrate, plant-based eating pattern it associates with official dietary guidelines (and, by extension, vegetarian/vegan diets) is not merely less optimal than a low-carb diet but an active cause of specific physical harm: it names a 'very low-fat, vegetarian, or vegan diet' as something that leaves a person 'especially vulnerable to problems with your gall bladder', and states as settled fact, citing one 1978 study, that 'kidney stone formation is more common on a high-carb diet, not a low-carb one' - the reverse of the usual caution about low-carb/high-protein diets and kidney stones. The book also dismisses a named vegan physician's dietary position outright, calling it 'dietary dogma' and 'the make-yourself-sick diet', without engaging its substance.
myths.verdict: Not supported by mainstream nutrition science as stated - flagged here as a claim to address, but this project has not yet located a Strong source to cite for the rebuttal (see gap below).

explanation.text: The book frames the entire premise of official dietary guidance as a cause of the chronic-disease epidemic, using correlation presented as causation. It first states: 'In just the past few decades, the rates of obesity, diabetes, heart disease, and other chronic illnesses have gotten considerably worse. And do you know what's most shocking about that? The spike in all of these ailments coincides almost perfectly with the implementation of the government's Dietary Guidelines in 1980. Coincidence? I think not.' After an intervening sentence comparing this to the definition of insanity, it goes on: 'The government ignores studies that don't fit within a preconceived template of a low-fat, low-salt, calorie-restricted, high-carb, plant-based diet.' This sets up the book's recurring framing that high-carbohydrate, plant-forward eating (not just excess calories or specific food choices) is itself the causal problem.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: On gallbladder health specifically, the book states: 'if you have been on a very low-fat, vegetarian, or vegan diet, you can be especially vulnerable to problems with your gall bladder,' quoting a named low-carb expert's general statement ('If you don't use it, you might just lose it') rather than a study. No citation is given for this claim anywhere in the surrounding text.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: On kidney stones, the book asserts the reverse of the common concern about low-carb/high-protein diets: 'kidney stone formation is more common on a high-carb diet, not a low-carb one, as shared in a British Journal of Urology study published in December 1978.' This project has not independently located or verified this specific 1978 citation, and the claim is stated as a settled, general fact about 'a high-carb diet' without distinguishing diet quality (e.g. refined versus whole-food carbohydrate sources, of which a well-planned vegan diet is typically the latter).
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book dismisses, by name, one of the best-known vegan physicians' public position on low-carb eating without engaging its substance: 'I would be remiss if I didn't include the position on ketosis from one of the most outspoken proponents of a vegan diet... Dr. John McDougall... Google it and listen in for one of the most entertaining examples of what dietary dogma looks like,' going on to quote his view that ketosis is 'the make-yourself-sick diet' and characterising his position as dogma rather than addressing his reasoning directly.
explanation.label: illustration

gaps: This project has not yet located and read a Strong source (a systematic review or government/health body statement) directly assessing whether a low-fat vegetarian/vegan diet is a specific risk factor for gallbladder problems, or whether high-carbohydrate (as opposed to low-carbohydrate/high-protein) diets are a specific risk factor for kidney stones - needed before this myth entry can carry a confident 'verdict' line per BRIEF.md rule 10. Do not publish the verdict as stated above until that source is found and cited directly, not assumed from general knowledge.

The 1978 British Journal of Urology citation named in the kidney-stones quote has not been independently located or verified by this project - flagged as an uncheckable citation, not confirmed as either accurate or fabricated.

The book's own correlation argument (1980 Dietary Guidelines implementation coinciding with rising rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease) does not itself rule out other explanations (e.g. rising overall calorie intake, processed food availability, reduced physical activity) - this reasoning gap is worth naming plainly in the eventual rebuttal rather than simply asserting the opposite conclusion.

When this is eventually written for readers, make clear these are claims from one low-carb-advocacy book, not a finding from a health body reviewing plant-based diets - an anxious reader should come away understanding that a well-planned vegan diet has not been shown here to specifically harm the gallbladder or kidneys, only that this one book asserts it without a clear supporting citation.

myths.claim: The mainstream recommendation to eat plenty of dietary fibre, especially cereal bran, is presented as a harmful 'trap' rather than a genuine health benefit: high-fibre eating (particularly bran/added fibre) is claimed to inhibit absorption of iron, calcium, zinc, phosphorus, magnesium and vitamins A, D, E and K, to be a contributing cause of osteoporosis, Alzheimer's disease (via an aluminium-absorption mechanism) and rickets, and to make irritable bowel syndrome worse rather than better - with the Burkitt fibre-cancer hypothesis (fibre protects against colon cancer) described as a weak, unsubstantiated theory that media and commercial interests exaggerated into dogma.
myths.verdict: The myth's dramatic claims are not supported by current mainstream evidence: no Strong source links ordinary, recommended fibre intake to osteoporosis, Alzheimer's disease or rickets, and the specific 'fibre blocks mineral absorption' mechanism the book blames is, in current nutrition science, mostly driven by phytate (a separate compound that travels alongside fibre in whole grains, legumes and seeds), not by fibre itself. That said, this is not pure fabrication: there IS a real, narrower, dose-dependent kernel of truth here, which this project's own fibre.json card already documents under 'cautions' - at very high total fibre intake (above roughly 50 g/day) or with large amounts of isolated/added bran, reduced absorption of vitamins, minerals, protein and calories is a genuine, if usually minor, concern, mostly via the phytate that travels with that fibre rather than the fibre itself. This does not apply to the moderate, whole-food-based fibre intake (roughly 21-38 g/day) this project recommends throughout.

explanation.text: The book states this under a section literally titled 'The High Fiber Trap' and 'Fiber-caused Diseases on the Rise,' listing specific claimed consequences: 'eating fiber-enriched foods or foods containing rough fiber can significantly inhibit the absorption of iron, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sugars, proteins, fats and vitamins A, D, E and K'; that bran 'depletes the body of' calcium, iron, zinc, phosphorus, nitrogen, fats, fatty acids and sterols; and that this contributes to osteoporosis ('now a leading cause of death'), Alzheimer's disease (via an aluminium-absorption mechanism) and a resurgence of rickets.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book draws a real, worth-preserving nuance that should not be lost in any rebuttal: its target is specifically BRAN/cereal fibre (and, separately, added/isolated fibre), not fibre from whole fruits and vegetables, which it explicitly calls 'quite harmless for the body' and even recommends ('it is much better for the body to obtain fiber from fresh fruit, salads, cooked grains, beans and vegetables'). The book's own position is narrower than a blanket anti-fibre claim, so a rebuttal should not straw-man it as one.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book's critique of the Burkitt dietary-fibre/colon-cancer hypothesis has some real nuance of its own (noting the hypothesis was originally about vegetable fibre, not bran, and quoting Burkitt's own research partner, Dr. Hugh Trowell, making that distinction in 1974). The underlying point - that the fibre-cancer link is more complex and less settled than 1970s-80s 'eat more bran' messaging implied - has some genuine basis in the nutrition-science history of that specific hypothesis, even though the book's broader claim that fibre in general harms nutrient absorption and bone/brain health goes well beyond that narrower, defensible point.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The key scientific distinction this myth blurs: much of the real 'fibre reduces mineral absorption' effect is actually driven by PHYTATE (phytic acid), a separate compound that travels alongside fibre in whole grains, legumes and seeds - not fibre itself. A Tufts University nutrition expert, answering this exact question directly, states that high-fibre cereals also tend to be high in phytate, so 'it is hard to pick apart how much of the inhibition of absorption of these minerals is due to phytate alone' versus fibre - but that for calcium and magnesium specifically, 'most of the inhibition... is thought to be due to phytate rather than fibre' (with a smaller, separate effect of cellulose reported for calcium). The same source states that at typical, ordinary fibre intakes, no chronic adverse effects from mineral malabsorption have been seen.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: This project's own nutrient cards already carry the mainstream phytate framing the myth conflates with fibre: NIH states that vegetarians/vegans may not get enough zinc partly because beans and grains contain phytates that reduce zinc absorption, and ICMR-NIN advises that soaking, sprouting or fermenting beans and grains lowers phytate content and improves zinc absorption - standard, well-established preparation advice, not a reason to eat less fibre.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: This project's own fibre.json card already carries a real, much narrower version of this caution, correctly scoped by dose: 'Total daily fibre intake above about 50g may raise the risk of intestinal blockage, and excessive fibre intake has been linked to reduced absorption of vitamins, minerals, protein and calories generally - though this is unlikely to be a problem for healthy people eating fibre within the usual recommended ranges.' The myth source takes this genuine, dose-dependent, high-intake caution and wildly overstates it into a blanket warning against the ordinary, moderate fibre intake (roughly 21-38 g/day) this project recommends throughout - and then layers on specific disease claims (osteoporosis, Alzheimer's, rickets) that go well beyond even that existing caution's scope.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: Current mainstream guidance (NIH MedlinePlus, citing the Dietary Guidelines for Americans) sets the adult/adolescent fibre target at 21-38 g/day - well above typical intake of about 16 g/day - and lists established benefits (fullness/weight control, aiding both constipation and diarrhoea, helping lower cholesterol, supporting blood-sugar control) with no mention of fibre causing mineral-absorption harm, osteoporosis, Alzheimer's or rickets at these levels.
explanation.label: official recommendation

explanation.text: On osteoporosis specifically: this project did not find a Strong source (government/health body statement or systematic review) directly testing and confirming 'high fibre intake causes osteoporosis.' Available observational research is mixed rather than confirming the myth's claim - some large population studies link higher fibre intake to better bone density and lower hip-fracture risk; others find a weak, inconsistent association with lower bone density at one specific site (the femoral neck) at very high intakes; still others find no association at all. No study found establishes fibre as a cause of osteoporosis, and none of this research is about bran specifically. This is graded as 'not supported by available evidence' rather than a fully 'disproven' claim, since mixed observational data cannot rule out every possible narrow effect.
explanation.label: open question

explanation.text: On Alzheimer's disease specifically: no mainstream health body treats aluminium as an established cause of Alzheimer's at all, let alone via a fibre-driven absorption mechanism. The Alzheimer's Association's current position is that 'no single food, ingredient or supplement has been shown to prevent, treat or cure Alzheimer's'; an earlier version of the same organisation's myths page stated plainly that 'studies have failed to confirm any role for aluminum in causing Alzheimer's.' The aluminium-Alzheimer's hypothesis itself remains a contested, unproven minority position even within the scientific literature on its own terms - and this project found no source anywhere, mainstream or otherwise, connecting fibre-driven aluminium absorption specifically to Alzheimer's risk. That particular two-step claim (fibre raises aluminium absorption, which then causes Alzheimer's) appears unique to this one 1997 book.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: On rickets specifically: a 2019 peer-reviewed review of the history of nutritional rickets states plainly that vitamin D deficiency, 'usually in concert with dietary calcium deficiency, is the leading cause,' historically linked to overcrowding, indoor living, poor air quality and a greater dietary reliance on bread, and in its modern resurgence to reduced sun exposure. It does not mention dietary fibre or bran anywhere as a cause. The current, mainstream peer-reviewed account of what causes rickets has no place for fibre, and centres on vitamin D, calcium and sunlight instead.
explanation.label: established fact

gaps: No systematic review was found directly and specifically testing 'does ordinary high fibre intake cause osteoporosis' as its own research question - the osteoporosis finding above is built from several mixed observational studies via general web research, not one dedicated Strong review read in full. Flagged for a closer, more targeted search if this card proceeds toward publication.

This project read the 1997 book's own claimed 'mechanism' for the Alzheimer's/aluminium link (fibre affecting aluminium absorption) but did not trace it back to any primary study the book itself might cite - the book's genre (alternative-health/longevity, pre-2015) makes its internal citations unreliable, and no matching claim was found anywhere else in the literature to independently verify or refute the specific mechanism, only the much broader (and separately unsettled) question of whether aluminium causes Alzheimer's at all.

Separate, secondary finding worth flagging to the owner even though it is outside this card's direct scope: fibre.json's own existing '>50g/day' caution is labelled 'established fact' but is sourced only to book-encyclopedia-of-diets, which sources.json itself grades Moderate (not Strong) and flags pre-2015. That existing label may be slightly stronger than its source supports - not something this myth-card task is authorised to fix, but worth the owner's attention alongside this card's own Gate 2 review.

No current Strong source was found giving a single, settled view on whether very high fibre intake has any meaningful effect on IBS (the myth's claim that fibre 'makes IBS worse'); fibre.json does not currently address IBS at all. Flagged rather than addressed, since it was outside this task's specific brief.
myths.calmLanguageNote: This card needs careful, reassuring framing because it concerns a nutrient this project otherwise describes as one that 'looks after itself' on a vegan diet. The eventual reader-facing version must make unmistakably clear that the ordinary, whole-food-based fibre intake this project recommends everywhere else (roughly 21-38 g/day, from whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit) is NOT what is being cautioned about here, and is not dangerous - the dramatic claims (osteoporosis, Alzheimer's, rickets) are not supported by mainstream evidence at any ordinary intake. At the same time, be honest rather than dismissive: there is a real, narrow, already-documented caution (fibre.json's own '>50g/day' note) about very high total fibre intake or large amounts of isolated/added bran, mostly via the phytate that travels with it - this is a different, much smaller, much less common situation than what the myth implies, and should be framed as routine, sensible context (soak/sprout/ferment grains and legumes; a varied diet rather than large amounts of one isolated bran/fibre source) rather than a new worry. Avoid any wording that could make a reader cut back on the fibre-rich foods (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit) this project recommends elsewhere.

myths.claim: Human teeth, saliva pH, stomach shape, intestine length (claimed to be '12 times the length of the body' versus '3 times' for carnivores), and sweat-gland distribution are presented as settled anatomical proof that humans are natural herbivores (not omnivores), making meat-eating 'an acquired habit and wholly unnatural' rather than a dietary choice supported by human biology.
myths.verdict: Not supported, and the specific numbers are wrong, not just the overall conclusion. Mainstream comparative anatomy and physiology classify humans as omnivores - not strict herbivores and not strict carnivores - with a mix of herbivore-like and carnivore-like features. Independently checking the specific gut-length figures this claim (and its two source books) repeat: a 2025 peer-reviewed review gives humans a small-intestine-to-body-length ratio of about 5:1, which is closer to carnivores (dogs, about 6:1) than to herbivores (ruminants, about 12:1) - the OPPOSITE of what this claim asserts. Human stomach acidity (pH about 1.5) is also carnivore-like, not herbivore-like. The one point that does cut toward omnivory/starch adaptation is salivary amylase, which humans have in abundance and obligate carnivores largely lack. None of this says anything about whether a vegan diet is healthy, which rests on nutrition science, not comparative anatomy - it only says this particular argument for veganism is inaccurate and should not be used.

explanation.text: The book presents this as a settled scientific case, introduced as 'incontrovertible scientific facts' under the heading 'Scientific and Anatomical Basis of Vegetarianism.' It lists several specific anatomical comparisons as proof: carnivores 'perspire through the tongue and not through the skin' while 'all naturally vegetarian animals perspire through the skin, as humans do'; 'our anatomical structure is not adapted to a meat diet... we have no claws to kill and rend prey'; 'the human alimentary canal is twelve times the length of the body [while] the carnivore canal is only three times the length of its body'; and 'humans secrete alkaline saliva, the carnivore secretes acid saliva.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: A second book, Timeless Secrets of Health and Rejuvenation, makes the same argument independently and in similarly absolute terms: 'Man's entire anatomy (jaw, teeth, and digestive system, hands and feet) shows that he must have evolved for millions of years living on fruits, grains, vegetables, nuts, and seeds'; 'Our dental structure is only conducive to the cutting of vegetables with incisors and to the grinding of grains and fruits with molars... We have, indeed, nothing in our anatomy that compares with the sharp claws of a tiger or an eagle'; and 'The human hand with its opposable thumb is better suited for harvesting fruits and vegetables than to killing prey.' Recorded here as a second, independent instance of the same claim pattern, not a separate myth.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: A 2021 comparative study across many mammal species (Duque-Correa et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B) directly tested the 'textbook' assumption that herbivores reliably have longer intestines than carnivores - the same assumption this claim leans on. It found diet does have a real average effect on intestine length in the expected direction, but the strength of that pattern depends heavily on sample size and which animal groups are included, so it 'cannot be considered a fixed biological law.' In plain terms: gut length is a loose tendency across many species, not a clean two-category rule that lets anyone read a single species' diet off its intestine length with confidence - the method behind this whole argument is shakier than the claim assumes, even before checking the human-specific numbers.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: A 2025 peer-reviewed review (Clemente-Suarez et al., Metabolites) addresses humans specifically and gives the numbers needed to check this claim's own figures - and they do not hold up. Humans are classified as omnivores with 'omnivorous flexibility and partial carnivorous specialization', not herbivores. On intestine length: the human small intestine is roughly 5 times body length, not 12 times as the claim states - and that puts humans closer to carnivores like dogs (about 6 times) than to herbivores like ruminants (about 12 times, the figure the claim misattributes to humans). On stomach acidity: human stomach pH is about 1.5, in the carnivore range (about 1-2), not the much less acidic herbivore range (about 4-7) - the opposite of what the claim's 'acid-stomach-means-carnivore' logic would predict for a 'natural herbivore.' One point does genuinely support an omnivore/starch-adapted picture: humans have abundant salivary amylase (an enzyme that starts digesting starch in the mouth), where obligate carnivores like cats have little or none - so the honest picture is a genuine mix of features, not a one-sided case for either herbivore or carnivore.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: Separately from the anatomy argument, a distinct but closely related claim in book-cosmic-nutrition-taoist - that spirulina, alfalfa, miso and tofu are reliable natural sources of vitamin B12 for vegans - is a more safety-relevant inaccuracy and is recorded as a CONFLICT with this project's own existing, better-sourced vitamin-b12.json content in drafts/llamaparse_findings/cosmic-nutrition-taoist.md, rather than drafted as a second myths card here, per BRIEF.md rule 6.
explanation.label: illustration

gaps: This card's Strong-source gap is now closed with two independently-read, peer-reviewed sources that directly address comparative digestive anatomy and the human case specifically. Remaining for a human reviewer before final publication: a calm-tone, reader-facing rewrite (see calmLanguageNote), and a decision on whether the reader-facing card should include the corrected numeric figures (5:1 vs the claimed 12:1) or keep things simpler by just stating the conclusion without re-litigating specific numbers - including exact ratios risks reading as pedantic to a reader who only wants to know 'is this a good argument to use or not.'

Note for the owner (unchanged from the original draft): this card differs in kind from the project's other myth candidates, all of which debunk a claim used AGAINST vegetarian/vegan eating. This one debunks an overstated argument used FOR it. Worth confirming the owner is comfortable with the myths deck including this type of card before Gate 2, since the calm-language and framing needs are different (reassuring a sceptical reader that veganism doesn't need this particular argument to be well-supported, rather than reassuring an anxious vegan reader that a scary claim against them is weak).
myths.calmLanguageNote: Needs its own calm-tone pass for the final reader-facing card, written here mainly to record the claim and evidence accurately. The eventual card should make clear that the WEAKNESS of this anatomy argument does not weaken the actual evidence for a well-planned vegan diet's healthfulness (which rests on nutrition science, not comparative anatomy) - the point is that vegan readers do not need this particular argument, and should stop using it, not that veganism itself is in question. For the busy-sceptic reader specifically, this card is actually a gift: it lets them say 'yes, that gut-length claim going around is wrong' without it costing them anything, since the real case for a vegan diet's healthfulness doesn't depend on it.

myths.claim: The Paleo diet holds that grains (including bread), legumes of any kind (beans, lentils, peas) and dairy should be excluded entirely, not just moderated, because the human body was 'designed' for a hunter-gatherer diet of meat, fish, vegetables, fruit, nuts and seeds. A specific health claim is attached to the exclusion: grains and dairy, eaten in the quantities modern commercial food supplies make available, are said to directly cause lactose intolerance, gluten intolerance and 'other allergies', and their starch content is said to make weight loss difficult.
myths.verdict: Not supported by mainstream nutrition science as stated - flagged here as a claim to address, but this project has not yet located a Strong source to cite for the rebuttal (see gap below).

explanation.text: The Cheat Sheet states the exclusion as a simple rule with no caveat: 'Do not eat processed foods, junk food, fast food, salt, refined sugars, grains, dairy, or lentils' - grouping grains, dairy and lentils (a legume) in with junk food and refined sugar as equally to be avoided - and frames this as how the body is meant to eat: 'Our bodies were designed to thrive from this diet.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The Training Guide attaches a specific, nameable health claim to the same exclusion, not just a preference: 'We are naturally adept at digesting lean meats, fruits, vegetables, and nuts and seeds... The types of foods that became commonly and commercially available to us through farming, foods like grains, corn (which is technically a grain), and dairy products consumed in an abundance can cause the body many issues. Lactose-intolerance, gluten intolerance, and other allergies abound from commercialized and common staples foods of this nature. Not to mention, several of them are very starchy, which can make it difficult to lose weight.' No citation, study or named source is given for this claim anywhere in the document.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The same Training Guide lists legumes as a full category to avoid, with no exceptions and no distinction between legume types: 'Beans, lentils, peas, etc. Basically, no legumes of any kind,' alongside 'Grains. Yes, this includes bread!' and frames the reasoning as these foods containing 'additives that are difficult for our bodies to process' that are 'clouding our minds and clogging our arteries' - a specific, if unreferenced, claim of harm rather than simply a dietary preference.
explanation.label: illustration

gaps: This project has not yet located and read a Strong source (a systematic review or government/health body statement) directly testing or rejecting the claim that whole grains and legumes, as commonly eaten, cause lactose intolerance, gluten intolerance, 'other allergies', or meaningfully impede weight loss through their starch content alone - needed before this myth entry can carry a confident 'verdict' line per BRIEF.md rule 10. (Note for whoever closes this gap: lactose intolerance is a dairy-specific digestive condition unrelated to grain or legume consumption, and conflating it with a general 'grains and dairy cause allergies' claim is itself worth flagging in the eventual rebuttal text, not just citing a counter-source.) Do not publish the verdict as stated above until that source is found and cited directly, not assumed from general knowledge.

The source documents for this card give no author name and no reliable publication year anywhere in the extracted text - the Training Guide's own PDF metadata reports 'year: 1970', which is implausible for a Paleo-diet eBook referencing modern commercial food supply chains and is almost certainly a metadata artefact, not a real publication date. Treated as unknown/pre-2015 for recheck per BRIEF.md rule 5, rather than trusting the metadata.
myths.calmLanguageNote: Needs its own calm-tone pass once the Strong-source rebuttal is in hand - written here mainly to record the claim accurately, not as finished reader-facing text. When this is eventually written for readers, note that grains and legumes (dal, rice, roti, chana, rajma) are core everyday foods for most vegan readers in this project's audience - the eventual card should be especially careful not to alarm a reader who eats these daily, and should make clear that whole grains and legumes are well-supported staples in mainstream nutrition guidance, not a fringe choice needing defence.

myths.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (2 Nov 2026) - current Strong-source check complete and independently verified by the main session (American Cancer Society's 2025 'soy foods are healthy and safe' wording, the Wei et al. 2019 meta-analysis's '3% reduced risk per 10mg/day isoflavone' figure, and the Oliveira et al. 2021 'no association' finding on soy infant formula and puberty were each re-fetched directly and matched exactly), then given the owner's own direct sign-off given the topic's sensitivity, per BRIEF.md's own instruction for this card. Myths module has not formally started; KEPT HELD for whenever it begins. This directly fulfills Enhancement Backlog item #3 (soy/oestrogen myth-mining). The verdict has flipped from the original cautionary framing to a reassuring one (soy foods do not raise breast cancer risk and may lower it), with the whole-food-vs-supplement caveat and a doctor's-advice line for hormone-sensitive cancer treatment kept intact. The birth-sex-ratio and precocious-puberty extension was checked specifically and not found to have any credible support - see gaps.
myths.claim: Vegan diets, particularly through heavy use of soy-based products, may increase the risk of breast cancer because soy's plant oestrogens (phytoestrogens/isoflavones) act like the body's own oestrogen. The same source extends this to a claim that vegan mothers have a 'disproportionate number of female babies' and that these daughters show earlier (precocious) puberty than daughters of non-vegetarian mothers.
myths.verdict: Busted, with one caveat the card should still carry. Current evidence from major cancer bodies and large population studies does not show that eating soy foods raises breast cancer risk - if anything, several studies associate typical soy intake with a small reduction in risk, and some evidence suggests soy may support better outcomes for breast cancer survivors. The caveat: this reassurance is about whole soy foods (tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk) at ordinary dietary amounts, not about concentrated soy isoflavone supplements, which major bodies still treat with more caution (not because they're shown to be harmful, but because there's less evidence behind them and they're not the way this benefit has been studied). The separate claim that vegan mothers have 'a disproportionate number of female babies' with daughters reaching puberty earlier was checked directly in this pass and found to have no credible scientific support - it appears to be an unsupported, fringe extension, not an established finding, and is not something this card should repeat even as a 'myth to bust' without that caveat being front and centre.

explanation.text: The American Cancer Society's own current page (2025) states soy foods are 'healthy and safe' and that human studies have found soy isoflavones either have no effect on breast cancer risk or may reduce it - especially among populations with lifelong higher soy intake. It explains the original scare directly: early studies in mice and rats found high-dose soy isoflavones promoted breast cancer cell growth, but rodents process isoflavones differently from humans, and the doses used were far higher than typical human diets - so that finding never translated to people.
explanation.label: official recommendation

explanation.text: The American Institute for Cancer Research gives the mechanism in more detail: isoflavones bind to oestrogen receptors differently from the body's own oestrogen - more like a different key that happens to fit a similar lock - and in some cases this seems to switch on genes that slow or limit cancer cell growth rather than promote it. Studies show soy protein or isoflavone intake has no effect on breast-cancer-risk markers such as hormone levels, breast cell growth or breast density.
explanation.label: official recommendation

explanation.text: A large prospective study of over 300,000 Chinese women, combined with a dose-response meta-analysis pooling 631,498 women across prospective studies, found moderate soy intake was not associated with increased breast cancer risk, with no meaningful difference before or after menopause - and that each extra 10 mg/day of soy isoflavone intake was linked to a 3% reduction in breast cancer risk. This is the kind of direct, large-population evidence (from a group with genuinely higher lifelong soy intake than most Western diets) that the two health-body sources above are drawing on.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: For women already living with breast cancer, AICR's own Continuous Update Project (a global systematic-review programme) rates the evidence as 'limited suggestive' that eating soy is linked to greater survival and lower recurrence, including in oestrogen-receptor-positive cancer, at around one to two standard servings of soy a day (tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk) - with no extra benefit found from eating more than that.
explanation.label: established fact

explanation.text: The caveat worth keeping, stated plainly rather than glossed over: this reassurance is specifically about whole soy foods at ordinary amounts. For cancer prevention, the American Cancer Society does not recommend soy isoflavone supplements, and recommends getting nutrients from whole foods instead - not because supplements have been shown to cause harm, but because they can contain much higher isoflavone amounts than naturally occur in food and have not been studied as thoroughly. AICR's own reading is similar in spirit: isolated soy protein does not appear to carry extra risk, but it also does not have the fibre and fuller nutrient range of whole soy foods, so whole soy is the better-evidenced choice either way.
explanation.label: official recommendation

explanation.text: The claim's second half - that vegan mothers have 'a disproportionate number of female babies' with daughters reaching puberty earlier - was checked directly in this pass and not found to have credible scientific support anywhere. No study was found linking a vegan or soy-rich maternal diet to the sex of a baby. A systematic review and meta-analysis specifically on soy-based infant FORMULA and puberty timing (a different, narrower question - about a baby's own feeding after birth, not the mother's pregnancy diet) found no meaningful difference in precocious puberty risk or age of first period between formula-fed infants given soy formula and those given other formula.
explanation.label: open question

explanation.text: Tracing where the sex-ratio idea might come from: the only genuine research found anywhere close to this topic is a single 2008 study (flagged here as pre-2015 and not re-verified since) which looked at mothers' total calorie intake before conception, not veganism or soy specifically, and found the opposite pattern to the myth - women eating more calories were somewhat more likely to have sons, not daughters. This does not support the original claim; it is included only so the claim's likely origin is on record rather than left as an unexplained gap.
explanation.label: open question

explanation.text: The claim comes from an academic reference encyclopedia (not a popular diet book), which states there is 'some evidence that vegan diets may actually increase the risk of breast cancer in women, particularly in those who use large amounts of soy-based products' due to phytoestrogens, and separately that soy phytoestrogens 'may also explain why committed vegans have a disproportionate number of female babies, and why these girls have a higher rate of precocious puberty.' No inline study citation was given for either claim in the text captured.
explanation.label: illustration

gaps: Concentrated soy isoflavone supplements are not covered by the same reassurance as whole soy foods - major cancer bodies still recommend getting isoflavones from whole foods (tofu, tempeh, edamame, soy milk) rather than supplements, and this card should keep that distinction rather than reassuring readers about soy in general without it.

No source read in this pass addresses whether the soy/breast-cancer reassurance changes for women currently on hormone-sensitive cancer treatment (e.g. tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor) - this is exactly the kind of situation where BRIEF.md's 'talk to your doctor' safety rule should appear on the published card, not a blanket all-clear.

The birth-sex-ratio and precocious-puberty claims remain unsupported by any source this project could find, including a direct, specific search for them - this card should present that clearly as 'checked and not supported' rather than silently dropping the claim or treating it as merely unconfirmed.

All evidence read here on soy-and-puberty specifically concerns soy-based infant formula, not a pregnant or breastfeeding mother's own vegan diet - a narrower question than the one the original claim poses, so this card should not overstate how directly that evidence answers the maternal-diet version of the claim.

The encyclopedia source's own bibliography was not traced further in this pass to find whether it drew on the 2008 calorie/sex-ratio study or something else entirely; this is a minor loose end, not a blocker, since the claim itself was independently checked and found unsupported regardless of its origin.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. From the dedicated Soy article in The Gale Encyclopedia of Diets (2008) - the SAME BOOK as the original uncited claim above, read in full in a later pass specifically to check whether it gave a clearer citation or rebuttal, per this task's instructions. It does - directly, and from a named health body (American Heart Association), which is a real improvement on the original uncited claim, though still secondhand (quoting the AHA's committee findings, not the AHA's own primary report read directly) and flagged pre-2015. This does NOT fully resolve the myth card (see gaps - the birth-sex-ratio/precocious-puberty claims are still untouched), but it meaningfully strengthens the 'likely outdated/not well-supported' lean already in this card's verdict field for the breast-cancer part specifically.
candidateAdditions.text: This book's own dedicated Soy article states that an American Heart Association (AHA) committee investigated soy isoflavones directly (citing 'American Heart Association Science Advisory Board, Soy Protein, Isoflavones, and Cardiovascular Health, Circulation 113(2006):1034-44' as its source) and found 'no evidence that, as some experts have suggested, soy increases the chance of post-menopausal women developing breast cancer.' The same AHA committee also found no evidence that soy isoflavone supplements can treat or prevent breast, endometrial or uterine cancer in women (or prostate cancer in men), and separately found isoflavones have no effect on menopausal hot flashes - directly contradicting the estrogen-mimicking mechanism the original uncited claim leans on. This is a named, dated, health-body source actively investigating and not finding the claimed breast-cancer risk - a real citation the original Veganism-article claim lacked entirely.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Also from the dedicated Soy article (2008 book, flagged pre-2015) - noted for completeness since it is the one place this book comes close to the children's-development angle of the original claim, though it does not address birth sex ratio or precocious puberty at all.
candidateAdditions.text: The same article notes that, as of this book's writing, a long-term study was underway tracking isoflavone blood levels in children who drank soy infant formula, planned to run about 20 years, with no results available yet. This is not evidence either way on the original claim - it is included here only so it's on record that this book's own soy-and-children content is this single not-yet-resulted study, nothing more specific to sex ratio or puberty timing.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

myths.calmLanguageNote: This is exactly the kind of claim that could alarm a reader if published carelessly (breast cancer, babies' sex, children's puberty are all high-stakes topics), so the finished card needs to be calm and evidence-led without swinging too far into blanket reassurance either. Guidance for the final reader-facing wording: (1) Lead with the plain, calm bottom line - 'the evidence does not show that eating soy foods raises breast cancer risk, and some evidence suggests it may help' - never 'soy prevents cancer' or any cure/prevents language, which the evidence does not support. (2) Keep the whole-food-vs-supplement distinction visible, not buried - it is the one genuine caveat, phrased as practical guidance ('choose tofu, tempeh, edamame and soy milk over isoflavone supplements') rather than as a warning. (3) Add a plain 'talk to your doctor' line for anyone currently being treated for a hormone-sensitive cancer, per BRIEF.md's safety rules - this is a real gap in what this project could verify, not a formality. (4) Handle the sex-ratio/precocious-puberty half gently but honestly: say plainly that this project looked for evidence and found none, rather than either repeating the claim uncritically or mocking it - a reader who has heard this claim deserves a straight, calm answer, not silence. (5) Never say 'you are deficient' or anything alarming about soy itself; this card should leave a vegan reader feeling less anxious about soy than before they read it, not more.

myths.status: GATE 2 APPROVED (22 Oct 2026) - verified by independent review: all four explanation quotes confirmed exact against cache/chinese-nutrition-therapy-tcm.txt (pp.69, 71, 73, 97, plus the 'For vegetarians:' clinical note), and the 'only such note found' claim confirmed by a whole-file search. KEPT HELD - the Myths module has not formally started, so this stays a Gate-2-approved candidate for whenever it begins. Same evidentiary gap as the existing blood-type-diet and metabolic-typing myth candidates: no Strong mainstream source has yet been found to directly test or reject this theory.
myths.claim: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) dietetics holds that plant/vegetable foods are inherently more 'yin' (energetically cooling) than meat, so a vegetarian or vegan diet is, on its own, energetically unbalanced - and will tend to cause cold-type symptoms such as fatigue, poor digestion and cold intolerance - unless deliberately corrected with warming cooking techniques, warming spices, or meat.
myths.verdict: Not supported by mainstream nutrition science as stated - flagged here as a claim to address, but this project has not yet located a Strong source to cite for the rebuttal (see gap below).

explanation.text: This claim comes from TCM's 'food energetics' theory (thermal nature: hot/warm/neutral/cool/cold), under which foods are classified by an energetic quality unrelated to their actual temperature, calories or nutrient content. The book states this directly and repeatedly: baking is described as 'a way for vegetarians to supply their body with yang energy and balance the cooling effect of the yin foods that make up the biggest share of a vegetarian diet'; long-simmered vegetarian stews are said to lose energetic value with cooking time so that 'warming spices should be used instead... to increase the energetics of the meal'; warming spices are described as 'recommended for a vegetarian diet to balance the cooling effect of vegetable foods'; and the book's own general-recommendations checklist for patients includes 'When following a vegetarian diet, ensure your diet contains enough energetically warming foods.'
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The claim is framed as a built-in property of plant food itself (its 'yin' character), not as a preference, a cultural habit, or an individual difference - the same pattern as the blood-type-diet and metabolic-typing claims already on file, which frame meat-need as an innate biological property rather than a choice.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: The book's own preface concedes, in its own words, that 'current Western scientific methods are not yet able to offer plausible explanations for the concept of energetics in Chinese nutrition' - a direct acknowledgement, from the source itself, that the yin/yang thermal-nature framework has no established mechanism in mainstream nutrition or physiology. This is useful context for why the claim is flagged, but it is the author's own framing, not an independent rebuttal, and does not by itself satisfy BRIEF.md rule 10's requirement for a Strong source.
explanation.label: illustration

explanation.text: Notably, the same book is less absolute elsewhere: in one clinical example (general weakness/low blood pressure), it offers a direct 'For vegetarians:' substitution using only grains and warming spices/vegetables, with no suggestion that the substitution is inadequate. This is the only such note found in the whole book, but it shows that even within the book's own internal logic, a fully plant-based approach is treated as workable with adjusted cooking and seasoning choices, not as something that fails without meat.
explanation.label: illustration

gaps: This project has not yet located and read a Strong source (a systematic review or government/health body statement) directly testing or rejecting TCM food-energetics/yin-yang theory as applied to vegetarian or vegan diets - needed before this myth entry can carry a confident 'verdict' line per BRIEF.md rule 10. Do not publish the verdict as stated above until that source is found and cited directly, not assumed from general knowledge.
myths.calmLanguageNote: Needs its own calm-tone pass once the Strong-source rebuttal is in hand - written here mainly to record the claim accurately, not as finished reader-facing text. When this is eventually written for readers, keep the 'For vegetarians' internal-consistency point (last explanation bullet) prominent - it is the most reassuring angle for an anxious reader, since it shows the theory itself does not require abandoning a plant-based diet, only adjusting cooking methods.

herbs.name: Amla

traditionalUse.text: This card is about amla as a concentrated Ayurvedic/therapeutic supplement or extract - capsules, standardised extracts, powders taken at therapeutic doses, and classical multi-herb preparations such as Triphala and Chyawanprash. This project already has a separate Foods-module entry for amla, 'Amla (Indian gooseberry)' (its data file is unusually named goosberry.json - a naming slip in the file name only, not a different food), covering amla as an everyday vitamin-C-rich fruit: its vitamin C content, an iron-absorption pairing tip, and preparation notes (fresh, murabba, pickle, candy, powder). This card does not repeat that vitamin-C-content framing; where vitamin C is mentioned below, it is only to explain a study's own mechanism, not as new food-composition data. Readers after the everyday-fruit information should see that Foods entry instead.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Like this project's Guggul card (Commiphora mukul/wightii), amla's two scientific names are a genuine taxonomic naming change over time, not a mix-up between two different plants: Phyllanthus emblica L. is the currently accepted name, with Emblica officinalis Gaertn. as an older synonym still very widely used in the research literature and on product labels - both names are used interchangeably throughout this card's sources.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Amla's fruit is one of Ayurveda's most important traditionally used ingredients, officially recognised by Canada's own health-product regulator as traditionally used as a 'Rasayana' (rejuvenative tonic), as a digestive tonic for Amlapitta (hyperacidity/dyspepsia), as a mild laxative for occasional constipation, and as an eye tonic. This project's own cached Ayurvedic academic text independently describes amla as 'arguably the most important medicinal plant in Ayurveda' and separately describes the broader Rasayana-therapy concept (restorative remedies claimed to support immunity, nutrition and healthy ageing) at length - corroborating that this traditional reputation is genuine and long-standing, not that any specific health claim below is proven.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Amla is also the base ingredient of two well-known classical multi-herb preparations, which matter for the vegan check in howToUseVegan below: Triphala (amla combined with two other fruits, haritaki and bibhitaki) and Chyawanprash (an amla-based herbal jam combined with roughly 50 herbs, traditionally including ghee, sesame oil and honey). Neither preparation's own evidence (where it exists) is treated in this card as evidence for amla alone, since a combination product needs its own evidence, not the evidence of one ingredient.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol and lipids are amla's best-researched therapeutic use. The single most rigorous review located (Brown et al 2023, using the stricter Cochrane RoB 2 risk-of-bias tool, 9 RCTs, 535 participants, mostly small Indian trials of 2-12 weeks) found significant falls in LDL ('bad') cholesterol (-15.08 mg/dL), VLDL cholesterol (-5.43 mg/dL) and triglycerides (-22.35 mg/dL), and a significant fall in hs-CRP, an inflammation marker (-1.70 mg/L) - this hs-CRP finding was also the single most consistent result in the whole review, with the trials agreeing with each other almost perfectly (I-squared of 0%, versus 62-96% for every other outcome). HDL ('good') cholesterol did not change significantly, and neither did systolic or diastolic blood pressure, despite very high disagreement between the pooled trials on both of those two measures.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: That same review's own summary overstates its own numbers in one place: although HDL cholesterol did not reach statistical significance in its results table, its Discussion and Conclusion describe HDL improvement as a significant finding alongside the genuinely significant ones. This card follows the review's own results table rather than its more confident-sounding discussion.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Two further reviews, pooling smaller and partly overlapping sets of the same small pool of worldwide amla trials, reach a broadly similar positive conclusion on cholesterol: a 2023 review focused specifically on dyslipidaemia (4 RCTs, 227 participants) found total cholesterol and LDL both fell significantly, HDL rose significantly, and triglycerides did not change significantly - but its own authors rate this 'low certainty of evidence' and call for trials comparing amla directly against statins. A separate 2023 review (5 RCTs) reports significant falls in CRP, blood glucose, LDL, total cholesterol and triglycerides and a significant HDL rise, but its own published abstract gives no effect sizes or heterogeneity figures to check those claims against - a real reporting gap. Because so few amla RCTs exist worldwide, this card treats these three reviews as one small evidence base sliced three different ways, not as three independent confirmations of the same finding.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: No trial comparing amla directly against a statin medicine was found by any of these reviews - all explicitly call for one. Most of the underlying trials are small (several under 20 participants), short (2-12 weeks), mostly conducted in India, and use varying forms (extract strength, raw fruit versus extract) - this card does not treat amla as a settled or reliable substitute for prescribed cholesterol treatment.
