whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Blood pressure shows the same kind of single-trial-versus-pooled-review conflict this project has already documented for other herbs. A single, well-designed 8-week Iranian trial added 500 mg amla three times daily on top of patients' existing blood pressure medicine (81 completers) and found a significantly greater fall in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure than adding a placebo, with no significant change in blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, or liver/kidney markers, and no reported side effects.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Set against that one positive add-on trial: Brown's 2023 pooled review (which included some of the same kind of hypertension-population trials) found no significant effect on systolic or diastolic blood pressure overall, with extremely high disagreement between trials (I-squared of 96% and 89%). This card treats blood pressure as a genuinely open question, not a settled benefit, and does not suggest reducing a prescribed blood-pressure medicine on the strength of amla.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Blood sugar is amla's thinnest and least independently checkable researched use. The most rigorous review located for cardiometabolic outcomes (Brown et al 2023, above) did not test blood glucose at all - diabetes was only a trial-eligibility characteristic, never a measured outcome. The only review found that did test blood glucose (Setayesh et al 2023, 5 RCTs) reported a significant fasting-glucose reduction in its own abstract, but without giving the pooled effect size or heterogeneity needed to judge how reliable that finding is - a clear step down from the more fully reported lipid findings above. Because of this gap, this card treats amla's blood-sugar evidence as a real but still thin and largely unproven interest, and does not add amla to this project's own Diabetes health topic as a supported option on the strength of it; the caution about combining amla with diabetes medicines further down still applies regardless, since even an unproven blood-sugar-lowering effect matters for that specific risk.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Amla's traditional 'Rasayana' reputation is often read as including immune support, but this card could not find reliable human evidence that amla measurably improves immune function specifically. The richest consumer clinical-reference source found for amla reports only animal data under its own 'Immune' heading (a multi-herb Triphala preparation raised neutrophil activity in stressed rats in one experiment; a plain amla extract had no effect on stress hormone release in another) and gives no human immune-outcome trial anywhere on the page. Because of this genuine evidence gap, this card does not add amla to this project's own Immune function health topic - its Rasayana reputation is treated here as a real traditional use, not a confirmed immune benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Hair is where amla's very well-known traditional use (as a hair oil) and its actual clinical evidence point in genuinely different directions, and this card keeps that distinction clear rather than blurring it. A single small triple-blind trial (60 women with female-pattern/androgenetic hair loss, 12 weeks) found an ORAL amla fruit syrup, taken three times daily, significantly improved the proportion of hairs in their active growing phase compared with a placebo syrup, with only one mild side effect (constipation) reported. This is a genuine, if small and unreplicated, signal for oral amla specifically - not for amla hair oil.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: By contrast, this card could not find any published clinical trial of amla hair OIL used on its own. The one topical trial located tested a leave-in hair serum combining amla extract with several other active ingredients (coconut water solids, a selenium-containing peptide, peanut shell extract) in 42 people, with no placebo or comparison group and funding from the ingredient manufacturer - a design that cannot show what amla itself contributed, and a materially weaker kind of evidence than the oral trial above. Amla hair oil remains, on the evidence this card could find, a genuine and very well-known traditional/folk practice, not a clinically tested one - the same honest distinction this project's Guggul card drew between a single small trial and a confident-sounding 'Possibly Effective' rating.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Plain dried fruit powder (churna), juice and standardised-extract capsules or tablets are plant material - naturally vegan. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Triphala (amla combined with haritaki and bibhitaki fruit powders) is vegan by composition as a plain powder or capsule product - all three ingredients are fruit, with no ghee, honey or other animal ingredient in the formula itself. Classical instructions for HOW to take the powder sometimes suggest mixing it with honey, milk or warm water depending on the condition being treated - this is a traditional way of taking it, not an ingredient of the product, so a plain Triphala powder or capsule stays vegan as long as it's mixed with water rather than honey or milk.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Chyawanprash is a genuinely different, stronger vegan-ingredient flag, the same way this project's Guggul card flagged ghee in Yograj Guggulu: ghee and honey are both FORMAL, STANDARD ingredients of the classical recipe, not just a traditional way of taking it. The classical process fries the amla paste with cow ghee and sesame oil, then stirs in honey once the mixture has cooled. This is not vegan as classically made, and commercial variation is wide (anywhere from about 25 to 80 ingredients across different brands) - anyone wanting a vegan version would need to check the full ingredient label of a specific product rather than assume a jar labelled 'Chyawanprash' is plant-only, and this card does not know of a standard vegan version.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Amla hair oil, where used, is typically a plant-oil base (commonly coconut or sesame oil) infused with amla - naturally vegan as a concept, but as with any commercial cosmetic product, check the full ingredient label, since some hair-oil and hair-serum products on the market combine amla with many other active ingredients of varying origin.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding safety data for amla at therapeutic/supplement doses is genuinely lacking, not reassuring - this card does not say amla is safe in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Canada's own health-product regulator requires a 'talk to a healthcare practitioner' caution for breastfeeding on every amla product, and for pregnancy specifically on any product providing more than 3 g of amla a day; a separate professional monograph independently states plainly that information on pregnancy and lactation safety 'is lacking.' Talk to a doctor before using any amla supplement if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: A genuine, if not fully settled, bleeding/antiplatelet caution is worth flagging clearly, and this card treats it as more credible than a simple 'theoretical' label might suggest. A 12-week human trial of a standardised amla extract found it significantly reduced two different markers of platelet clumping (ADP- and collagen-induced platelet aggregation) in obese adults, with the effect on one of those markers still measurable 2 weeks after stopping; a separate small human safety trial independently found amla significantly shortened prothrombin time (a clotting-speed blood test) after 4 weeks. Despite this, the consumer monograph reporting the platelet-aggregation finding separately states 'Interactions: None well documented' elsewhere on the same page - an inconsistency this card does not resolve by picking a side. Anyone taking a blood-thinning or antiplatelet medicine (such as warfarin, aspirin or clopidogrel), anyone with a bleeding disorder, or anyone with surgery scheduled should talk to a doctor before using an amla supplement.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: If you take blood pressure medicine, be aware that amla may add to its effect - the one dedicated add-on trial found amla significantly lowered blood pressure further when combined with an existing antihypertensive medicine. This is not necessarily a problem, but it is worth discussing with a doctor, including whether blood pressure should be monitored more closely while combining the two.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: If you take insulin or any other diabetes medicine, talk to your doctor before using an amla supplement and watch for symptoms of blood sugar dropping too low (shakiness, sweating, confusion) if you do combine them - amla's blood-sugar-lowering effect is still an open research question (see above), but even an unproven effect is relevant to this specific interaction risk, the same cautious approach this project's Tulsi, Ashwagandha and Moringa herb cards take for their own less-than-certain blood-sugar findings.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: The safety picture in the small human trials actually completed is reassuring, though based on short studies with few participants: an 18-week crossover trial in 13 healthy adults found no adverse events, and no meaningful change in liver enzymes (ALT fell slightly, AST unchanged, all values stayed in the normal range), kidney markers (creatinine and urea nitrogen unchanged) or blood counts; a separate 8-week add-on hypertension trial likewise found no significant change in ALT, AST, BUN or creatinine and no reported side effects. This project could not find a documented human case report of liver injury, kidney harm or serious allergic reaction linked to amla specifically - a notably cleaner safety record in the sources checked than this project has found for some other herbs (Moringa and Guggul both have at least one documented case report of liver-related harm). This does not mean amla is proven safe for everyone, only that no clear warning signal turned up in what this card could independently verify.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Amla is traditionally used in Ayurveda as a mild laxative; Canada's own health-product regulator lists a laxative effect as a known, expected adverse reaction at the doses it allows on product labels (3-6 g dried fruit a day), and separately warns not to use amla as a laxative if you have a fever or any undiagnosed gastrointestinal problem.
cautions.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive, talk to a doctor before using any amla supplement, extract or concentrated preparation - not the everyday fresh fruit, which this project's Foods-module entry already covers separately.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take a blood-thinning or antiplatelet medicine, have a bleeding disorder, or have surgery scheduled, talk to a doctor before using an amla supplement.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take insulin, another diabetes medicine, or blood pressure medicine, talk to your doctor before trying an amla supplement, and ask about monitoring if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Do not use amla as a laxative if you have a fever or an undiagnosed gastrointestinal problem - see a doctor instead.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice, and is about amla as a concentrated supplement, extract or classical preparation. It does not change this project's own Foods-module guidance that fresh amla is a normal, nutritious, vitamin-C-rich fruit in everyday vegan eating.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength or in vegan status. The human trials behind this card's cholesterol, blood-pressure and safety findings used plain standardised fruit extract capsules or dried fruit powder - never Chyawanprash or Triphala. A mild cup of amla in warm water is a different matter from a standardised extract capsule dosed to match a clinical trial, and both are different again from Chyawanprash, which this card's research found is not vegan as classically made.

preparationForms.note: The form used in most of the human trials cited above, typically 250-1500 mg/day. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
Traditional dried-fruit-powder form, typically 3-6 g/day per Health Canada's own regulatory monograph; also the form used in some individual blood-sugar and cholesterol trials (1-3 g/day in water).
An everyday-food form already covered by this project's own Foods-module entry for amla; not separately reviewed for therapeutic dosing in this card.
A classical three-fruit combination, vegan by composition as a plain powder or capsule - but check that it is mixed with water rather than honey or milk if you want to keep the whole routine vegan.

Combines amla with roughly 50 other herbs; ghee and honey are both standard, classical ingredients of the recipe itself, not just a way of taking it - not vegan as classically made, and this card does not know of a standard vegan version. Any clinical evidence for Chyawanprash is evidence for the whole product, not for amla alone.
A very well-known traditional practice with no isolated clinical-trial evidence this card could find; naturally vegan as a plant-oil base, but check the full label of any commercial product.

herbs.name: Ashwagandha

traditionalUse.text: A root herb used for centuries in Ayurvedic tradition as a 'rasayana' (rejuvenating tonic) and adaptogen - traditionally understood to help the body adapt to stress, strengthen and nourish the nervous system, and support general vitality. Its Sanskrit name (roughly 'like a horse') refers to the strength it is traditionally said to confer, and its distinctive earthy smell and taste come from withanolides, the steroidal compounds the root contains.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 9 randomised controlled trials (558 participants) found significant reductions, versus placebo, in perceived stress, Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores, and serum cortisol. 4 of the 9 trials reported mild-to-moderate adverse events, and the authors call for more long-term safety data.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: This is a genuinely mixed picture, not a settled one: a separate, later meta-analysis pooling a different, more recent set of trials confirmed the cortisol-lowering effect again but found NO significant effect on perceived stress specifically. Clinical-reference sources independently describe the overall evidence the same cautious way - modest effects from standardised extracts, small studies, more research needed - and a major US cancer centre's own herb-information page reaches the same conclusion for sleep, anxiety and cognition specifically.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: A small, older human trial (39 participants total, 6 weeks) found a trend toward ashwagandha extract outperforming placebo for anxiety symptoms, and a separate, different human trial (300 mg twice daily, standardised to 1.5% withanolides, 81 participants total) found a bigger reduction in anxiety scores in a group receiving ashwagandha alongside counselling and relaxation techniques than in a group receiving counselling and relaxation alone - though with several components combined, it is not possible to say how much of that effect came from the ashwagandha specifically.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Most of the broader claimed benefits (fertility, muscle strength, cholesterol, joint pain, cancer) rest on animal or laboratory studies, or on very preliminary human data - a major US cancer centre's own page states plainly that anticancer effects seen on cell lines have 'not been observed in humans.' This card does not treat any of these broader claims as established.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Root powder is the traditional form, naturally vegan on its own. It is commonly stirred into warm liquid before drinking - a plant milk (almond, oat, soy) works just as well as the dairy milk some recipes default to, since the herb itself carries no animal content either way.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules, tablets and standardised extracts (such as the KSM-66 extract used in some of the trials above) are also widely available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy and while trying to conceive - this is the strongest-worded caution across every source checked, with some evidence it may increase miscarriage risk. Breastfeeding safety is not established either; talk to a doctor first.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar. Combined with diabetes medicines (insulin, sulfonylureas, metformin and similar named across sources) this could cause hypoglycaemia; anyone with diabetes should talk to their doctor before trying ashwagandha and monitor blood sugar closely if they do.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood pressure. Caution is advised for anyone on blood pressure medicine (examples named across sources include captopril, amlodipine and furosemide) or anyone who already runs low blood pressure.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May increase immune system activity, which could reduce the effectiveness of immunosuppressant medicines (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone/corticosteroids named across sources) - and may trigger or worsen autoimmune conditions (multiple sclerosis, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis named). This is not a theoretical concern only: one case report describes kidney transplant rejection in a patient taking ashwagandha. Anyone on immunosuppressants, with an autoimmune condition, or with a transplant, should avoid it or discuss it with their doctor first.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May cause drowsiness/sedation. Combined with sedatives, benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants or barbiturates (examples named across sources include clonazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam, diazepam, zolpidem) this could cause excessive sleepiness.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May raise thyroid hormone (T3/T4) levels - the opposite direction from tulsi's own thyroid caution, but still a real interaction. Anyone on thyroid medicine should talk to their doctor and may need thyroid function monitored with blood tests; this caution is independently corroborated by three separate sources here, including real case reports of thyrotoxicosis (which resolved after stopping). See this project's own Thyroid health topic and Tulsi herb card for the related but opposite-direction caution.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid with stomach ulcers or liver disease. Liver problems, including rare case reports of more serious liver injury (acute steatohepatitis), have been reported with ashwagandha use and generally improved once it was stopped.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May raise testosterone - a caution specifically for anyone with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, who should avoid it.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May slow the central nervous system; stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery and tell the surgical team. This specific surgery caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently confirmed by every other source checked for this card.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Buy from a reputable brand: one case report describes hemolytic anaemia and abdominal pain from an ashwagandha/mucuna product found to contain high lead levels - a product-quality and contamination issue, not a property of the herb itself, but a real reason to be careful about sourcing, especially for an unregulated supplement market.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you take diabetes medicine and start ashwagandha, watch for hypoglycaemia symptoms (shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness) and talk to your doctor promptly - do not adjust your medicine dose yourself.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: See a doctor promptly for signs of liver problems - unusual tiredness, nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes - and stop ashwagandha until you've been checked.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before starting ashwagandha if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive, have an autoimmune condition, have had an organ transplant, have liver disease or a stomach ulcer, have diabetes, have low or medically treated blood pressure, have hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, take thyroid medicine, or have surgery scheduled.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - traditional root powder stirred into a drink is typically far gentler than a standardised capsule extract (such as KSM-66, used in some of the trials above), and the cautions above apply most to the stronger, concentrated forms.

preparationForms.note: The traditional root-powder form, commonly stirred into warm liquid (water or a plant milk) before drinking.
Standardised extracts (such as KSM-66) and tablets are widely available; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.

herbs.name: Brahmi

traditionalUse.text: A small creeping marsh plant used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is described as a 'medhya rasayana' - a class of herbs traditionally believed to improve mental health, memory and intellect and to promote rejuvenation. Its main traditional uses are memory improvement, insomnia, epilepsy and as an anxiolytic (anxiety-calming herb); its Sanskrit-derived name refers to Brahma, the Hindu creator deity.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This is the single most important thing to know before using this herb, and this card puts it first rather than burying it in the cautions: the name 'Brahmi' is genuinely used in India for two different plants - Bacopa monnieri (the plant this card is about) and Centella asiatica, also called gotu kola or Indian pennywort. The two are not interchangeable - they are different plants with different chemistry, uses and safety profiles. This is not a rare mix-up: it is independently confirmed by a US medical reference (RxList), an NIH-hosted clinical reference (StatPearls), and this project's own cached academic book, which makes exactly this error (see the next point).
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: A real, documented example of this exact mix-up, found during this project's own research: a cached academic nutrition book's table of Ayurvedic anti-cancer herbs lists 'Bacopa monnieri' as the scientific name and 'Brahmi' as the Sanskrit/Hindi name, but then gives the English name as 'Indian pennywort' - the common English name for Centella asiatica (gotu kola), not for Bacopa monnieri. The same table correctly lists Centella asiatica as its own separate entry a few rows later (Sanskrit 'Mandukaparni', English 'Gotu kola'), so the two plants are not fully merged into one line - but the English-name column for the Bacopa monnieri row is still wrong, borrowing the other plant's common name. This is the same kind of species mix-up this project has already caught for Tulsi (confused with culinary basil) and Shatavari (confused with vegetable asparagus).
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This is not just one book's slip: a major consumer medical reference (Merck Manual) independently makes a version of the same mix-up, describing Bacopa itself as 'also called Brahmi, Indian pennywort, water hyssop, and herb of grace' - folding Centella's common name into Bacopa's own name list. A more clinically careful source (StatPearls) does not do this, listing Bacopa's own names only as 'brahmi, water hyssop, thyme-leaved gratiola, and the herb of grace,' with no mention of pennywort. This tells readers something useful: 'Indian pennywort' showing up in connection with Bacopa is a real, recurring naming mix-up across more than one published source, not a one-off error - a good reason to check the Latin name on any 'Brahmi' product rather than trusting the English name alone.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Memory is this herb's best-supported use. A 2012 systematic review pooling 6 randomised, placebo-controlled human trials (12 weeks or longer, standardised extracts) found Bacopa improved performance on 9 of 17 tests specifically in the domain of memory free-recall, with little evidence of benefit in other cognitive domains. The review's own conclusion was cautious: research on its effects was 'in its infancy,' and more consistent testing methods and dose comparisons were needed.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: A later, larger 2014 meta-analysis pooling 9 randomised controlled trials (518 participants, 437 analysed) found a different kind of benefit: faster performance on the Trail B test and quicker choice reaction time - both measures of speed of attention, not specifically free-recall memory. The authors concluded Bacopa 'has the potential to improve cognition, particularly speed of attention,' but said only a large, well-designed head-to-head trial against an existing medicine would give definitive proof. Worth knowing: these two reviews, run two years apart on overlapping but not identical sets of trials, point to benefit in two different cognitive domains (free-recall memory vs. speed of attention) rather than confirming the same effect - a sign the underlying evidence is still not fully settled on exactly what this herb does best.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Beyond memory and attention, the evidence is much thinner. A US clinical-reference site rates irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) as 'Possibly Ineffective' - a real trial found Bacopa no better than placebo at preventing IBS symptoms returning after remission. Anxiety, epilepsy, asthma, backache, mental illness, joint pain and several other traditional or claimed uses are all rated 'Insufficient Evidence to Rate.' A US government-hosted clinical reference separately notes some trials have reported reduced anxiety and improved mood alongside the memory benefit, and that combining Bacopa with gotu kola (Centella asiatica - the other plant also sometimes called Brahmi) has shown anxiety benefits in some trials - but this combination finding says nothing about Bacopa taken on its own.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Most of the other proposed mechanisms (antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective effects, and benefits for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and stroke recovery) come only from animal or laboratory studies, not human trials. This card does not treat any of these as established in people.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Leaf and whole-plant material are naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules and standardised extracts are widely available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Do not confuse Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri, the plant this card is about) with Centella asiatica, also called gotu kola or Indian pennywort - a different plant that is also sometimes called 'Brahmi' in India. See the traditional-use section above for a real, documented example of this exact mix-up found in this project's own research. If buying a 'Brahmi' product, check the Latin name on the label, since the two plants are not interchangeable.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May raise thyroid hormone (T4) levels - the same direction as this project's own Ashwagandha herb card, not the opposite direction seen with Tulsi. The underlying evidence here is thinner than for Ashwagandha: it comes from one animal study (an approximately 40% rise in T4 in mice), but two independent clinical-reference sources (RxList, a consumer medical reference) extend this into a caution for people, advising anyone with a thyroid condition or taking thyroid medicine to use Brahmi cautiously or avoid it, and to have thyroid function monitored with blood tests if they do combine them. See this project's own Thyroid health topic for the related caution.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May slow the heart rate (bradycardia). This could be a problem for anyone who already has a slow heart rate, and the mechanism (increased acetylcholine activity) is also why this herb may worsen stomach ulcers, asthma or other lung conditions, or urinary tract obstruction - all are named as reasons to avoid or use this herb cautiously.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy - reliable safety information is lacking, and clinical-reference sources advise against use. Breastfeeding safety is also not established; the same sources advise avoiding use.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Drug interactions worth knowing: Brahmi may reduce the effect of anticholinergic ('drying') medicines (examples named include atropine and some antihistamines or antidepressants) and may increase side effects when combined with cholinergic drugs or Alzheimer's medicines that work the same way (examples named include pilocarpine, donepezil and tacrine). It has also been shown in laboratory studies to inhibit several liver enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4) that break down many common medicines (examples named across sources include warfarin, glipizide, diltiazem, losartan, fluoxetine, and some chemotherapy drugs), which could raise or lower blood levels of those medicines. Anyone taking regular prescription medicine should talk to a doctor before starting Brahmi.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: An animal study found Brahmi reduced sperm count, motility and quality in male mice at a relatively high, sustained dose, without affecting libido - an animal-only finding, not confirmed in humans, but worth knowing for anyone trying to conceive.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Short-term use (up to about 12 weeks, the typical length of the human trials above) is generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal side effects (looser or more frequent stools, stomach cramps, nausea, dry mouth, fatigue) the most commonly reported. Longer-term human safety data is limited.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine, talk to your doctor before trying Brahmi, and ask about monitoring thyroid function with blood tests if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you already have a slow heart rate, a stomach ulcer, asthma or another lung condition, or urinary tract obstruction, talk to a doctor before trying Brahmi.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before using Brahmi if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, trying to conceive, or take any regular prescription medicine, and always check the Latin name on a 'Brahmi' product to make sure it is Bacopa monnieri and not Centella asiatica (gotu kola).
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - the human trials behind this card's memory and attention findings used standardised capsule extracts at specific, studied doses, not loose powder or home-made tea, and the cautions above apply most to the stronger, concentrated forms.

preparationForms.note: Standardised extract, typically 300-450 mg/day standardised to 10-55% bacosides depending on the product - the form used in most of the human trials cited above; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
Crude dried herb, traditionally 5-10 g/day in Ayurvedic use - a far gentler, less concentrated form than a standardised extract.
A liquid 1:5 extract, traditionally 10-20 mL/day - not separately tested in the human trials this card cites.

herbs.name: Giloy (Guduchi)

traditionalUse.text: A climbing shrub whose stem is used in Ayurveda as a rasayana (rejuvenating herb) - traditionally taken for general vitality, fever and immune support, and widely used across South Asia for centuries.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis) is the one use with a genuinely positive rating: a specific extract (sold under the brand Tinofend) significantly reduced sneezing and nasal itching after about 2 months in a clinical trial. This is a brand-specific finding, not a general statement that any giloy product works the same way.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Almost everything else this herb is traditionally used for - diabetes, cholesterol, cancer, arthritis, general liver support, immune 'boosting' - is rated insufficient evidence in humans, resting mainly on animal or laboratory studies. A handful of small human studies exist (a diabetic foot ulcer study, one short cognition trial, a preliminary arthritis trial), but none are large or rigorous enough to confirm a benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Worth knowing when reading about this herb online: a 2024 review's own highlights claim it 'could fight against coronavirus disease,' but the review's own body text gives no human data for this - COVID-19 research on this herb is described only as 'in the clinical trial stage.' This is a case of a source overselling in its summary what its own detail actually supports, not a reason to dismiss the herb's traditional use, but a reason to read past headline claims.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Stem, root and leaf are all plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Taken as a boiled-stem decoction (kwath), tablets, or syrup in the documented case reports - this card does not recommend a specific form or dose, given the safety concerns below.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: This is the most important thing to know about this herb: real, published, peer-reviewed clinical case reports describe serious liver injury linked to Giloy/Guduchi use, including one death. A 2021 case series (6 patients) reported jaundice and acute hepatitis after a median of about 3 months of self-prescribed use, with very high liver-enzyme and bilirubin levels; one patient died of liver-related complications about 4 months after first presenting. A separate, larger 2022 study across 13 hospitals in India reported 49 similar cases. This is not a single isolated report - it is two independent, peer-reviewed findings.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: This finding is genuinely disputed, and this card presents both sides rather than picking one: critics have raised real points, including that the larger study did not report how many total patients were screened to find its 49 cases, that typical reported doses may have been higher than usually recommended, and that some cases may actually involve a different, visually similar plant (Tinospora crispa) rather than this one. India's government AYUSH Ministry has also publicly disputed the link. None of this proves the herb is safe either - it means the exact cause is still being argued over, which is itself a reason for caution rather than reassurance.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Notably, in the 2021 case series, 4 of the 6 patients had underlying silent autoimmune-featured liver disease found on biopsy, and the authors propose the herb may trigger an autoimmune-like hepatitis or unmask an existing autoimmune liver condition someone did not know they had. This connects directly to the separate caution below about avoiding this herb with autoimmune conditions.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding - not enough is known about safety in either situation.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar - combined with diabetes medicines (insulin, glimepiride, glyburide and pioglitazone named) this could cause hypoglycaemia. Anyone with diabetes should talk to their doctor first and monitor blood sugar closely. See this project's own Diabetes card for the related caution note.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May activate the immune system - avoid with autoimmune conditions (such as multiple sclerosis, lupus or rheumatoid arthritis), where it could worsen symptoms, and it may reduce the effectiveness of immunosuppressant medicines (azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus, prednisone/corticosteroids named).
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery, because of possible effects on blood sugar.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Long-term safety (beyond about 8 weeks) has not been established even by sources that otherwise rate short-term use as probably safe - combined with the liver-injury findings above, this card does not treat 'natural' or 'traditional' as a reason to use this herb for months at a time without medical guidance.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Stop taking Giloy/Guduchi and see a doctor promptly if you notice yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusually dark urine, pale stools, persistent nausea, loss of appetite, or unexplained tiredness - these can be signs of the liver injury documented above, and need medical attention, not waiting to see if they pass.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you have any known liver condition or autoimmune disease, talk to a doctor before using this herb at all, given the documented connection between Giloy-linked liver injury and underlying autoimmune liver disease.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before using this herb if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, have diabetes, take immunosuppressant medicine, or have surgery scheduled.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: Given this herb's documented liver-injury risk, this card does not recommend any particular form or duration of use - the case reports describe injury after weeks to months of ordinary self-prescribed use, not only from an unusually strong or impure product.

preparationForms.note: Boiled stem preparation - the form used by most patients in the documented liver-injury case series.
Also used in the documented case series; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
A less common form, also used in the documented case series.

herbs.name: Gotu Kola

traditionalUse.text: A small creeping plant in the carrot/parsley family (Apiaceae), native to the wetlands of Asia, with the above-ground leafy parts used to make medicine. It is used across Ayurveda, Traditional Chinese Medicine and Siddha medicine (where it is known in Tamil as Vallarai), with traditional and purported uses spanning wound healing and skin conditions, venous/circulatory problems (varicose veins, venous insufficiency), and memory, cognition and anxiety. A US government-hosted health database states plainly that none of these purported benefits 'have been proven in controlled human trials,' and that gotu kola is not approved in the United States as therapy for any medical condition, though it is sold over the counter.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This is the naming question this card was specifically asked to re-verify, from gotu kola's own side rather than only repeating what this project's Brahmi herb card already found: the name 'Brahmi' is genuinely used in India for BOTH Bacopa monnieri (the subject of this project's separate Brahmi card) and Centella asiatica, the plant this card is about - and that overlap now checks out independently from two of gotu kola's own clinical-reference sources, not only from Bacopa's side. RxList's own gotu kola page lists this plant's 'other names' as 'Brahmi, Indian Pennywort, Hydrocotyle asiatica, and Mandukaparni.' A separate US federal government database (NCBI Bookshelf's LiverTox chapter, run by the NIH's NIDDK) independently lists this plant's names as 'Gotu kola, Asian pennywort, spadeleaf, coinwort, tiger grass, Brahmi, Centella.' Two different clinical-reference sources, read directly for this card, both apply the name 'Brahmi' to Centella asiatica on Centella's own page - confirming the mix-up is real and bidirectional, not a one-way error on the Bacopa side alone. See this project's own Brahmi herb card for the original, more detailed documented example of this mix-up (a cached Ayurvedic academic book and Merck Manual both making a version of it).
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This mix-up has real practical stakes, not just a labelling curiosity, and the evidence this card gathered below makes that concrete: this project's Brahmi card shows Bacopa monnieri has two independent systematic reviews/meta-analyses of human trials finding a real, if modest, memory or attention benefit. Gotu kola's own best-available pooled evidence for cognition (see whatEvidenceShows below) found NO significant benefit in any cognitive domain tested. A reader who buys a 'Brahmi' product hoping for Bacopa's documented cognitive benefit could, because of this naming overlap, instead receive Centella asiatica - a different plant whose own pooled cognitive evidence did not reach statistical significance. Checking the Latin name (Centella asiatica vs. Bacopa monnieri) on any product labelled only 'Brahmi' remains the one reliable way to know which plant, and which evidence, a reader is actually getting.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: A separate, unrelated naming point worth knowing: a US government-hosted health database states gotu kola 'should not be confused with kolanut' (the caffeine-containing kola nut used in some beverages) - gotu kola itself contains no caffeine and has not been shown to have stimulant properties.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Venous insufficiency (varicose veins, leg swelling) is the one use a US consumer clinical-reference site rates with a positive effectiveness rating - 'Possibly Effective' - stating that taking gotu kola or a specific standardised extract by mouth for 4-8 weeks 'seems to improve blood circulation and reduce swelling' in people with venous insufficiency, at a typical oral dose of 60-180 mg/day of extract. A dedicated 2013 systematic review (8 RCTs, 1981-2001, 17-99 participants each, mostly testing a titrated triterpenic extract called TTFCA) found statistically significant improvements in several surrogate circulation measures - transcutaneous oxygen pressure, transcutaneous CO2 pressure, and the venoarteriolar response - versus placebo.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Checked specifically for the kind of overclaiming this project has already documented in Tulsi, Nettle, Shatavari, Giloy, Guggul, Amla and Hibiscus's reviews, and found here too: that 2013 venous-insufficiency review's own Conclusion states its 8 trials 'all reported beneficial effects' - a stronger framing than its own risk-of-bias analysis supports, since only 1 of the 8 trials had low risk of bias from blinding of both participants and outcome assessors, and sequence generation was unclear in 6 of the 8. The review's own Discussion separately warns that the surrogate measures it pooled 'lack well-established normal values,' meaning a statistically significant change on them may not translate into a clinically meaningful one for a patient - yet its own abstract still describes these same measures as 'significantly improved.' This card treats venous insufficiency as gotu kola's best-evidenced use by volume of trials, but a genuinely imperfect evidence base, not a settled, well-proven benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Wound healing and skin repair is gotu kola's next best-known researched use, and the evidence is real but still early. A US consumer clinical-reference source rates topical use for wound healing as 'early evidence' only, with a proposed mechanism of increased collagen production. A dedicated 2022 systematic review - the first of its kind on this specific question - found only 4 small human trials in total, covering diabetic foot wounds, burns, anal fissure and post-laser skin, with different designs and comparators in each; its own authors state 'it was not possible to conduct a meta-analysis' given how few and how different the trials were. Results were mixed: diabetic-wound and burn trials reported faster healing, but the anal-fissure trial's own healing-time result 'did not reach significance (p=0.07).'
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Overclaiming check on that same wound-healing review: both its abstract and its own conclusion attribute the healing effect to a specific mechanism - improved angiogenesis via collagen I, FGF and VEGF production - that none of its 4 included clinical trials actually measured; this mechanism comes only from separate background animal/in-vitro studies cited elsewhere in the paper, not from the clinical evidence just reviewed. The same conclusion section goes further still, adding that the findings also 'suggest a promising effect in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis' - a claim resting on an animal study, with no rheumatoid-arthritis trial anywhere in the review's own evidence base. This card treats gotu kola's wound-healing evidence as genuinely early and not yet meta-analysable, considerably more modest than the review's own concluding language suggests.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cognition and memory - often the reason gotu kola gets reached for BECAUSE of the 'Brahmi' naming overlap documented above - is, on gotu kola's own evidence, the weakest of its three best-known uses, not the strongest. The most rigorous pooled review located (Puttarak et al. 2017, 11 RCTs, 5 testing gotu kola alone and 6 testing combination products) found NO statistically significant difference versus placebo in ANY cognitive domain tested - overall cognitive status, attention, executive function, information processing, language, or working/verbal/visual memory all crossed the line of no effect, with high disagreement between the pooled trials (I-squared 61-88% for most domains). The only significant findings in the whole review were single small trials, not the pooled result: one 14-person single-dose trial for working-memory time, and three results from combination products (which, by definition, cannot isolate gotu kola's own individual contribution).
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Overclaiming check on that cognition review: its Discussion states gotu kola 'may improve working memory' despite the pooled working-memory result being null, and credits gotu kola (in combination with other herbs) for attention, executive-function and information-processing improvements even though the paper's own text admits those combination-product results 'could not show the direct effect of C. asiatica' specifically, since other herbs in the mix may explain them. The Discussion also states the mood results 'support the traditional use of C. asiatica as a brain tonic' and that it 'may improve mood disorders' - even though the trials pooled enrolled mostly healthy volunteers (one enrolled children with ADHD), none assessed a diagnosed mood disorder, and the positive alertness and anger findings each rest on only 2 small studies. This card follows the review's own results table (null on every pooled cognitive domain) rather than its more confident Discussion.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Anxiety has one genuine but very early human signal: a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial gave 40 healthy adults a single 12 g oral dose of gotu kola or placebo and measured the acoustic startle response (ASR), a physiological, involuntary startle-reflex measure linked to anxiety/fear circuitry - not a self-rated anxiety scale. Gotu kola 'significantly attenuated the peak ASR amplitude 30 and 60 minutes after treatment' compared with placebo, but had NO significant effect on self-rated mood, heart rate, or blood pressure. The authors' own conclusion was explicitly preliminary, stating plainly 'it remains to be seen whether this herb has therapeutic efficacy in the treatment of anxiety syndromes' - this was a single-dose physiological-marker trial, not a treatment trial, and this card does not treat it as evidence that gotu kola treats anxiety.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: A genuine structural gap worth flagging honestly, rather than forcing a link to the wrong place: venous insufficiency/circulatory health appears to be gotu kola's single best-evidenced use by volume and consistency of trials (see above), but this project currently has no dedicated venous/circulatory health topic among its health_topics files (anaemia, bones, diabetes, gut-health, heart-and-cholesterol, immune-function, kidney-health, mood-mental-health, pcos-hormonal-health, skin-hair-health, thyroid, weight). Because of this, and because gotu kola's own cognition/anxiety evidence is too thin and inconsistent (see above) to support a primary link to this project's Mood and mental health topic even despite the Brahmi naming overlap discussed earlier, this card does not add gotu kola as a primary link to that topic - the same honest 'no primary link found' approach this project's Moringa card already took when its own evidence did not clear the bar, rather than stretching a link to a topic that doesn't genuinely fit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Fresh or dried leaf, tea/infusion, and plain powder are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing in gotu kola itself to check. In parts of South and Southeast Asia the leaves are also eaten as a fresh salad green or cooked vegetable (for example as Tamil 'Vallarai Keerai'), a straightforwardly vegan everyday use distinct from the therapeutic doses discussed in this card.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules and standardised extracts are widely available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist, and at least one secondary ingredients database lists gelatin as an example capsule-shell ingredient on some gotu kola products specifically.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: This card's own research found no standard, documented classical preparation that formally combines gotu kola with a non-vegan ingredient such as ghee or honey, the way Chyawanprash does for amla or Yograj Guggulu does for guggul - the consumer and government clinical sources checked describe gotu kola only as tea, dried leaf, powder, standardised extract capsules, or a topical cream/ointment, with no combination formula requiring a non-vegan ingredient named anywhere. This card says so plainly, the same honest approach this project's Hibiscus card already took, rather than forcing a finding that isn't there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Topical creams and ointments (sometimes sold under names like Madecassol) used for wound healing are typically a plant-extract base - naturally vegan as a concept, but as with any commercial cosmetic or wound-care product, check the full ingredient label, since formulations vary and some combine gotu kola with other active ingredients of varying origin.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Do not confuse gotu kola (Centella asiatica, the plant this card is about) with Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) - a different plant, covered in this project's own separate Brahmi herb card, that is also sometimes called 'Brahmi' in India, and whose own documented cognitive evidence is meaningfully stronger than gotu kola's own (see traditionalUse and whatEvidenceShows above for this card's independent confirmation of the mix-up and why it practically matters). If buying a product labelled only 'Brahmi,' check the Latin name to know which plant - and which evidence - you are actually getting.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Liver safety is a real, if rare, concern backed by more than a passing case-report mention. A US federal government liver-injury database (LiverTox) documents a 2005 case series of three Argentinian women (ages 61, 52 and 49) who developed jaundice 30, 20 and 60 days respectively after starting Centella tablets for weight loss. The 61-year-old's case is the most detailed and significant: she recovered after stopping, with normal liver tests at 2 months, then had the injury recur on rechallenge about 7 months later when she restarted the product for just 2 weeks - a positive rechallenge, one of the stronger forms of evidence for attributing an injury to a specific product. LiverTox separately notes one further published case (a Swiss woman in 2011, after use for acne), and gives gotu kola its own likelihood score of 'C' - a probable rare cause of clinically apparent liver injury. People who already have a liver disease such as hepatitis are advised to avoid gotu kola, and anyone taking another drug that can affect the liver (acetaminophen, methotrexate, and statins are named as examples) should be aware gotu kola might add to that risk.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May add to the effect of sedatives or other CNS depressants (zolpidem and lorazepam are named as examples), causing excess sleepiness or drowsiness - for this reason, stop using gotu kola at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery, because of the risk of added sedation with anaesthesia-related medicines.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: In laboratory (in vitro) studies, gotu kola inhibits several liver enzymes that break down many common medicines (CYP1A2, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4 and 2C19) - this could in theory raise or lower blood levels of drugs metabolised by those enzymes, but a US government-hosted clinical reference states plainly that the 'clinical relevance is undetermined' in people, so this card treats it as a real but unconfirmed interaction risk rather than a settled one. Anyone taking regular prescription medicine should mention gotu kola to their doctor or pharmacist.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding safety data is genuinely lacking for oral use, not reassuring - one consumer source rates topical use 'POSSIBLY SAFE in pregnant women when applied to the skin,' but is explicit that oral use should not be taken in pregnancy at all ('don't take it by mouth'), and advises avoiding gotu kola entirely while breastfeeding.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Side effects at ordinary intake are generally mild: oral use can cause nausea and stomach pain; topical use may cause itchiness, redness, or allergic contact dermatitis in some people. A government-hosted clinical reference separately notes potency can vary widely depending on where the plant was grown, which may affect how a given product behaves.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you already have a liver disease such as hepatitis, or notice signs of liver trouble (unusual tiredness, nausea, abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stools, yellowing of the skin or eyes) while using gotu kola, stop and see a doctor promptly - do not restart it afterwards.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are pregnant or trying to conceive, do not take gotu kola by mouth; if you are breastfeeding, avoid it altogether. Talk to a doctor before using even topical gotu kola in pregnancy.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you have surgery scheduled, stop using gotu kola at least 2 weeks beforehand because of a possible added-sedation risk with anaesthesia-related medicines.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take any regular prescription medicine - especially one that affects the liver, a sedative, or one broken down by common liver enzymes - talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting gotu kola.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - and is about gotu kola (Centella asiatica). Always check the Latin name on a product labelled only 'Brahmi' to make sure you know which plant, and which evidence, it actually refers to: Bacopa monnieri (this project's separate Brahmi card) or Centella asiatica (this card).
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength or evidence. The venous-insufficiency and wound-healing trials and reviews this card cites mostly used standardised extracts (often a specific titrated triterpenic fraction, TTFCA) or clearly defined oral/topical doses - not a casual cup of gotu kola tea or an unmeasured sprinkle of powder; the one human anxiety trial used a single large one-off 12 g dose, not an ongoing daily regimen, and should not be read as a dosing recommendation.

preparationForms.note: Naturally vegan; also eaten as a fresh or cooked leafy vegetable in some South/Southeast Asian cuisines - a different, everyday use from the therapeutic doses in the trials this card cites.
Dried-leaf powder, typically 600-1800 mg/day per a US government-hosted database's own dosing figures - naturally vegan.

Purified/standardised extract, typically 60-120 mg/day per a government-hosted database, or 60-180 mg/day per a consumer source's venous-insufficiency dosing - the form used in most of the venous-insufficiency trials cited above. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
Used for wound healing and skin in the small trials this card cites; naturally vegan as a plant-extract base, but check the full ingredient label of any commercial product, since formulations vary.

herbs.name: Guggul

traditionalUse.text: A yellowish gum resin (oleo-gum-resin) tapped from the bark of a small, thorny tree native to India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Ayurvedic medicine has used it for centuries to treat arthritis, obesity, skin disorders and high cholesterol, and a standardised extract is approved for marketing in India as a cholesterol-lowering medicine.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Unlike some other herbs this project has checked, this is not a mix-up between two different plants: the scientific literature genuinely uses two botanical names for this same tree - Commiphora mukul and Commiphora wightii (and, in older texts, Balsamodendrum mukul and Balsamodendrum wightii) - reflecting a taxonomic naming change over time, not two different herbs being confused with each other.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: The purified resin on its own (sometimes called Shuddha Guggulu) is one traditional form, but guggul is also very often combined with many other herbs in classical Ayurvedic tablet formulations, such as Yograj Guggulu - a detail that matters for the vegan check below.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol is this herb's best-known researched use, and the evidence is genuinely split rather than one-sided - this card shows both sides rather than picking one. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 7 randomised trials (380 participants, mostly standardised guggul/guggulipid extracts, about 12 weeks average) and found an average fall in total cholesterol of about 16.8 mg/dL and in LDL ("bad") cholesterol of about 18.8 mg/dL, with a small rise in HDL ("good") cholesterol and only minor side effects reported overall.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Worth knowing when reading that same review: its own data is shakier than its summary conclusion suggests. The 7 pooled trials showed high variability (statistically, I-squared of 75%, right at the review's own cut-off for trusting a pooled result), and the authors state one single older trial "strongly influenced" the overall effect - with most of the trials run in Western populations, by the review's own count, apart from two exceptions. The review still concludes guggul is "moderately effective," which reads more confident than this underlying unevenness fully supports - a pattern this project has flagged before in other sources' summaries.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Set directly against that pooled finding: a rigorous 2003 US trial (103 adults with high cholesterol, eating their usual Western diet, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 8 weeks) found guggulipid did NOT lower LDL cholesterol - LDL actually rose by 4 to 5% in the guggulipid groups, against a 5% fall on placebo - with no significant change in total cholesterol, HDL or triglycerides either. Six of the guggulipid-treated participants also developed a hypersensitivity skin rash, versus none on placebo. The authors concluded guggulipid "did not appear to improve" cholesterol over the short term in this population and might even raise LDL.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Clinical-reference sources reflect this same unresolved split rather than settling it: a US consumer medical reference rates the cholesterol evidence "insufficient... inconsistent," noting guggul may lower cholesterol for people eating an Indian-style diet but not for people eating a Western diet, while an older nutrition encyclopedia describes early Indian studies as promising but "limited in scope," making their results "unreliable." This card does not present guggul as a settled or reliable way to lower cholesterol.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Acne is the other traditionally and clinically explored use. A small 1994 Indian trial (20 patients with nodulocystic acne, 3 months) found oral gugulipid reduced inflammatory lesions about as well as the antibiotic tetracycline (68% versus 65% reduction, not a statistically significant difference), with people who had oily skin responding particularly well.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: But sources disagree on how much weight that single small, old trial should carry: a US consumer reference rates acne "Possibly Effective" largely on the strength of it, while a cancer-centre clinical database's own review states plainly that "evidence is lacking to support this claim for guggul alone." This card treats acne as a genuinely open question, not a confirmed benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For weight loss, most research suggests guggul does not meaningfully reduce body weight in people who are overweight or obese - rated "Possibly Ineffective" by a US consumer medical reference. Early, small studies hint at possible pain improvement in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, but the evidence here is rated insufficient to draw a conclusion either way.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: The gum resin itself, and the purified resin (Shuddha Guggulu), are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Standardised extract (guggulipid) capsules, dosed by guggulsterone content (commonly 2.5 to 3.5%), are the form used in most of the human trials cited above. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: A genuine vegan-specific check worth making, the same way this project flags gelatin capsules: classical multi-herb Ayurvedic tablet formulations that include guggul, such as Yograj Guggulu, are not vegan as traditionally made - ghee is a direct ingredient in that recipe, and honey or buttermilk is the traditional way the tablets are taken. Choosing a plain guggul or guggulipid extract product, and checking the full ingredient label on any combination "guggulu" product, is the safer route for staying vegan.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: Likely unsafe in pregnancy - it may stimulate the uterus and menstrual flow, so a US consumer medical reference rates it "Likely Unsafe" in pregnancy, and an older nutrition encyclopedia independently makes the same point ("probably unsafe for pregnant women"). Not enough is known about breastfeeding safety either, so the same sources advise avoiding it.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May raise thyroid hormone activity. A cancer-centre clinical database lists guggul as able to elevate TSH, T3 and T4 on lab tests, an academic nutrition textbook describes Commiphora mukul as showing "strong thyroid stimulatory action" in animal research, and a consumer medical reference advises using guggul only under a doctor's supervision if you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine. See this project's own Thyroid health topic for the related caution.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May act like oestrogen in the body - avoid with breast, uterine or ovarian cancer, endometriosis or uterine fibroids, and avoid combining it with oestrogen-containing medicines or birth control pills.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May slow blood clotting - use caution with a bleeding disorder, and avoid combining with blood-thinning medicines (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, heparin and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are named) without medical advice. Stop taking guggul at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May change how the liver breaks down several medicines (it can affect the CYP3A4 liver enzyme), which may make some medicines less effective. Examples named across sources include some statins (lovastatin, atorvastatin), some antifungal and allergy medicines, and tamoxifen - one source states plainly not to combine guggul with tamoxifen. Anyone on regular prescription medicine should check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Skin hypersensitivity (an allergic-type rash or itching) is a real, documented reaction - seen in a formal clinical trial (6 of 67 people taking guggulipid, versus none on placebo) and in contact-dermatitis case reports linked to topical slimming or anti-cellulite creams containing guggul.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A small number of case reports describe raised liver enzymes or liver injury linked to guggul-containing products, but this project treats the signal as real but unproven, not a confirmed guggul-specific risk - weaker and more confounded than the liver-injury finding this project has documented for Giloy. The reported cases involved combination products (one alongside red yeast rice, one alongside usnic acid and green tea), and the reviewing source itself says it is unclear how much guggul, versus the other ingredients, was responsible. Separately, a 2020 US government toxicology study found no dose-related organ damage in a 3-month animal study, though this is animal data, not proof of human safety.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Milder, more common side effects include stomach upset, headache, nausea, vomiting, loose stools or diarrhoea, belching and hiccups - more likely at higher doses (around 6000 mg/day in the sources reviewed).
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medicine, talk to your doctor before trying guggul, and ask about monitoring thyroid function with blood tests if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take blood-thinning medicine, have a bleeding disorder, have surgery scheduled, take tamoxifen or another hormone-sensitive-cancer medicine, or take any regular prescription medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using guggul.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Stop taking guggul and see a doctor if you notice a widespread rash or itching, yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusually dark urine, or persistent nausea - these need medical attention, not waiting to see if they pass.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - avoid guggul if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and check with a doctor if you are trying to conceive or have a hormone-sensitive condition.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - the human trials behind this card's cholesterol and acne findings used a standardised guggulipid extract dosed by guggulsterone content, not raw resin or a multi-herb tablet. Classical combination tablets such as Yograj Guggulu also raise a separate, vegan-specific issue: ghee is a direct ingredient in that recipe, so check labels rather than assuming any product called "guggul" or "guggulu" is plant-only.

preparationForms.note: Raw or purified resin, a traditional Ayurvedic form - naturally vegan, but not the form used in the clinical trials cited above.

Standardised extract dosed by guggulsterone content (commonly 2.5-3.5%). The Western cholesterol trial used 1000-2000 mg guggulipid three times daily; the acne trial used a dose giving 25 mg guggulsterone twice daily. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.

preparationForms.form: Tablet (classical multi-herb formulation, e.g. Yograj Guggulu)
preparationForms.note: Combines guggul resin with many other herbs; ghee is a direct ingredient in this classical recipe, and honey or buttermilk is the traditional way to take it - not vegan as traditionally made. Choose a plain guggul/guggulipid product instead to stay vegan, and check the full label.

herbs.name: Hibiscus

traditionalUse.text: This card is about Hibiscus sabdariffa L. (family Malvaceae), the plant most often sold as a herbal tea, extract or capsule for blood pressure and general wellness. A government horticultural database (Singapore's National Parks Board) confirms this scientific name and family, with several botanical synonyms (Hibiscus gossypiifolius, Abelmoschus cruentus, Hibiscus digitatus, Sabdariffa rubra, Hibiscus sanguineus) still sometimes seen in older literature. The part used is the fleshy red calyx (the structure that encloses the base of the flower, often loosely called the 'flower' in everyday speech) - not the leaves, which are also eaten as a sour vegetable in some cuisines, or the seeds.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This is the naming question this card was specifically asked to resolve, and the honest answer is: both 'roselle' and 'sorrel' are genuinely used as common names for this exact plant, AND 'sorrel' is also, separately and confusingly, the common name of a completely different, unrelated plant. 'Roselle' is the common name used most widely in English-language scientific and horticultural sources (confirmed independently by the government database above and by this card's consumer sources). In Jamaica, Trinidad and elsewhere in the English-speaking Caribbean, the same plant - and the drink made from its calyces - is instead called 'sorrel,' 'red sorrel' or 'Jamaica sorrel' (confirmed independently by the same government database, by a consumer supplement monograph, and by a drinks-reference source). The genuine ambiguity: 'sorrel' is ALSO the standard common name of Rumex acetosa (garden sorrel or common sorrel), a sour-leaved vegetable in a completely different plant family (Polygonaceae, the buckwheat/dock family) grown and eaten in Europe and elsewhere - an unrelated plant that has nothing botanically to do with Hibiscus sabdariffa (Malvaceae, the mallow family). A drinks-reference source makes this exact point explicitly: 'This should not be confused with sorrel (Rumex acetosa), a perennial herb.' This is the same kind of real, documented common-name collision this project has already flagged for Tulsi (confused with culinary basil), Shatavari (confused with vegetable asparagus) and Brahmi (confused with Centella asiatica/gotu kola) - not a rare mix-up, but a genuine naming ambiguity worth knowing before buying a product labelled only 'sorrel.' Checking for 'Hibiscus sabdariffa' on the label, rather than relying on 'sorrel' alone, avoids the confusion.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Traditional and everyday uses include the calyx steeped as a hot or cold drink (sold worldwide under various regional names - karkade in Egypt, zobo or bissap in West Africa, agua de Jamaica in Mexico, sorrel in the Caribbean), used as a natural food colouring and in jams, with young shoots/leaves eaten raw or cooked as a sour vegetable in some cuisines. The same government source states plainly that 'research supports the traditional use of roselle for ulcers,' while describing most of its other traditional medicinal reputation (pain relief, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, antimicrobial effects) as coming from animal studies only, not confirmed human evidence - a distinction this card keeps clear throughout rather than blurring traditional reputation with proven effect.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Blood pressure is hibiscus's best-known and most researched claimed benefit, and the evidence is genuinely mixed depending on which review and which comparator is used - this card shows the range rather than picking a single number. The largest and most recent pooled review (17 trials in total, across blood-pressure, lipid and blood-sugar outcomes combined) pooled roughly 11-12 of those trials specifically for blood pressure - the review's own text says 12 reported blood-pressure outcomes, while its own reference list and table for that outcome show 11, an inconsistency this card did not try to resolve - with 819 participants allocated across the blood-pressure trials specifically (415 to hibiscus, 404 to control). That blood-pressure analysis found hibiscus significantly lowered systolic blood pressure compared with placebo (-10.05 mmHg) and compared with all non-drug comparators pooled (-7.10 mmHg), but did NOT find a significant fall in diastolic blood pressure against placebo, and found NO significant difference from pharmaceutical drugs on either systolic or diastolic blood pressure in the 4 trials that made that comparison directly. Heterogeneity (disagreement between the pooled trials) was very high for almost every result (I-squared 81-96%), and the diastolic-vs-placebo finding was fragile: removing just one included trial from the pooled analysis would have flipped it from non-significant to significant and sharply cut the disagreement between trials - a sign that one study is doing outsized work in that particular number.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: That same 2022 review's own Discussion overstates what its results table actually shows, the same kind of overclaiming this project has already documented for its Tulsi, Nettle, Shatavari, Giloy, Guggul and Amla reviews. It describes hibiscus as a 'viable alternative' to diuretics or ACE-inhibitor blood pressure drugs, even though its own head-to-head drug comparisons were not statistically significant and came from only 4 trials with very high disagreement between them. It also says a statistical check called trial sequential analysis 'supports' the blood-pressure effect, even though its own systolic-blood-pressure result did not actually cross the specific statistical boundary that check requires to call a finding reliable. And it suggests a dose-response relationship (higher doses working better) that its own subgroup data do not actually support. This card follows the review's own numbers rather than its more confident-sounding discussion.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: An earlier, more cautious systematic review (4 RCTs, 390 patients, searched through January 2009) found far less to work with: no placebo-controlled trial even met its inclusion criteria, and of the 4 trials that did, 2 compared hibiscus with ordinary black tea (hibiscus did better than tea) and 2 compared it directly with a real ACE-inhibitor blood pressure drug - captopril in one trial, lisinopril in another - with hibiscus performing worse than the ACE inhibitors in that review's own reading. Nearly all of the underlying trials, bar one, were rated short-term and of poor methodological quality (Jadad scores below 3). This review's own conclusion, quoted directly, was blunt: the trials 'do not provide reliable evidence to support recommending Hibiscus sabdariffa' for treating primary hypertension in adults. A separate, broader 2013 review covering 10 RCTs (5 on blood pressure, 5 on cholesterol) reached a middle position - calling hibiscus 'promising' while explicitly saying many of the included trials were low quality and that preparations, doses and plant parts varied so much across studies that comparing them was difficult.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Hibiscus HAS been tested directly against a real antihypertensive drug - in fact, in at least three separate trials, which is more direct drug-comparison evidence than this project has found for some other herbs (amla and guggul, for example, have no such trial). A 2004 Mexican trial (90 enrolled, 75 completing, 4 weeks) found hibiscus extract and captopril did not differ significantly in blood-pressure-lowering effect, in how many people responded to treatment, or in tolerability (100% in both groups) - though the diastolic-blood-pressure result in that trial was itself only borderline significant (P<0.06) despite being described as significant in the trial's own abstract. A larger, separate 2007 trial by the same Mexican research group (not independently re-read in full by this card, cited via a secondary review) instead found hibiscus performed WORSE than lisinopril.
