A 2016 Nigerian trial (78 enrolled, 75 completing, 4 weeks) found hibiscus's systolic-blood-pressure reduction was actually significantly GREATER than lisinopril's own reduction at every weekly check from week 2 onward. Put plainly: the three head-to-head drug-comparison trials found in this card's research point in three somewhat different directions (roughly equal, worse than the drug, and better than the drug) - a genuinely unsettled picture, not evidence that hibiscus reliably matches or beats a real blood-pressure medicine.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Worth knowing when weighing the Nigerian trial above: it was reported across two separate published papers by an overlapping author group - one on blood pressure and renal/diuretic outcomes, one on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system markers - from what appears, on the details given (78 participants, same three groups, same mild-to-moderate hypertension, same 4-week duration), to be the same underlying 78-person trial rather than two independent studies. This card treats the two papers as one piece of evidence, not two confirmations of the same finding, when judging how much weight this particular result deserves.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: A genuine, reasonably well-evidenced diuretic effect does exist, separate from hibiscus's blood-pressure effect, and this card treats it as more than a theoretical claim. A dedicated 2013 review states plainly 'there is evidence that HS acts as a diuretic,' citing animal studies showing dose-dependent diuresis and at least two human studies finding statistically significant increases in sodium or chloride excretion (a natriuretic/chloruretic effect) - the reviewers compare hibiscus's effect profile to potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone. Separately, the 2004 captopril-comparison trial above observed a natriuretic effect with hibiscus, and the 2016 Nigerian trial found hibiscus significantly increased urine volume compared with placebo at every time point measured, and increased it MORE than lisinopril did (an ACE inhibitor, not itself a diuretic, which is a less direct comparison for this specific point than it might first appear) and significantly raised creatinine clearance, a kidney-filtration marker, versus placebo.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol and blood-sugar evidence for hibiscus is considerably thinner and less consistent than its blood-pressure evidence, and this card could not independently verify a reliable effect on either from the sources it directly read. The 2013 review covering 5 cholesterol-focused RCTs called results 'promising' but, as above, noted low trial quality and highly inconsistent preparations across studies - this card did not find a separate, specifically cholesterol-focused meta-analysis it could independently verify in full. For blood sugar, this card's own direct research turned up conflicting small human trials (at least one small positive trial reporting lower fasting glucose; at least one placebo-controlled Iranian trial finding no significant effect on blood glucose or HbA1c), and could not independently verify a reliable pooled blood-sugar effect size from a source it read in full. Because of this genuine evidence gap, this card does not add hibiscus to this project's own Diabetes health topic as a supported option, and does not claim a lipid or blood-sugar benefit as established fact.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Dried calyx (loose or in tea bags), plain powder, and standardised-extract capsules or tablets are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing in the hibiscus itself to check. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin; most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: This card's own research found no standard traditional hibiscus preparation that formally combines it with a non-vegan ingredient the way Chyawanprash does with ghee and honey for amla, or Yograj Guggulu does with ghee for guggul - plain hibiscus tea, powder and extract are vegan by composition, and this card says so plainly rather than forcing a finding that isn't there. The one thing worth knowing: traditional Caribbean 'sorrel' drink recipes commonly add a sweetener (sugar, or sometimes honey) and are sometimes served with rum added at serving time. Honey is a recipe choice, not a fixed ingredient of hibiscus itself, and sugar or a vegan sweetener works just as well in the same recipe; rum is an optional alcoholic addition at serving time, not part of the hibiscus preparation. Plain hibiscus tea or extract, taken on its own or sweetened with sugar or a plant-based sweetener, stays vegan.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding safety data for hibiscus at supplement/extract doses is genuinely lacking, not reassuring, and more than one consumer source goes further than a simple 'talk to your doctor' - one states that animal data suggest possible harm including miscarriage, and advises against use in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; a second separately advises avoiding it while pregnant or nursing because safety 'may be unsafe for you and your baby.' This card treats avoidance as the safer reading rather than a milder 'ask your doctor' framing alone.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: If you take chloroquine (for malaria treatment or prevention), be aware of a real, sourced interaction caution, not an urban-legend-style claim: older human pharmacokinetic studies, independently reviewed in a 2013 primary-literature paper on hibiscus's effect on drug-metabolising enzymes, found hibiscus-containing beverages significantly reduced chloroquine's bioavailability - meaning the drug may not reach effective levels in the blood if taken alongside hibiscus. A separate consumer source independently confirms hibiscus tea 'may interfere with some anti-malaria drugs,' without naming chloroquine specifically. The exact mechanism isn't fully worked out - the 2013 paper's own laboratory data classify the extract as only a weak liver-enzyme inhibitor overall, yet its own discussion separately warns that its converted dose-equivalent values for several of those same enzymes are high enough that in-body inhibition is plausible. This card treats the chloroquine caution as real and worth taking seriously precisely because it is independently sourced and consistent across more than one kind of source, while being honest that the underlying 1994 human study was not re-read directly by this card, only reviewed via a later paper's own citation and summary of it.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: If you take a blood-pressure medicine, be aware hibiscus may add to its effect rather than simply doing nothing alongside it - this is the flip side of hibiscus's own researched blood-pressure effect (see whatEvidenceShows above). Combining the two isn't necessarily a problem, but it's worth discussing with a doctor, including whether blood pressure should be monitored more closely, and this card does not suggest reducing a prescribed blood-pressure medicine on the strength of hibiscus. Separately, if you already have naturally low blood pressure, a consumer source names a blood-pressure drop as a possible hibiscus side effect in its own right.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Hibiscus has a genuine diuretic (urine-increasing) effect, covered in detail in whatEvidenceShows above - this matters for more than blood pressure. If you take a diuretic medicine (a 'water pill,' including hydrochlorothiazide), a reviewed animal study specifically flagged a possible interaction and the reviewing authors warned against combining the two on that basis; if you take any other medicine affected by fluid or electrolyte balance, or you have existing kidney disease, talk to a doctor before combining hibiscus with it, and watch for signs of dehydration or excessive fluid loss if you do.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: If you take acetaminophen (paracetamol) or diclofenac, be aware of weaker but genuine interaction signals from small older human pharmacokinetic studies: hibiscus water extract has been found to reduce acetaminophen's elimination half-life (without a significant change in total drug exposure, so the clinical meaning of this specific change is unclear) and to reduce diclofenac's metabolic clearance. The reviewing authors describe these as real findings from real human studies, while cautioning that the clinical significance of both is still unclear and that more in-vivo research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about combining hibiscus with these or other medicines broken down by the same liver enzymes - named examples of other such medicines include phenytoin, carbamazepine, theophylline and digoxin, drugs where even a modest change in blood level can matter.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: If you take insulin or another diabetes medicine, a consumer source lists diabetes medicines among those to discuss with a provider before using hibiscus - worth knowing even though this card could not independently verify a reliable blood-sugar-lowering effect for hibiscus (see whatEvidenceShows above), since even an unconfirmed effect is relevant to this specific interaction risk, the same cautious approach this project's Tulsi, Ashwagandha, Moringa and Amla herb cards take for their own less-than-certain blood-sugar findings.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Side effects reported across consumer sources are generally mild at ordinary intake: gas, stomach discomfort and constipation are named as common; dermatitis, headache, nausea and tinnitus (ringing in the ears) are also named by a separate source. A more serious caution appears on one consumer monograph: possible liver damage (hepatotoxicity) with regular high doses or when combined with other liver-affecting medicines, with named warning symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain, fever, fatigue, itching, poor appetite, pale stools, dark urine, jaundice) - this card could not find a specific published human case report of hibiscus-related liver injury to check this caution against, so it is shown as a sourced precaution rather than a confirmed, documented harm.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Allergy: avoid if allergic or sensitive to hibiscus, roselle, or other plants in the Malvaceae (mallow) family, and seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, facial or throat swelling, hives, rapid heartbeat or fainting.
cautions.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive, avoid hibiscus supplements or concentrated extract and talk to a doctor before using any hibiscus product beyond very occasional tea.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take chloroquine for malaria treatment or prevention, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using hibiscus in any form - the interaction caution here is sourced to real human studies, not folklore, and could mean the malaria drug doesn't work as well.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take a blood-pressure medicine, a diuretic ('water pill'), insulin or another diabetes medicine, acetaminophen, or diclofenac, talk to a doctor before starting hibiscus, and ask about monitoring if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Seek medical help immediately for signs of an allergic reaction (breathing difficulty, facial or throat swelling, hives, rapid heartbeat, fainting) or signs of liver trouble (nausea, abdominal pain, fever, fatigue, itching, poor appetite, pale stools, dark urine, jaundice) while using hibiscus.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice, and is about Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle/sorrel) as a tea, extract or capsule. Always check that a product labelled 'sorrel' actually names Hibiscus sabdariffa on its ingredient list, since 'sorrel' is also the name of an unrelated plant (Rumex acetosa) with no connection to hibiscus's own researched effects or cautions.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength. The human trials behind this card's blood-pressure and diuretic findings used a brewed infusion or decoction of dried calyx at specific, studied amounts (roughly 10-20 g dried calyx per day, or standardised equivalents) - not a casual cup of hibiscus tea at an unmeasured strength, and not a sweetened bottled hibiscus drink, which is a different matter again from a standardised extract capsule dosed to match a clinical trial.

preparationForms.note: The form used in most of the human trials cited above, typically made from about 10 g dried calyx per daily dose in the studies this card checked. Strength varies a great deal by how much calyx is used and how long it's steeped, so a casual cup is not the same dose as a studied one.

Widely sold as an over-the-counter supplement; no optimal dose has been established for any condition, and product quality and active-ingredient content vary between manufacturers, per a consumer source. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
Dried, ground calyx - naturally vegan, with nothing specific to check beyond sourcing and purity.

A traditional sweetened and spiced version of the tea, known regionally as sorrel (Caribbean), karkade (Egypt) or zobo/bissap (West Africa). Vegan as long as it's sweetened with sugar or a plant-based sweetener rather than honey, and served without rum if an alcohol-free version is wanted - neither honey nor rum is a fixed ingredient of the plant itself.

herbs.name: Licorice Root
aliases: Gan Cao (Chinese licorice, usually Glycyrrhiza uralensis)

traditionalUse.text: This card is about Glycyrrhiza glabra, a perennial legume (family Fabaceae) whose dried root, rhizome and stolon are used in herbal medicine and as a flavouring - not about liquorice-flavoured confectionery, which this card addresses separately below and in howToUseVegan, since the two are genuinely easy to conflate. Two government-hosted clinical references independently confirm the botanical identity and plant parts used (root, root and stolon, root and rhizome), and that Chinese liquorice (Glycyrrhiza uralensis, called Gan Cao) is a related but separate species sometimes used interchangeably in Traditional Chinese Medicine. In Ayurveda the root is called Yashtimadhu or Mulethi (Jethimadh); in Western herbalism and on supplement labels it is usually just 'licorice' or 'liquorice' (the British spelling for the same plant).
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: The naming/identity point this card was specifically asked to resolve: to most readers, 'licorice' means the chewy black or red confection sold as candy, not the herb. A US government-hosted consumer clinical reference states this plainly: most licorice-flavoured candy made in the United States is actually flavoured with anise oil and contains no real licorice/Glycyrrhiza extract at all. European and UK liquorice confectionery (for example Haribo's Pontefract Cakes, a well-known British liquorice sweet) more often does contain real liquorice extract as a declared ingredient - and, per this card's own vegan-check research below, these real-liquorice sweets commonly also contain gelatin, which the candy itself does not need botanically but which manufacturers add for chewy texture. This card's cautions, dosing and evidence below are about the herb/root - taken as tea, powder, standardised extract or DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) tablets - at doses well above what casual candy-eating would deliver, not about occasional sweets.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Traditional and purported uses span coughs, sore throat, bronchitis, asthma, peptic ulcers and gastritis, heartburn/indigestion, hepatitis and other liver complaints, skin conditions (used topically for eczema and minor skin irritation), and general use as a demulcent (a soothing, coating agent) and flavouring agent, across Ayurveda, Traditional Chinese Medicine and Western herbalism. A US government-hosted database states plainly that licorice root is 'generally considered safe as a food ingredient' but that there 'isn't enough high-quality evidence to clearly support licorice for any health condition' at therapeutic/supplement doses - a notably more cautious framing than licorice's long traditional reputation might suggest, and consistent with this project's standard practice of treating traditional reputation and proven effect as two separate things.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This project's own Gut health topic file already had a pending candidate note (sourced to a Gale reference encyclopedia) naming licorice root as a traditional remedy people reach for to help 'rebalance stomach acid output' for heartburn, alongside other home remedies such as banana, aloe vera, chamomile and ginger. That book source gives no specific study citation of its own for licorice, so this card treats it only as a starting lead confirming licorice's traditional reputation for this use, not as evidence in itself - the actual evidence check for this use is in whatEvidenceShows below, drawn from this card's own independently fetched trials.
traditionalUse.label: illustration

traditionalUse.text: Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is a specifically processed form of the same root with most of its glycyrrhizin (the compound responsible for licorice's best-documented safety risk, covered in detail in whatEvidenceShows and cautions below) removed. A current Health Canada natural-health-product monograph (dated 31 January 2025) sets this out precisely in regulatory terms: a finished DGL product 'must not contain more than 3% of the original quantity of glycyrrhizic acid found in the source material.' The same monograph authorises DGL, specifically as a demulcent, to help relieve minor gastrointestinal inflammation and abdominal pain/burning in the stomach - but only in dosage forms that are chewed (chewable tablet, chewable gel/gummy, granule to be chewed, or chewable bar), because the monograph's own direction for use states DGL must be 'chewed between meals or 20 minutes before meals' and 'mixed with saliva' to work - implying its benefit (where shown at all - see whatEvidenceShows) is understood as a local, in-the-mouth-and-oesophagus effect rather than a systemic one. This single regulatory fact drives much of this card's howToUseVegan and preparationForms sections below: DGL is not simply 'licorice with a different dose,' it is a distinct product made specifically to separate licorice's digestive reputation from its hypertension/potassium risk.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Licorice's single best-documented effect is a real, well-established pharmacological mechanism called pseudohyperaldosteronism (also written pseudo-primary aldosteronism), and this card independently verified it across five separate sources rather than relying on any one source's diagram. Glycyrrhizin, licorice's main active compound, is converted in the gut to glycyrrhetinic acid, which inhibits an enzyme called 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11-beta-HSD2) in the kidney. That enzyme's normal job is to convert cortisol into inactive cortisone in kidney tissue; with it blocked, cortisol builds up locally and - because cortisol and aldosterone act on the same mineralocorticoid receptor - starts acting like aldosterone. The practical result, confirmed in the same terms by a US government fact sheet, a government-hosted cancer-centre herb database, a Merck Manual consumer page and a 2023 peer-reviewed narrative review: sodium and water retention, potassium loss (hypokalemia), and a rise in blood pressure, sometimes with tissue swelling (oedema). This is a textbook example of pseudo- rather than true hyperaldosteronism because renin and aldosterone themselves are typically suppressed, not elevated, on lab testing - the receptor is being over-activated by cortisol standing in for aldosterone, not by excess aldosterone itself.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: How severe this gets, and at what dose, varies by source and by individual susceptibility - this card shows the range rather than picking one number. A 2023 peer-reviewed narrative review (independently fetched and read by this card) collected 104 published cases of clinically significant licorice toxicity: 84 required hospitalisation and 2 were fatal, with complications ranging from muscle weakness and rhabdomyolysis to dangerous heart-rhythm changes and hypertensive encephalopathy; the same review notes glycyrrhetinic acid blood levels were only actually measured in 4 of those 104 cases, so diagnosis in practice relies mostly on history and clinical picture rather than a lab-confirmed level. On everyday dosing: a US consumer clinical-reference site states licorice doses as low as 5 g/day can cause these effects in people with high salt intake or existing heart, kidney or blood-pressure problems, and cites a 2011 FDA alert that eating more than 2 ounces of black licorice candy a day for at least two weeks can cause hypokalemia and irregular heartbeat, with adults over 40 at particular risk. Separately, European regulators have historically worked from a different kind of figure: the EU's Scientific Committee on Food assessed a maximum intake of about 100 mg/day of glycyrrhizic acid as being of no health concern for most people (while explicitly flagging that real-world intake is likely underestimated by that same figure) - a tighter, population-level regulatory threshold rather than the US source's per-person symptom-onset estimate. Both figures point the same direction (licorice's mineralocorticoid risk is real and dose-related) without being the same number, and this card shows both rather than picking one.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: For digestive use specifically - heartburn, dyspepsia and peptic ulcers, the traditional use this project's own Gut health topic file already had a pending candidate note about - the evidence is real but considerably thinner than licorice's long traditional reputation suggests, and this card found a genuine overclaiming pattern to flag, the same check this project has run on every herb's reviews to date. The clearest single trial is a 2011 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of GutGard (a flavonoid-rich, low-glycyrrhizin standardised root extract, not literal DGL) in 50 adults with functional dyspepsia: 75 mg twice daily for 30 days produced significantly lower total symptom scores and Nepean Dyspepsia Index scores than placebo at both day 15 and day 30, and was well tolerated. However, independently checking the paper's own author list (not just its stated conflict-of-interest line) found that seven of the eleven authors, including the corresponding author, are staff of Natural Remedies, the Bangalore company that developed GutGard and that itself also designed the trial's own randomisation sequence - a direct manufacturer relationship built into the trial's authorship, not merely an undisclosed funding line hidden in acknowledgments. The paper's conclusion also states GutGard is 'a safe and effective remedy for patients with functional dyspepsia,' a firmer claim than a single 25-per-arm, 30-day, sponsor-run trial with a baseline age/blood-pressure imbalance between groups can really support, and the trial found no benefit over placebo for one specific symptom (early satiety).
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) specifically in peptic ulcer - as distinct from the low-glycyrrhizin GutGard extract above - this card independently fetched two of the older trials behind DGL's traditional ulcer reputation and found them pointing in different directions, shown here per this project's rule to show both sides rather than pick a winner silently. A 1975 uncontrolled retrospective endoscopic survey of 32 patients with chronic duodenal ulcer found the ulcers had healed on repeat endoscopy, with the mucosa looking normal in most patients after DGL tablets - but this was not placebo-controlled, so a real treatment effect cannot be separated from natural healing or expectation. Set against that, a 1971 double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial in 90 men with relapsed chronic duodenal ulcer, running glycyrrhizinic-acid-reduced liquorice (760 mg three times daily) for six weeks against placebo, found - quoted directly - 'the results do not show any advantage for the active treatment when compared with the placebo,' on pain frequency/severity, antacid use, and both doctor and patient ratings. A current Health Canada natural-health-product monograph for DGL (2025) still authorises a demulcent GI-soothing use based on this same older literature, but requires no specific adverse-reaction or contraindication statement on the label - reflecting DGL's good safety profile more than a settled efficacy case. This card treats DGL's digestive benefit as a genuine traditional use with real but mixed and dated trial support, not a settled, well-proven effect.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Pregnancy safety is a genuinely debated area where this card independently verified both the original research signal and a formal government critique of it, and shows both rather than resolving the debate itself. The signal comes from a long-running Finnish cohort (begun in 1998 with over 1,000 pregnant women): a 2002 paper found heavy prenatal glycyrrhizin exposure (≥500 mg/week) roughly doubled the odds of preterm delivery, with a stronger association for very early preterm birth (adjusted odds ratio 3.07 for delivery before 34 weeks); an earlier 2001 paper from the same group had already found heavy exposure linked to about 2.5-times higher odds of delivery before 38 weeks, with no significant effect on birth weight itself. Later papers from the same research group (2009, then a 2017 follow-up of the same children at around age 13) reported that children of high-licorice-consuming mothers scored lower on cognitive tests and showed more ADHD-type behaviours and, in the 2017 follow-up, earlier pubertal development in girls, with a proposed mechanism that glycyrrhizin's 11-beta-HSD2 inhibition (the same enzyme covered above) could let more maternal glucocorticoid reach the fetus. A formal 2023 assessment by Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR), independently read by this card in full, evaluated this same body of work directly (citing the 2009, 2010 and 2017 papers by name) and - agreeing with a separate 2018 Norwegian food-safety panel opinion - concluded that 'the data collected in the study are not suitable for making reliable statements about a possible causal relationship between the consumption of liquorice during pregnancy and the physical and mental development of the offspring,' citing retrospective (not prospective) exposure recall, roughly two-thirds loss to follow-up by the later assessments, and the general limits of observational studies for proving causation; the BfR notes the original authors themselves have since agreed their data cannot establish causality. A separate 2014 methodological critique, also independently read by this card, recalculated the 2002 preterm-birth paper's own statistics and found its central result only bordered on significance (OR 2.18, 95% CI 0.98-4.86, p=0.056) once measurement and selection-bias concerns were factored in. Despite this genuine causality debate, the BfR's own bottom line is NOT 'licorice in pregnancy is fine' - it explicitly maintains a decades-old precautionary recommendation (first issued in 1999 by its predecessor body) that pregnant women, along with people with hypertension, cardiovascular disease or diabetes, should avoid regularly consuming large amounts of liquorice, reasoning from licorice's separately well-established sodium/potassium/blood-pressure mechanism rather than from the still-debated cognitive/behavioural findings.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: A researched hormonal (anti-androgen) effect exists but is thin, and this card deliberately does not add a PCOS link on the strength of it - the same honest 'evidence too thin to link' approach this project has already taken for Shatavari (skipped a diabetes link) and Moringa (skipped a primary link entirely). The actual direct human evidence located and independently fetched is a single small 2004 trial: 9 healthy women given 3.5 g/day of a commercial licorice preparation for two cycles saw total serum testosterone fall significantly (from about 27.8 to 17.5 ng/dL by month two), reversible after stopping, with the authors proposing a mechanism (inhibition of 17-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and 17,20-lyase) and suggesting licorice as a possible adjuvant therapy for hirsutism/PCOS - but with no control group and only 9 participants, this is a preliminary signal, not proof. A separate, better-known 2007 trial from the same Italian research group, in 32 women with PCOS taking spironolactone with or without 3.5 g/day licorice, is sometimes cited for PCOS but this card found - independently checking its own reported results via the only abstract text it could access - that it measured mineralocorticoid/side-effect outcomes, not androgen levels: blood pressure fell with spironolactone alone but not with the combination, volume-depletion symptoms occurred in 20% on spironolactone alone versus none on the combination, and renin-aldosterone-system activation was lower with the combination - the authors' own conclusion was that licorice's mineralocorticoid effect can offset spironolactone's diuretic side effects, not that it adds an androgen-lowering benefit. This card could not independently verify the 2007 trial's primary journal text directly (only a university-repository-hosted abstract), and says so here rather than treating it as fully confirmed.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Dried root, root tea/decoction, plain powder, and standardised whole-extract capsules or tablets are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing in the herb itself to check. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin; most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) specifically needs its own vegan check, because a current Health Canada monograph (see traditionalUse above) authorises it only in dosage forms that must be chewed: chewable tablet, chewable bar, granule, and - the one that actually needs checking - 'chewable gel,' explicitly noted in the monograph as meaning a gummy. Gummy supplements of any kind commonly use gelatin as their gelling agent; plant-based DGL gummies exist (using pectin or a plant gum instead) but this is exactly the kind of product where 'gummy' should not be assumed vegan without reading the label, in the same way this project already flags for any other gummy-form supplement.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: The vegan check that matters most for licorice specifically, and that this card was asked to run precisely because it doesn't come up for this project's other herbs: liquorice CANDY is a different product from the herb/supplement covered by this card, and the two need separate vegan answers. Real liquorice-extract confectionery - the kind most likely to carry genuine Glycyrrhiza glabra extract as a declared ingredient, such as British/European liquorice sweets (Haribo's Pontefract Cakes is one well-known example this card checked directly) - commonly lists gelatin among its ingredients, added for chewy texture rather than for any property of the liquorice itself; that gelatin is typically pork-derived. By contrast, a US government consumer source notes most American 'licorice' candy (Twizzlers is the best-known example) is actually anise-oil-flavoured and contains no real licorice at all, and is widely reported as gelatin-free - though this card found at least one specific commercial example where a product's own front-of-pack 'gelatin free and vegan' claim did not match its own printed ingredient list, which still showed gelatin - so a vegan reader should check the actual ingredient panel on any specific product, never a front-of-pack claim alone, and also watch for other non-vegan confectionery ingredients unrelated to licorice itself, such as beeswax, shellac or carmine (a red dye from crushed insects), which appear on some liquorice sweets regardless of gelatin content.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: This card's own research found no standard, documented classical preparation that formally requires combining licorice root with a non-vegan ingredient, the way Chyawanprash does for amla or Yograj Guggulu does for guggul - the clinical and government sources checked describe licorice root only as tea/decoction, powder, standardised extract, or DGL tablets/chewables. One home-remedy detail worth flagging rather than hiding: some traditional mulethi/Yashtimadhu preparations are made as a milk decoction rather than a plain water tea - that is a recipe choice (plant milk works just as well for the same preparation), not a fixed ingredient of the herb itself, the same distinction this project's Hibiscus card already drew for honey and rum in traditional sorrel drink recipes.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: Licorice's defining caution is the hypertension/potassium-loss (pseudohyperaldosteronism) mechanism covered in full in whatEvidenceShows above - this matters at ordinary supplement/tea doses taken regularly, not only at extreme intakes. People with existing high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney disease, or a high-salt diet, and adults over 40, are named across multiple sources as being at higher risk of symptoms at lower doses (as little as 5 g/day of licorice root per one consumer source). Watch for unusual tiredness, muscle weakness, headache, swelling, or an irregular heartbeat, and stop use and see a doctor if these occur.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: avoid regular or large-amount use. This card's own independent research (see whatEvidenceShows above) found a genuine scientific debate about whether licorice causes the specific cognitive/behavioural effects reported in Finnish cohort studies, with a 2023 German government risk-assessment review concluding the existing data cannot establish that causal link. That same review, however, still recommends pregnant women avoid regularly consuming large amounts of liquorice as a precaution, based on licorice's separately well-established sodium/potassium/blood-pressure mechanism rather than on the still-debated cognitive findings - and separately, a US government fact sheet states that consuming oral licorice extract in large amounts (around 250 g of licorice per week) during pregnancy is unsafe and can raise the risk of delivery before 38 weeks. This card follows the precautionary recommendation rather than waiting on the unresolved causality question.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: This general pregnancy caution is corroborated, in passing, by a mainstream consumer nutrition book independently checked for this card: a 2006 American Dietetic Association nutrition guide lists licorice among a general run of herbs 'identified as potentially harmful' for pregnant or nursing mothers, alongside many other herbs (aloe, buckthorn, chamomile, ginseng, senna and others). That book gives no licorice-specific mechanism, dose or study citation of its own - it is a generic herbal-safety list, not independent pregnancy research - so this card relies on the specific, independently fetched studies and the 2023 German government review above for its actual pregnancy guidance, and cites this book only as a secondary, non-specific corroboration that licorice's pregnancy caution is not a fringe position.
cautions.label: illustration

cautions.text: DGL is specifically made to reduce this pregnancy/blood-pressure risk profile (no more than 3% of the original glycyrrhizic acid remains, per the Health Canada monograph), but this card did not find dedicated pregnancy-safety data for DGL itself, and a consumer health source notes pregnant people should only use DGL under a healthcare provider's guidance given how little pregnancy-specific data exists for it specifically - this card does not treat 'DGL' as an automatic green light in pregnancy on the strength of its lower glycyrrhizin content alone.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Medicine interactions, independently compiled across this card's sources: digoxin and other cardiac glycosides (licorice-induced low potassium can increase toxicity risk); diuretics/'water pills' (added potassium loss); blood-pressure medicines (licorice's own sodium/water retention may work against them); corticosteroids such as cortisone/hydrocortisone/prednisone (licorice may raise their effect/side-effect risk); warfarin (case reports of reduced effectiveness or a sudden INR drop); oral contraceptives and other oestrogen-containing medicines (reported to increase or decrease their effects); and, per one source, possible interaction with MAO inhibitors. Because glycyrrhizin content is not stated on most retail licorice packaging, a German government risk body notes consumers cannot tell from the label alone how much they are actually getting - another reason to mention any licorice use to a doctor or pharmacist rather than assuming a 'small' dose is safe with these medicines.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Contraindications named by a US consumer clinical-reference source: congestive heart failure, hypertension, hypokalemia, diabetes, severe kidney impairment, cirrhosis or cholestatic liver disorders, and hormone-sensitive conditions including breast, ovarian or uterine cancer, endometriosis, and uterine fibroids (licorice has documented estrogenic activity in preclinical research). Use with caution with any existing liver-function impairment.
cautions.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: Duration: a consumer clinical-reference source advises against using whole licorice (not DGL) for more than 4-6 weeks at a time at typical doses; a US government fact sheet separately notes that licorice products without glycyrrhizin (i.e. DGL) might be used for longer, up to about 4 months, though it gives no further detail beyond that figure. General side effects at ordinary intake include fluid retention/swelling, headache, lethargy, muscle weakness or pain, decreased libido, and menstrual changes; a liver-injury—focused government database separately states that hepatotoxicity (liver damage) from licorice extracts or glycyrrhizin itself has not been reported, which this card notes as a point in licorice's favour distinct from its well-established mineralocorticoid risk.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Stop use and seek care promptly for signs of licorice's mineralocorticoid effect: unusual muscle weakness or pain, irregular heartbeat, severe headache, confusion, or new or worsening swelling - these can signal dangerous potassium loss or a hypertensive crisis, and have been fatal in rare documented cases at high or prolonged intake.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive, avoid regularly consuming licorice root in any form - tea, powder, extract or DGL - beyond very occasional, small amounts, and talk to a doctor before using any licorice product, including DGL, since dedicated pregnancy-safety data for DGL specifically is lacking.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes, a hormone-sensitive condition (breast, ovarian or uterine cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids), or liver disease, or if you take digoxin, a diuretic, a blood-pressure medicine, warfarin, corticosteroids, or hormonal contraceptives, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting licorice in any form - plain product labels do not state how much glycyrrhizin a given product actually contains.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice, and is about licorice ROOT (Glycyrrhiza glabra) as a tea, powder, standardised extract, or DGL supplement - not about liquorice-flavoured candy. Occasional sweets are a different matter from the doses discussed in this card, but if you do eat liquorice confectionery regularly or in large amounts, the same sodium/potassium/blood-pressure caution above still applies, and a real-liquorice sweet's own label should be checked for both its liquorice content and (separately, for vegans) gelatin or other animal ingredients.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not interchangeable, and this matters more for licorice than for most herbs in this project because its two best-known research angles (digestive use and hypertension/potassium risk) pull in opposite directions on glycyrrhizin content. Whole root, tea and standard extract contain glycyrrhizin at a variable concentration that most retail labels do not state. GutGard, the extract behind this card's main dyspepsia trial, is a specific low-glycyrrhizin (≤0.5% w/w) standardised extract, not literal DGL. DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) is a distinct, regulated product required to contain no more than 3% of the original glycyrrhizic acid, and its own traditional-use trials used specific chewable dosage forms taken before meals - not a cup of ordinary licorice tea at an unmeasured strength.

preparationForms.note: Traditional preparation; glycyrrhizin content is not standardised or stated, so strength varies with how much root is used and how long it is steeped. Naturally vegan; some traditional mulethi recipes use milk instead of water - a recipe choice, not a required ingredient.

Dried, ground root - naturally vegan, typical cited dosing around 1-4 g taken up to three times daily per a consumer clinical-reference source, with a general recommendation not to exceed 4-6 weeks of regular use.

Includes products like GutGard (a specific low-glycyrrhizin, flavonoid-rich extract used in this card's main dyspepsia trial, dosed 75 mg twice daily in that trial) - check the capsule shell isn't gelatin, and that the glycyrrhizin content is actually stated on the label.

preparationForms.form: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) chewable tablet, chewable gel/gummy, granule or bar
preparationForms.note: Must contain no more than 3% of the original glycyrrhizic acid, per a 2025 Health Canada monograph, and must be chewed (not swallowed whole) between meals or 20 minutes before meals to work, since the claimed benefit is a local, in-the-mouth/throat/stomach effect. Check any chewable-gel/gummy form specifically for gelatin.

Used in small trials for canker sores and post-intubation sore throat, per a US government fact sheet; naturally vegan as a concept, but check any commercial lozenge for gelatin and any rinse for other non-vegan additives.

preparationForms.form: Liquorice-flavoured candy (for comparison only - not the subject of this card's cautions)
preparationForms.note: A different product from the herb. Real-liquorice-extract sweets (common in UK/European brands) commonly contain gelatin and sometimes beeswax, shellac or carmine; most US 'licorice' candy is anise-oil-flavoured and contains no real licorice, and is more often (though not always reliably) gelatin-free - always check the actual ingredient panel, not a front-of-pack claim.

candidateAdditions.status: CANDIDATE - pending Gate 1/Gate 2 review. Flagged honestly rather than forced into a link now, the same approach this project used for Gotu Kola's venous-insufficiency topic gap.
candidateAdditions.text: Licorice's anti-androgen/testosterone-lowering signal (Armanini 2004, n=9, no control group) is a genuine but very preliminary research lead for PCOS/hirsutism that this card deliberately did not use to add a pcos-hormonal-health link, since the evidence is far thinner than Shatavari's own PCOS evidence already backing that health topic's primary herb link. If a larger controlled trial of licorice specifically on androgen levels in PCOS is published in a future review pass, this should be revisited.
candidateAdditions.label: open question

herbs.name: Moringa

traditionalUse.text: This card is about moringa as a concentrated herbal supplement or extract, and about plant parts not normally eaten as food (especially the root and root bark), used for traditional and therapeutic purposes. This project already has two separate Foods-module entries - Moringa (drumstick) leaves and Drumstick (moringa pods) - covering moringa leaves and pods as an everyday vegetable, with their own nutrient content, portions and cooking/pairing tips. This card does not repeat that nutrient-content information; where a nutrient is mentioned below, it is only to explain what a specific study tested, not as new food-composition data.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: A fast-growing tree native to the Indian subcontinent, known in Ayurveda as 'Shigru'. Different parts of the plant have genuinely different traditional uses: the leaves and pods are eaten as an everyday vegetable (the Foods-module entries above), while the leaves, flowers, seeds, bark and root are all separately used in traditional and folk medicine for a wide range of claimed purposes, including infections, diabetes and high cholesterol.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: This project's own cached Ayurvedic academic text lists 'Moringa oleifera' under its Sanskrit/Hindi name 'Shigru' in a table of traditionally used Ayurvedic herbs, and separately names 'Shigru (Moringa olifera)' as an ingredient in a classical gruel (yavagu) formulation traditionally used for excessive thirst - a symptom Ayurveda has long associated with what is now understood as diabetes. These are plain name-table and ingredient-list entries with no outcome data given, so they confirm genuine traditional use and naming, not that moringa treats diabetes or any other condition.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Worth flagging clearly before anything else on this card: the root and root bark are traditionally recorded as having been used to try to end a pregnancy, and are chemically different from the leaf in ways that matter for safety (see Cautions). This is not a reason to be concerned about eating moringa leaves or pods as a vegetable - that everyday use is well established and considered safe - but it is a real, separate safety issue for anyone considering a root or root-bark preparation specifically.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Blood sugar is one of moringa leaf's two best-known researched therapeutic uses, and the research is genuinely unsettled rather than one-sided. A 2021 meta-analysis (Phimarn et al.) pooling 7 studies (257 participants, mixing randomised and non-randomised trial designs, 28 to 90 days) found fasting blood sugar fell by a weighted average of 14.81 mg/dL and post-meal glucose fell by 64.73 mg/dL, with no significant change in HbA1c (the 3-month average blood sugar measure).
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: That same 2021 review's headline finding is considerably shakier than its own conclusion suggests, and sets up a direct conflict with a more rigorous, newer review: the fasting-glucose result had extremely high statistical variability (I-squared of 97.8%, meaning the individual trials barely agreed with each other), and the review pooled randomised trials together with non-randomised ones rather than restricting itself to randomised controlled trials (RCTs) only. A stricter, RCT-only 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis with formal GRADE quality grading (Crisan et al., 9 RCTs, 341 people given moringa versus 308 controls, mixed populations including prediabetes, type 2 diabetes and overweight adults) found no significant effect on fasting glucose or HbA1c, rating the certainty of evidence 'very low' for both. The 2025 authors' own conclusion, in their words: 'Current evidence does not support consistent cardiometabolic benefits of moringa supplementation in adults.'
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: A separate, specific finding worth knowing: one clinical-reference source notes that adding moringa tablets on top of an existing sulfonylurea diabetes medicine did not improve blood sugar control any better than taking the sulfonylurea alone in the trial it cites - a direct test of moringa as an add-on to real diabetes treatment, not just moringa alone.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol and lipids are the other main researched therapeutic use, and the same two reviews disagree here too. The 2021 meta-analysis's own conclusion describes an improved lipid profile with a rise in HDL ('good') cholesterol, though this card could not independently confirm the exact pooled lipid figures beyond that stated conclusion, because the original paper could not be fully rendered through this project's fetching tools - a genuine verification limit, noted here rather than smoothed over.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: The stricter 2025 RCT-only review found no significant effect on any lipid measure tested - total cholesterol, LDL ('bad') cholesterol, HDL or triglycerides - again rating the certainty of evidence 'very low' for all of them. A cancer-centre clinical database independently describes human studies on moringa as 'quite limited', with only small preliminary findings hinting at a modest positive effect on lipids, and calls for well-designed studies in people with diabetes or prediabetes specifically.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Taken together, the single most rigorous review available for both blood sugar and cholesterol found no reliable benefit, with very-low-certainty evidence throughout - a notably less confident picture than the earlier 2021 review's own headline wording suggests. Because of this, this card treats moringa's diabetes and cholesterol research as a genuinely studied but still unproven therapeutic interest, not as an established benefit - this project's Diabetes and Heart-and-cholesterol health topics do not list moringa as a supported option on the strength of this evidence.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Leaf powder, leaf capsules and leaf tea are plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there beyond the capsule shell itself: as with any capsule supplement, check it isn't gelatin.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Root and root-bark preparations are also plant material, so they raise no separate vegan-ingredient issue - the reason to avoid them (see Cautions) is a safety concern, not a veganism one. This card keeps those two questions separate deliberately, so a safety caution about the root is never read as a reason to doubt the leaf's vegan status or its everyday safety as a food.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

cautions.text: This is the single most important safety point on this card: moringa root and root bark are genuinely different from, and more concerning than, the leaves and pods eaten as a vegetable. Root and root extracts are rated 'possibly unsafe' to take by mouth, and the root contains spirochin, described as a toxic substance. By contrast, the leaves, fruit and seeds eaten as food are rated 'likely safe', and leaf or seed used medicinally short-term is rated 'possibly safe'. This card's safety information about the root therefore says nothing against eating moringa leaves or pods as a vegetable.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Pregnancy safety genuinely differs by plant part, and this card keeps that distinction rather than giving one blanket warning. Root, bark and flowers are rated 'possibly unsafe' in pregnancy - traditional use of the root and bark aimed to cause miscarriage, and chemicals in these parts may make the uterus contract. A dedicated 2023 review of moringa leaf use in pregnancy and breastfeeding (12 studies, leaf powder/extract/capsules only, no root or bark studies) found that none of the studies it reviewed reported contraindications to leaf-based use - but its silence on uterine effects reflects that its scope never included root, bark or flower studies, so this reassurance applies to leaf-based forms only, not to root, bark or flower preparations.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Worth noting for balance: a cancer-centre clinical database states more simply that pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid moringa use altogether, without separating this by plant part. This card shows both positions rather than picking one - readers who are pregnant or breastfeeding and considering any moringa supplement, in any form, should talk to a doctor first.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: The thyroid picture is genuinely mixed, not a simple 'raises' or 'lowers' story, and this card does not overstate it in either direction. Animal studies conflict with each other: some found moringa leaf extract raised T4 by blocking the conversion of T4 to T3, others found it lowered T4, and one found both T3 and T4 rising with TSH falling at high doses. The one human trial found (in people with an underactive thyroid, not healthy adults) found TSH fell in the moringa group, but TSH also fell somewhat in the placebo group, and T3/T4 were not reported - too thin and poorly isolated a result to draw a clear conclusion from.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: The clearer, more practical thyroid-related caution is a different kind of interaction entirely: moringa may reduce how well the body absorbs levothyroxine (a common synthetic thyroid medicine), rather than directly changing the body's own thyroid hormone levels the way this project's Ashwagandha, Brahmi and Guggul herb cards describe. Anyone taking levothyroxine should talk to their doctor before using moringa and consider timing the two apart.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Moringa may lower blood sugar, so combining it with insulin or diabetes medicines (sulfonylureas such as glimepiride or glyburide, and others such as pioglitazone or rosiglitazone) could cause hypoglycaemia (blood sugar dropping too low). Close monitoring and possible medicine-dose changes are advised for anyone combining the two.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Moringa may add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect of blood pressure medicines (examples named include captopril, enalapril, losartan, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide), and may slow how the liver breaks down several other medicines metabolised by the CYP3A4 liver enzyme (examples named include the statin lovastatin, and the antifungal/allergy medicines ketoconazole, itraconazole and fexofenadine), potentially raising their effects and side effects.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A documented but rare case report describes acute liver inflammation (hepatitis, without jaundice) linked to a moringa-containing product that also listed vitamin C on its label; the person's liver tests worsened again after they stopped the product and later restarted it, a pattern that supports (without fully proving, since the product's exact ingredients weren't specified) a real link to the product. The reviewing database rates moringa as only a 'possible but rare' cause of liver injury, and notes there were no other published reports of this kind before this case.
cautions.label: open question

cautions.text: Rare but genuine allergic-type reactions have been reported in case studies: a severe skin reaction (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) after eating food containing moringa leaves, skin toxicity in a woman using moringa powder for weight loss, and a serious whole-body allergic reaction (anaphylaxis with widespread swelling) after eating moringa leaves. These remain uncommon, documented reactions rather than an expected effect.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: A preclinical (mouse) study found moringa genotoxic only at a very high, 'supra-supplementation' dose (3,000 mg per kg of body weight) - far above any typical food or supplement amount, and an animal-only finding, not a normal-use human safety concern.
cautions.label: open question

redFlags.text: Avoid root, root bark and flower preparations - their safety profile is genuinely different from, and more concerning than, the leaves and pods eaten as food, and this applies with particular force in pregnancy.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive, talk to a doctor before using any moringa supplement, in any form - not just the root.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take insulin or any diabetes medicine, or any blood pressure medicine, talk to your doctor before trying moringa, and watch for symptoms of blood sugar dropping too low (shakiness, sweating, confusion) if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take levothyroxine or another thyroid medicine, or any regular prescription medicine broken down by the liver (including some statins), talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using moringa.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Stop taking moringa and see a doctor if you notice yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusually dark urine, a widespread rash, or facial or throat swelling - these need medical attention, not waiting to see if they pass.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice, and is about moringa as a concentrated supplement or non-food plant part. It does not change this project's own Foods-module guidance that moringa leaves and pods are a normal, nutritious vegetable in everyday vegan cooking.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength or in safety - the human trials behind this card's blood-sugar and cholesterol findings used leaf powder or leaf extract, never root or root-bark preparations. A mild cup of leaf tea is far gentler than a standardised leaf-extract capsule, and both are a different matter entirely from a root or root-bark preparation, which this card does not recommend at all given its documented, more concerning safety profile.

preparationForms.note: The form used in most of the human blood-sugar and cholesterol trials cited above, typically a few grams per day. Check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
A gentler, less concentrated everyday form than a standardised capsule extract; not separately tested in the trials this card cites.

A traditional and folk-medicine form, not used in any of the human trials behind this card's blood-sugar or cholesterol findings. This card does not recommend this form: the root is rated possibly unsafe by mouth, contains the toxic compound spirochin, and root/bark preparations have a traditional association with attempting to end a pregnancy. Not the same plant part as the leaves and pods covered in this project's Foods entries.

herbs.name: Neem

traditionalUse.text: Called 'the wonder tree' and 'nature's drugstore' in Ayurvedic tradition - every part of the tree (leaves, bark, seed oil) has a long history of therapeutic, dental and household use across the Indian subcontinent, among the most widely used plants in traditional Indian medicine.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Folk/home-remedy use leans heavily topical and external: neem leaf powder dusted on skin, mixed into a paste, or used in a bath, traditionally for various skin complaints. This is traditional practice, not independently verified clinical evidence.
traditionalUse.label: illustration

whatEvidenceShows.text: An honest, Indian-dermatology-specific peer-reviewed review states plainly: 'Although there is no evidence of efficacy, neem is extensively used for medicinal purposes in India,' and that 'the scarcity of human trials has obscured its role in modern medicine.' For most skin conditions neem is traditionally used for - acne, eczema, pruritus, scaly scalp, dermatophytosis, scabies, psoriasis among them - the same review finds only traditional use or preclinical (lab/animal) data, not real clinical trials.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: The few real human trials that do exist are small, old and not treated as settled even by the review that reports them: a single 50-patient 1994 trial (oral neem alongside topical tar and salicylic acid) for psoriasis; a small randomised proof-of-principle study for tungiasis (a skin parasite, using neem and coconut oil); and a 1992 pilot study for scabies (neem and turmeric). None of these are large or recent enough to be treated as confirming neem's effectiveness for these conditions.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Laboratory and animal studies suggest antimicrobial, antifungal and anticancer activity (including against drug-resistant bacteria and several cancer cell lines), and a small study of HIV-positive volunteers found an extract increased CD4+ cell counts. These are early-stage or preclinical findings only - a major US cancer centre's own page states plainly there are no human studies showing neem to be an effective cancer treatment, and this card does not treat any of these as an established human benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For oral hygiene, early research is mixed: a neem leaf gel applied to teeth and gums was linked to reduced plaque in one study, but a separate 2-week neem mouth-rinse trial did not reduce plaque or gingivitis.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Neem leaf, bark and seed oil are all plant parts - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there. Given this card's cautions below, topical (on-skin or dental) use has the better evidence and the lower-severity risk profile compared with swallowing neem oil or seed, which carries the most serious documented risks.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules and standardised leaf-powder products are available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Taking neem oil or neem seed by mouth is rated 'Likely Unsafe' for children - this is this card's single most important caution. Serious side effects in infants and small children can happen within hours of swallowing neem oil, including vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, blood disorders, seizures, coma and brain disorders. This is independently corroborated by two further sources, including a peer-reviewed dermatology review that states oral neem is contraindicated in children under 12 and reports documented child deaths from neem oil ingestion.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding: neem oil and bark taken by mouth are rated 'Likely Unsafe' in pregnancy and can cause miscarriage. A peer-reviewed dermatology review independently states oral neem is contraindicated in both pregnancy and lactation.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May harm sperm - avoid when trying to conceive. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently cross-confirmed by this card's other sources.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May activate the immune system - a caution for autoimmune conditions (such as multiple sclerosis, lupus or rheumatoid arthritis), where it could worsen symptoms, and for organ-transplant recipients, where it could reduce the effectiveness of anti-rejection (immunosuppressant) medicines (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate and corticosteroids named). Both cautions are sourced to one clinical-reference site here; a second source separately found neem extract inhibits several liver enzymes (CYP3A4/5, 2C8, 2C9) that many medicines rely on, in laboratory testing, though its own clinical relevance 'is not known.'
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar - combined with diabetes medicines (insulin, glimepiride, glipizide and pioglitazone named) this could cause dangerously low blood sugar. Anyone with diabetes should talk to their doctor before trying neem and monitor blood sugar closely if they do. The blood-sugar-lowering direction itself is corroborated by a second source's own separate finding of improved glycaemic control in one small metabolic-syndrome study; the specific diabetes-drug interaction caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May reduce lithium clearance (acting somewhat like a diuretic), which could raise lithium to harmful levels in anyone taking it for a mood disorder - a dose adjustment may be needed. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Large doses or long-term oral use are rated 'Possibly Unsafe' and might harm the kidneys and liver - this is a different, broader caution from the acute child-poisoning risk above, and applies to adults too.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Topical use is not automatically risk-free either, worth knowing specifically for a skin-and-hair-focused herb: allergic contact dermatitis to neem oil has been reported (including on the scalp and face when used for hair loss), chewing neem twigs has caused lip leukoderma (a patchy loss of skin pigment) in a case series, and one case report describes neem oil applied to blisters triggering a flare of an existing autoimmune blistering skin condition (bullous pemphigoid). A peer-reviewed review states plainly that 'the exact compounds and the mechanisms of cutaneous adverse effects remain unclear.'
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Freshness and sourcing matter: neem twigs (sometimes chewed as a traditional toothbrush) are often contaminated with fungi within about 2 weeks of harvest, and home-remedy preparations more broadly can carry a fungal/aflatoxin contamination risk - a reason to avoid chewing twigs and to buy packaged products from a reputable brand rather than assuming any neem preparation is automatically safe.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May interfere with blood sugar control; stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery and tell the surgical team. This specific surgery caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently confirmed by every other source checked for this card.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Never give neem oil or neem seed by mouth to a child, in any amount - this is the clearest, highest-stakes rule in this entire card. Serious poisoning in infants and small children can happen within hours, and child deaths from neem oil ingestion are documented.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Seek emergency medical care immediately if a child or adult swallows neem oil or seed and develops vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, or any altered consciousness - do not wait to see if it passes.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Stop using neem on the skin and see a doctor if you notice a rash, blistering, significant redness or a worsening skin reaction after topical use.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before using neem (oral or topical) if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive, have an autoimmune condition, take lithium, have diabetes, take immunosuppressant medicine or have had an organ transplant, or have surgery scheduled.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are genuinely not equivalent in risk for this herb specifically, more so than for most others in this project: topical/dental use has the evidence and safety profile described above, while swallowing neem oil or seed carries this card's most serious documented risk (see cautions and redFlags) - the form matters here as much as the dose.

preparationForms.note: Applied to skin, e.g. for traditional skin complaints - not risk-free either (see this card's own cautions on contact dermatitis), but a lower-severity route than swallowing neem oil or seed.
Standardised leaf-powder products and capsules are available; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
The form carrying this card's most serious documented risk - never given to children, and this card does not describe a safe way to use this form at home.

herbs.name: Nettle

traditionalUse.text: A European herbal tradition (leaf and root) reputed as a 'blood cleanser' and general tonic - traditionally used for anaemia and excess menstrual bleeding, and as an old European remedy for rheumatism and arthritis, brought to Britain by the Romans and later naturalised in North America. Traditionally considered rich in calcium, magnesium and iron.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

traditionalUse.text: Also named in a herbal-medicine reference list with the functions: diuretic, tonic, astringent, prevents haemorrhaging, anti-allergenic, reduces prostate enlargement.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Osteoarthritis is the one use with the strongest rating across the sources checked here - 'Possibly Effective,' not just 'insufficient evidence' - for leaf preparations taken by mouth or applied to the skin, which 'might reduce pain' and the need for pain medication. A second independent source corroborates this directly: 'clinical trials support the topical use of nettle for arthritis,' though it adds that larger studies are still needed. This is a genuinely better evidence picture than most of the other claims on this card.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Nettle's best-known traditional reputation - as a 'blood builder' that helps anaemia - is not actually supported by the evidence: a clinical-reference site explicitly places anaemia in its weakest evidence category ('more evidence is needed... for these uses'), the same bucket as asthma, cancer and wound healing. This card's primary link is to this project's own Anaemia health topic precisely because of how often the traditional claim comes up, not because the evidence backs it - readers relying on nettle instead of the iron-rich foods and B12 care already covered there would be relying on folklore, not evidence.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH, an enlarged prostate - not covered elsewhere in this project) has a more substantial but still unsettled evidence base: a 2016 meta-analysis (5 trials, 1,128 patients) found favourable effects on symptom scores, urine flow and prostate volume, with no change in PSA (a safety marker) - but reported no adverse-event data and no risk-of-bias assessment at all, despite still concluding the herb is 'effective and safe.' A more recent, more rigorous reassessment by a different research group (a larger pool, 6 trials, 1,210 patients) reached a more cautious verdict: risk of bias mostly unclear or high, and 'very low' certainty for the main symptom-improvement finding. The honest picture is 'promising but genuinely uncertain,' not settled either way.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Diabetes evidence conflicts across the studies cited: one 8-week trial in people with advanced, poorly controlled diabetes found no blood sugar benefit, while a separate 3-month trial in people already on diabetes medication found lower blood sugar and HbA1c. A second source separately reports a trial finding improved glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes. Taken together this is a real, worth-knowing lead, not a settled benefit.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Hay fever/allergy relief at the first sign of symptoms is an early-research-only lead, rated insufficient evidence to confirm either way.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Leaf (fresh, dried or cooked) and root are both plant material - naturally vegan. Cooking (as in a soup) or drying deactivates the sting, so nettle is eaten as a cooked leafy green in some cuisines as well as taken as tea, powder or in capsules.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules are also widely available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy - rated 'Likely Unsafe,' since nettle may stimulate uterine contractions and cause miscarriage.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid while breastfeeding, both by mouth and applied to the skin: a case report describes a breastfed infant developing urticaria (hives) after the mother used nettle-boiled water on cracked nipples - a directly relevant caution for anyone considering a 'natural' topical remedy while nursing.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May reduce how well the body clears lithium (acting somewhat like a diuretic), which could raise lithium to harmful levels in anyone taking it for a mood disorder - a dose adjustment may be needed. This is the same lithium-clearance pattern already seen in three of this project's other herb cards (Ashwagandha, Neem, Shatavari). See this project's own Mood and mental health card for the related caution note.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar - combined with diabetes medicines this could cause hypoglycaemia; a real case report describes this happening in a 78-year-old man taking a nettle-containing remedy. Anyone with diabetes should talk to their doctor before trying nettle and monitor blood sugar closely if they do. See this project's own Diabetes card for the related caution note.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood pressure further in combination with blood pressure medicines - caution advised, especially for anyone already prone to low blood pressure.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Large amounts may cause drowsiness, adding to the effect of sedatives or other CNS-depressant medicines.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Contains vitamin K, which may reduce the effectiveness of the blood thinner warfarin - the same mechanism this project's own vitamin K2 card already describes for leafy greens generally. Blood tests and a dose adjustment may be needed for anyone on warfarin.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Real but uncommon hormonal side effects have been reported: gynaecomastia (breast tissue growth) in a man and galactorrhoea (unexpected milk production) in a woman, both linked to nettle tea in case reports. Separately, nettle pollen exposure has caused allergic rhinitis in documented cases. (A different, unrelated plant - the Australian stinging tree, a different genus entirely - has caused severe reactions requiring intensive care in separate case reports; this is not the same plant as the common nettle this card is about, noted here only so the two are not confused.)
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Touching the fresh plant causes skin irritation (the 'sting' the plant is named for) - wear gloves when handling or harvesting it.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Laboratory studies suggest nettle may inhibit liver enzymes (CYP450 family) that many medicines rely on, and animal studies suggest an additive diuretic effect with diuretic medicines - in both cases, the clinical relevance in humans 'has yet to be determined.' Worth mentioning to a doctor or pharmacist if taking multiple medicines regularly, even though this isn't a confirmed human risk.
cautions.label: open question

redFlags.text: Avoid nettle (by mouth) during pregnancy, and talk to a doctor first if trying to conceive.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If breastfeeding, avoid nettle by mouth and don't apply nettle preparations to the breast or nipples, given the documented infant reaction above.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take lithium, diabetes medicine, blood pressure medicine, sedatives or warfarin, talk to your doctor before trying nettle.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - nettle tea or cooked leaves are typically far gentler than a standardised capsule extract, and the cautions above (especially the drug interactions) apply most to the stronger, concentrated forms.

preparationForms.note: Dried or fresh leaves steeped in hot water - the most common everyday preparation.
Cooking (as in a soup) deactivates the sting, so nettle is eaten as a cooked leafy green in some cuisines.
Dried leaf powder and capsules are widely available; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.
Applied to skin for the osteoarthritis use this card's whatEvidenceShows describes.

herbs.name: Psyllium Husk

traditionalUse.text: The crushed seed husk of Plantago ovata (fleawort), a plant native to parts of Asia, the Mediterranean and North Africa - long used as a gentle, bulk-forming laxative for constipation, similar in this role to oats and wheat bran.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: Constipation is psyllium's best-established use: it absorbs liquid in the intestines and forms a bulky, easy-to-pass stool - a well-understood mechanism, not a traditional claim alone.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: For irritable bowel syndrome, real trial evidence exists but fades over time: a 275-patient, 12-week trial found psyllium better than placebo in the first two months but not by the third month, and a smaller 80-patient trial found an 82% response rate versus 53% on placebo. This is a genuine, if time-limited, lead rather than a settled cure.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: For ulcerative colitis, one open-label trial (105 patients already in remission) found psyllium comparably effective to the medicine mesalamine at maintaining remission - a real but limited finding (a single, non-blinded trial), not strong enough to suggest replacing prescribed treatment.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question
