whatEvidenceShows.text: Cholesterol-lowering is a commonly cited use for psyllium and soluble fibre generally, though this card has not independently verified the specific clinical-trial evidence behind it in the same depth as the gut-health findings above - see this project's own fibre nutrient card and heart-and-cholesterol topic for the better-established, food-based soluble-fibre/cholesterol evidence.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Small studies have found psyllium does not meaningfully reduce how well the body absorbs vitamins or minerals - a reassuring point given how often fibre supplements in general are assumed to interfere with nutrient absorption.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: The seed husk is plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Powder or granules must be mixed in about 8 oz (240 ml) of liquid immediately before taking, followed by a further full glass of water - this is not optional good practice, it is specifically needed for psyllium to work properly and to avoid the choking/obstruction risk covered in this card's cautions. Capsules and wafers are also available; wafers should be chewed thoroughly.
howToUseVegan.label: official recommendation

cautions.text: This is the most important caution for this herb: taken without enough liquid, psyllium can swell and block the throat or oesophagus. Mix each dose in about 150-240 ml of liquid immediately before taking it, and drink a further full glass of water afterwards - and do not take it at all if you already have difficulty swallowing.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Take other medicines at a distance from psyllium, since it can reduce how well they are absorbed: specifically avoid taking digoxin, aspirin/salicylates or nitrofurantoin within 3 hours of a psyllium dose.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Avoid psyllium if you have a bowel obstruction, faecal impaction, symptoms of appendicitis or an acute surgical abdomen, gastrointestinal ulceration, difficulty swallowing, or rectal bleeding - these need a doctor's assessment first, not a fibre supplement.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Allergic reactions, including rare but real anaphylaxis, and occupational asthma from repeatedly inhaling the powder, have both been documented - avoid inhaling the powder while mixing a dose, and stop and seek care for any allergic symptoms.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Sugar-free psyllium products often contain phenylalanine - relevant for anyone with phenylketonuria (PKU), who should check the label.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: For some people with inflammatory bowel disease, taking too much psyllium can worsen symptoms rather than help - a reason to start low and go slowly if trying it for this reason, under medical guidance, rather than assuming more is better.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: one source describes psyllium as generally acceptable in pregnancy and, since it is not absorbed systemically, unlikely to pose a breastfeeding risk - though this is a general statement, not dedicated trial data for either situation, so checking with a doctor first is still reasonable.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Psyllium is a fermentable fibre, which can aggravate symptoms for the specific subset of people managing irritable bowel syndrome or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) on a low-FODMAP diet - a narrow, condition-specific caution, not a reason for most people to avoid psyllium.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Stop immediately and seek medical care for chest pain, difficulty breathing, or any sensation of food or the supplement being stuck after taking psyllium - these can signal choking or an oesophageal blockage and need urgent attention, not more water and waiting.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: Do not start psyllium if you already have difficulty swallowing, a known bowel obstruction, or rectal bleeding without your doctor's clearance first.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take digoxin, aspirin or an antibiotic such as nitrofurantoin, space your dose at least a few hours apart from psyllium, as advised above.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in risk for this herb specifically: all forms carry the same choking/obstruction risk if taken without enough liquid, so the liquid-mixing instruction below applies regardless of which form is used.

preparationForms.note: Must be mixed in about 8oz (240ml) of liquid immediately before taking, followed by a further full glass of water.
A more convenient form, but does not remove the need to drink plenty of water alongside it.
Should be chewed thoroughly, then followed with a full glass of water.

herbs.name: Shatavari

traditionalUse.text: A root used in Ayurveda as a rasayana (rejuvenating tonic), traditionally regarded as a female reproductive tonic and adaptogen, also used for digestive complaints (dyspepsia, gastric ulcers) and as a traditional galactogogue (breast-milk aid). Its Sanskrit name is traditionally translated as 'she who possesses a hundred husbands.'
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: The only genuine, independently-readable primary trial on file for this herb in a PCOS population is a 2026 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (70 women, 66 completed, 12 weeks, one 300 mg capsule/day standardised to at least 10% total Shatavarins). The trial's own stated primary outcome (ovarian volume) showed no significant difference from placebo; BMI, hormone levels and lab values also showed no significant difference. It did find a significantly greater decrease in follicular count and a significantly greater improvement in perceived stress scores versus placebo - real findings, but on secondary outcomes, not the trial's own chosen primary one. The paper is also inconsistent within itself about which outcome is primary - its Abstract and Conclusion lean on the outcomes that were significant (follicle count, and a separate increase in endometrial thickness) rather than the one named primary in its Discussion. This is a genuinely mixed result, not a confirming one - it does not support a confident 'shatavari helps PCOS' claim on its own.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Shatavari's traditional use as a galactogogue (to increase breast milk) is directly contradicted by the one human trial that tested it properly: a randomised trial found no increase in prolactin, the hormone that drives milk production, and concluded the preparation tested 'has no lactogenic effect.' Worth knowing specifically because this is one of the herb's best-known traditional uses.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: A second, more recent human trial (2024, 70 postmenopausal women, 8 weeks) found a significant improvement in a menopause-specific quality-of-life score versus placebo. This is a different population from PCOS, so it does not confirm anything about this herb's PCOS-specific effects - and it has its own real quality problems worth knowing about: its own results tables disagree with its own methods on how many participants were in each group, and it directly contradicts itself about whether the adverse events reported were mild or not mild. Its own conclusion ('a safe alternative to modern drugs') reads as more confident than a small, short, internally-inconsistent trial can really support.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Most of shatavari's other traditional uses (pain, anxiety, stomach spasms, uterine bleeding, PMS, diarrhoea, bronchitis, diabetes, dementia, alcohol withdrawal) are rated 'Insufficient Evidence' by a clinical-reference site, which states plainly there is 'not enough information available... to know how it might work for any medical use.' Most of the pharmacological activity reported anywhere (antiulcer, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, antidiarrhoeal, and others) comes from animal or laboratory studies, not human trials.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Root powder and standardised root extract are both plant material - naturally vegan, with nothing to check there.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

howToUseVegan.text: Capsules are also widely available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin - most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: This is the most important caution for this herb, and it directly complicates the traditional view of shatavari as a pregnancy-safe tonic: a rat study (root extract, 100 mg/kg/day for 60 days) found increased fetal resorption, malformations, intrauterine growth retardation, smaller placentas and litters, lower pup weight and length, and developmental delays. This is an animal-only finding, from a review with real quality problems of its own (noted in its own source entry), but it is a specific, identifiable study, not a vague claim - and it is a real, serious reason not to take Ayurveda's own traditional 'safe even in pregnancy' framing at face value.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Independently, a clinical-reference site advises avoiding shatavari in pregnancy and while breastfeeding on separate grounds - not enough is known about human safety either way - 'stay on the safe side and avoid use.' Combined with the animal finding above, and the fact that the one proper human trial of its traditional lactation-boosting use found no effect at all, this card does not treat shatavari as a safe or evidence-backed choice for pregnancy or breastfeeding.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May reduce how well the body clears lithium (acting somewhat like a diuretic), which could raise lithium to harmful levels in anyone taking it for a mood disorder - a dose adjustment may be needed. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site here. See this project's own Mood and mental health card for the related caution note.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Do not confuse Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus, the Ayurvedic root herb this card is about) with ordinary vegetable asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) - a different plant entirely. This is a real, documented mix-up, not a hypothetical one: a general-audience health and nutrition book checked for this project actually makes this exact error, describing vegetable asparagus as 'also known in India by the name Shatavari.' The two plants' safety and nutrition profiles are not interchangeable.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Overall safety is genuinely less well established than for the other herbs in this project so far: a clinical-reference site states plainly 'there is not enough information available to know if asparagus racemosus is safe,' and does not list specific side effects. One acute-toxicity animal study of a different shatavari-containing product found no deaths even at a very high dose - a reassuring data point for ordinary short-term use, but it does not resolve the separate pregnancy-specific concern above, since it tested a different question.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: Avoid shatavari during pregnancy and while trying to conceive. Despite its traditional use as a pregnancy and lactation tonic, the actual evidence points the other way (a real animal study found fetal harm, and a real human trial found no lactation benefit) - talk to a doctor rather than following traditional use here.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you take lithium for a mood disorder, talk to your doctor before trying shatavari, and watch for signs of lithium levels running high (tremor, confusion, nausea, unsteady movement) if you do combine them.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - given how little is established about this herb's safety overall, treat it with more caution than you might a better-studied herb, and talk to a doctor before use if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, trying to conceive, or take lithium or any other prescription medicine.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - traditional root powder is typically far gentler than a standardised capsule extract (the 2026 PCOS trial above used one 300 mg capsule/day standardised to at least 10% total Shatavarins), and the cautions above apply most to the stronger, concentrated forms.

preparationForms.note: The traditional root-powder form.
Standardised extracts are available, as used in the clinical trials this card cites; check the capsule shell isn't gelatin.

herbs.name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)

traditionalUse.text: Long-standing use in Ayurvedic tradition as an adaptogen - taken as fresh chewed leaves or steeped as a tea to help the body adapt to physical and emotional stress, and traditionally understood to support general immune resilience.
traditionalUse.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: A systematic review of 24 human studies (1,111 participants) found favourable results across three domains: metabolic measures (blood glucose, lipids, blood pressure, uric acid), immunity/viral-infection markers, and stress/mood/cognition - the review's authors suggest tulsi may work as an adjunct alongside standard treatment for diabetes and metabolic syndrome, not as a replacement for it.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: On safety specifically: across those 24 studies, 15 reported no adverse events, 8 did not describe any, and 1 reported occasional mild nausea - genuinely reassuring for short-term use, but the longest trial ran only 13 weeks, so this does not establish long-term safety.
whatEvidenceShows.label: established fact

whatEvidenceShows.text: This evidence should not be read as more settled than it is: the review's own authors note only a small minority of the 24 studies were high quality, most lacked double-blinding, doses and formulations varied widely and were often unspecified, and they state tulsi's effects 'may be overestimated' by the body of evidence as it stands - a more cautious conclusion than the review's own abstract wording suggests. A separate academic herb-information page from a major US cancer centre independently reaches the same cautious note for stress, sleep, anxiety, cognition and oral/eye health specifically: small studies suggest possible benefit, but 'further research is needed to substantiate these findings.'
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

whatEvidenceShows.text: Laboratory (cell-line) and animal studies have explored other possible effects - including anticancer, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and a topical tulsi-containing formulation reducing oral mucositis in cancer patients receiving chemoradiation in one study. These are early-stage or preclinical findings, not established human clinical benefits, and are not a reason to use tulsi in place of medical cancer treatment.
whatEvidenceShows.label: open question

howToUseVegan.text: Fresh tulsi leaves, chewed or steeped as a tea, are the traditional and simplest form - naturally vegan, with nothing further to check.
howToUseVegan.label: established fact

howToUseVegan.text: Dried leaf, powder, tablets, capsules and liquid extracts are also available. As with any capsule supplement, check the capsule shell isn't gelatin (most modern capsules use a vegetarian cellulose or HPMC shell, but gelatin ones still exist) - the herb itself is plant-only either way.
howToUseVegan.label: illustration

cautions.text: Avoid in pregnancy and while breastfeeding, and if trying to become pregnant: animal studies show large doses can interfere with a fertilised egg implanting, and human safety has not been established either way.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower blood sugar - early research suggests a blood-sugar-lowering effect in type 2 diabetes. Combined with insulin or sulfonylurea medicines specifically, this could cause hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar); people with type 2 diabetes, or anyone on these medicines, should talk to their doctor before trying tulsi. The specific insulin/sulfonylurea interaction is sourced to one clinical-reference site here, not independently cross-confirmed by the second - flagged honestly rather than overstated.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May lower thyroid hormone (thyroxine) levels and could worsen hypothyroidism - people with hypothyroidism are advised to avoid it. This caution is sourced to one clinical-reference site only; a second checked separately (RxList) does not mention thyroid effects at all, so this is not cross-corroborated the way some of this card's other cautions are.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: May slow blood clotting. Taking it alongside a blood-thinning or antiplatelet medicine (aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin named specifically) could increase bruising or bleeding risk, and it could increase bleeding risk during and after surgery - stop at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery and talk to a doctor if on any of these medicines.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Reported side effects beyond the above include nausea, headache and feeling agitated.
cautions.label: established fact

cautions.text: Holy basil should not be confused with ordinary culinary/sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) - a different plant with a different safety profile. This mix-up is a real, documented one (at least one otherwise-reliable food-reference source mixes up the two botanical names), so always check which basil a product or recipe actually means.
cautions.label: established fact

redFlags.text: If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea medicine for diabetes and start tulsi, watch for hypoglycaemia symptoms (shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness) and talk to your doctor promptly if they occur - do not adjust your diabetes medicine dose yourself.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: If you are on a blood thinner or antiplatelet medicine, or have surgery scheduled, and notice unusual bruising or bleeding, tell your doctor - and mention tulsi use before any planned surgery.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

redFlags.text: This card is general information, not a substitute for medical advice - talk to a doctor before starting tulsi if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive, have a thyroid condition, have diabetes, or take any prescription medicine.
redFlags.label: official recommendation

herbs.preparationFormsCaveat: These forms are not equivalent in strength - a tea made from fresh leaves is typically far gentler than a standardised capsule extract, and the cautions above apply most to the stronger, concentrated forms.

glossary.definition: Compounds naturally found in grains, legumes, nuts and seeds that bind minerals such as iron, zinc and calcium, reducing how much of them the body absorbs. Soaking, sprouting or fermenting a food lowers its phytate content.
A compound found in some plant foods, such as spinach, that binds calcium and iron, reducing how much of them the body absorbs. Blanching or lightly cooking an oxalate-rich food reduces this effect.

A general term for natural plant compounds - including phytates and oxalates - that can reduce how well the body absorbs certain minerals and vitamins from a food. Soaking, sprouting and fermenting all reduce them.
Natural substances in some foods that can interfere with the body's ability to absorb or use iodine. Ordinary amounts in a varied diet are not a concern as long as iodine intake is adequate.
How much of a nutrient the body can actually absorb and use, as opposed to how much is simply present in a food.
A nutrient has been added to a food that didn't naturally contain it, or not in that amount - for example, B12-fortified nutritional yeast or a fortified plant milk.
How much of a nutrient eaten actually gets taken up into the body, rather than passing through unused.
Not getting enough of a nutrient to meet the body's needs.
Beans, lentils, peas and similar pod-bearing plants - a broad food group and a key everyday source of plant protein and fibre.

A process in which bacteria or yeast break down parts of a food, used to make dishes such as idli-dosa batter, kanji and plant yoghurt. It can also add live cultures and improve how available some nutrients are.
Letting a seed, grain or legume begin to germinate before cooking it - a traditional step that reduces antinutrients like phytates and can improve mineral absorption.
A protein source that provides all nine essential amino acids in useful amounts. Soy foods such as tofu, tempeh and edamame are complete plant proteins.
The amino acids - protein's building blocks - that the body cannot make itself and must get from food.
Plant compounds found in soy foods that can bind to the body's oestrogen receptors, though they act differently from the body's own oestrogen.
Plant compounds, including soy isoflavones, that loosely resemble the body's own oestrogen but act differently from it.
Recommended Dietary Allowance: the average daily amount of a nutrient judged enough to meet the needs of most healthy people, set by a body such as NIH or ICMR-NIN.
A study that collects and summarises all the available research on a specific question, following a pre-set, documented method.
A statistical method that combines the results of several separate studies to produce one overall, more reliable estimate.
Studies in which participants are randomly assigned to receive a treatment or a placebo, used to test whether something really causes an effect.
A study that follows a group of people over time to see how their habits relate to health outcomes, without assigning anyone a treatment.
An inactive treatment, such as a dummy pill, given to a comparison group in a trial so a real treatment's effect can be measured against it.
A state in which the body's cells respond less well to insulin, making it harder to keep blood sugar levels steady.
A calculation from a fasting blood test - using glucose and insulin levels - that estimates how resistant the body's cells are to insulin.
An age-related change that makes the body less efficient at using dietary protein to build and maintain muscle.
The gradual loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with ageing.
A condition, more common with age, in which the stomach lining produces less acid - one reason the body's ability to absorb vitamin B12 from food falls as people get older.
A liver enzyme that breaks down many common medicines. Some herbs can speed up or slow down how it works, changing how well those medicines act.

A mechanism, well documented for licorice root, in which a compound blocks a kidney enzyme, causing the body to retain sodium and lose potassium as if a hormone called aldosterone were raised, even though it isn't.
A traditional term for an herb believed to help the body handle physical or emotional stress more easily.
A herbal preparation made by boiling plant material, such as a root or stem, in water to draw out its active compounds.
Lower than normal potassium levels in the blood.
Swelling caused by fluid building up in the body's tissues.
Plant compounds, found in tea and coffee, that reduce how well the body absorbs iron from plant foods. Having tea or coffee between meals rather than with them helps.
Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten damages the lining of the gut.
An amino acid in the blood; a raised level can be a sign of low vitamin B12 or folate.
Live beneficial bacteria, often found in naturally fermented foods, that add to the gut's own bacterial population.
A type of fibre that feeds the beneficial bacteria already living in the gut, rather than being digested itself.
The point when a woman's menstrual periods stop permanently, usually in her late 40s or 50s.
Low-density lipoprotein, often called 'bad' cholesterol because higher levels are linked to a higher risk of heart disease.
High-density lipoprotein, often called 'good' cholesterol because it helps carry cholesterol away from the arteries.
A type of fat carried in the blood, usually measured alongside cholesterol as part of a routine blood lipid test.
The medical term for indigestion - discomfort or pain in the upper stomach, often after eating.
Irritable bowel syndrome: a common digestive condition causing bloating, pain and altered bowel habits.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease: ongoing heartburn or acid reflux caused by stomach acid moving back up into the gullet.
Relating to the body's hormone-producing glands and the hormones they release.

The type of iron found in plant foods such as dals, millets and greens. The body absorbs it less efficiently than haem iron (the iron in meat, fish and poultry), which is why pairing it with a vitamin C food helps.
